Author: @naestein3216
Content:
Adhd can present in 3 ways: You may have trouble focusing, you may be hyperactive, or both. Now, the inattentive version is often underdiagnosed, but regardless, 50-70% of people with autism have adhd, (as far as we know, they are both super underdiagnosed), but not everyone who is autistic has adhd. Pretty much, a lot of the adhd things, from the surface, can look like autistic traits, and there is a lot of overlap, but someone can have adhd and not autism, and someone can have autism and not adhd. Like the whole focus thing, an autistic person might care even less about a thing, or even more about a thing, but not caring and not being able to focus I think are different, (I'm not sure if that difference actually exists or not, that's just what I think I gathered, so take it with a grain of salt, but), and maybe needing to stim to calm yourself down or express yourself when you're happy is different from maybe needing to move in order to focus or just moving instinctually, unable to sit still, but that's just my interpretation of those seemingly overlapping traits, one feeling out of emotional necessity, and one rooted in focus, but I'm not an expert. ADHD and autism both are very different, but I'd say the community around autism is way worse because it's on a spectrum, and saying 'a spectrum' doesn't do it justice. There are many different spectrums of many different traits, and you may have some in lower degrees in some parts and higher degrees in others. It's not just one line between hardly autistic and super mega harsh autistic. 

A lot of autistic traits that set it super apart from adhd is stuff like sensory issues, which may include stuff like always needing to wear noise blocking headphones, but it can also just be someone super picky about food, or someone who can't handle wearing clothes with certain fabrics or seams, or someone who can't stand having their hands be super slimy, or feels stressed out when they smell something too strong. There are a wide spectrum of traits and a spectrum of severity of each of them. A lot of autistic people mainly stick with one food to eat for months on end, and there are probably some autistic people who don't experience anything like that. 

Another thing is not understanding social cues. Stuff from not understanding tone, to people's boundaries, to thinking that something people said as a metaphor or an analogy or expression is literal when it isn't. Maybe you talk too much about something you really care about to a crowd of people most people would know is not interested, or maybe, like me, (I'm autistic btw, if you couldn't tell), you tried to become best friends with someone you hardly knew in one day back in middle school, or maybe (I'm gonna be projecting a lot, especially since I don't really watch your channel, *sorry*, but it's okay if you don't experience autism this way, that's perfectly fine), you would hear an analogy and then ask about the specifics until everyone else told you to stop because you were taking it too far, or maybe you didn't even notice it, got confused, and needed clarification, or maybe you (still projecting) couldn't figure out what everyone was laughing about a lot when you were younger. Maybe you would ask way too personal questions, or had frequent issues with communication in general. This is really hard on a lot of autistic folk that have these issues, and I'm gonna talk about it more later.

I think the last main issue that entirely sets autism apart from adhd is trouble with adjustments. A lot of autistic people have trouble with changes and find it anywhere from 1000 to 1 million times more comfortable sticking with a routine instead of trying something new. A lot of new experiences can be especially scary on autistic folk, and they may have trouble adjusting to new environments. I should have probably mention stimming in it's own section, but I briefly referenced it at the start of this insanely long message. Anyway, if you don't know what a stim is, it's short for self stimulatory behavior, look it up. 

Now not everyone is going to have all of the things in each section, some people might not even have traits from all the sections. Also, Autism, as well as about a million other mental health disorders are super underdiagnosed. Pretty much everyone everywhere who comes out saying they're autistic anywhere will get the comments 'you don't look autistic' because it is on such a wide range and people have a certain idea of what looks like 'actual' autism to them, which, while may not be an inaccurate representation of some autistic person, does not envelope anywhere near all of them. Plus, a lot of autistic folk people think of as only affecting kids, which is dumb, since it carries through a person's entire life. This is why I believe there needs to be major improvements in the autistic community. Because the biggest issue comes next.

If someone is autistic and doesn't know it, they often do a thing called 'masking', where they try to cover up their autistic traits. For me, I started laughing whenever people said something I thought they intended to be funny, often tried not to speak if I wasn't directly asked something, (or at least someone asked the audience something for anyone to answer), I tried to make eye contact a little more, I would try to suppress my urge to stim when I was happy, tried to just guess where I was in every relationship I had (if I knew someone enough to have lunch with them, if I knew someone enough to ask for help with a thing, if I knew someone enough to share my autistic interests, ect) blindly, without having a good point of reference, tried to copy what other people were doing, sometimes even harder than they were, maybe pretend to like a thing I perceived as something other people liked, some people get overly apologetic, copy things other people do to try and fit in, and generally suppress behaviors that make someone seem 'autistic' or just 'different', just to seem normal. This can cause you to look like a practically completely different person outside versus at home, maybe with people with lower functioning autism it can cause you to break down whenever you got home, and masking traits may leave you forever undiagnosed or might even lead to autistic burnout. 

Autistic burnout is where you basically try to live up to the NT standard for long periods of time, and, unable to do so, leave you feeling burnt out (hence the name). Now, the National Autistic Society describes it as "a syndrome conceptualised as resulting from chronic life stress and a mismatch of expectations and abilities without adequate supports. It is characterised by pervasive, long-term (typically 3+ months) exhaustion, loss of function, and reduced tolerance to stimulus." according to Dr Dora Raymaker in the article "Understanding Autistic Burnout" published March 01, 2022. A lot of people who struggle with stuff like loud noises, talking to people (I forgot to mention it, but autistic people tend to have trouble making friends, both because NT people don't like them as much, and because it's just harder to communicate or find the energy to in general, maybe this is you, maybe it isn't idk), their clothes, frequent strong smells, retaining eye contact, constantly searching for social cues, ect, may end up getting it. So it's really important that people learn that they're autistic so they don't feel the need to mask as much, or take on more than they can handle in that regard, rather than assume they're just weak and try even harder, to make sure they take the time they need instead of burning out and not being able to do anything while feeling miserable for 3 or more months. Unfortunately, autism, in my opinion, is the worst out of all the mental health communities, at having their stereotypes reach a large % of people. There are stereotypes of practically every mental health issue, and that tends to mean they're all underdiagnosed, but I'd say autism is probably the broadest one of them all, so it's probably the most underdiagnosed of them all. Also no Tylenol and vaccines will not make you autistic.

I am not a long time fan of your channel or anything, I hardly watched it, but I have seen some of your content via other people, and I've seen you on other people's channels as well, and I will say, I did not know you had ADHD, I did not know you had Autism, and yet I am completely unsurprised. Practically every other creator has ADHD online, and whether or not you had ADHD and Autism from the little parts of your content I've seen (and I haven't even seen that much) felt so ambiguous that this had occurred to me multiple times whenever I was reminded you exist. I didn't mean to say that in a mean tone, I'm sorry if that came out that way, I also won't be hurt if you don't read all this, it's a century long, and I'm glad you got diagnosed in a world where most autistic people never come to that realization, and I'm glad you tried to send this message. I'm also curious how your channel would have changed had you been neurotypical, but that doesn't mean your channel is wrong.

Author: @rachaelmessenger1125
Content:
I used to work with severely autistic adults as my day job and grew up with autistic brothers. I personally disagree with getting rid of the terms "high functioning" and "low functioning" in regards to autism. The difference being whether or not you can perform self cleaning tasks and communicate basic needs. 

Using that term in my job gave better descriptions of the needs of a person without having the person there, but the spectrum is still there. 

For example, my brother is high functioning but not independent with limited verbal response, this means he can clean himself effectively and communicate his needs, but can not live alone and uses limited amounts of verbal communication. I love my brother dearly, but to talk about him without context would be a disservice to others when I describe his giant bear hugs that you have to scream "Gentle!" or you risk injury and how he will insist on kissing old people on the head when saying goodbye because he associates it with Snow White when she kissed the dwarves on the head. Just saying he has autism without the further context makes his actions seem weirder than they are, and with context makes the funny things he does adorable instead of alarming.

Author: @S.H.O.D.A.N_1
Content:
Dude. I've loved Trains since I was a kid. Even built a very large HO Scale Model Train in my bedroom. And stood on a bridge with very heavy traffic with a buddy so we could catch a GG1 that was still in service in Connecticut. And my buddy got the photograph of the legendary Engine as it crossed a Railroad Bridge over a marsh that served as an incredible reflecting pool. 

I like Trains too. 

And in many, many cases, Autism actually is a gift. Although it does impede learning in many unexpected ways, these same people overcome those challenges, and also have talents that truly amaze me.

I've known that you have ADHD, would it surprise you to learn that most - virtually all of the top YTubers in the Gaming space have ADHD? Like Kevin, like SymbaLily (a favorite of mine and a very special person). And just go down the list. Once you learn to recognize some of the specific traits of ADHD, it is obvious, and truly stunning to see this phenomenon in the top Tubers.

I, as someone who doesn't have Autism or ADHD, I am consistently blown away by how their brains work and process information in ways I could only dream of doing.

I watched SymbaLily play Alice: The Madness Returns and witnessed her processing five, six, eight streams of incoming data so fast that I felt significantly inferior.

But interestingly, she would consistently walk right past little details and pick-ups in the game that I always noticed.

So there is a huge gain in some very important areas, but a bit of a deficit in others. A give-and-take situation.

But I will tell you right now that I could not do so many things that she smashed out of the park on her first try.

Same thing with Cuphead and Dark Souls. Cuphead is just insane. That game is specifically designed for people like her. And like you. I just cannot do that sh|t. Not even an option.

Same goes for Bloodborne (don't come at me for my terrible spelling - I already know) and Dark Souls. She was beating most Bosses on her first or second try. And you know how many people struggled with those games. People like me going up against bosses again and again and again, trying to work out the patterns and best strategies. But she was blowing right through them. I think her worst showing in Bloodborne was seven tries to defeat a Boss (I think it was against the long haired Witch in the church).

So I envy what comes naturally to you and others with your Superpowers. It's likely that you'll miss the little stuff, the small details and secrets. But you can process multiple points of hectic, chaotic information so quickly and so successfully that I am rendered mute.

Autism and ADHD have their challenges. But they also have their many rewards. It's not a deficit, it's a different way of processing information. More than likely an evolutionary step forward in our species.

You guys lead at the front, and people like me, with slower processing abilities will take note of the finer details that you guys will pass over.

Our different brains, you and I, actually compliment each other very well.

And as far as I can tell, it's not a Diagnosis. It's a compliment. I don't know if you and your partner (is it Gabby?) are still together - I hope so - but make sure that you are paired with someone who processes like me, and you both will go very, very far...

Content:
I meant to comment on this video back when you posted it and I just..failed to (executive dysfunction 😂) so here we are lol. I have no idea if you’ll see this or read it, but if you do: I just wanted to let you know that I was also late diagnosed or late discovered Autistic. It wasn’t until I was 33 that I was diagnosed - I’m 37 now. And I’m still going through the process of discovering what it all means and how to navigate life properly. 

I gotta say, as a fellow autistic person, it brings me a ton of joy to see you embrace it and to see you just…unapologetically do the things that you need to do in order for you to maintain a healthy balance in your life. Honestly, that’s probably why you became one of my most favorite YouTubers to watch long before realizing that you’re also autistic as well. 

The fact that a while back, you prioritized your mental health and physical health instead of trying to “mask” and “perform” for your audience and that you were going to just be your most genuine self and that you were going to play things that you wanted to play - and if you didn’t like the thing, then you wouldn’t finish it, period. And if people didn’t like it, too bad. I personally, really respected that decision. 

I mean, masking like that for so long can very easily lead to intense autistic burnout (not to be confused with normal “burn out” - when an autistic person gets burned out in this very specific way, it is horrific and we shut down in a really really bad way that can take us out mentally and physically for days, weeks or longer in some cases; depends on the person).

And now, to see you in your element and, as an autistic person, catching onto your autistic traits and noticing certain things (because of course now I’m paying attention 😅😂) it brings me a ton of joy. 

Especially in today’s specific…”climate” shall we say, at least where I live. Specifically because of how horribly autistic people are being treated and talked about and scrutinized and such. 

I’m not sure how it is where you live Sean, but here in the US, it’s basically a nightmare. I don’t regret getting my diagnosis. But I am so angry every day with my country’s “healthcare” system. 

Which…honestly is why I’m so very thankful every day that you and your channel are around. 

So…I guess this is just a super long way for me to say: thank you for being you. And thank you for being so willing to share this amazing part of your life with us. It gives people like me that little extra feeling of community and solidarity.

Author: @MaxineMcAllister
Content:
hi! im sure no one is gonna see this considering its been seven months since this video was posted, but i wanted to share my experience in hopes someone else might read it and feel something in their life make sense

I was young when I started watching jacksepticeye’s videos and loved how hyperactive he was, I had a toxic home environment and had no real father figure in my life but sean and multiple other content creators filled that gap and made me feel comfortable in a house that couldn’t provide that. (unrestricted internet access allowed for me to branch out to most of my favourite creators today, even if… a bit vulgar LOL) 

Seeing people today in these comments, supporting and having each other’s backs heals something in my inner child that I never knew I needed. I used to cry when I got overwhelmed and would often seek out attention by tantrums and sometimes even getting into trouble. 
Of course now I’ve matured to a degree and realize the consequences of my actions, but if someone out there is confused or scared or even angry at themselves for not being ‘normal’ or ‘responsible,’ know that you might have long road ahead, but with the right resources you can manage it faster than you think.

I’m sixteen now, I have a loving boyfriend who is also on the spectrum, my mother and stepdad both actively encourage my growth and I’m finally catching up in school! :D it gets better, I promise you.

Content:
Hello Seán!

I've been diagnosed with Autism and ADHD back in 2021, I've been a long time subscriber and for some reason I understood your jokes (I don't get jokes) and I felt that you're quite relatable. Content: My 3 year old daughter is the most extroverted person I ever met, and has never done stranger danger. She still will only drink out of a bottle, but she'll usually fight hard against having to drink unless I bribe her with dancing afterwards, and sing the whole time that I am giving it to her. We discovered in OT that we can get her to eat pudding and cream of chicken soup if we put YoGabbaGabba on. Author: @FaalKoriims
Content:
I haven't been diagnosed yet. I cannot afford it, and I'm quite certain any of the specialists around me won't be specialized in autism in women. Not where I live. I should look into that, though. Everything that you described resonates very strongly with my experience in life, especially the analyzing and studying everyone around me at any given time to get a read on them part. I have so much anxiety about interacting "incorrectly" with others that I have taken to minimizing my existence, only asking about them and rarely talking about myself, and making sure to only interact with a person in a way that suits their personality. More casual with some, more formal with others, a little open with one person, or completely shut off from another. All depending on their personalities and how they come off through body language/facial expressions. It's exhausting and a little lonely. I don't really feel a connection with anyone anymore because of how bad this has gotten. I don't know how to just genuinely be me without putting up people-specific masks. I want to stop with it and figure out how to just be me, comfortably, without the anxieties. Sometimes it's just too much, and when I find myself overwhelmed, I isolate from others. I'm currently going through an extensive period of isolation, though I suspect it will ease up in a couple months. 

I have been stuck in an abusive relationship for the last year and a half and just got out last week. I'm finally free. I am hoping to relearn myself and grow over the next few months enough to be more comfortable being me. Here's to striving for something good for a change.

Author: @lauralagier9404
Content:
Hey Jack! Just got diagnosed about 6 months ago with AuDHD at age 25. Had digestive/ asthmatic/ sensory issues since I can remember. So much sickness due to stress and masking. I’m now still high masking but I’m learning to be okay with myself. My biggest struggle is advocating for myself. Sharing this diagnosis is scary due to stigmatization. Thank you for sharing your diagnosis with us and for all the insight you provide to those who may struggle but not know why. We all need compassion for ourselves and our process. Much love to you! Thanks again!

Edit, random neurodivergent signs I never realized were AuDHD:

-eating the same thing everyday/ food phobia/ food aversion
-allergies, skin sensitivity (CUT THIS DAMN TAG OUT OF MY T SHIRT)
-wearing same clothes/ buying multiples of the same shirt because it fits well and is comfy
-digestive issues
-struggle keeping a steady job
-employers may say you are: lazy, unmotivated, disorganized, unproductive, distracted, take too long to complete tasks/ complete tasks “the wrong way”
-you experience symptoms of: anxiety, depression
-you may have scored high on the ACE test (adverse childhood experiences) and may have experienced some sort of traumatic event in childhood 
-you struggle with understanding or processing (or feeling) your emotions. Maybe you always feel numb, or feel like your emotions are just out of reach, or you don’t know why you feel angry/sad etc.
-you have specific interests, or what I like to call rotating hobbies 
-exploring new things is either awesome or absolutely terrifying (or both simultaneously) ADHD = novelty; ASD = routine

There are so many more signs but here’s a few just to get your mind going, if you think you may be neurodivergent, or if you were just curious! Either way thanks for reading if you did, and take care, awesome human

Author: @coroixiwa
Content:
"If you knew why didn't you tell me?" Dude I am still currently trying to understand myself right now and going into being 31 soon, I am STILL trying to understand my own autism as it is (Diagnosed a two years ago be cause I finally got the courage to do it). All I can say is welcome and you're one of us (Been one of us). Seriously this is going to be oversharing a bit, but I have a laundry list of health conditions that my doctors and whatnot diagnosed me with back to back for over six months straight, it has been STRESSFUL. Slowly getting a rein on it all, but it'll take more time still even though it's been a few years for the overall of them (First one was PTSD back in 2017, and then in 2022 it was back to back nonstop results from testing and stuff ending, for now, in March of 2023 with my autism diagnosis).

I used to be a Residential Aide until 2016 then a Bus Aide until 2022. Been a librarian since and meet a lot of children in my storytime group that know about my conditions (Because I've discussed it with curious parents, to the limit of what I am willing to discuss about myself) and some of those children are similar to me with some of their conditions. Including one who has never met an autistic adult until me.

Early on with learning I had ADHD and Autism (Diagnosed with ADHD around the same time as PTSD back in 2017):
I was told by my first few doctors that "Oh you're just depressed" or they kept pushing different pills on me like Prozac (Which I learned I'm allergic too, and yes they kept telling me to take it after they wrote down I was allergic to it). Took until my SIXTH doctor to finally have any breakthroughs, because they were willing to LISTEN and not just look at me and judge; previous doctors, the latter two literally said I needed my mom to be in the room with me, which yeah she was there because I can't drive due to PTSD (It's related) but do you know how demeaning that is? They were talking to my mom, not me, about MY health and stuff, in my late twenties. I know I'm 4'10" and look younger than I am because my mom's half of the family are baby-faced, but still. Sixth doctor is how we got answers finally and not just prescribed something just to get me out. I was fine with learning I was masking autism and stuff, just needed to learn how to demask and adjust. What the issues was actually is when people gave me issues like I should be ashamed or hiding it? Or the few times people had said "You need to act right" or "Act your age" or "You're too old to be autistic" (That last one irked me, because it doesn't go away, so what world did they live in there). It was rough for the first year, especially when my boss got involved but they couldn't fire me because I didn't mess anything up and just had to adjust to myself. No, the issues with my boss was that they were extremely judgemental of autistic people and saw anyone with autism as being "slow" or "dumb" which is definitely not true (Graduated with an Associate's Degree in Computer Programming before all of that). That boss wound up getting fired by the board and our current boss is LEAGUES better. Current boss? It's like night and day, I swear. In fact my boss has OCD and when they learned I had autism they said they had a feeling but felt it was ADHD and didn't want to just assume. Current boss eventually went to go through testing to see if maybe they were autistic and it came back that they weren't, but they said doctor always scared them and I get it (The reason I didn't go for so long, grew up in the '90s with a prejudice school, a lot of other things that went on, but to summarize it my school did something super illegal and got nailed when parents find out but nobody checked if their children did actually have health concerns, and my mom was too busy working four jobs to do it).

So yeah, come 2022 it was a surprise, but we nailed down it was likely due to my school way back that was working to "correct" children that showed any signs of learning disabilities that lead to me seeming normal because I was masking. Or as my doctor lovingly says "Monkey see, monkey do" (They apologized if it sounded offensive to me but I honestly chuckled at it because I thought of Little Monkies Jumping on the Bed the book). Demasking has been ROUGH, but it is so worth it. I always wondered why I felt like I was living a lie in everything I did, now we know why. Also learned I'm actually ambidextrous but the masking didn't let me use my left hand due to the "learning" at my childhood school. Should say my mom immediately pulled me and my brother into homeschooling us right after she learned what the school was doing, but it was around 9/11 that took place so a lot of stress weighed on her with my older (Now estranged) brother being in the military. My old school is actually finally being torn down brick by brick, and nobody cares, they stopped caring after they pulled that crap.

To give an example of how the school did this: They saw a child with signs of something, didn't know what but if it wasn't "normal" they'd pull you into "The Extra Class" for "special teaching". If you did anything out of the norm, even so much as using your left hand instead of your right, you got your desk smacked by a ruler and yelled at in front of everyone. The method they used was to make ONE student an "example" and seeing them get chewed out the rest would "correct" themselves to "act right". In reality they took thirty children and conditioned them to mask and hide any signs of disability. Many of my classmates went home crying or screaming because of it. It lasted a few months until the teacher they threatened and put into it to "fix our writing" wound up whistleblowing and reporting to parents immediately. That teacher quit soon after because she was disgusted, and rightfully so (Her son was autistic and you had the school you worked for saying "Autism is nothing but a child refusing to be normal, teach it out of them" essentially).

By homeschooling, I mean cyber. Nowadays looking back, I would recommend other forms of homeschooling and NEVER cyber, because it was toxic both the students and teachers.

Its not "ADHD" or "autism". 

Look up Carl Yung's cognitive functions and MBTI. 

You're just an ENTP (look at their cognitive functions -> Ne, Ti, Fe, Si. ENTPs are very intuitive, creative, curious, logical and charming, but struggle with sensory stimulation (sensory sensitivity, difficulty focusing in the present moment) and repetitive activities or too much organisation. 

If you study and understand Carl Yung's cognitive functions you' ll see that everyone with underdeveloped Si has ADHD (Ne, Se people) and everyone with underdeveloped Fe, Fi and Si (and possibly high Ne or Ni, especially if the person is an introvert) is laballed as autistic and of course its a spectrum depending on your specific type (extroverts tend to be "high functioning", like you (ENTP. Look up Bobby Fisher who was an INTP). 

All these pharmaceutical companies want to classify everyone who isn't an SJ type (people with well developed Si, especially if combined with Te) as sick like with ADHD (and low functioning autism) and put everyone in a box. 

The solution is simple.

IN THE NEXT VIDEO!" To me, stims like that are quite charming and what made you unique and entertaining to me. I was diagnosed when I was 14 and back then, the DSM-5 hadn't changed yet, that research in women (or afab people in my case) hadn't really been done, so they were very adamant about the fact that I specifically had add because I didn't appear to be hyperactive at the time. Now, this was at a time where my depression was at an all time high, so I was extremely unmotivated in general, but if any of my friends heard that, they would've immediately called bs. I am so chatty when I'm comfortable with people and I can be extremely bubbly and charismatic. I also overthink and daydream a lot. I had all the "girl" symptoms, and that was at a time where it really felt like add was for girls and adhd was for boys. So I'm very glad that more research around these topics is being done and improved on because it's really helped me understand myself better and like Jack said, be kinder about a lot of things. It's so comforting to know there's at least a reason why I don't always read social cues great and I have some sensory issues sometimes, and it's allowed me to really give myself a lot more grace. So I'm glad Jack's able to do that as well

Content:
I was diagnosed at 30 I'm 31 now spent from about the age of 12 just accepting I was mental, would struggle with a lot of meltdowns around routine changes big swings in moods feeling overwhelmed easily as well as many other things again just thinking I was mental just got unlucky with the brain I was given.

Problem is I've never had a job or had one long enough to really count it I feel frustrated that jobs mainly the descriptions and application process feels like such a barrier to even getting a chance at an interview let alone the interview and if the job itself could be accommodating in small ways, leaves me feeling frustrated and like I'm worthless to society yet I have wealth of knowledge in working on cars and taking things apart fixing things people didn't think could be fixed knowledge of photography down to the technical and practical level and many other things but I can't prove them without work history of qualifications so I feel very stuck in this regard and I'm not quite sure where to turn. 

Anyone of thinking of getting a diagnosis for ASD/ADHD or any other condition you think you might have I'd highly recommend it also look if you are eligible for right to choose it's a bit like going privite but having the NHS pay for it and wait times can be quite short depending on the provider, I hope we do see a shift in how mental health is viewed in society and that it would probably benifit everyone to include people with brains that do work a bit differently.

Content: Admittedly I'm self diagnosed. However I have taken some fairly reliable tests like the RAADS-R. I get overstimulated and overwhelmed very easily, And the first time I got drunk I basically told this one woman who was friends with my mom.... "What is wrong with your son." I hid in the bathroom through the rest of the party. Being autistic has allowed me to know more, and have more creative skills than the average person. However It's a pain knowing that I'll always have to work twice as hard to be like the normal person. I'm big into cinematography, video editing, music production, woodworking, gardening, arts and crafts, etc. I love creating. Author: @MidnightRose98
Content:
Can I just start off by saying thank you so much for coming out and being honest with us? It took a lot of courage to come forward and be honest and maybe feel a bit vulnerable. What you said- it really is important though. Neurodivergent individuals are deeply misunderstood. And you’re right, autism isn’t really normalized enough! It isn’t the same for everyone, and because of masking it can be severely under diagnosed.

I myself wasn’t diagnosed with ADHD until I turned 19 and took myself to my very first psychiatrist appointment with my new insurance. It was scary, very scary. But it helped me to understand that I wasn’t stupid or lazy, I just have my brain running its own little unique program while most people are running on brand name systems. 

Heck, 9 years later and I’ve been absolutely wrecked at the very thought that I might be autistic too. How can I tell my family? Will people treat me differently if I am diagnosed with it? But you? You just went right out there and said it! 

I do hope that if I am diagnosed, or if I’m just a bit more quirky than some folks, I really hope that I can unmask and be as amazing as you. You don’t let this new diagnosis stop you from being yourself, you let it help you shine even brighter. I’m really proud of you for coming out with this. Thank you, for helping those of us who are struggling with doubts and fear to work up the courage and strength to talk about this and other issues with our trusted doctors, friends, and or family. Thank you, Sean!

Author: @georgiablainey9061
Content:
Context: I have undiagnosed autism. I have worked with autistic children for over 10 years. I have autistic friends. Much experience.

Autism. We're different, but where one struggle lies, a superpower hides.

It is SO misunderstood, and it is SO obvious once you've experienced all the different kinds of people with autism and all the different kinds of ways it presents.
Yes it is difficult but it almost always comes with superpowers!
Yes, some are non-verbal, stim more, struggle more, some do sign language some don't, but often they have a skill that comes so naturally to them it is superhuman (-> see that girl that plays piano).
Then some who can talk but struggle with normal conversation or social interactions, get them to talk to you about their special interest and they are very quickly the smartest person in the room and have every bit of potential to be a top specialist in that area (those kids that know the ins and outs about how a train works and the names of them and even technical terminology).
Then you get all of us who are 'just weird' and yeh we may not like certain textures or get 'too loud' when we're excited or don't take hints as easily as others, but goddamn we can see patterns better than others or hear exactly what song is playing in a busy loud shopping centre that noone else even knew music was playing in.

Content:
As a fellow AuDHD you can ultra-mask to do tasks that would otherwise be sensory overload; referring to around the 9m50s mark of the video. Though after doing this one or more times; I have four kids; you may have to take a break or find a way to discretely stim afterwards. That said my wife has told me that I do not need to hideaway or privately shutdown, just do it where ever in the house.

Our cat of 20 years recently passed away last week and my neurotypical wife couldn't look at him at all, but with what I call the flip of a switch was able to get some lockets of hair, whiskers, and clean his fur, before preparing him for cremation. I had to stim a lot after that to deregulate, but if you learn how to flip that switch then you can endure a lot of sensory overload, to an extent before shutting down if you are unable to deregulate.

Noise cancelling headphones are your friend, and if you are in a place with many flashing lights then even shades.

Author: @beez1717
Content: I was diagnosed in second grade and so I've had around 29-30 years of being diagnosed. It's amazing how having autism has changed from everyone thinking you're nonverbal and stimming all the time to many people understanding it's a spectrum and that no two people display and experience autism the same. Because I've had my diagnosis for so long and for most of my life, it's really helped me understand what my limits, needs and areas I need help with are. For example, I have a really hard time with executive functions like keeping appointments, remembering to make them and even making sure to clean up my apartment, and I have learned to tell people that I can sometimes use the wrong tone of voice and I may not know I'm talking too loud, and thus end up saying things in ways I don't intend. I also learned that I have a real issue with being awake all day unless I take certain medications that also allow me to focus on what I want to for far longer. I've also learned that I do best in social situations when there is some structured activity going on like playing a board game, video game, or watching something, because I spend far less energy doing those things than when I talk to others. I need to have a predictable schedule because I don't do well with sudden changes, and knowing what my schedule is ahead of time helps me budget my energy so I'll have enough for everything. The best thing is that I'm in a program where I live in an apartment and they have a case manager that helps me with a lot of aspects in my life, such as asking my team to make an appointment for me because I forget frequently, remind me to take my meds, and I even asked the program to set up a D&D game with others in the peogram so I would have some fun social time each week, and also be able to work on my social skills in a fun way.

Author: @pizapocket477
Content:
I think autism issss... Overexaggerated at times..?
There's a ***spectrum.*** Yes, there are life-changing cases, but there's also cases where-... It, doesn't affect your ability to function much.
I've been diagnosed with autism, depression and anxiety, (which I can't take medication for the last two because they'll effect the parts of ny brain where ny epilepsy is) but I wanted tooo... Wait? At least until I had a good idea of how I could sustain myself. I didn't want to know until I gave everything a genuine shot, y'know? Being diagnosed can be discouraging, that's why I wanted to wait until I knew myself what I am and am not capable of, and can endure.

The stereotypes? I don't mind.
The excuses/crutches? I very heavily mind.
People will get diagnosed with something so mild they're told "you show signs, but you're clearly still able to function normally" and just start using it as an excuse to no longer want to learn, to not do anything, as a shield or trump card if they get themselves into trouble. By THAT point, this metaphorical person is just objectifying the term as an excuse to do whatever they want, insulting the people that have it worse than them. I'm glad you're not doing that. Remaining the same person.

"Be kind and ***hope*** people are kind back" is EXACTLY the mindset everybody needs to be. Hope is the key word there. We shouldn't expect kindness from anyone, especially nowadays where certain audiences of hate have had time to develop online.
But there is a difference between ambition and genuine goals versus overworking. There are some people that have something they want to chase that may require a lot of work, and they'll need support to fall back on especially if they have poor time management and overwhelm themselves.
If anything, learn your limits, but don't grow complacent either. Yes, you're no Shonen protag that's shattering limits every other Saturday, but you're human at the end of the day, still capable of growth, learning, controbution, despite what you may want to convince yourself at times.

I do know that ***not*** sharing weaknesses is a pretty hard thing to do, but what if I told you that was my weakness?
In favor of others getting help first, I often tough things out, say I'm fine and to focus on either the less capable, less skilled, those I personally value more, things like that. I have to practically be forced to admit "okay, I hurt" or "okay, this made me feel bad," with the defense of "but it's something I'm no stranger to healing over time, so I don't think it's worth the attention towards me."
It took fracturing my spine in two places for me to finally tone down on what all I do at work. (I practically still do work easily 3-4 positions daily while there are at leaat 5 people standing around on their phones? I may leave soon though, as my productivity -especially in its high phases- makes the managers standing around ignoring customers look bad, and people will actually assume I'm a manager when one of the managers is standing right next to me. They've started inconveniencing people that associate with me, since they know that inconveniencing my day personally isn't going to make me quit. I love it there, but my friends there that actually socialize and work I don't want having bad days just because of me still being there, even if I'm not the direct cause and it's the manager trying to get me to leave. The boss loves me. Lmao)

But, THANK YOU for voicing the opinion of "worst case scenario? You're in the same situation you are now," and not feeding the self-diagnosed or those barely on the spectrum that use the term as a defense for everything they do.

Content: Hello, Since you have a platform you can tell people in the UK that for ADHD and ASD assessment yes, the NHS waiting list is long but there is something called "Right to choose". Author: @robinpike3780
Content:
Sean i swear you're just becoming more relatable day by day. I also have all those things and have been watching and growing with you since you were in the 100k sub count, maybe earlier.. 
Late diagnosis can be difficult, I can attone to that. Especially as a high masking autism it can have a lot of imposter syndrome in it. The ADHD I find masks a lot of the ASD in me so I'm just telling everyone who is late diagnosed AuDHD that wondering if you're "autistic enough" or "adhd enough" is part of it, use the diagnosis to your benefit. It def taught me a lot about how to care for myself

The hardest part though, is the skill regression in high masking AuDHD. Learning to unmask is a fuckin hassle and worst part about it is you find yourself aware of things you suppressed, especially the difficulty in tasks we used to push through. Allowing yourself the opportunity to regress will help a lot, not being on it all the time is the best gift you can give yourself in being neurodivergent <3

Love to all of you, take care of yourself and drink water for heavens sake!

But once you embrace it, you feel pretty good with yourself~! Just always remember that you are what you are. Nobody should tell you otherwise.

One of the worst parts of OCD is repetitive and reoccurring thoughts that are quite uncomfortable and out of your control. For example: My OCD has a repetitive thought about wanting to have sex with older men. Content:
Thank you for making this video and saying all the right things! Despite being such a common and natural thing, autistic people are seen as aliens by way too many people. And when you brought up that people had asked you "Why do you admit to that?", I really felt that.

People close to me had no problems before I was diagnosed when I was 15. But after that, they started talking to me less since the confirmation bias attached to the diagnose made them think I was weird and uncomfortable to talk to. They made no effort to educate themselves about autism, so their ignorance distanced them even more from me. The funny thing is that I got a lot of social training the years after the diagnose and managed to become so much more comfortable in my own skin, but still, my relatives were stuck in their confirmation bias loop.

Today, I'm not sure if the diagnose was actually right since I had some childhood trauma, bullying and lack of social training early on that complicates things. But regardless, the diagnose made me learn a lot about autism and the nuances of being on the spectrum. It has made me much more aware of neurodiversity and accepting of those who possess it than I could have been if not for the diagnose. I always try to educate people if they lack knowledge about autism and I stand up for them if someone shows hostility towards autists. I really wish we would have gotten further by now.

Content:
I'm in the process of talking to my doctor about getting diagnosed because when I was a child I never had what people call "social cues". I would talk and talk and talk while people around me would get annoyed and I just thought that's how they would listen. Most people don't like to be rude and say "hey, can you let someone else say something?" 
I'd just keep going. 
On top of that, when people would say something like "it's a gray area" I'd get super freaking confused and say "what do you mean? It's super colorful in this place." 
My doctor told me masking is a huge part of growing up Autistic, and if I do have it more than likely because I grew up with the parents I had, masking was a big thing in childhood. 
It's not uncommon for kids to mask all the way into their teenage years and adulthood.

yeah, DUH... But here is the kicker. It makes it easier if you can figure it out yourself, rather than others trying to put you in a box. Second Time, I answered truthfully, and god a definitive inside the spectrum. After that, it took over 1 year before I dared get a professional diagnosis. My absolutte best tips. Be truthfull to yourself. be Truthfull to you, not what you believe is expected of you,. Drop the mask for yourself first.

Content:
I didn’t know until I was 35. It really didn’t change me or bother me to know that I had autism, it just gave clarity to my suspicions I had internalized. I can absolutely relate with treating yourself nicely. I always say that no one is more critical to me than myself. Sometimes you just get into a slump and just mentally shutdown. 
It also makes sense why I can trust so deeply but cross or betray that trust and it is heartbreaking and excruciatingly difficult to rebuild. 
If you are worried about being stigmatized professionally that is valid. I probably would have never been able to serve the military if I would have been diagnosed earlier in life. People seem to distance themselves from what they truly do not comprehend which I understand because it can be a lot to unpackaged at times. Unfortunately that misunderstanding can be carried to the workplace and you can be treated differently when all you desperately want is to let people understand how capable and competent you are. 
Don’t be afraid to be who you are though because being autistic and being different is not inadequacy, it is simply just being different like every other person on this planet. Everyone has a different journey in life to experience and they vary vastly from one person to the next. We are all on this planet together though, so may as well be understanding and accepting of others journey even if we can’t quite understand what everyone could potentially be experiencing, be kind. But anyways autistic ramble done. Cheers!

Content: Hi, Just want to intrude a  bit because the only way misconceptions are cleared  up is by speaking about them. Author: @simonmcglary
Content:
“If you knew I had autism why didn’t you tell me?” After 50 years I was told because I would research it to the nth degree! When, at the end of a talk, meeting or appointment you get asked if you have any questions, never, until 2 or 3 days later I had a complicated, in depth, in detail question! Look at any autistic comedian and they are amazing at picking apart the stereotype of autism. 
The more I have learnt about neurodivergence the more it appears that our brains may work slower, but in an increased level of thinking. We all think very differently, not so much outside the box, more there are boxes? Neurotypical is about neat, ordered and working within defined definitions, adhering to fixed descriptions. We get bored and find crossover, further details, new ways of looking at things, completely new ideas in general, going off at a complete tangent (and sometimes coming back with a genius world changing explanation and way of understanding the world!) We’re all very different, very diverse thinkers with very diverse backgrounds and, if biographies of historical figures are to be believed, potential life changers for others! Amazing examples why diversity is good and should be celebrated! You don’t knock difference, you try and understand it and develop from there.

Author: @AmirSylvane
Content:
Core Components Of ADHD:
1. Craves novelty
2. Difficulty regulating attention & focus
3. Difficulty with social cues due to focus & attention issues
4. Hyperactivity & impulsivity
5. Inhibition difficulties

Core Components Of Autism:
1. Craves familiarity
2. Finds comfort in repetitive behaviors
and routines
3. Difficulty reading allistic social cues
intuitively
4. Strict adherence
to routines
5. High need for verbal context

Overlap Of Both:
1. Stimming
2. Sensory differences
3. Interception issues
4. Impulse control difficulties
5. Emotional regulation difficulties
6. Higher rates of substance abuse, suicidality, depression, eating disorders, anxiety, bipolar & OCD
7. ND communication patterns (info-dumping, connecting over shared interests, story swapping)
8. Webbed/interconnected thought patterns
9. Executive functioning difficulties
10. Increased risk of victimization
11. Special interests & passions
12. Task-switching difficulties
13. Neurodivergent masking
14. Eye contact differences
15. Social differences
16. Passionate focus

These are obviously generalizations & will not resonate with everyone's individual experiences. There is a lot of diversity among Autistic and ADHD people & each person's journey is very VERY different.

I wish people who talk about adhd and autism where more educated, but I guess that’s why licensed professionals exist.

I digress however. Needless to say, at its very core, ADHD and Autism are not the same thing, despite having some overlap.

I'm annoyed that autism gets conflated with other things because it seriously undermines what actual autistic people live through. Keep in mine, a lot of these people ARE verbal, but they still have many of the stereotypical expressions. I swear, mental health care is in the dumps now that it's everywhere. We need to chill.

Author: @sibertiger1970
Content:
It should be mentioned that autism is your brain is wired differently to neurotypicals, It is not caused by immunisation or lack of breastfeeding or all these other myths. It is genetic. It is nothing parents "did" to their child, but at least one of those said parents likely has autism (in varying degrees).
I was diagnosed at 40. My two daughters both diagnosed when they were 18 and had finished school - when their masks and coping mechanisms were no longer required. It is a disability in a world of "typicals" but is in itself a beautiful and crazy individualism.
We are all different to each other but also all the same. It is a journey of learning and lightbulb moments of "oh, so that's why I do this".
I thank you for bringing awareness to this and I wish you nothing but goodwill as you go through this journey.

Author: @hannatheresia
Content: As a fellow late diagnosed person, diagnosed last year when I was 30, I 100% think it's amazing and important that you are talking about this publicly. I saw a psychologist that brought up that I might be autistic twice, once when I was around 20 and the next time when I was around 25, and I did not take that well. I am ashamed but I had prejudices about autism that didn't really get better by all my friends saying that there's no way that I'm autistic considering how good I am at communicating. I could've gotten my diagnosis ten years earlier if I had understood that autism can look like a bunch of different things and that it would've, for me at least, helped me have a better life. With a diagnosis it's possible that I wouldn't have pushed myself to do things that ultimately only hurt me and I might not have stretched myself so thin that I've now experienced burnouts several times that makes it harder and harder to gain energy back. I sometimes think about how useless I felt earlier in life when for example a project was being made in class and everyone just knew what to do and I went outside of the room and cried because I didn't know how to do what they did. Now I know that I can do a spectacular job if my instructions are just a little clearer. I feel so bad for that girl, for the girl that thought she was lazy, untalented, stupid. I resisted before but ended up fighting for my diagnosis.

Author: @MusicSparkleStar09
Content:
Welcome to the AuDHD club! It means so much to have creators like you sharing your experiences and to be so kind in the way you talk about it. I'm able to relate to a lot of the points here <3

Was Dx with ADHD on its own in HS, meds helped out somewhat but they didn't solve all my self-perceived problems. I spent most of my 20's feeling like I was missing something, like there had to be more explanation for what I was experiencing in my brain. I even went to college for Psychology partially to try and understand myself better. It wasn't until a few years ago while watching Tik Tok compilations of ADHD & ASD folks sharing their lived experiences that I started making connections to myself. Like you I grew up in an era where ASD was primarily seen as only including nonverbal kids, especially boys.  It was seen as a very debilitating condition from the low amount of awareness I had. There was very little attention paid to girls and acknowledging that they could have it too. I was even tested in elementary school but I scored so high academically that my parents were told I couldn't have it because I was too successful. (Ofc the social differences started becoming more apparent around that time but since I was smart I *had to be fine*, right? 🙃) Back to the 2020's, once I learned more and more about the nuances and variety of ASD experiences, I asked my therapist (who'd I'd been seeing for a while by then) to help me out and thankfully that organization was able to get me the papers. (I am super aware that I got very lucky and so many people have to wait years and/or spend a ridiculous amount of money to get the same thing :( )

Author: @rwild9356
Content:
Lots of creative people have either ADHD or autism, because the first is a dopamine deficiency that makes ADHD people VERY driven to seek out novelty and new creations and entertainment, and autistic people have hyperfixations that make them very good at very specific things and allow them to put in the hours that most people just can't do otherwise. That's why, even though ADHD and autism can have some inconvenient symptoms for some people, they've persisted evolutionarily- ADHD at least is genetic and inheritable. They tend to not be great for the standardized school system (at least some of the time, everyone's traits are different) but they exist for a reason.

Musicians, artists, actors, etc have a very high propensity for having one or both because those are the kind of people that end up in those jobs. I'd recon a lot of scientists and inventors have/had autism too.

Obligatory: people shouldn't need to be useful to be worthy of dignity and decency, but these things aren't bad things. And understanding why they persist in human populations can help some people who have them figure out how to best direct their qualities into fulfilling and successful lives.

Author: @D-a-n-c-i-n-g_R-a-c-c-o-o-n
Content:
0:30 something very common with autistic people, especially adults diagnosed with autism later. "But you're so social, and great at communicating"

Sometimes we can be masking and not be aware of it. For years I just thought everyone was tired after talking to folks, but that's because of masking. A lot of adults can subconsciously mask autism without realizing it because they are taught that it is wrong to act different from early on. (Masking behaviors are exceptionally common in women, which is why they often go undiagnosed)

1:10 another common thing; autism & ADHD. I was diagnosed with ADHD a few years before my autism diagnosis, and they are very often mistaken for eachother. ADHD people and autism are also very often tied together.

1:48 children with autism often experience "outsider syndrome" where other kids perceive them as weird so they are often left alone, or may even be bullied. I experienced the bullying aspect of this, mainly in elementary.

3:42 this was the same for me. When I heard back from my phsycologist that I very likely have level 1 autism, it was a big relief, unexpectedly. Likely because it provides reasoning as to why I struggle with the things I struggle with, why I can't be in loud environments, why I go completely silent when I have to talk in a group.

7:04 it's a good thing for people to be diagnosed with autism, not because it'll change anything about them or the way they are, but because it allows them to accept themselves and allows them to realize that they don't have to be ashamed of how they are because it's different from the people around them.

9:04 adaptive behavior. Picking up on other's behavior, tone of voice, what they do with their hands, what they talk about, so that you can use some of that and apply it to how you communicate with that person.

9:47 me with vomit. Specifically dog vomit. Specifically when there is a lot of it, and it's slimy. Same with foods. Any slimy or jello-ey foods, I'll just vomit it up right back on the plate. Like toothless and cloudjumper lol.

But that kind of shit sucks because you want to do it, you want to be independent, you don't want to burden someone else with doing it, and you feel terrible about it, but physically you can't do it because you *will* vomit or pass out.

10:12 for me, my triggers are overwhelming unexpected lights and sounds (if I'm going to a concert, I can prepare myself because I KNOW the environment I'm going into), slimy or semi-solid foods like jello (as previously stated), warm drinks, strong scents (poop smell, cat piss smell, certain food smells like fish or beef stew or something, perfumes and deodorants, which suck, as a highschooler surrounded by Christmas-ey perfumes and axe body spray), a lot of people, especially gathered close together, people being behind me, dust, smoke, light touches like hair or someone grazing you lightly with a bag or shirt or something, probably more that I'm forgetting rn. I will actually vomit on you if there is a loud high pitched noise or strong smell or slimy texture. I will and have.

10:34 the waiting list at my therapy place was like 5 years. I went to a phsycologist (or phsyciatrist, I mix the terms up, it's the one that doesn't give you medication for it) in about 6-12 months after the initial talk.

Unmasking Autism is helpful for folks who know they are autistic, think they might be autistic, or just for folks that want to learn more about a variety of autistic perspectives from the interviews in the book. 

It’s also a bit of a “self help” or guidance book that helps you reshape or reframe how others may have made you feel about yourself.

Author: @Chocoboy_James
Content:
Want to thank you for this in-depth video, Jack. 
I myself have been diagnosed when I was 21, and now ten years later I still struggle with it every day. People around me still 'getting used to it' or 'forgetting.' 
And sometimes I do feel myself wondering what could've been different had it been diagnosed earlier, etc.

But for me it was also very funny to go back in time and smile at some stuff I did because "Ah that explains, that was my Autism." Always wanted plushies in my bed in the same order otherwise  I couldn't sleep. Almost every weekend I sat in my bedroom taking out all my jigsaw puzzles and solved them on my bedroom floor and covered most of the floor just with jigsaws. (And then videogames came xD)

But yeah, before I ramble with my stories, thanks for coming out with it and taking the time to share your story and giving more awareness to it that Autism isn't indeed not only non-verbal. I think that's the thing I struggled with most. Just like you said. "BUT YOU'RE ALWAYS SO COMMUNICATIVE." yeaaah... masking. Hopefully it'll make people see their own selves with it too, and make them realise that Autism isn't bad. 

Keep being you, Jacko, proud of you ^^!

Content:
I think it's great that you want to help change the industry, just please stay aware of your health while you go about it. There's so much wrong and unknown in the industry as a whole, nowadays, and it can be soul-crushing. My high school principal's attempts to keep resources from us, along with a somewhat unsupportive dad, gave me a lot of anxiety and depression. But the support I did get did wonders, the therapies I got gave me the tools I needed to learn to deal with myself and others even through higher education.

Author: @distractedcolorist
Content:
I was THRILLED when I finally got diagnosed at 31! It validated soooo much of my life that was previously so confusing. I feel so much less alone now. I am happy I figured it out and sought a diagnosis. I also use comedy as my tool for coping and communicating. Everything you are describing is my exact experience, as well! I am also introspective and had suspected I was autistic for a year or so before that, but I ended up seeking a diagnosis because I ended up in burnout and subsequently a mental health crisis because I was overextending myself. Now that I am diagnosed, and nearly 2 years have passed, I am slowly trying to test my limitations to see what they *_actually_* are and not what I thought they should be based on the non-autistic people around me. 

Also, for context, as a nonbinary AFAB person who lives in the US, getting a diagnosis as an adult was unnecessarily scary and complicated. There aren't any psychologists/psychiatrists/doctors who are qualified or willing to do a proper adult assessment in my area, and I live close to a decent-sized city. I am on Medicaid (low-income government insurance) and finding a doctor/psychologist who does assessments via telehealth for adults who also took my insurance, was impossible. I found 0, and my therapist and psychiatrist were helping me search, so I know it wasn't just because I didn't know where to look. Additionally, the standard assessment itself is geared toward children. There is no standard adult autism test in the US. requires an adult family member to answer questions, and does not account for high masking. So one alternative I was given by my psychiatrist was sending me for neuropsychological testing with a neurologist, but the waiting list was over a year long and my insurance wouldn't even cover it. Since I am not employed, I couldn't afford the cost of the appointment out-of-pocket.

I ended up sending my regular psychiatrist, who manages my ADHD and anxiety meds (who does not regularly do full autism testing), *_ALL_* of the online self-assessments from the "Embrace Autism" website with added notes for clarification. I also wrote out the DSM criteria and provided examples of my experiences from both childhood and how each criterion presents now beneath each one in a 4-page google doc. My therapist who also works at that practice, also sent him notes from our session and talked to him I was super nervous he was going to laugh it off or be dismissive or say it wasn't enough, but he thanked me for being so thorough (lol) and said "Wow, this is great. I wish all of my patients could send me such detailed information. That just made my job so much easier!"  He asked me more clarifying questions after he read through my notes with me, and said that it was definitely enough information to add an official autism diagnosis to my chart! 

There are a lot of barriers, and I know I am extremely lucky that I was able to get the diagnosis, but I want to thank you for sharing your experience! You making this video will definitely help people! I just got stuck writing this for like an hour instead of doing something I needed to do (classic lol), so I hope this helps someone lol 😮‍💨🥴🫶

Author: @GameJam230
Content:
Recently I've been coming to better understand my own ADHD and Autism symptoms. Specifically from the ADHD side of things, it affects my ability to study and learn new things in longform ways. I can't just sit down and read a book or watch a 3 hour complete tutorial on using Ableton, my learning style works by being able to ask questions when I have them and get immediate feedback for them. It's the same way I learned to code, and it's how I learned to analyze stories and construct my own.

In highschool, I was sitting at a grade of 31% at the start of the second-last week of classes in Physics, but I took a few days of tutoring where we essentially went over the notes for each chapter, I asked questions and got immediate feedback, I was able to retake every exam in the class (due to the teacher's policy) and bumped it up to an 81% before the year ended. The tutor himself wasn't the solution, it was the ability to learn at an accelerated pace and to take the knowledge in the way I needed it, instead of the way somebody else organized it.

This is one of the things I actually believe AI has a lot of positive potential for. It's currently in a bad place because of the legal rights associated with it and the moral issues with people who are using it as a replacement for actual artists, voice actors, and writers, but I think there's a few very specific tasks that AI is capable of that are inherently NOT possible without it. Examples include unique interactive experiences like games where the NPCs can respond to more complex situations than current ones, the ability to generate specific TYPES of images that humans are not really able to make due to the math behind how they're constructed (would recommend watching Stand Up Maths' video on jigsaw puzzles that can be arranged in multiple unique ways for an example), but the most important feature, and the one specific to the previous topic, is as an accessibility tool for people with ADHD.

Imagine, for all of you who prefer to learn the same way I've described earlier, if instead of reading through a text book, you could instead just be told a list of chapter categories, given a handful of questions in each, and instead of needing to read through the entire textbook, you could just ask it about the chapter and what it says about the topics in the question for how you would determine how to solve it? To be clear, I'm not saying to ask for answers, but instead to ask it to explain the meanings of only details you want to know so that you can work towards it yourself.

If you want evidence of this being possible, I just finished writing an essay this way. To be clear, no plagiarism occurred, nothing was directly copied from the AI into the essay, and none of the ideas it provided were actually used IN the essay, everything was my own ideas in my own words. So, what DID it provide me? Well, we need to cite examples of quotes in the texts we're referencing in order to make our arguments, so knowing that the texts I was using HAD examples of what I was looking for (I had already discussed it with my professor), so I simply provided ChatGPT with the PDF of the book the texts were contained in and asked it to provide EXACT quotes that conveyed the idea I needed. Then, I can Ctrl+F to find the quotes in the original story to get a page number. All of this was only done to save me the time of reading the entire story when I already understood the premise of it enough to argue an idea in an essay, and with it, instead of forcing myself to take hours and hours struggling to force myself to finish reading the story, only to have forgotten the moment I needed to cite because I zoned out while reading, I was just able to write the essay.

AI is an accessibility tool for ADHD if it's used right, we just need to stop people from using it wrong.

Author: @scritch.scritch
Content:
IMPORTANT DISTINCTION BETWEEN AUTISM AND ADHD:
while the _symptoms_ can appear as a Venn diagram, the _root causes_ of those symptoms vary greatly. this is why ADHD meds work *only* for regulating ADHD and are ineffective for autism. the difference in root causes is why each has their own diagnostic criteria. for example: if you're distracted, is it due to focus issues or sensory issues? ADHD meds will help with the focus for a moment but cannot address the sensory issues (i.e. can't focus in class because of the sound of electricity buzzing through the lightbulbs and my clothes feeling wrong to the point of overwhelm and/or anger).

i comment this because there are a lot of "theories" and strange discourse online arguing that we should get rid of the distinction between autism and ADHD because of that Venn diagram of symptoms. we really shouldn't do that because of the treatment differences between the two; reducing two distinct neurotypes into one is harmful to those who may seek help. it also erases the experiences of people who are both autistic and ADHDers, aka AuDHD. so i encourage pushing back against saying the two are "basically" the same.

sincerely, an AuDHDer :)

Author: @elektrikhd
Content:
This sounds a lot like me--and I self-diagnosed as autistic close to 3 years ago. I'm 40 now for perspective. It's very affirming to hear an experience similar to mine.
For me, there was never an ADHD component; while I have some traits that match, they're better explained by depression, PTSD, or autism. I was always one of the "weird kids" in school, despite managing to have a small circle of friends. I learned to mask because I didn't like how people reacted to me being me. What really made things fall into place for me was reading an article about how autistic people struggle with working, and for the first time I read about an experience that matched my own. Since then I've found a few other people who feel the same way, all autistic or AuDHD. Work has always been a struggle for me, and knowing why I need to, or what good things it can do for me, has never made me feel more comfortable with it. I have to genuinely want to do what I'm doing, otherwise I burn out very quickly.
I think it's more than just YouTube, but capitalist society as a whole, that pushes us to constantly be productive, and makes us feel guilty for time relaxing or having fun. I think autistic people have an easier time seeing through that because we see and approach the world differently in the first place.

Author: @keith_5584
Content:
I think the testing criteria and diagnosis bias is too wide for what they are calling Autism. The scope is huge, and not exclusive. 

There needs to be more defined exclusion criteria and subsets of what they are calling Autism. More than just a line that says if this bad, patient may need treatment.

If it is supposed to classified as a problem and not just a personality trait worth notating, it’s grossly lacking in identifying those who do not need treatment. If it was just notated as a personality trait, then it would be fine. (What that means is a patient may be more likely to have a specific set of criteria if exposed to extreme factors) 

When you over-diagnose or do not narrow the scope by adding subsets of the scope (IE smaller clusters: for example Asperger’s) it waters down the clarity and treatment for the cases that really need help with their condition. It also adds resistance to a patient taking their condition seriously if suddenly everyone else has it diagnosed in common. 

To be perfectly clear, this is not me saying Jack or someone else does not have Autism or does. I am just pointing out that there is a clear deficiency in narrowing things down to how to help a patient. 

TLDR If suddenly all your patients have Autism but have completely different symptoms, how do you help those who are counting on your guidance. Eventually, if your data is wrong you will loose the trust of the patient.

Author: @RikaRoleplay
Content:
Diagnosed from a super early age of 7 (or 8? 2nd grade), I would make friends with my teachers, stay in for recess, and talk to them about their fields of study rather than hang out with my peers.  I volunteered to stay in the 2nd grade since I didn't want to switch teachers, and my one friend I did have was held back for other reasons I never was informed about and they worried I would do poorly without socializing with my peers which I was about half a year younger than them.  

School was fun to me for the structure, the regularity of the schedule, but the coursework was mind numbingly simple for me, and I just was in coast mode until I repicked up pre-calc in High School (which I learned algebra, geometry and pre-cal in 1st grade).  The homeschooling I do think was the major reason it was such a strong diagnosis, though it did run on my father's side of the family subtly, my brother and sister ended up also eventually being diagnosed later in life.  

I struggled in University, since I never studied for tests, and so I had terrible study habits in University admittedly, which really hit my sense of pride at the time and sense of self worth.  I no longer was at the top or near the top of my class without any effort, and I didn't know how to climb.  It was a struggle to fail in many of my ambitions and goals at that time.  I have changed a great amount since then, and I can't even say that I would change some of my darkest hours, as it might have lead me onto another path that could be a greater crash down the road.  

I wish more people could take a look at the world free of their own backstory, and see the world from a sky-high point of view, divorced of the every day mundane task and goal and any personal biases, and really see things from the top down instead of the bottom up.  I would think many would consider this similar to a form of enlightenment, but I do not, there is so much I wish to know more about, and yet so little time to know it.  

Sorry for the late night thoughts and ramblings resulting in this wall of text, the title alone of this video just brought back a lot of memories and nostalgia.  

Have a good night, or, you could say, "Last of the Night To Ya Jack!"

It is 2:10, and high time for bed.

Since I realized that I almost certainly have adhd, I've recontextualized a lot of my childhood and even adult life, and it's a lot easier to extend grace to myself knowing that I'm probably just experiencing symptoms of a disorder and I'm not *just* lazy and unmotivated. Content:
I am part of the generation of autistic women who didn't get diagnosed until adulthood because of the stereotypes around autism (namely the myth that women can't have autism). I was diagnosed in 2021 when I was 27. And I wept when I got the diagnosis. Because it made me realize that it wasnt my fault that I was struggling to exist in this world that wasn't built for me. Like you, I also have menagerie of nurodivergencies onto of it, so trying to figure out was diagnosis affects what parts of my life are really difficult. 

But 3 years later, I know myself and I understand myself better. I have a found family (also all neurodivergent and autism and adhd are the one I see the most in my fam). Therapy has also obviously helped. But the community is what helps the most because when I'm struggling with something, someone in the community has my back with hacks, tips,and tricks. And if they don't have a solution, they point out what I should talk to my therapist about.

Thank you for speaking about your diagnosis. The more we talk about it, the more good we can do. We can't smash more stereotypes, make the mental health industry more ethical and ND friendly, and overall just make better lives for ourselves.
