Author: @deborahwunderman8567
Content:
You are absolutely amazing! I am totally with you about changing the paradigm around Autism and other ways of being in the world that are different than "Normal"! What you say around minute 14... what if "we" (the ones who have autism) flip the script on the neurotypicals. Those individuals who appear to be super productive, super feminine or super masculine, super cool, super perfect with no signs of weakness anywhere or anytime... WHAT IF THEY ARE THE ONES WHO ARE MASKING?   

I am almost 60... and in the last two to three weeks, I have come to realize I am autistic and have ADHD and I have been masking my entire life. I am going to get an official diagnosis because I just want to know and like you, I find it super interesting to learn about myself.  However, I have taken three online tests that all put me on the spectrum around 160ish.  I have never felt like I fit in since childhood.  I have super abilities of smell, sounds, and I am fascinated by light and reflections and shadows. But, I also get gag reflexes to the exact same thing when my dog gets poopy butt... I can smell her a mile away, but I have to call my husband to clean her or there will be two messes to clean up!  

I realize now that when I am talking to people... I am taking in massive amounts of information, including how they smell, body movements, facial expressions, posture, tone of voice, words used and not used... and I am processing all this information in real time to figure out how to move with the conversation, just as you explained so well!  It is exhausting!!!  Because once I get all this information inside my head, it does not go away.  I continue processing it 24/7 and adding it to new information coming in... almost like a super computer with no off switch.  I have digestive issues and joint issues. I have depression and constant anxiety.  I have lived through hell in the workplace because I am not afraid to point out to my superiors when they are wrong... and in our world -- wrong is right if you have the proper title or high enough level of status.   

I hate the status quo.  I hate how neurotypicals seem to so easily ignore that which they don't want to know, don't want to feel, don't want to bother with... I believe our world is drowning right now in Ignorance... break it down -- ignore...ance.  We are taught from small children to ignore that which is not convenient to us, that which will suck too much of our time or our wealth or our status.  I have written an entire novel about this crisis of consciousness (published earlier this year), but evidently it is too complicated for the "average" reader to engage or understand... that's another story!

Your story is what drew me here, and I like your style!  I like your sentiments!  I like your thinking!  I think we need to change how people think about individuals with "disabilities" 'cause maybe our disability is actually a super power the neurotypical world desperately needs NOW. My daughter headed Best Buddies through her high school years and I helped a lot with activities and what neurodivergent individuals have (meaning individuals who have a much greater difficulty navigating the neurotypical world because we choose to ignore difference and don't build in accommodations)... but what these individuals have that my neurotypical "friends" lack is EMPATHY, KINDNESS, COMPASSION, JOY, FUN!  We need so much more of that in our world today... we are dying from lack of these super powers... exactly what us in the neurodivergent spectrum are said to be SUFFERING FROM... when did KINDNESS and EMPATHY become a disease?

Content:
Wow, everything you said in the video, I relate to SO SO much. I got diagnosed with autism at 17, like Jack because I want/need to have answers about myself. I believed I had ADHD (Most likely just ADD cause I've never been extremely hyperactive) since I had been diagnosed previously with only Generalized Anxiety and (Mild) Major Depressive Disorder, although I had those answers as reasons for my uncommon mood issues and anxiety, I felt like that wasn't it.. I knew there was something more and I believed maybe it was ADHD. When I went to get my ADHD evaluation the Phycologist noticed other signs that are common within persons with autism. I'm so happy I got the phycologist I got to do my evaluation, me being female, many mental health things are so much different for me/us (other biological females) than males. If she wasn't as dedicated to my case as she was, my evaluation would probably have been wrong or come up as no different from my previous one. Many things express itself differently depending on your physiological make-up, there are some similarities but sometimes it appears less often or very differently. I've always been one to do my own thing if others didn't want to join, I overanalyze everything (sometimes I even have to reconstruct my entire way of thinking just to understand something new, like in Math even though I excell in both Math and Science.. History and English are the most difficult for me), and sometimes, although being one of the smartest/top students in my school, my processing speed can be extremely slow which shocked school staff.

Learning about my autism has helped me a lot, I feel so much more content understanding why I feel and do some of the things I do or feel. Even if I can't get prescribed anything to help with it, I feel so much better just knowing.

Thank you Jack, even though I don't watch many of your videos anymore (I used to watch your extremely old content).. Thank you! I'm so glad that I subscribed to you back when I was just a nugget. 💙

Content:
I was diagnosed with major empathy at 16. Not fake tik tok egirl empath, I have actual clinically diagnosed empathy. I thought I was autistic but its not at all the same. to this day I'm still not sure what to tell people when they wonder what the hell makes me so anxious and isolative, tired. I don't have it in me to tell people they are making me anxious cause i can feel their moods so deeply. I don't want them to think its their fault or that I blame them for something that they don't understand. Oh random reader, the hardest part is always that no matter what I say about this, I can feel that no one understands what I'm talking about and I sound nuts trying to elaborate on it. I've failed numerous times in my definitely selfish attempts to feel genuinely understood by someone else, and decided to let go of those selfish expectations. Which at its core is a general rule that I just don't talk to people much anymore, even if I'm interested in what they are doing/ talking about. Cause if they open up, so do I, and that can of worms always leads to me wishing I hadn't started a conversation at all. How the fuck do you explain to someone Empathy and Psychopathy are just opposite sides of the same coin without sounding self centered/ like a psychopath? Kind of a self fulfilling catch-22 type thing I guess. Mainly because so many people left, I let go of the idea anyone wants someone who sounds like (and through years of isolation might be) a looney for a friend. Guess I figured this would be interesting to share because not everyone who's here, or a loner, ect. is autistic, some of us are just deeply hurting and misunderstood people who don't want to hurt others. We all however, are misfits here, and we accept each other.

Author: @SamSepiol127
Content:
The "funny" thing is, when I was a kid back in the early '90s, being different, having issues, having divorced parents, or even just wearing glasses was a disadvantage. I wasn’t invited to birthdays because I had divorced parents.
Now, in 2024, having a few traits that lean toward the non-disabling end of the autism spectrum has become a superpower. If you have a disabling illness? You’re the coolest! And if you talk about it on social media, you’re the king of cool...
When I was diagnosed with ADHD, it wasn’t trendy yet, so I was just the "slow kid," and they told my mom it would be better if I didn’t pursue further education because I didn’t have what it took—I couldn’t sit for 8 hours with a book. Nowadays, if you can’t focus on one thing for a minute, you’re awesome because you probably have some disorder.
People self-diagnosing illnesses to excuse their lack of effort in anything, scrolling TikTok 24/7: "Leave me alone, I’ve got autism/ADHD."
Maybe it’s because of the times, maybe it’s the difference in diagnoses, but for me, it was anything BUT a superpower.
I’m happy for you and wish you all the best! Big hug.

Author: @KovarrBlue
Content:
I want to thank you for posting what is a personal journey, for us to follow.

I was diagnosed with ADHD about 6 years ago.  I'm now 50 yrs old. I had a lot of people say to me, "Well, why bother getting diagnosed NOW, it's not like you need extra help in school or anything."  But suddenly realizing why I was the way I was - why I couldn't concentrate, why I was so forgetful, meant so much to ME.  I suddenly realized I wasn't "broken".  My self esteem was poor all my life because of this.  My first day on meds, I sat down and cried, because finally I felt like a real person.
I've always known there was a link between ADHD and Autism, and while I knew it was a spectrum, I still thought I would be very "different" if I had it.  
Thanks to you mentioning that you're going to get tested, I started thinking maybe I should as well.  It would explain why I have issues with other parts of my life.
I'm making arrangements to be tested in the new year.  Whether I am diagnosed with Autism or not, I thank you, Sean, for being a waypoint for me.

Content: I hope if you ever see this you don't take it the wrong way, but I'm really fascinated to see if your opinion on seeing the diagnosis as a positive always stays that way, and maybe if already being successful has an affect on things. But now, since unmasking and trying to give myself the grace and time I need in order to stop having repeated burnout, I am experiencing massive skill regression I never expected. I think its a mix of my age and learning that I really do have different needs than nuerotypicals, but I am absolutely falling apart and becoming unable to take care of myself monetarily, which is leading to a collapse of everything else too. I used to be able to force myself through these minimum wage, entry level jobs for around 6 months at a time to be able to support myself partially, but have never been able to fully support myself (now 30f). Trying to get my mind on something I'll be able to do to support myself once my family is no longer able, or if I am ever left without a partner to help me, feels almost impossible and like I'm sailing a sinking ship. I do hope your journey continues to be positive, and congrats on your new understanding of yourself!

Author: @_x..Jamie..x_
Content: I'm also AuDHD! I was diagnosed with adhd at 15 but don't have an official autism diagnosis. I'm unsure if I want an official diagnosis because in Finland you get the same support for adhd as you do with low support needs autism  and having an autism diagnosis automatically makes the adoption process longer here and I hope to adopt someday. I also experienced very much the same outsider feeling as a kid as well as when I got my adhd diagnosis. My sister who I've always related to the most was diagnosed first with adhd when she was like 19-20 (I was 13-14) and that led to us convincing my parents to get me tested. However after the initial euphoria of having an answer my sister and I started having a lot of misunderstandings and arguments and that alongside interactions with other adhders left me still feeling like I was an outsider even within adhd people. That eventually led me to tell my sister that I sometimes wondered if I was on the spectrum and us falling down a rabbit hole of research (we both knew quite a lot to begin with, me having researched prior for answers and her being a youth social worker). That was 4 years ago and by now I'm certain I am autistic and have gotten validation for my self diagnosis from a range of autistics and adhders as well as multiple professionals who deal with adhd and autism issues including my psychiatrist (to an extent of course, they never want to comittally agree on a diagnostic term without an actual diagnosis). Your autism seems to present quite similarly to mine, I struggle with sensory issues a lot but I also have issues with non-surface communication and being able to manage all aspects of life at once. I've been trying to unmask for about 2 years now and as a nursing student working part time it's been hard. Especially when even the person who at one point was the one I related to and who understood me the most (my sister) seems to now misunderstand me a lot.

Author: @mezzomae_1
Content:
Welcome to the family, man!


Yeah, ADHD and autism do have a lot of the same symptoms 
It’s absolutely felt like a weight lifted from my shoulders since I was diagnosed. In elementary school, I blamed myself so heavily for the way I was. I honestly thought that everyone around me had those issues earlier on and just coped with them better than I did. I thought I was weak and I felt helpless in a way.

I honestly was so self conscious that even when I was in kindergarten, in the back of my mind, I could never properly say how I felt or perceived anything. 
I’ve always been a very picky eater. Even when I’m fully awake, I struggle to feel like I can bring myself outward and *show* that I’m there. I struggle to see the real person trapped within me to finally reveal itself when I look in the mirror.
Looking back now that I’ve turned 18, I think the question that was always in my mind was in school was, “How many birthdays do I have before I implode?”
Humor, musical theatre, and art has always been a major part of how I can get as close to communicating my voice outward as I can.
I just always felt that way. 

I’m glad I’m not alone in having this and I hope you and everyone like me can bring themselves outward and live as contentedly within themselves as possible😊

Author: @mintybirdy3850
Content:
Welcome aboard! I hope you are doing well! As for what you are saying, I totally resonate with it. Despite having an early diagnosis of Autism and ADHD as a young girl/toddler in the 90s. So yes, I too know what it is like to feel like an outsider even when you have places you can relate to but don't entirely fit the mould. And yes, I have anxiety, I have had depression and I also have mild hypermobility, joint pains and a sensitive stomach and I also had asthma that I grew out of as an adult! :D

Yes, people then and still today - despite awareness campaigning (but I will say that it is certainly better than the 90s) - think the more extreme end of the spectrum is what ALL autistic people LOOK like. Some people - more in the 90s and earlier - even confused this with down syndrome despite them not being related at a core level. This from my own experiences has caused people to constantly overestimate my ability or underestimate me. Especially as an autistic person that can articulate herself and convey my emotions without having a meltdown. (I have shutdowns more than I have ever had a meltdown in life) Also there was little to no support for me going from pediatric autism support services to adult ones. I believe that still to be the case today that child support is vastly better than adultcare too. I also find that the biggest thing I have ever wanted is to be normalised which usually comes with understanding and acceptance and this has yet to be achieved. 

Especially in a world as that currently likes to accentuate difference rather than recognise it and accept it. I was very fortunate to be brought up in a household that saw me as just ME rather than someone that has autism. But going outside my house, going into school - especially middle school and higher and so forth - made me realise how much my difference seems to define me and not the person I AM. This was quite an isolating experience. (It did not help that I experienced bullying because of my quirks.) I had been taught the opposite, to accept people and try my best to understand them in turn. I have found in my life that I have had an easier experience understanding and accepting others but finding that others - especially those with a lack of awareness - find it very difficult to understand me. Especially with people who have no intention to change their minds as well on what autism is (and what caused it which is a painful regurgatation of fear-laced hypothesis that have scientifically have long since been squashed.)

There is also the issue that people - even if they have more awareness - do not see individuality in a person with autism. They have an idea that all individuals with autism are the same. Which is why the old 90s point of view still exists today. I know I could walk into a room with a bunch of autistic people and know they will all be different to me, even if we have some similarities. Just like going into a work place or school, I don't expect people to all be like me. It just feels like common sense since despite human beings being a social species, we are largely individualistic. That is why we are different from one another, even if we are like-minded and I think that is something to be happy about and to encourage. After all, having different perspectives makes innovation happen! :D

I am also very, very glad that you are seeing this as a positive and being kind to yourself! I do believe there is merit in understanding one's own different ways of getting things done or simply just not being at the same level as other people and accepting that. No good comes from working yourself ragged to attain a standard that just doesn't work for you. Being kind to yourself is important in general too! :3

Content: i think they mostly talk about the stimming/nonverbals a lot, even amongst mental health professionals, because I have a theory that these labels were created in essense to estrange these types of people from the "normal" ones. They only take the most intense cases, the people with it, but who slipped under the radar, were never considered because they were more likeable/tolerated. I still have a hard time coping with my own diagnosis, due to the historical meaning of mental health diagnoses, but I'm sorry that this essential piece of information, part of you, key to understanding yourself better, has taken so long to come by. It's a blessing and a curse, I'll say that. Once I got diagnosed with schizophrenia, I felt like it was my own key to feeling better. It really wasn't, i tried jamming that key into doorknobs that wouldn't fit it. I really believed my diagnosis was all that I was. I want you to take this information and remember it. You may have autism, and that is a key to understanding yourself, as a part of you, but it is not all that you are. You may not feel the way i felt about mine, immidiately, but i see it happening with other people who have been diagnosed for a while. Stay true to yourself - old time watcher <3

Author: @emilydb444
Content: i first started to suspect that i was autistic when i saw a few tiktoks about autism and really related to them. i dove into the research reading 4 books, listening to podcasts, reviewing the dms-5 criteria over and over again. i knew i was autistic. all of the signs were there. i asked my prescriber to be put on a waiting list to be assessed. she said it would take a while. it took over 2 years. i had to practically beg her to assess me. it was a long process but in the end i was officially diagnosed as autistic level 1. she said i was teetering on level 2 but i was so high masked that i was able to stay in level 1 cause my support needs weren’t as high because of my ability to mask. i got diagnosed one month before my 21st birthday. all my life i knew there was something different about me. (now im pretty sure i also have some sort of dissociative disorder because of trauma but that’s different lol) i was self diagnosed as autistic for about 1-1/2 years. people think that self diagnosis means you watched 10 tiktoks and now you think you’ve got whatever disorder they were talking about but that’s not the case. yeah, it started because i saw some relatable tiktoks but after that i did immense amounts of research. it took me so long to actually get properly diagnosed by a doctor. what i mean by this is, autism is a spectrum, self diagnosis is valid, and neurodivergence is never a bad thing!

i just now got the notification for this vid and jack probably won't see this but this is for anyone in a similar situation. i had to literally fight for my diagnosis. i went to 3 different psychiatrists and had to convince my long term one i was autistic. i researched autism and autistic traits from online advocates who were autistic themselves for over a year and yet i was told by a psychiatrist who had to study the definition and memorize the basic traits of it for a test and a degree. i got diagnosed after i told my psychiatrist i knew more about autism than he did and explained my own traits. guys, there's a reason it's called the autism SPECTRUM.

many people go undiagnosed or self diagnose because they don't fit a single possible manifestation of autistic traits out of infinite possible outcomes.

Author: @Cerasum_chrysanthes
Content:
I have been diagnosed with ADHD a year ago, at 31 years old. I have asked my psychiatrist if I could get tested for autism when I was around 25-26.
I have been scared to ask again because of the way he dismissed me. He said "You're crying, you're looking me in the eyes. You can't be autistic."

At that time I didn't know all that much about it either, but since then I've read and heard so much more about autism from people who are diagnosed and from researchers and I keep finding more and more things that just... fit.
It's so obvious. It's all there. But people STILL have this old and narrow-minded view of what autism really is. 
As if there is a specific checklist of things you need to have to count as autistic. (In some way, yes, that is obviously how it works, but you know what I mean. As if only those very specific things mean you can be autistic! I don't like trains, I'm bad with numbers and I can look people in the eye when I'm masking!)

I think my psychiatrist was definitely not educated on autism or still held very old views about it that obviously wouldn't fit with new research of autism, especially how autism presents itself in AFAB individuals.

I also often still think about the question he asked me: "What would a diagnosis do for you?", he asked. But he didn't accept my answer. I just wanted to know, I just wanted to understand myself. According to him, people with autism don't ask those questions... obviously that is bullshit. You notice how you're different, how you're sometimes even outcast because of how different you are when you're autistic. 

The fact that JSE has his diagnosis honestly just shows me once again that autism is not just this one specific picture people have in their mind. Autism is a huge spectrum. 
Luckily I have a new psychiatrist now and I also found a clinic that specializes in autism in adults, so maybe I can soon try and get tested again and not just be dismissed again.

Honestly. Good for you, Jack. Thank you for sharing this and for giving people hope.

Author: @JessicaHayes-lewis
Content: ADHD and Autism definitely have similarities but they are not the same thing. Their similarities though is what leads lots of people to get confused between the two. Most commonly are communication and attention difficulties. I have ADHD and Autism and I was diagnosed as a child so I grew up understanding both. I’ve started running a vlog discussing experiences, difficulties and positives of both conditions. Anyway, there are a lot of conflictions that come with having both. One example is in behaviour. If you have ADHD you come across more hyperactive which sometimes breeches the gap in communicating difficulties because your mind is running a million miles an hour. So your anxiety sometimes doesn’t have time to catch up, but when it does it’s like being hit with a freight train 😅. However, commonly people with autism actually come across as more withdrawn unless faced with an intense interest. Both definitely need more awareness and more discussion both socially and scientifically. And of course all characteristics and behaviours are largely dependent on the severity on the spectrum and individuality. Ok, I’ve written a lot so I’m gonna come to a close now. But I think the gist of the whole discussion is whether you were diagnosed a long time ago or recently, people should never allow themselves to be led to believe either condition is a disadvantages. There are struggles and issues that most need support with, but there are just as many strengths. And at the end of the day it is just a part of what makes you who you are. So embrace it and don’t let anyone tell you that you are stuck with the difficulties and they will never get easier to manage. You are intelligent. You are charismatic. And there are always others who can understand where you are coming from even if you feel alone. 😁👍

When I tell people I have autism, they tell me I’m lying because I don’t have too many issues socializing or speaking even. Yes, I rely on patterns. Yes, I fixate on small details. Yes, I am awkward and don’t like crowds. Yes, my brain goes in overdrive and take in too many things at a time and it doesn’t filter out. I struggle to know what to say, when I have to say it, how I have to say it. When it’s wrong, I feel anxious. I hate the fact that I look at someone and trying to figure them out like they’re some puzzle. I struggle with shutting down my brain and making eyecontact with people. Some tastes, some textures triggers me. Once I smell, hear, see or taste something, I fixate on it and can’t “undo” it. But no, I am not incapable of socializing. I have an issue with all the stigmas and stereotypes. So ya…. Ranting over

Author: @Femmeenby
Content:
Putting this up top bc I realize I rambled for far too long: I’m so happy for you Sean, and I’m so thankful that you’re speaking openly about this, and that you generally want to shift the tone on mental health conversations. This is a big thing, and you are brave for doing it not because you’re autistic (like how some folks do the “oh my god you’re soooo brave🥺” thing) but because you have such a large platform, and you are willing to risk the negativity from ill informed individuals to get the message out. You’ve been so outspoken about various issues, and frankly it’s part of why even tho my preferred type of game is story based type stuff like TWD, TLOU, undertale, even FNAF to a more casual (sort of… aside from security breach…) sense, which doesn’t seem to be quite as big these days, I still try to tune in to you, mark, & Ethan as often as possible. Y’all speak up about these topics that folks still treat as something to be ashamed about or whatever. It means the world that y’all also speak on things like LGBT+ rights, including trans people. Just… everything you’ve done for various communities & causes is so amazing, and I wish I had the power you do to also speak up and make a significant difference.

On the topic of picking apart one’s life… I also love it! As a young kid I was quite excitable which drew in other kids, but I rarely initiated, and for the most part that only got more apparent as I got older & found out I like books more than people, so the only friends I had were either folks who felt bad for me at first but then got to know me, who saw some “likeness” in me through observation, got paired w me, or who I reached out to solely bc I realized that bc bullies weren’t gettin the “right” responses from me, they were targeting this other person. 
When it comes to “play,” especially as a kid, for as long as I can remember it looked like me silently putting dolls together/staging littlest pet shops into “scenes,” appreciating it, perhaps internally imagining scenarios & conversations (w/o moving them) then I’d change scene, move the toys, and do it again. 

Even now, at nearly 27, I found out Wizard101 has the option to move furniture in homes in “illogical” or “hyper specific” ways, which I’ve spent hours on at this point, just ever so slightly rotating presents & wrapping paper in my “Christmas” house for realism, sizing up pets & mounts to be closer to their real size, etc. 

I also feel like I can “read” people very well, for better or worse, for similar reasons. The “humor” is usually just me unmasking to a degree, which comes across as humorously overdramatic, or it’s me studying people casually, without interacting, and using that info to adjust my behavior. This means my personality is… I feel like less developed…? Bc I’ve always been a “fill in the gap” type of person. If my friend is quiet and reserved, I remain a comforting presence but I’m simultaneously the “impulsive” one, or I’m the “defensive” one if necessary (like walking around at night or at a Halloween haunt, I’ll take on a more protective attitude) and the opposite is true too. If my friend is loud & impulsive, I still match them in a sense, but I’m also more likely the voice of reason, the nurturing one. 

And textures… as a baby I loved the bright orange baby mush food, w carrots & sweet potato & whatever, I almost exclusively ate that to the point where I started to turn orange around my lips, eyebrows, and nose apparently. As a young kid who would wake up hours before my parents, I would whisk eggs w a fork & microwave them, or eat hotdogs right out of the package. Constantly. 

Now I can’t stomach any of those things, even 20yrs (at LEAST) later. 

Can’t do chewy bits in my food. Chunky mashed potatoes despite my LOVE of potato dishes, and forget about ribs, steaks that are juicy due to fat content, etc. if I have a single bit of fat I’m immediately gagging & having to spit it out. My spouse even says I get this look in my eyes, think it was like… zombie deer in headlights, if I bite down & feel that awful texture of having chomped on a bit of fat. Even coarse ground sea salt is too much! Why are there tiny pebbles in my mouth?? Bits of garlic bigger than finely minced? (Loooove garlic) especially if they’re on anything other than garlic bread which should be equally as soft due to oil, I can’t do it. 

And flavors!!! BEGONE sweet and savory!!! The devil!!! Even a lot of fresh garlic on steak is too much, bc cooked garlic has just a little too sweet of a taste for me on well seasoned steak. 

Socks gotta be inside out bc of the seam, shoes gotta be a size up and wide for toe space, I want comfy comfy clothes in nice textures, Sherpa is evil, my hair cannot be touching my ears, I’ve currently got a mullet-Mohawk (death hawk??) of sorts, and the hair at the back keeps curling and tickling my ears making me freak tf out… 

Nevermind the missing certain social cues, in settings where I don’t feel the need to study folks, or the insanely high sense of justice (dangerous since I’m 5’3 & 130 at best. I don’t even work out.) that will have me toe to toe w someone 6ft+ 200+lbs. I beef w management. I have to work part time which doesn’t pay the bills bc otherwise I’ll burnout in a year anywhere other than fast food (retail seems to be the only other place that will take me other than my seasonal haunt actor job, and retail will likely be the death of me)

Downside- I cant be a gamer bc the controls never make sense. I even struggle w wizard101 (that, undertale, ACNH, & mariokart are about the only games I can actually play half decent) I can’t seem to develop the skills for any sort of art (makeup, paint, craft, etc) bc that requires time, patience, dedication, and focus.

I’m trying to write a fanfic which has now been on hiatus for 3mo (most due to working my main job & as a haunt actor, but then after I’ve just been so drained…) 

Worst part is- even if I got diagnosed, I’m now married so I wouldn’t get shit for support, and my spouse NEEDS support too. So I HAVE to work. I HAVE to keep crushing shit down and biting my tongue to the best of my ability. 

Being diagnosed would run me the risk of fr putting my name on the “fire asap” list bc I live in an “At will” state meaning they could fire me for truly no reason at all if they really wanted to. 

All of this, & folks will still assume I’m not autistic, or brush it off as some joke when I say I am, unless they are ALSO autistic in which case they’re like “yeah, obviously” (being “peer reviewed” is the funniest thing ever, I love it)

Author: @wispisang
Content:
Bro is probably never gonna see this but SO MUCH said in this video I can relate to, as someone who is already diagnosed. I don’t exactly have ADHD, I was told that I have a provisional diagnosis which from how they explained it is like “You could be diagnosed with ADHD but most of your ADHD behaviors can be attributed to the autism.” After I was diagnosed it made me able to understand and recontextualize my whole life and why so many things that were “easy” for most people were so hard for me. It made me feel so validated in how I exist in the world and not just “willful and lazy” like my parents would always assume. It made THEM finally understand me and why I couldn’t do things the same as other people.

I also have an extreme issue with bad smells!! One time I was left home alone with our family dogs and the moment one of them shit on the floor I boarded myself up in my room and cried because I couldn’t handle it. Recently someone threw a stink bomb in a haunted house I was working at and I literally couldn’t get myself back inside the building until it was completely aired out, thankfully my stage manager was very understanding and I wasn’t the only person with those sensory issues working there. I’ve never been able to handle certain mushy and slimy foods and can only eat very specific shapes of pasta. I like to use music to block out sounds around me in a noisy place, it helps me regulate my brain, back before I was diagnosed I’d cry if I’d have to go into a mall without headphones or earbuds and now I finally get why it was so distressing for me. I have trouble taking showers because I don’t like the feeling of soap in my hair and being wet afterwards. All throughout my life I’ve used vocal stims, I still do, my coworkers have all just accepted that “I’m a rat” because that’s one I’ve been stuck on recently. At the bakery I used to work at I’d just start meowing unprompted sometimes and my boss would go “Ope, Hannah’s meowing again” She would call me the white rabbit because I jumped around and paced back and forth so much.

I find in a lot of social situations I enjoy more to just sit back and listen to people talk, I never know how to contribute to conversations without it being incredibly disjointed or one sided. If I’m having a good down I MIGHT be able to manage. I’m very fairly at masking though, I feel like part of it factors into my acting skills. My whole life has been acting out certain emotions for people. I find that I have to put energy into emoting and when I’m tired and drained I literally am just deadpanned, being expressive becomes exhausting. In the following years of my diagnosis I was just able to notice so much of how it really was my reality in the smallest of ways, which made any thoughts of the imposter syndrome just die out for me. I have no doubts that I’m autistic, even if other people might say I don’t “look” the part. A lot of people just don’t think I’m autistic because they think I’m pretty and I wear too many cute clothes which is just… bruh. But as the years go by the depression and self hatred doesn’t go away but it gets a hell of a lot easier, and just easier to deal with life because you actually understand that you’re different and not just going about things like everyone else and thinking “why the hell can’t I manage this what’s wrong with me?” Having autism is hard and sometimes you hate it, I know I do, but there are also plenty of things to love about it. My attention to detail and artistic inclination, my ability to look at every aspect of a situation to easily weave together my stories and my interest in how human minds function and develop for writing my characters. My ability to sing music pitches on command and being so particular with them and making sure they are in tune. My ability to just not give a shit about sticking out like a soar thumb and being myself, not feeling the need to conform to things. My ability to see through certain bullshit manipulation tactics int society and think for myself.

There are a lot of us out there, thankfully since I work in more creative settings I tend to be around a lot of other autistic people. A couple weeks ago me and my co workers went to Chili’s and I mentioned I had autism and turns out like everyone else did too and we were able to just talk about it and relate to each other and that kind of stuff is just so nice. A bunch of very particular people working together can get on your nerves, but we all understand where we are coming from. It’s so nice to see such a big youtuber being open about autism and trying to normalize it, it shouldn’t be something people have to hide and be ashamed of.

Content: Welcome to the cool kid club!! Going through my own process of getting diagnosed with Autism was really healing. It helped my to judge myself less, take care of myself better, and express my needs to others. It’s hard growing up autistic, struggling to relate to my peers. Author: @cayotoledo6970
Content:
Jacksepticeye, I realize that I don't frequent your channel and that I am not familiar with you. However, I am ABSOLUTELY on your side all the way. 

Why? Because I am also on the autistic spectrum. Specifically, I was diagnosed with Asperger's syndrome. I am a Filipino Aspie here in the Philippines.

Even in my childhood, there were times when I with full awareness asked myself:
"Why am I like this?"
"I know I'm different from others, but I have no idea why."
"I am intensely interested in this/that and I want others to share that same satisfaction I get."

I remember when I was still in high school and my parents suddenly pulled me aside one night. It was then they revealed my Asperger's condition: my laser focus on everything that piques my interest, me not being wired to be socially adept like the others, my senses being heightened and more sensitive, my going through my school years wanting to study and work the way only I want, how there are many famous people on the globe who have Aspergers or any other autistic form. 

And yes, you mentioning how you prefer to talk to everyone behind screens instead of in real life? That is EXACTLY how I conduct my business and I tell you, I'm doing splendidly. It is a nightmare and a drain on my being to make extended social interactions in flesh-and-blood settings.

Personally, I have found my new desire to be a writer who has my own goals for literature.

Our species anywhere on the autistic spectrum may have been treated as outcasts back then, but with the increased awareness of our own neurological and psychological profile, you and we can wear it as a badge of pride and honor. 

We know that we are not stupid to think that having any autism at all makes us any less human. Autistic or neurodivergent, WE ARE STILL HUMAN BEINGS worthy of dignity and capable of bringing good into the world. 

We are just as badass as the "normal" people. And I for one, wholeheartedly welcome you into this gigantic community where we are not afraid to be one with ourselves and to live our lives to the best of our ability. It really is beautiful that we are able to be free to live our lives the way we want it and we show the world that we are indeed human beings.

I could write a whole library of my experiences on Asperger's, but this is something I wanted to say to express my solidarity with you.

Live well, Jacksepticeye
👍😉

Author: @BonnieCalderwoodAspinwall
Content: YES SEÁN! I'm so happy for you to be learning more about yourself. Before I realised I'm AuDHD I spent years trying to follow advice for ADHD or advice for autism and neither worked, because it turns out combined AuDHD is its own specific neurotype with its own particularities. I'd also recommend you look into PDA profiles (not uncommon in autism), because learning about this changed my life. It has a bunch of dumb names that people argue about, but basically it's where perceived loss of autonomy activates a threat response in us, putting us under huge physiological and psychological stress. It often leads to "rebellious" responses, or complete overwhelm shutdowns, social hibernation, "running from responsibilities" etc. and was a big part of leading me to burnout, because I was trying to power through it instead of understanding that these responses were my body/brain sending me signals that I was over-committing myself and giving up control over too many aspects of my life (or allowing myself to feel like I had lost control when I hadn't truly, but was just feeling beholden to too many other people). It helped me change my relationship with friends, work, responsibilities, etc, reframing them from demands whenever possible. Feels like this could help with your relationship to Youtube/fans maybe? Sending much love and support ✌

Author: @LightYagamiSOS
Content:
I haven't been diagnosed officially and i dunno if /when i will be mainly because i go back and forth between  'bruh im autistic as hellll'  to 'nah ain't no way'.
Then when I do truly think i'm autistic, I back out of making any steps towards getting assessed because I feel like i'm taking away an assessment from someone who is autistic. For every 5 autistic traits I have, there's always one I don't think I fit that makes me decide i'm not. 
I have an older brother who is diagnosed with autism. My parents noticed him so I figured that if I was, they would've gotten me assessed too. I did more research and since im a girl it's different and due to the lack of research on autism in girls, it's no surprise my parents didn't notice. 

As a kid, I spent most of my time alone. I'd read or just stare at bugs, plants...whatever I could to pass the time. Teachers would always ask why I wasn't playing with the other kids, but the other kids didn't like me and I didn't know why and I couldn't explain that to the teachers because they'd just say 'Oh they don't dislike you! Let's go ask if you can play with them!' It was such an awful feeling. So we'd approach some kids who were playing and the second I was basically forced onto them, they'd stop playing and make excuses to leave the moment the teacher left. I was a really lonely kid, but I didn't know how to make people like me because as far as I knew, i wasn't doing anything wrong. I wanted to hang out with kids my age, but they also felt very immature to me. Yeah duh, they're kids. I felt more confident talking to the teachers than the people my age. Talking to kids felt so incredibly awkward. 

I can't make eye contact. It's physically uncomfortable for me. I had a boyfriend who made it his duty to force me to make eye contact and it made me so anxious every single day. I ended up breaking up with him because he wouldn't stop. I have issues with certain textures. Microfibre is a material created by Satan. I hate the way it clings to your fingers. I always have to rub my hand on my leg afterwards because I can still FEEL IT. I seek out stuffies with beads in them because I love the feeling of them. I like marbles too. 
I rock constantly when i'm thinking, watching something. Side to side if i'm typing something, back and forward if i'm watching something on youtube or somewhere else. As a kid, I would wait for my eldest brother to get home from work at night and 'take the cold away' - when I was around 4/5 this also meant putting my cheek on people's cold feet. I shudder at the thought. I just loved cold skin. It was so soothing. 

I think my mother suspects that i'm autistic. She was telling me about how a boy I went to school with was diagnosed with autism and how he's a homebody 'like me' and I could see the cogs turning in her head. My older sister was talking to her about how autistic people tend to isolate themselves and have a lot of alone time, like my older brother who's autistic and she looked at me like 'oh...and you'. 

Maybe one day i'll look into a formal diagnosis, just in case.

Author: @Serechor
Content:
I had a friend who had AuDHD, and it felt like night and day compared to me (just Autism). We were both hyperfixated on things, but I found that she was much more... energetic overall in how she acted, and my bar for sociality and energy was much lower. She was also a lot more socially conscious than I was, and tended not to have as much stereotyped movement compared to me. I, on the other hand, have said things rather recently that "don't make sense" or offend someone accidentally.

I do wonder if self-conciousness is an AuDHD thing, or I passed by that "portion" of autism. My friend was extremely self-concious, in a rather internal way. She tends to be her worst hater. However, I generally have no qualms with myself. I know that my self-worth is strongly conncected to success, but I have alleviated much of that by reminding myself that "C's get degrees" and all that. I am, however, not a good masker, but that is likely because like 60% of my family is autistic, 39% is adhd/add and then there's my grandma

In general, ADHD and Autism seem to combine into rather unique people, rather separate from ADHD and Autism as a whole. It's all rather interesting!

Author: @ArcaneSequence
Content:
I might get some hate for this, but this is something I'm starting to see a lot.

Before you attack me, I'm autistic myself, which prompts me even more to talk about this.

Autism is spreading, and it's spreading everywhere. Prevalence has increased so much that it might as well be 50/50 that anyone you talk to has it. It's so common in 2024, however, a few decades ago it was extremely rare. You might be thinking 'What's wrong with that?', well, I think some people forget that ASD is a disorder, and it's called that for a reason. I think everyone already knows Autism is not a good thing, and people will say that there is nothing wrong with being Autistic. Of course you should not be discriminated against for it, that's horrific, but I think people need a wakeup call that this is a negative thing. If Autism spreads enough that most people in the world have it, it's gonna get much worse. The reality is that we have defective brains - we don't just work differently, we work worse. And I feel like for us to be the best versions of ourselves, we need to come to terms with the fact we aren't perfect instead of being in blissful ignorance. Coming to terms with my issues has helped me become better overall, and I think it's helped me overcome a lot of my issues related to ASD.

Autism is not a normal thing. It's an anomaly - and I firmly stand by my belief that finding a cure for such a fast spreading hereditary disorder should be at the top of our priorities. Screw the people that say it's fine and we don't need to find a cure. This is an issue, and it needs to be solved. My goal here isn't to make anyone feel bad about themselves, but how good would you feel if there was a cure for the disorder that actively hinders your ability to learn or interact with the world? I sure would want one. And so would my family.

Autism can destroy families. It can tear them apart, and it hurts the world as governments are having to pour money into supporting them. While this only applies for severe cases, this is still an issue. Don't just dismiss me and call me a hater, I've been through it all. I've seen the weakest cases all the way to the strong ones. It's heartbreaking to see how much damage is done to the lives of children who could have been normal kids and the families who have to raise a child with a condition they didn't prepare for. If there's a chance we can get rid of this disorder for good, then I would do anything to take it.

Author: @allyabasta2783
Content: I have ADD, non hyperactive, and I’ve been diagnosed since kindergarten. I was always allowed to have extra time for tests and assignments in school but it still never helped and teachers got fed up with me and my “procrastination” and “laziness”. I developed anxiety and depression over time because I didn’t understand why my brain would process all the learning but couldn’t put pen to paper and answer a homework question. I over analyze everyone constantly and shift my personality and the way I present myself depending on who I’m with to try and make them like me or actually want to stay friends with me. I’m constantly masking to fit the social norm and when I get home I’m exhausted and then I have a meltdown because it’s so exhausting. I’ve had sensory issues since I’ve been born and everyone just says I’m picky or that I’m “so ocd” about things for no reason and I don’t think that’s the case. Everything makes noise and it’s so overwhelming. Cars and lights humming, fabric rubbing together, people breathing and talking is so irritating and when I can hear them all at once i can feel it in my ears and on my skin and I freak out. I hated jeans because they were “prickly”. I didn’t wear socks in 6th-8th grade because I hated the way they felt on my feet. I cant eat oranges with the white pieces or juice with the pulp. Too much lotion on my skin makes me want to peel my skin off and I can’t wear pants if the waistband is too tight on my stomach because I feel like I can’t breathe. I didn’t start taking pills until last year and I suffered through everything adhd-wise and pain-wise because no matter how hard I tried it was impossible to swallow them. You get the point. I want to get an autism assessment because I’ve always been this way and it’s exhausting. I’m scared to though, I’m afraid to get laughed at for bringing it up or something. I always think I’m wrong and I’m afraid to do things in front of people in fear that I’ll get yelled at or even laughed at, even when I know what I’m doing is correct. I feel like if I get a better understanding of myself and the reason why I am this way then maybe I’ll learn how to properly balance my emotions and my daily life. Should I do it?

Author: @murphysletsdraw
Content:
To anyone considering getting evaluated for autism and/or ADHD, if I may give some advice (I'm an audhd-er and have helped a few people through their own diagnosis process): it can really help to bring someone with you to the assessment meetings. They should be someone you trust, ideally someone who can appear "normal" (respectable, well dressed, not visibly disabled themselves) and who can help share their insights into whatever you do that points to autism/ADHD. 
"I've known x since high school and even then they struggled with y". "X is my brother and he's always been a bit z", etc. 
It can really help with your credibility if someone "normal" believes you might need help - it shouldn't have to be like that of course, but in my experience it often is, especially if you're marginalized in other ways or have the bad luck of meeting a specialist who's suspicious of self diagnosis or "drug seeking behavior". And even if your specialist is a lovely person who'll take you at your word, it can still be nice to have moral support and someone to help you remember everything you wanted to say.

Glad you learned more about yourself, Jack!

Author: @rednecknick4832
Content:
When I saw that popular YouTuber, Jackcepticeye, had posted a video about him having autism, I was intrigued. I watched the video and felt a sense of connection to Jack, as I myself have autism. I was proud of him for being open and honest about his struggles and felt empowered by his bravery. 

However, when I mentioned Jack's autism in my third period art class, it didn't go over so well. My classmates stared at me, some even snickering behind their hands. My teacher looked at me with a concerned expression on her face. I realized that I had unwittingly outed Jack as autistic in a public setting, without considering the implications or thinking about how it might affect others. 

I could feel my cheeks flushing with embarrassment as I tried to backtrack and explain myself. I didn't mean any harm by mentioning Jack's autism, I was just trying to relate to him and share my admiration for his openness. But it was clear that my classmates didn't see it that way. 

I left class feeling upset and ashamed. I had inadvertently made a mistake that could have serious consequences for Jack and for myself. I realized that I needed to be more mindful of how I talk about sensitive topics like autism, especially in a public setting. 

I learned a valuable lesson that day about the power of words and the impact they can have on others. I made a promise to myself to think before I speak and to always consider the feelings of those around me. And while I may have faced some backlash for my slip-up, I am grateful for the opportunity to learn and grow from my mistake. 

In the end, Jackcepticeye's video taught me an important lesson about empathy, understanding, and the importance of being mindful of how we discuss sensitive topics. I am grateful for his bravery in sharing his story and for the opportunity to reflect on my own actions and behavior.

Author: @scp-049iq3
Content:
As someone with autism who shares most of the traits you've mentioned you yourself have, I thank you for making this video. It addresses the false stereotypical mindset around what autism is (False in the sense that not EVERYONE with autism is non-verbal or have speech impediment. There's way more Individualism than that.) and goes into easy to digest details on how autism is actually an entire spectrum and it's effects on our side of the spectrum. Yeah, we can be a bit slow at times and maybe occasionally need things broken down a little bit but that doesn't mean we are any less capable and if anything it can even make us naturally ahead in some things. Like you said some senses can be hyperactive and the ability to kind of break down a person to get a better feel for who they could be as a person as well as occasional talents for things like art and in some cases even computer programming. Hopefully this video reaches everyone's ears and puts a more understanding light on autism, the existence of an entire spectrum and it's Individual effects. (and hopefully people stop putting all autism in a "incapable" category. like I've unfortunately experienced in my childhood.) Additionally I agree that the whole "Be tough, Don't show weakness" side of the internet is just silly to put it kindly. There's nothing wrong with Self-Improvement but trying to be some "tough macho with no emotion" isn't improvement, It's just insecurity.

Anyways Love to you Jack, Again thank you for making this video. ❤

Content: I'm so glad you brought this up. Ever since I was a kid, I always watched your videos and would rewatch them over and over again. I started doing my research on autism since I was 14 and learned that I could potentially have it. As soon as i saw this video I was shocked, I would've never assumed you had audhd but at the same time this video opened my eyes and me feel more confident and also made me realized that I relate to those symptoms similarly to you. Most of my life I wanted to socialize but I was bullied for reasons I never seen back then. So, I was always emotional and cried on the spot or get upset if anyone would make a joke or confront me about a little thing because I assumed everyone was out to get me since I never gotten along with the kids my age and I kept to myself until I learned how to mask, I also over analyze behavior to figure people out, and filter out and water down my actual personality to fit in and it has become second nature, I've also struggled with sensory issues as well. I always have to wear sandals indoors because I don't like the feeling of dirt on my feet, and if i don't wear them I just stand on the sides of my feet. It even made me struggle with doing chores and even taking care of myself since textures like dirt, sand, and unknown liquids and oils in dirty areas overstimulated me. And my sensory issues would only heighten if I was functioning on a full stomach. I'd gag for either walking too fast and feeling the food move in my body, smell anything slightly strong no matter if it smells good or bad, seeing something slightly or remotely disgusting and hearing a disgusting sound or someone describing a nasty thing. So to prevent myself from that I'd just isolate myself, stand or sit in place, close my eyes and hold my breathe whenever It would get too bad. I even struggle brushing my tongue because I always gag whenever I try cleaning my tongue. And on top of that whole mess I got a buttload of hyper fixations like human evolution, cannabis science, science news, animal biology, the color purple, the 2000s decade. etc. I know this comment looks like im re-writing the Declaration of Independance, but I just want to thank you for sharing this with your community, and sharing your experience, I especially look up to you because I've enjoyed your content since I was a child. Thank you <3

Content: I too got diagnosed with autism this year, same age as you (1990), and I can relate to how much the past of my life suddenly makes more sense to me. I thought I was stupid or weird (but I never felt like it, nor would I want to change, because I was just being me, and that wasn't "wrong"), but I still had a lot of friends and we played games together a lot. In my more grown-up days I lost touch with my friends as school was over, work and family started happening in peoples life. Now I am more or less without friends, though I live with my fiancé, whom I love more than anythign in this world, and I still love life by just being alone with my better half and play games. I miss having people to do stuff with, but neither me nor my fiancé consume alcoholic beverages (due to allergy and choice), and going out usually means drinking. I am sad to say that getting drunk seems to be the way to "socialize" nowadays, which makes it harder to find people to hang with as we both get uncomfortable around people not being themselves (drunk). We go both got diagnosed, and we both enjoy playing together or separate on our own screens (while sitting next to eachother). The alone time can be a sweet sweet blessing sometimes, but the longing for a group of friends linger always.

Content: Hey Jack, if you read this, I recommend looking into toxic shame. I have AuDHD too, alongside other stuff (like CPTSD), and I’d say neurodivergent people are more likely to develop toxic shame. I’d say this is at the root of all trauma, and it basically is a feeling of “I’m not good enough or somehow bad” that is stuck inside of you, which is then protected by defenses you have (like  thinking you’re better or worse than people sometimes). Because this feeling is really painful, we start having these defenses. I recommend the YouTube Heidi Priebe, who made videos on this and how to heal from it. I would say that we need to spread more awareness about this. It’s a feeling, and working through it means working through childhood traumas too, and we can learn how to integrate it and heal from it

Content:
I'm still not really sold on the whole idea. I've thought for a while that I may have ADHD, and wanted to get tested, but recently came to the conclusion that it doesn't matter and doesn't really change anything, I shouldn't let that define me. 

I've never genuinely met anyone who claims to be Autistic and thought "yeah that makes sense" because they've got a disorder, but because they have specific characteristics that are for whatever reason considered not normal, but a ridiculous percentage of the world's population now is considered to have ADHD or Autism, meaning that it's slowly becoming so wide that eventually we'll all be considered Autistic or something along those lines. 

15 years ago it was pretty specific and not something many people would get diagnosed with, but it seems they've expanded the criteria so much that it's slowly starting to include basic personality traits. I do believe it exists, but in the extreme cases, like those people who need 24/7 care. I think fairly normal people like myself, my friends, Jack, and any others than get diagnosed with it are just shifting the blame away from Anxiety which is the real problem with most of us.

Author: @MyNameIsNotActuallyRosco
Content:
Here's my story: (sensitive content warning)
When I got diagnosed with Autism at age 13, I initially felt good about it. However, during that time I didn't really process it all that much. I ended up going into a deep depression, where I thought about hurting myself all because I felt like my life was a lie. I was harkening back to all these memories from when I was a child in situations where I was treated differently compared to the other kids by teachers and whatnot. As a result of overthinking combined with teenage angst, I let this out on my parents. They definitely didn't deserve to be treated that way, and the more I argued, the more suicidal I got. As I couldn't really explain to them what I was feeling concisely without bringing up the diagnosis - which I found really hard. I was paranoid, distrusting others while questioning my own abilities and interests more frequently. On New Years Eve, 2023, I made a new years resolution to develop more optimism and look at life more positively. 

I'm 15 now, and I'm happy to say that this worked out! I've slowed down a bit this year to build up more confidence and in doing so I've achieved so much and effectively fucked autism in the ass XD. But in all seriousness, there really needs to be more societal awareness when it comes to mental health stigmas. I've always loved your content, Jack, and It really got me through that terrible time. FOR EVERYONE WHO'S GOING THOUGH A SIMILAR PIRIOD, PLEASE KEEP PUSHING THOUGH!!! It sounds simple but you have to think more of yourself in order to succeed.

Author: @Bendylife
Content:
Im really glad you have found an answer to how you have felt and I'm glad it's helping you. I just also want to say that Autism and ADHD and not "basically the same thing," and believe it to be misinformation to claim they are. They are two separate conditions with some over lapping symptoms. You can have both at the same time. I, for example, have ADHD, but not Autism. I think its important to be accurate about this kind of thing because it can be very confusing for others and could lead people to confuse the two conditions. They both require unique accommodations and treatment and it's important that people understand that having autistic like symptoms doesn't mean you don't have ADHD. 

Untreated ADHD can really negatively affect someone's life, as it did with my own for a long time. Treatment in very important and I don't think it's entirely helpful to say things that could confuse people and convince them to possibly stop pursuing treatment they need too early. 

Im glad you've found some answers and I hope this can be a comfort to others with Autism that can relate to your experiences.

Author: @harrisonmccartney4878
Content:
I completely get the "denial" element of having a diagnosis. The way I see things is that we're living in one of the most unnatural epochs in human history. All this technology, all these sedentary lifestyles, unhealthy diets (gut/brain connection), all this endless scrolling on social media and putting your brain in gear at 500 mph all the time because we're forced to feel like we're not keeping up, I just cannot believe that there is ANYONE who is mentally healthy in this unnatural world we now live in. If you're able to tough out the state of the world and be a functional person in it, I'm pretty sure you just have undiagnosed psychopathy with a very convincing mask, because for the rest of us the DSM-5 is basically a horoscope for the human condition in the modern world. Just as everyone has a star sign that correlates to the date of their birth, so too does everyone have something in the DSM-5 that explains how their brain is reacting negatively to this unnatural world. The list of mental illness has expanded to include everything under the sun, and it's all because we live in a world that is completely unnatural. We have so many things disrupting our sleep, we have a culture that glorifies alcohol and drugs, a culture that insists people be on the "grind" 24/7, a culture that makes us focus on consumerism and being unhappy with what we have so that we constantly want something else to fill the void in our lives and to keep the capitalist economy running, and a culture that is being divided along ideological lines by people in power who don't want their citizens to rise against them. Show me one person who is happy and healthy in a world like that, because I haven't seen one yet.

That's not to say that I don't think there are actual mental illnesses like ASD, depression, ADHD, etc., because I believe they exist, but rather I don't know what parts of mental health are a consequence of living in this unnatural world, and what parts would still exist if the world wasn't inundated with these things that push mental health to the brink in everyone.

Author: @BallisticCryptid
Content:
Hey guys, for anyone who may still not understand what ASD (Autism Spectrum Disorder) is like, something that helped me understand is this: picture everyone's brain like a computer. You're running a different operating system than everyone else. You can fundamentally do a lot of the same things, but the way you do them and the ease to which you can do them is different. Like imagine using Windows or Linux in a world where everyone "normal" uses MacOS. It'll be confusing and annoying that others don't get why you have trouble with things, but once you realize what OS you're using, you can find the guides needed to help you learn to live with it. 

Sean, thank you so much for making this video. As someone who was diagnosed with ASD when I was just a kid, you have no idea how much this means to me. Seriously, thank you.

Author: @Hal_Law26
Content: The "why did no one tell me?" at the beginning really got me. I have not been formally diagnosed with autism, although I have discussed it with various doctors in the past few years to figure out how to go about it (all of whom were literally no help :/), but I am 99.9% certain that I am on the spectrum. It had taken me until I was 25 to realize that I am autistic. I had been asked by my pediatrician, at 18, if I had ever thought that I was autistic, which my response (being ignorant of the real range of the autism spectrum) had been "no, I don't think so." Once I had figured it out though and had told my family (who were unsure at first, until they also did research and were like "yeah that fits" lol), my mom ran into my former pediatrician at the store one day and had asked if she had remembered that conversation, as well as asking why she had asked. because we were very sure that I am autistic now. My former pediatrician said that she had figured I was, but did not continue the conversation with me or my parents because she felt that I was "handling it well." Meanwhile, she was very much aware that I had struggled with debilitating (at times) anxiety and depression. I, too, always felt that neither diagosis fit entirely with what I was experiencing. On the one hand, I do understand her thought of not wanting to bring it up, if it was going to be a non-issue, however, on the other it also makes me unreasonably angry. I had spent years of my life feeling always at least slightly different than others (despite having a reasonably sized friend group) and I feel that if I had known this sooner then maybe some of my struggles could have been lessened or even avoided entirely, and I would have been more compassionate with myself.

Author: @CherryZomb13
Content:
Im not around on this channel a ton these days, but i wanted to tune in here and be one of the voices saying, we get it! We love you. Youre welcome here.

There can often be a mourning period after finding out about all the things you didnt know you needed and were missing out on, even if thats just personal understanding. Please take care. 

I so greatly appreciate having a public figure like yourself who will advocate for those of us that fly under the radar. Ive gotten the exact same "but you communicate and make eye contact so well!". 🙄


Edit: Okay, i wasnt expecting the bit about ambition. That one hit hard.

Just today, i was thinking about the way people ask God for strength. The strength to get up and do hard things, to endure stress and tragedy. "The strength to change what you can, and to accept what you cant," or however the saying goes. 

I realized that i *only* do that. I only ask for help with struggle, i constantly run head-first into strife and try to force my way through because if i ever feel like im not making progress, i get horrifically discouraged and end up doing something to mindlessly occupy myself.

I dont tend to let myself make art, or consume it, or read books, invest in my homekeeping, my looks (im vain alright), or even my hygiene because i feel selfish and hate having the things i do while knowing how much others suffer without. 

I realized that, if anything, i should be asking God for help in just being. In living with the blessings They've entrusted to me.

That isnt to say i should stop caring or trying to help other people, but that i cannot expect to continue doing so when i dont care for myself. I know i have that ambition in me-- but i dont have compassion for myself. I treat it like a reward hard to be earned rather than food for energy, something needed to thrive.

Its time for a lot of us to change how we view ourselves. May it only get better from here. <3


For those concerned, i know well that "God" is a complicated concept and unsuitable to all-- so trust me, righteous haters, when i say i dont put everything on prayer. Just thinking over my relationship with work and rest. ☮️🤟

Author: @stormydragonkai
Content:
Eeeeeyyy!!! Autism gang, woooo!!!! Thank you so much for talking about this. I super appreciate you explaining some things that are difficult for you because it's so important, as an autistic person especially, to be able to relate to other people. I haven't heard anyone talk about the SHEER AMOUNT of processing it takes to have a single conversation, but I'm so glad you did. It's so difficult to explain to neurotypicals. It's so difficult to get them to understand not only how fast we have to filter information in order to be able to respond at a socially acceptable and/or non-awkward speed, but also *how many filters there are*, like you said, from tone to body language and expressions, to social expectations and rules, to implications and subtext, to-- Then to run your own potential response through almost those same filters to make sure that you come across and will be received exactly how you intend to... Not to mention the amount of brainpower it takes to do that, again, with every interaction... It's so hard.

So proud of you, Sean! Here's to a year of self discovery and understanding, being kinder to one's self, and taking a stand against the difficulties of the industry and negative stereotypes against neurodivergency. Thanks for being you. :)

I wouldn't say that ASD and ADHD are on the same spectrum. They can be similar, but they are their own things.
I have both of them.
All those "if you have X you likely have Y" should always be taken with a grain of salt.
As studies like those are suggestions, and the results don't cover the whole population of the world.
So it's not always like that, which I think is an important thing to keep in mind.

As is the fact that you can have "traits" from a diagnosis, without actually having that diagnosis.
For example. Not everyone who struggle with keeping eye contact has ASD, despite it being one of the common "traits".
Not everyone with a hyperfixation has ASD, even though it's a common "trait."
That is something important to keep in mind.

Author: @Marc-dg2en
Content:
I love all the positivity, but one thing I am always careful with (for me its just ADHD) is seperating yourself from your condition. Something like "Im not actually like this, i just have ADHD". Or "it's not my vault, I have ADHD and can't control it". Those statements are false, you are like this and the things that you do are your responsibility. It's just way harder for you and there's nothing wrong with that. For example, I super easily forget people's Birthdays. I don't want that to suddenly become an ok thing to do just because I have ADHD. Forgetting a birthday is and will always be a "bad" thing. I am just someone that often forgets it and that's perfectly fine and does not make me bad person. At the same time, if someone doesn't want to be friends with me because I always forgot their birthday even after I explain to them that I didn't do it because I don't care abotu them, then that's fair too. ADHD is a part of me and not something that influences me. 

In autism for example some people are often seen as "rude", or "inconsiderate". Even for small stuff like unenthusiastic greetings or unintentional insults. I have seen someone with Autism talk about how annoying they find that people think that way. He wanted people to understand that he's not being rude and that he's just autistic. Again, that's not true, being rude is not the same as being malicious. It's not a state of mind or intention but a set of actions and when you are doing something that is considered rude or impolite, then it doesn't matter why you did it or how good your intentions were, you were just rude. Not saying hello to the cashier (or your cultural equivalent) IS rude. The problem is that other people will assume that you are doing so because are malicious, selfish or narcissistic. You have to understand that that is just the way you are and that it does in no metric make you "bad". The thing is we all technically know that cheerfully saying good morning to the cashier is a waste of time, but precisely because of that fact, it's a subliminal communication of respect. "I am sacrificing time and effort for you to show you that I view you as a person on the same level as myself and that I am trying to pay attention as to how my actions affect you" is essentially the information that gets communicated in a simple "good morning". Most neurotypical people don't even realize it and do it "automatically". Most of politeness comes from showing that you are paying attention to and are aware of others needs. Even with the useless stuff it's still "the thought that counts". And if you have that type of Autism that is something that is just way way harder for you. Neurotypical people have this insane separate parallel analysis system that is evolved precisely for social cooperation and communication. Don't let people who have it easy judge you for struggling in their turf. Not having access to this "algorithm" doesn't make you a bad person or give anyone the right to judge you. But it's sometimes true when they say that you are being inconsiderate. You just have to understand that you are not doing this out of malice, narcissistim or selfishness like everyone thinks. There is absolutely nothing wrong with you being that way.

Author: @Dotveg
Content:
Hi Jack, highly doubt you'll see this but everything you said resonated with me. As a diagnosed autistic person and stay-at-home dad, it took me four burnouts to finally get a diagnosis. Four burnouts caused by the very mentality you condemn in your video. Do better, do more, be interesting, bring something new to the table, be the best at what you do — and you know what? I failed at all these things. I failed tremendously hard because I was trying to do something I am literally not wired to be able to do as consistently, as effectively, and as mindlessly as it needs to be done to succeed. When I reached my fourth burnout, I had my first hardcore autistic meltdown — and no, while I'm sure that sounds like a cool album title, it was absolutely not cool: I was unable to speak for an entire week. I lost my ability to go outside on my own. I'm still trying to recover some of my minor motor functions from back then. That burnout fried something bad.

So your message is important. It's one more people should hear. It's one I desperately needed when I was the outsider kid, the kid whose parents were never proud of despite the fact he got straight A's in primary school, the kid who got bullied by anyone that saw he wasn't 'normal' and an easy target because of how already bruised his mental health was at a very young age from both his parents' abuse and the fact he could not understand social cues or regulate his emotions. I needed someone to be there and tell me "hey, this is normal. It's just who you are, you just function that way, and it's okay. You're okay. You're not alone."

So thank you. Thank you for sharing your diagnosis, for the lonely, misunderstood kids out there. For the then 14-yo me's wasting hours of their life in front of an editing software because it's the only place that feels like home, regardless of how bad both mental and physical health are getting. For the young TikTokers who are going to go through the same hell if they're not already there. For the influencers. For those who live with a camera pointed at them every moment. Thank you for letting people know, there might be a reason. They might just belong after all. But belonging does not have to be synonymous with destroying yourself for some stupid numbers on the internet. I was, and to some extent still am, a victim of this mentality. I am glad you're speaking up against it.

Content:
Yeah, I got my own testing for this stuff recently through Workforce Solutions. Generalized anxiety, autism, depression, but not ADHD. Turns out I just have anxiety so severe that I have the focus, thought patterns, and issues of ADHD, just none of the treatments or techniques for dealing with it do anything for me.

The distinction is found in those assessment tests; ADHD is an impairment in certain areas they can test for, these tests remove the emotion and consequences from those things, so if you can complete them fine, then it's not actually ADHD because it's not a cognitive impairment ruining your focus. Turns out my average results are above-average in all cognitive areas; no signs of any impairment, which means it's all emotional impairment holding me back.

Certainly feels nice to hear you have a similar attitude as me; different reasons, though. I consider finding out a win, but more because I want a problem to solve, not to keep sitting around feeling helpless and hopeless because I can't accomplish anything and there's no-one in my life to talk to.

Still need to find something that actually helps. Just haven't found out how to live my life. Good luck with your own crap.
