Author: @stickywiggit
Content:
I was studying to be a scientist but really struggling. My grades were fine but I forgot things constantly and... let's just say the signs were always there. I was diagnosed with generalized anxiety disorder and depression and given SSRI's but they made me feel incredibly sick. I went in to ask about testing for ADHD and the psychologist looked at my grades and said it was impossible because I had good grades. I accepted that at the time but by the end of grad school I had not one but THREE friends who were professional scientists who were diagnosed with ADHD which made the psychologists's hot take sus. 7 years later at age 40 I pulled a middle-aged-angry-white-woman (ew) and INSISTED on getting tested and, lo and behold, I had it.

Since then I've been very open about my diagnosis and I have discovered that there are an ASTOUNDING number of neurodivergent people in the sciences. Which, I mean, duh. A career where you can have a single minded obsession over a single topic? The ability to close yourself in a lab day in and day out without having to converse or make small talk with others? How about an intensely physical job where getting distracted looking at bugs or listening to bird calls is considered a positive trait? Neurospicies are EVERYWHERE in the sciences and I think the variety in neurotypes is really important for careers that require creative thinking (of which science is one of them).

I want to echo jack here and say: getting the diagnosis helped me understand that I wasn't a terrible person or an idiot. It didn't change anything about me except that I finally understood how my brain works and could cut myself some slack and help other people understand what to do when I was having a bad day. The biggest downside has been that, because neurospicy folk tend to gather together like dopamine-starved wolves, I stopped masking almost entirely and have forgotten that bursting randomly into song is considered odd to most people. Oh well.

Author: @mop7316
Content:
brickwall-sized comment ahead, you've been warned

so, when i was a kid, i was unironically convinced everybody gets a little handbook when they're small, basically a guide to life that explains how everything works: friendships, relationships, getting shit done, having interests, maturing—you name it, i couldn't figure it out, and everyone else apparently could, and the difference was so striking i was genuinely convinced i missed out on something essential growing up. the feeling didn't go away until age 21, when i was diagnosed with autism. and suddenly it all made sense in a very heartbreaking sort of way, because suddenly all the alienation i experienced as a kid because i never seemed to do things as effortlessly or as thoughtlessly as everyone else did—there had been a reason for it the whole time. nothing was wrong with me, i had simply been undiagnosed, and that made me the weird kid that had to (unknowingly) mask in order to not get weird looks for half the things i said or did.

i'm 23 now, it's still not easy. my main autism-related struggle now is that i have the same interests now as i did in high school, and most other people don't, and i feel incredibly immature and lonely sometimes. i have to keep reminding myself that everyone, me included, goes through life at their own pace, and i could spend a lifetime doing these same things that bring me joy and still be worthy of love and capable of community. i've had the utter luck to meet some people recently that don't know about my autism, can tell that i'm a little weird (not in the "i'm weird, i'm a weirdo, i don't fit in" sense, but in the "masking but still visibly neurodivergent" sense) and have fully embraced me exactly as i am, and it's so relieving it makes me want to cry a little sometimes. it makes not masking and being myself instead a lot easier, and hopefully i will be able to shed all this childhood trauma of exclusion and alienation and wrongness and embrace myself too, eventually.

tldr, thank you so, so much for sharing this. it's good to see the conversation around autism always expand to include people that aren't 6 y/o train-obsessed nonverbal boys. it helps those of us who are nowhere near that side of the spectrum, remember that we are valid too. wish you all the best <3

Author: @firstviicar
Content:
I highly doubt you'll see this at all, but funnily enough I got diagnosed with ADHD combined type at almost the exact same time you announced your own diagnosis of Autism. And... hearing the way you put it into words in a way I felt I could not describe before is so... freeing. I struggled so much of my childhood and even my now adult life trying to understand why I felt the way I felt. Why I did things the way I did things. I knew I was never neurotypical, but I also didn't know if it was just the depression/anxiety/ptsd/trauma responses doing their best to make things difficult... or if it was actually ADHD. 

I went for the same reason: For answers. I wanted to understand why my brain was the way it was. I wanted to understand why I thought the way I thought, and why I react the way I react to things. I didn't know if it was just my 'personality quirks' as my family put it, or if it was because of an underlying diagnosis that I wanted the answer for. My future husband also has ADHD, but he was full inattentive type. My best friend has ADHD but full hyperactive type. They presented so differently than myself, and I was so different from the stereotypical idea we have of ADHD... so I always told myself I was just probably embellishing it. That I couldn't have something like ADHD, because I've been relatively successful in school and in my social standing. I wasn't ever put in a separate category from others and was always put in higher curriculum standings. No one in my life from when I was a child, ever told me that I acted any different from your neurotypical child. I was called a 'gifted' kid, and I was always told by my family that gifted kids never had these issues-- I clearly have nothing wrong with me. I was always told those with ADHD would always struggle in school, and that you would be so hyperactive you couldn't stay in your seat. I wasn't like that. Though I'm sure the reason I wasn't is because my anxiety since childhood has always been so horrific, I was a people pleaser, and failure meant others would hate me. I couldn't have that. My psychiatrist and other medical professionals pointed that out to me as well. 

I work in mental health. I studied mental health, and still do as I go back for my masters degree. I always am so kind to others and know that mental health issues present in different ways. Not everything is linear and by the book. And yet... I denied myself the idea of having another underlying issue, simply because I had the preconceived notions from my family and my own line of thinking from how I was raised. I have never been nice to myself, and always told myself I'm faking it or it's something else. I told myself it wasn't possible, simply because I didn't present in a way that I felt was 'ADHD enough", simply for the reason that I didn't believe in myself, just like my family never believed me. It's so freeing to hear someone else share a similar sentiment (not all the same but yknow), and know that I'm... not as alone as I thought I was.

Content:
Hey jack, just wanna say im a huge fan and I love your vids and its crazy to hear this diagnosis (watching since happy wheels). I am very skeptical myself that I have ADHD, though I was doing just fine in life, because I have recognised that I am experiencing some symptoms that seem to match with ADHD, so I am considering getting a professional diagnosis soon. I just wanna remind everyone, including you, that people should never see ADHD or autism or any mental health issue as a disadvantage, but also as an advantage. I know a classmate of my little sister that is clinically autistic, and she tends to use it as an excuse for everything to get ahead of others. She gets away with bullying certain people and making racist jokes against others, as well as doing naughty things in class, all because she is autistic and supposedly cannot behave like a regular human being. What’s worse is that her parents condone this behaviour because they too have the mindset that this incurable disease will barricade her from becoming a good human being, so people need to excuse her behaviours. That’s a very prejudiced and disgusting attitude imo, because it is obviously false. Mentally ill people can absolutely succeed in life and grow into wonderful human beings. You are a prime example of that because when me and others watched your videos and interviews, your behaviours seemed normal, and you made it very far in life and grew to become an amazing person. 

I am no psychologist or a clinically diagnosed patient, but you should  leverage your mental illness not by exploiting the kindness of others, but by understanding it fully and using it to overcome countless obstacles, and working diligently towards your goals. Mental illness is not an impediment, but a limitation that can be overcome and sometimes an asset. This is something that must be comprehended by not only you, but your family, your friends and other members of your community.

Author: @peptobisman45
Content:
I realized I too am autistic about few months ago, now working on getting a proper diagnosis (it’s very expensive and I don’t have that type of money to spend tbh). 

Truly, I never even considered it for myself as I had such a pinpoint idea of what autism is and I wasn’t that (needing to stim a lot, being in your own world, not socializing in a neurotypical way, having meltdowns over things that seem small). 

I only really considered it for myself after a close friend of mine with diagnosed autism asked me if I had ever looked into getting an assessment done. At the time, I didn’t think much of doing an online evaluation because I truly thought I would get the result of not autistic. But after completing the cat-q, Aspie Quiz and the many free online evaluations I realized that I should probably seriously look into it. Every single evaluation I have done has came up with a positive for autism result (and I’ve been doing these evaluations over the course of 8 months, so even if my life is changing, the test results still stay the same). 

I too wonder why no one had told me sooner or got me assessed sooner. I would assume because the people around me also have that very pinpoint idea of what autism is. I do have memories of my elementary school teachers being a bit concerned and they did mention autism though usually went brushed off and rejected. Now after speaking with my parents about it more, they can understand a bit more why I am how I am a bit. 

I honestly am so relieved to know that I’m most likely autistic because it just makes everything about my life make so much more sense. I have sensory issues, I have social issues, I need structure and I work in a creative industry. I also got very specific interests that will end up wasting all of my time 😅. 

Usually I tend to get hate for the various things that I am. An example would be that I would get harassed for being queer by strangers on the street. At the time I was still figuring out my sexuality and wasn’t even presenting as anything other than straight man, yet somehow it was just clocked. I had a former boss of mine truly asking me if I was the not so nice word for autistic because of how I worked and interacted with my coworkers (also this was 1.5 years before I even started looking into me possibly being autistic). So I guess my common trend is, the bullies in my life honestly were correct in their assumptions (still shitty people though). 

It’s honestly a bit refreshing to hear that you (Sean) are also coming forward and saying you’re autistic. It’s refreshing in the way that you’re showing your audience that every autistic person and their experience is different yet similar. It allows people to understand that it’s not such a set in stone you must have debilitating symptoms of autism to be autistic. Autistic people can thrive with the right measures in place. Like at the end of the day, it’s just acceptance and accommodation. 



Also side note, my “pinpoint idea of what autism is” makes me laugh a bit because I’m all of those things I listed and didn’t even realize until I read over my comment just now. I’ve literally been stimming this whole time on autopilot, I used to truly just live within my own world until I realized that I had to conform and well I’ll just say, my social skills have been improving but they’re definitely not where they should be if I’m neurotypical, and yes I have some big emotional reactions to seemingly very small very nothing things (and very much no reaction to actual big and scary life events). Love to be self aware on a day like today amIright 🙃

Author: @batbratsdesigns
Content: I was diagnosed with autism in my 30s and I already was diagnosed with ADHD when I was a kid. My IQ is 200 and above because of my unique brain. I am very focused on certain things until I am an expert on the subject. At the same time I lose interest in things quickly if it's not a challenge. I can communicate well too but I can't read facial expressions so I have to read body language and lips. My senses are off the charts too and painful, my hearing is like a cat but I can't process speech. I can tell if someone is honest with me just by being in the same area with them. Also, I never played with kids in my youth, I hung out with my elders and learned how to cook and crochet. I have savant syndrome too so I have abilities that are natural for me like drawing and writing poetry. Everyone is different. Autism is a spectrum and not an illness. We are born uniquely autistic. I feel like a Gothic unicorn like human being, because I don't fit in one group I can fit in any group because I am kind and I understand a lot of things. Each of us have unique skills and disabilities. I understand how you feel. I knew I was different but I didn't expect autism but my mom and stepdad knew. They were excited for me to finally get the right diagnosis. My healthcare is better now and I have a legal guardian who takes care of me for life and I have in home assistance so I can live on my own. I am now 43 years old and I am proudly autistic. The reason it's good to get diagnosed is to get the right treatment for your unique needs. Autism can be painful with happiness in between. We are very sensitive people. Our immune systems don't work so well either, it's part of being autistic. Wheezing and lungs whistling while having asthma attacks. I recently got the right asthma treatment and I am on lots of inhalers and a stupid breathing machine. All because I was born uniquely autistic. I'm a walking mucus factory with an IQ higher than 0.1 present in society. That's like being a ghost that's not quite dead but still I'm pounding on the post and everyone is watching. I twitch and wobble when I walk because my brain has issues communicating to my legs too. I don't like attention but I accept it because I have a duty to my fellow autistic people to be a voice for the voiceless. I once was mute myself and now I can speak because of support and education in speech therapy and deep cognitive therapy. I don't take medication anymore because it doesn't help me, counseling helps me so when I need it I can request it from my doctor. I am happy for you, because you found yourself after you were in the dark for so long. I know it feels amazing and the release is great. Everything makes sense now. The pressure has been lifted. 😊❤ Welcome to the other side where everything is just right for your unique needs. This is how autism should be. We are the teachers of society too because we can speak for ourselves and people are ignorant and need to understand what we are so we all can live in peace and harmony.

Author: @venanreviews
Content:
My problem with diagnosis of autism and adhd is it implies a label that separates an idea of normalcy for the decision making processes of your mind. It's given a negative cannotation as a mental "illness" when a majority of the associated patterns are VERY common in everyone. "If you have autism you likely have ADHD", this feels like an umbrella in general as if to say your thought process being different means it's corelated to yet another "illness". "You likely have depression and anxiety", this compounds that because especially these days... who DOESN'T have depression or some form of anxiety due to the state of the world or one's country? "You likely have intestinal issues" also feels vague and happens to everyone as they age. "Hypermobility and joint issues", again... with age this comes too. Asthma feels a little out of place to label with that but I don't have enough knowledge to say anything more. The point of this rant is that you could be diagnosed one day under the consideration of your current mood and feelings, the current state of your mind with the anxiety of not meeting deadlines or being able to pay rent, with the depression that comes from losing a loved one, with the physical restraints that comes with age, and you qualify to be labeled as something people see as "inferior".

If we're ever going to evolve as a society and be comfortable being open about subjects like this, we need to stop labeling people and "sorting" these labels. We're segregating ourselves a little too easily these days. You can be "different" without being autistic, you can be "normal" with autism, and you can have all these symptoms without a label.

All that said, I agree with jack. As much as I don't like how easily it is to be labeled these days, it's only beneficial to understand yourself and each other better. It's like with depression, you can't just get rid of it, it's something you learn to deal with over time but you won't know how to deal with it until it's addressed. Learn about yourself, learn about your fellow man, become better by knowing better.

Author: @LeoVGaming
Content:
Not a subscriber, No hate against you, but just never watched your content despite your content aligning with some others that I frequently watch when I'm not hyper researching random shit. Will subscribe due to this video though. Not promising I'll watch, but that's because of my attention span more than anything. I was diagnosed officially with Autism late last year and ADHD this year and it wasn't even a thing I had been considering due to some unfortunate conditioning I had been given younger about being strong enough to fix my shit without asking for help, or therapy or really anything other than internalizing it. It was... A shock, not in a bad way really. Just hilarious how doing the assesment was like... ah, yes... mhm, yep. nope, that makes perfect sense. The shock was knowing that the vast majority of my life I had been hiding behind a mask, doing what I needed to to fit in and doing it so damn well that I kind of lost a sense of self for a really long time. Autism gave me a reason for alot of things in my life. A base point to start from to work on things. An opportunity to change not only what needed to change, but what I WANTED to change. Not just what others wanted me to.

I have been... Presented with people who already knew I was (very good friends of mine and new ones), coworkers who told me I should keep quiet about it and not talk about it (to which I told them to mind their own business and I'll talk about something I'm proud of all I want), to people who either straight up deny it because I seem to *normal* (jokes on them anytime I have an opportunity to unmask around them) to people who downplay it and tell me autism is overdiagnosed, to people who ask if this means I'm going to start using excuses for why I can't do some things certain ways (which quite frankly is the most insulting discussion to have with someone. As if I'm not good enough to meet midway like you would any other person and it's me who has to sacrifice to meet your expectations at the detriment to my mental health).

I just wanted to say that I felt this strongly, The video just randomly played while I was listening to DnD lore dives on the history and creatures of the forgotten realms, while playing Hardspace Ship breaker (a game that is literally geared to be a logic orient, task driven autistic persons wet dream), and I appreciate that you spoke up the sides of autism that people don't see, like the unwarranted hate and just negative behavior.

I appreciate that you used your platform to hopefully, even if it's just one or two, help people change their perspective on things a bit.

<3 Appreciate you my dude.

Author: @Sweet.peach21
Content: I’ve been going back n forth for a while now trying to figure out what’s different about me and everyone around me says I have autism, but I guess I’ve always mentally struggled to accept that definition because I’ve never felt like I’m not “autistic enough”. For a long time I’ve flipped through BPD (borderline personality disorder), OCD, CPTSD, or psychopathy just because of the way I think, especially the whole “analyzing ppl” thing. But what you said about how you communicate (bc Ive always felt that I can’t be autistic bc of the way I communicate) is exactly how I feel. I’ve been called multitudes of positive names for how i interact with others (“personable”, “understanding”, “logical”, “animated”, “engaging” etc etc), and while I know that I am, it’s always felt like a game to me almost, or like I’m working constantly at having ppl like me. My fiancé says I’m a people pleaser, and he’s right, but part of what I enjoy is the analysis. It’s like playing a more detailed, intricate version of the Sims where I’m trying to get full friendship with anyone I converse with 😂 yet it almost feels manipulative because I’m “picking the best dialogue options”. I’m still being me, I’m not afraid to disagree with others, but I can edit, cut, wittle down, soften, strengthen etc etc anything I’m saying to fit that person best. Constantly, the filter never stops. And I thought that’s what everyone did, until I was told by multiple people (neurodivergent but not autistic) that no, thats a me thing. So that’s when I started considering autism. Anyways, all this to say, Thank you Sean, this just helped me understand and accept myself a lil better :)

Author: @molkwi9077
Content:
As someone who diagnosed with ADHD and OCD (and I also show a fair few autistic traits) recently, I must say, it's true that it changes nothing about how I (or anyone else who gets a diagnosis) am and/or will be. Now, I know why I am a certain way, why I struggled where others didn't, and excelled in domains others couldn't keep up with. It only gives you answers, and explains and encapsulates all those long lists of mysterious differences you have, compared to other people. It doesn't change anything about me, except that now, if someone thinks I act "weird", I can explain to them that I have these conditions. I will never use them as an excuse, but I will use them as explanation, to ensure that people around me, friends, family, strangers, just anyone can understand that my brain is different, and I can't do anything to change it to fit with the norm. It brought me peace of mind, in a way, to finally get confirmation on my doubts. Having a doctor tell me this: "You, without the shadow of a doubt, have ADHD and OCD, and it's a right miracle you managed to make it so far in your life without struggling too much, not only shows that you are extremely intelligent, but also shows how much you can adapt to situations that wouldn't necessarily accommodate you." It's so liberating to be able to put words on why I struggled so much, and watched people surpass me despite me being considered a gifted kid in elementary school. The diagnosis only confirmed my doubts and suspicions, and now makes it a lot clearer, as I now have access to more resources and help, that I would have needed a long time ago, but am only getting now. 

If you also notice that you are different, or struggled with some things that others had no issues with, if at any point in your life you genuinely thought that you may have a certain condition, look it up, read about, listen to people talk about their experience with it, and once you're sure you found it, you can go see a psychiatrist, and maybe even a doctor later on, and maybe confirm your doubts, get answers, and the help you need and deserve.

Anyways, Jack, all the strength and love in the world go to you, I believe I speak for everyone when I say that we are happy you got answers and that you can get to know yourself better, because that is usually a huge relief, understanding ourselves better :)

Always remember, Average =/= normality, or total.
It's a number that compiles data, but not everyone is analyzed.

Author: @PikaCheeks
Content:
At first I didn't think I had anything but I always related to ADHD things but I always just thought I was just undisciplined and was the kind of person who thought ADHD was an excuse for bad and undisciplined behaviour.

A friend of mine who has ADHD and has been able to suspect who has ADHD or not suggested I might have ADHD. I didn't brush him off but I did consider it at that point.

It was until I started my new job for Data Entry where at first I loved the job and I still do but for some reason the more I worked there the more I felt like I was getting so bored it was driving me nuts. But I like Data Entry and I like my workplace, so what was wrong? I felt like had to drink a Coffee, Energy Drink and Can of Soft Drink in order to get by the day to do any important task. I felt like I constantly had to find a new song to play on repeat or find a new video to listen to just keep my mind preoccupied, all of that stuff is finite and it was affecting how I was at work. I was underperforming at my job but I knew I was good at typing, I know what I need to do and I know I am good at it but I just couldn't do it.

I finally decided to get diagnosed for ADHD but I had to wait for 6 months! Each day felt daunting, it was getting worse and worse for me.

I finally got diagnosed last month and yeah. The Psychiatrist at first thought I might have Autism but then the more I told my anecdote he decided it was just ADHD in th end.

I have always been great at connecting things to other things, via shared themes and etc or listening to one song and picking up that it sounds very similar to another song and it turns out they are, I just hear it, when I try showing it to other people they just think I'm crazy at first but the more I explain and show them they always end up saying "OOOOOH! Now I hear it!". 

I do video editing and I take a decent amount of pride in it and I am able to tell when a frame lasts abit too long or not down to the single frame @ 60fps even.

I like structure and being organized but I always end up falling through on them. It's either I'm totally organized or I'm a total mess.

At this point I think I may be a little autistic, so it's probs more correct for me to be AuADHD.

If you think you have ADHD I recommend getting a professional diagnosis because knowing already helps so much because you are not alone and it is not your fault. Knowing already is like 80% of the battle!

Content:
I grew up with autism since young, was non-verbal and slow at learning things for most of my kindergarten age until I received diagnosis of autism at age 6 and received speech therapy treatment after that diagnosis.

I definitely had a lot of obstacles that I overcame over the entirety of my life, both academically and socially facing with stereotypes.

Currently, I am a university student pursuing cybersecurity in one of the most prestigious universities in the world. I thought initially, i would never make it to university but I just didn't give up and did very well in college to get into one of the most well-known universities in Singapore. I have been enjoying watching your videos since the start of your YouTube channel and it's great that you decided to come out with a condition like autism.

Content:
Honestly, doesn't seem too surprising since ADHD and autism can go hand in hand for some folks, I've been wanting to eventually get screened for both myself and I've been putting it off lol. I'm so glad they're both better understood now than they were when I was a kid, my parents and teachers suspected I had aspergers since I was in preschool, I mean hell, I remember my parents talking about it when I was like 4 or 5 and I thought they were saying I was "artistic" XDDD, but my mom didn't get me screened because she feared special ed would hold me back. The clocking people easily thing, I feel that, hell I kinda like that about me because it makes giving people Christmas gifts way easier lol, but yeah it can also lead to anxiety when I attempt to find things to talk about to them.

Damn, I wrote a freakin' novel here but all this being said, I'm glad you're talking about this, I'm glad more public figures are talking about autism and adhd. We've come a long way since even 2012. I still remember hearing people talking about how Tim Burton was possibly autistic and why and as a 17 going on 18 year old back then, that's what got me wondering about myself over the years.

Author: @JustinMogollon199
Content: Well said Jack! You are definitely not alone. I have autism as well. Had it since I existed, and it is not that bad. There are different types of autism depending on different people. There is low functioning autism where people act crazy, struggle with speaking and processing, need the most help out of everyone. And then there are people like me who have high functioning autism, which means we can speak and think well, we don't need people to hold our hand (at least, not 24/7), and we are able to accomplish things with no problem. And I have accomplished a lot. I accomplished things that not only people like me couldn't, but also things that "normal" people could not (the reason I quoted normal is because let's face it, there's no such thing as being normal. It is just a social construct used by people to make themselves superior to others). You mentioned the symptoms of autism. I am autistic, but I don't have ADHD, I am not depressed nor have anxiety (complete opposite. I am happy and enthusiastic and I am a very calm and collected person), I don't have intestinal issues, I don't have hypermobility or joint issues, and I don't have asthma. Of course, I am different from others. You also mentioned that when you were the school, you weren't a popular guy. I on the other hand am every where I go. Because of my personality, hard work, passion, and talent. I am very popular for the right and wrong reasons (right because people are inspired by me and impressed with what I do and want to be like me. wrong because they want to use me for their own personal gain, like I am an ATM machine. Like, some expect me to carry them to victory). And there is nothing wrong with admitting that you are autistic. When someone asks me if I have autism, there are 2 different sides. One side is where my Mom and other people are like "Dude, what the fuck? Why would you ask that? What is wrong with you?". But when someone asks me that, I am like "Yes." All they are asking is if I am autistic. Asking someone if they are autistic is like asking if someone is black, white, citizen, immigrant, man, woman, basic things. It is completely normal, and it is a conversation that should be normalized. Now if someone were to ask me if I am retarded, stupid, or offensive stuff like that, then that's when it becomes a problem. By admitting that you are autistic and stuff like that, you are being honest to the world and accepting who you are. You are accepting you have this. Having autism doesn't make someone a different person. How people are is not determined by race, gender, nationality, or disabilities. It is the character, personality, the type of person someone is. No matter what we are, we are all individuals with a purpose in life and we strive for a better world. I have admitted multiple times on my channel that I am autistic, and I am not ashamed of that. I am embracing who I am, and I know that whether or not I have it, I am a hardworking and passionate person willing to inspire people, make people happy, and to make our world a better place. And I will continue to do that for as long as I live. I always take the "dis" in disabilities and replace it with "pro". I am proud of who I am, and you all should be proud of who you are.

Author: @YouveBeenMegged
Content:
This is definitely relatable as an autistic person who’s becoming more sure by the day that I’ve also got ADHD.
I was first diagnosed as a toddler, and so I grew up relatively familiar with how my brain works and what it means for me. But then, I’ve always had other issues that became more apparent as I got older, that I wasn’t sure autism really explained. Biggest one: I was convinced for _ages_ that I was just lazy, because I have huge issues with just sitting down and making myself _do_ things. But, recently, I’ve seen a few videos that talk about why people with ADHD might have this problem, and the way they described it just had me going “Wait… HOLY SHIT THAT’S IT, SOMEONE PUT IT INTO WORDS”. And  then the comment sections of those videos are full of people describing their experiences and I just go “Wait that has an explanation too?!” And then there’s my sister, who is actually diagnosed with ADHD (and who also thinks I should get evaluated). I looked through the written test-thing she had as part of the evaluation, and I was like “wait a damn minute.” So, not 100% sure and a bit nervous to self-diagnose, but it would definitely explain a lot.

Anyway, I could keep going on about that, but my point here is that diagnosis really can help you understand yourself, and go easier on yourself, just like you said. Welcome to the club, Jack!

One of us
One of us

Author: @c.a.5782
Content:
As the President & CEO of a mental health organization that provides psychological testing and mental health support to the Hampton Roads community, I want to say how truly proud and inspired I am by your journey. Getting tested and receiving a diagnosis is such a brave and empowering step. It’s amazing to finally have that clarity and to begin learning ways to navigate life with those insights.

Having observed you over the years, I could see certain traits that suggested autism, especially after you shared your ADHD diagnosis. The behaviors you’ve mentioned reflect a lot of learned social patterns, and they’re part of what makes you uniquely you. Honestly, when I read your announcement, I thought, “Well, of course—that makes perfect sense.” But more importantly, it doesn’t define you; it just adds depth to the amazing person you already are.

I’ve always believed that with mental health challenges often come extraordinary gifts. As someone who was also diagnosed with ADHD later in life, I can relate to those moments of discovery and the blend of challenges and strengths. For me, hypersensitivity—especially to odors—has been both a gift and a curse. In fact, it’s become a bit of a fun quirk where people challenge me to taste things and guess the ingredients. These traits may feel overwhelming at times, but they’re also what make us special and connected to the world in unique ways.

Thank you for sharing your story—it’s such a reminder of the beauty of embracing who we truly are. You truly are inspiring others to take the path to self-discovery and acceptance of who they are.

Author: @xxmelody777
Content:
Oh my gosh! I was diagnosed with Autism by doctors at around age 4. I'll be turning 30 this January. But I never actually knew about it until I was a young adult.
(I'm sorry if its long! I appreciate anyone who reads it regardless!)🌻 :) 

 I think I asked my father about Autism and if I was ever diagnosed(since I was researching mental health several years back, and was curious). Apparently, he kept it from me for a while because he was afraid I would see myself differently, in a bad way. He was going to tell me right around the time I asked him, when I was more mature and understanding. When I was diagnosed as a child, some adults at the daycare at the time, (and other adults) were suggesting my parents to put me in special school. My father was very furious about it because he wanted me to learn like all the other kids at school and to not be treated differently. He wanted me to succeed in life, have a good career one day, get married and whatnot. But yes, I guess for me I would call it closure and a sense of "Everything makes sense now!" Just hit me when I found out my diagnosis.

  I've been struggling with my mental health for the longest time. I was never good at socializing with others and its made it really difficult for me in my personal life and at work at one point. I would usually repeat myself often and get very fixated in things. I dealt with panick attacks and mental breakdowns at one point and its made it hard for me to maintain a job. I recently got diagnosed with Anxiety and PTSD. I have a feeling I might have ADHD but I would want an actual diagnosis later in the future. But that definitely changed alot of things in my life. This is why I now try to do things that help my mental health like listening to chill music and wearing noise cancelling headphones in public when I start to feel overwhelmed. 🌱
  I enjoy drawing, gaming and watching Youtube. I usually end up watching your videos which make my day! 🌸 I can't believe one of my favorite youtubers has Autism. I do agree talking about it and having awareness(in anything really!) is super helpful! 🌟
I appreciate you talking about mental health and I admire what you do especially with raising money for thankmas! 🎄Hopefully, I can donate even if its a very small amount this year. 😄

If anyone has read this far... give yourself a pat on the back!! 👏🏻🎉 I hope putting my experience on here can help others too. :)

Anyways, I hope everyone's journey through life goes well! 🙏🏻 Stay cool! 👍🏻Remember, don't forget to be yourself!! 🦄🌈💖🐥🐭🌸✨✨
Keep being awesome dude!! 😎

Author: @hideous_taco_michael_zacki
Content: Everyone has autism these days😂. It's a trend amongst doctors to diagnose it. I'm a son of a medical specialist and I can tell you this much- there's this thing called "hyperdiagnostics" or "overdiagnosis". Basically when there's some "new" or "trendy" or "fancy" disease and doctors become obsessed with it and they start seeing it everywhere, jumping to conclusions even without sufficient evidence, and start diagnosing people with it left and right. Of course, in most cases it turns out to be a false diagnose and people become victims of a "medical trend". We know this because this has happened before, many times in the history of medicine. Famous examples are: schizophrenia, clinical depression, ADHD, chronical prostatitis, and even bizarrely- Cancer. I'd wager that more than 50% of modern "autistic people" are overdiagnosed. So don't lose hope yet- you might NOT actually be one. Yes, this is a thing, doctors are not machines and they are also susceptible to trends, and sadly- they make mistakes ALL THE TIME. This is the biggest delusion people have about medicine- thinking that it's precise, that is not true at all. As my mother loves to joke- "Medicine is the third most precise science in the world... After Religion and Fortune-telling"🤣. You start to understand this the more you learn about it.

Author: @Tarrabyte
Content:
With 30M subs, I don't you'll read this but I grew up in special ed my entire life and one of the most annoying things about it is that here in the south if you are considered to have any type of mental disorder you were basically considered the r word. I've struggled getting diagnosed with autism because of money. I don't have  $1,500 to get tested unless there's another place that I can do it cheaper or free. I've always feared it because growing up in Georgia, it has (if always been) perceived as somebody that has to be looked down upon.

 Let's face it, in a good bit of society if you tell somebody that you have autism you'll be seen as slow, stupid, you don't understand things, the list goes on. I don't want that to happen to me but at the same time a lot of people also assume that if you're autistic you're like Sheldon and you're super smart and you understand; it's a double edged sword and you don't want to be treated that way. You don't want to be the guy that people are constantly coming to you and asking you 8 million questions because you know the subject but you know how stupid some people are and you don't want to deal with that. 

Growing up I've always been one of the smarter kids in my class because I didn't really have to try and I'm not saying that I'm a genius it's that I didn't really have to try too hard because I actually paid attention and I know what I was doing. The teachers liked me but I struggled with paying attention. 
Everyone wants to be autistic now and it pisses me off. I hate that everyone wants to be seen as "quirky" so it must mean they have Autism. Just because you have a hobby doesn't mean that you're autistic. It means that you have a hobby, that you enjoy painting or music or building computers. There's no reason why somebody is autistic just for a hobby. That's what pisses me off. 

When I think of mental disorder I'm not saying that I think of somebody that is erratic and belongs in a mental hospital or somebody that's in special ed. Being that there were people in regular Ed in school who are medicated and they did just fine. sadly, I was in the extreme side of it even though I didn't need to be because anybody that's seen any of my videos will tell you the same thing there is no reason for you to be in special needs if you are pretty mundane in society. 

But regardless of all that, it sort of pisses me off cuz I never thought that we'd get to a point in society where everybody wants to be considered autistic and I swear to God everybody does and if you aren't autistic and you've never been diagnosed by a doctor with testing and everything, which can take anywhere between 3 days to 5 days because I've looked into it, (I was about to get done till I realized it cost money) most people that are saying they're autistic probably aren't diagnosed. But anybody that's reading this comment if you haven't been diagnosed by a doctor, please don't claim that you're something that you aren't because it does seriously piss people like me off. You have no idea what you're talking about.

Content:
Thanks for sharing your story. I recently am going through this process after a medical practitioner let me know that I meet many of the signs of neurodivergence. For years I have struggled with depression, anxiety and social situations and it can get so frustrating. I felt like myself and those around me wonder why after years of therapy I wasn’t getting any better. I felt weird and frustrated that my mind couldn’t just get better. The sensory things that you spoke about, yessss! I’ve got a nose so strong it drives people crazy and am asked if I’m pregnant haha. 

I get what you mean when you say having the diagnosis doesn’t change you, it just helps you feel like you understand more about yourself and like you can be more kind to yourself. I feel like going through this and potentially finding out I have neurodivergence might allow me to not feel guilty for ‘not just getting over it’, instead finding peace within myself. 

Thanks for sharing, and yes, let’s talk more about mental health, disability and 
 neurodivergence, as it no longer has to be this negative or scary thing. Instead we need to speak about it to realise how many of us actually have things that are part of our daily life and make us who we are. 

Take care on your journey ❤

Author: @crowblin
Content:
Before I yap I want to say congratulations on your diagnosis. It makes me very happy that a public figure such as yourself can be open about this and help to de-stigmatize it.  

As someone who has Autism and ADHD (AuDHD as it's informally called), I do agree there is A LOT of overlap, but they are definitely NOT the same disorder. I've learned how to identify which behaviors of mine stem from Autism and which stem from ADHD. Like you, I was diagnosed with ADHD first (as a child) and then diagnosed with Autism much later (earlier this year) and I've also had the same problem with finding medications that work for treating my symptoms. Regular ADHD meds didn't work. But I'm on a new medication called Cymbalta (generic: Duloxetine) which is an SNRI (serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor) instead of an SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor). I'm hoping that it'll have a similar effect as the non-stimulant ADHD medication known as Strattera  (which is an NRI) while also treating my depression + anxiety. Fingers crossed.

Author: @hannahshaffer3745
Content: I was very fortunate to have been diagnosed with autism when I was 3 years old and grew up with resources and a support system to help me succeed in life. I used to be so ashamed of my diagnosis because I wanted to be like everyone else and fit in, but now that I am an adult, I love to talk about my autism and don't mind not fitting into the idea of being "normal." I also have been educating myself more on my diagnosis to help me understand who I am. I am so glad that more people talk about this because it is so important to understand and I love that you decided to come on the internet to be a part of the conversation and to help people see that autism isn't something scary or negative. I like to see that being diagnosed with autism doesn't change who you are as a person, it means that you can understand yourself a little bit better. You are still you but with an answer to a question you couldn't answer before! Thank you for coming into the conversation, you have no idea how much this means to me! Now I am a bigger fan of yours!

Little fun fact super mini infodump: Sean is saying this because they have a lot of very similar symptoms (ex: stimming, sensory processing difficulties, and communication), and as such can be hard to distinguish in oneself if you have both. This affects like a shit ton of people, because ADHD and Autism have a HUUUUUGE comorbidity rate (aka, most people have both than just one). Highest I’ve seen is 80% correlation but there’s a range. That being said, they are indeed 2 separate disorders, and you can indeed only have one. It’s just significantly less common, especially if you’re looking past formal diagnoses. :P

Author: @winter8748
Content:
As a student of clinical psychology and who is currently studying child psychopathology, i really think the dsm needs to be revised and the criteria for diagnosis should be revaluated. i say this because autism is not always characterized with inability to socialize or repetitive movements. it involves a lot of masking and a difference of symptom manifestation. not to mention, the primary criteria for diagnosis is 'if it causes any dysfunction to their lives.' the truth is an individual may mask their dysfunctions, blame themselves and force themselves to act a certain way while simultaneously effecting their mental health. not to mention alot of the standards of ethics need to be revaluated aswell such as making therapy a very formal thing. 
p.s a psychological assessment or evaluation is nothing to be scared off. it can sometimes be a very interesting and insightful experience. also one of the reasons why an assessment may take long to get back to you is because the scoring or analysis of a test is a very standardized procedure. not to mention, its a manual process, as in you need to do it by hand, computer software's are not used for it and above all, it is a tedious and meticulous process because the results will effect their life. sometimes psychologists may ask for multiple assessments to make sure they are not wrong. anyway i hope this gets a conversation flowing and helps someone :)

Author: @CiaranShade
Content:
From one autistic person to another, thank you so much for this video. I'm 35 now, but I was diagnosed at 18/19. Masking is hardcore exhausting, and the sensory issues are REAL (a lot of it is hearing stuff for me - electricity, fluorescent lights, etc.). 

I'd also like to point out that one of the reasons functioning labels aren't useful is because autism can be on a sliding scale even within an individual. Most of the time, people can look at me and not even know I'm neurodivergent. They might think I'm, at most, a bit quirky or eccentric. But, other times, when I've been masking for a long time and things are really weighing on me and the anxiety/depression get really bad, you might look at me and go, "Wow, yeah, that person is autistic." At my worst, I do go nonverbal under extreme stress, my stims become way more obvious, and you can absolutely forget any semblance of eye contact. (Honestly, among other things, watching your videos has helped me have something to focus on at some of those rough points - put on my headphones, focus on the cool, funny Irish guy playing video games, and laugh/be scared/feel emotions that aren't "life is overwhelming and I can't handle it.")

Anyways, sorry, this comment is getting kind of long. I just want to thank you again and send you the feeling of a warm hug. Welcome to the family, although you've been here all along.

Much love to you, Evelien, and BB!

Author: @AemesIsMe
Content:
Heck yes to this video! Finally no tiptoeing. No weirdness to autism. A lot of the times the “I have ADHD” was for some reason not bad, but “I have autism” is like ew or something. 

The positive look on “you have autism” is also I had. I am now a 27 year old woman, got diagnosed when I was around 24 because my whole life I was under constant stress and my body at some point was like: “now I will give you more clear body signals like constant nausea and sensitivity to back pain and wrist pain cause you are not listening to me!” So I started to reach out after my mom was like: please go to a doctor for it.

I will skip the rest of the details ( cause I was in depression ), but please I ask of you, if you feel like something is off… don’t give up if one person denies it but you still feel off. When they diagnosed me with autism and explained certain things to me (like Jack said, certain ways the brain and body perceives and processes things is different from the neurotypical way), it clicked and with medication (to help process things better) I feel so much better. Obviously meds don’t solve everything, but it’s a start.

Another thing (which may not be in every country), but there are people who are caretakers who can help you in your life making things clear, giving you rhythm, help to make things more clear and guide you. 

Last thing as a tip I got which helped me start and work on myself: it’s important to start by yourself, to love yourself and care for yourself before you can take on challenges or help others. 

Hope this helps <3

Author: @SaruCharmed
Content: Damn... I've suspected for a while I have adhd or autism or both. I didn't know that it often came with physical symptoms like intestinal issues, asthma, and joint issues... I've had a lot of anxiety and depression throughout my life, especially in my early life, and a lot of intestinal issues, especially now. I don't have asthma often but if I try to run for more than a couple minutes I'll be wheezing for half an hour. I was also super flexible as a kid (my parents called me double jointed but I don't think I'm truly double jointed) and I have a lot of joint and tension issues as an adult. I have also heard that a higher percentage of queer people tend to be nd and I am that as well. I was a really weird kid and always felt like an outsider. I preferred to read at recess instead of playing outside. I was way ahead of my class in everything even though I often didn't pay attention. But now as an adult it feels like I'm lagging behind others. But I've also become a lot more social. I often struggle to find the energy to do even things that I want to do and are fun to me, like playing video games or making art. I also have been really good at reading other people throughout my life which was a very necessary skill because I had a highly volatile, unpredictable, abusive stepfather. I want to get tested so I can finally confidently put a name to what I'm experiencing, but I haven't gotten around to it yet...

For three, this happens with today's most over diagnosed conditions.

Compare A: Hoeg Law had a stroke. The first thing he did was spend months doing intense physiotherapy for recovery. In the meantime, his wife updated his clients and audience. Then, after having taken the appropriate measures, and when able, he did a retrospective retelling of the events, noting how this changed his behavior, and how he'll proceed towards recovery in the future.
Compare B: Timothy Cain told an anecdote about a cashier who was ignorant of his colorblindness, and was confused at his question about the color of a button. He didn't tell this to celebrate an unserious thing, but to show it's a recurring matter-of-fact problem he deals with.

0:20 I didn't know because I'm not in a position to know, like engaging with the many forms of the subject for long periods of time, like a researcher or doctor. And pathologizing normal behaviors is cringe.

It's very much how I've experienced my diagnosis through the years as well. And like you said. Being able to be less harsh on yourself as well with this new information. I don't think people realize how valuable it is. How much. Of a RELIEF it can be, to learn that. It wasn't your fault. So, so often. It means so much. Representation matters. You're like me, and I think you're cool. So. Maybe I can think I'm cool someday too :)

I never thought I'd have kids art in my life because I don't want kids myself, but now I have a canvas from a previous client who said "it's you and me Teacher JJ! " when he pointed at the scribble of pencil and crayon on the canvas.

Author: @TheEmchu
Content:
A couple things I've learned overtime as someone with undiagnosed Autism (COVID was bad when I could afford to get testing so they weren't testing and now I don't have insurance @-@) ...

Apparently rolling your eyes isn't doing a full circle? It's looking up?

Other people don't like when you're too honest? Like not mean, but telling them the full honest answer to something, it's weird.

I still don't understand the answer "it's fine" to a question of me asking if you want me to do something. Does it mean it's fine go ahead or it's fine don't worry about it? So I always have to ask for clarity, and it's okay to do that. Sometimes things need a bit more communication.

Masking is very exhausting, and not good for you! HOWEVER I think a lot of us do it without thinking and I do it a lot because I don't feel safe (that's the closest word I can find for that) with some people.

I didn't realize that people can put socks on and they don't have to move it so it's perfect (I can't have knee socks right at my knees has to be lower or higher, the part where the toes goes needs to be a certain way)

Also with sensory issues I've learned several things. It seems that everyone has different ways that help them. Weighted blankets, dark rooms, silence, grounding techniques, earplugs (they have some that change how the sound hits your ear hair so it's less stimulation, and not necessarily blocking sound out), stimming, and all sorts of stuff. 

Fun facts: Normal people have a thing that sort of turns off senses when they do stuff (for example if you are leaning on a table with your hand and doing something else you stop focusing on that hand so much) with over stimulation that decides to not work so your body is literally over loading itself.


Panic attacks do not happen for a reason they are due to your brain going into fight or flight and refusing to stop! (thanks brain!)  Anxiety attacks tend to happen due to outside forces like something that happened that day or month.

I think that's about all I have in my noggin (of course I could be wrong about some stuff but I tried)

OH Please neurotypicals stop treating us like kids too. I don't know how many times it's happened to me. I understand everyone has different needs and someone may need to be treated that way, but please don't assume. @-@

Author: @BelindaShort
Content:
I also was tested and I'm so glad you were able to. It's so unattainable by so many adults here, because as a child you get a lot of resources but as an adult you have to pay out of pocket (for me it's yearly) for re-evaluation for the PTSD part of it, but you're looking at 2K or far more for doctors to do the testing.

Most insurance does NOT cover it for adults and when you have one that does, the doctors don't take it.

It's fucking awful.

And yeah, it's wild how many things have comorbidity. The EDS, Asthma, GI problems, hypersensitivity, all of it.

And I am SO glad more people are okay with the diagnosis, it used to be treated like some kind of death notice, when now giving a name to it and knowing that there may not be a lot of treatments, but you can figure out how the best way to live your life is.

When you're young you can't really control your environment and that makes it super hard too.

Lastly- I'm not sure why they didn't test you for this at the same time as the ADHD. A neuropsychologist usually will do both at the same time.

Author: @baileylawrence3927
Content: ADHD is not the same as autism. I have both. they are both neurodevelopmental disorders, yes. But simply put, ADHD is a dopamine deficiency, and autism is not. Though they present similarly on the outside in few occasions, they are still very different in many many different ways. I am happy he was able to find out this about himself because I know how hard it is to not have a name for the behaviors we have to grow up with, but please remember to not talk about it like this when you don't fully understand. Congratulations man, it's going to be really rough from here on figuring out things about yourself that you didn't know related to your autism. It's going to feel like your entire life was a lie but understanding yourself and taking off your mask will be so much better in the long run. I wish you the best of luck, please do more research into these disorders tho. 💚

Author: @shanoodle42
Content:
Hell YES. I fucking love that you want to use the platform to make good, genuine, and amazing change. Spot on with this video. We're a fun group :) Hello! 
I was so relieved after getting my ADHD diagnosis. It felt like "Yeah, this 100% makes sense". My interest in psychology, astrology, human design, neurology... likely were all ways I was trying to make sense of myself and the world around me. Everything felt so alien, so foreign, I didn't (and still don't) understand why certain aspects of society are the way they are. I wish I could say, in a group, "My social battery just died. This music is overstimulating and I no longer wish to be here, thanks for hanging out, I'm leaving." and then...leave, and have it be cool. Why can't that be more socially acceptable? (Well, to be fair, we're working on it, it's getting a bit better I think!) 

I really do think we can change. Us, as a whole, but it takes time, and awareness, as well as empathy, compassion, education, acceptance, and the fact that you are out here truly wanting and actually DOING to make those changes happen is incredible. I'm so thankful. 

One of us, one of us, one of us! We add another to our ranks.

Author: @TCWpower
Content:
I don't think it's an important "diagnosis" if you're going to a therapist specifically for the purpose of getting a diagnosis to find out more about yourself. As far as I'm aware, at least in the US, every therapist taking insurance must diagnose a patient for insurance purposes, so if you used insurance, the therapist may have forced the diagnosis to appeal to your insurance. If by chance you were diagnosed without insurance and the therapist truly put genuine thought into this diagnosis, they likely thought you are barely further along the spectrum than any other "normal/neurotypical" person and they thought to mention these concepts that may be helpful to you --- or anyone. Everyone is different, everyone is quirky. If it is not intruding upon your daily functionality, and in a way that physically,  mentally, or emotionally holds you back from succeeding in the game of life, then the diagnosis itself is not important.

 -and to be clear, I mean the title of the diagnosis, not the information, and you likely do not need traditional treatment; unless you are toning down the severity in your explanation. love the idea of normalizing mental health issues and making them aware to others, having those conversations without guilt or stress of judgment, but forcing the title of a mental health disparity upon yourself does not make it true or authentic. It does make you seem bold, transparent, and perhaps working towards an agenda. - which is seems you have, as you say you want males to be more open about weakness, care less about legacy, and generate funding for your charity. 

It's lovely that people in the comments are happy to accept this, and that's because they love you, likely not because you are suffering from Autism. 

Also a couple other things, liking video games does not put you on the spectrum, so many, millions of people age 30+ still play video games. Observing body language is certainly not an aspect of Autism, probably the opposite. Maybe thinking you can figure people out in 5 minutes is Autistic, because that sort of cocky attitude will hold you back from truly understanding people at a deeper level. Use of comedy in conversation often comes from coping with negative interactions with others and a feeling of desired inclusion, maybe even having been bullied. - that could be related, perhaps, but also sometimes people are just awful at a young age due to ignorance and naivety. Texture and sensory issues could be traits of Autism...

But I wonder why consider yourself Autistic if you may only be like, "5% Autistic"; its like saying I'm a Movie Director because I took a Single Film analysis course in college. The reason why I bothered to type all this, and I don't mind hate or judgment or to be ignored and lost in the comments, is because you, with money, cut the line for people who need assistance more than you. You're in your mid 30s and have coped however you have all you life. You're doing fine. You don't need to place yourself into the shoes of victimhood. If you're unwell mentally, I feel for you. It also discredits those who truly are irritated by their dispositions each day, whether they are strong and happy with their life or not. You wouldn't say you're a war veteran if you stubbed your toe on the kitchen chair because you experienced pain. Therapy could help, always, working things out in a sophisticated and organized manner, and so can a solid social group around you. A title does not do much, it's everything else but the title that matters. 

I think if you did this video, but did not diving so deep into the title of being Autistic, this would have been a beautiful thing, because I feel normalizing this topic is a very good thing. In my opinion, it seems like finding purpose could be beneficial to you. It's a really difficult thing to do. It takes courage and exploration. Simply fabricating purpose by attaching a title to yourself is not the answer. If you're doing charities, that could be an amazing purpose and helping people could be enough.

Author: @theawkwardartist12
Content:
Welcome to the AuDHD family, Sean :) 

I wanted to pop in real quick to make a little correction at the beginning of the video. ADHD and autism are NOT the same thing. They do share some traits due to executive functioning issues, but otherwise, they contradict each other.

The biggest differences are that autism needs routine, familiarity, and order while ADHD needs variety, newness, and functions well in chaos. The social differences are not the same either.

These disorders are highly co-occuring but they are not the same. The reason why many think they are no different is usually because of this high co-occurence with 80% of autistics having ADHD, and there is a lot of misinformation on ADHD traits due to many of these people having undiagnosed autism. 

Hope this helps and again, welcome to the family!! /pos

Author: @PotterFreak22
Content:
I’m a wordvomit commenter so I am sorry but not sorry.
A good analogy or metaphor I came up with for getting a diagnosis is that, you’re told to hold this really heavy bucket of water from the get go as a kid and you grow up accommodating for that bucket in everything you do. Decades pass and suddenly someone empties the bucket of water then tells you to function with that now for the rest of your life.
How are you supposed to that when you’ve LITERALLY SPENT YOURE ENTIRE LIFE with the heavy bucket of water, get used to the feeling, get used to having it around all the time and living your life with it. THATS the part I continue to be stuck on every day.
A good Dr that I’ve seen that has the ADHD/Autism/etc diagnoses once said that being neurodivergent is like “trying to run Windows on a Mac or a Linux. It just doesn’t work or make sense!” and I’ve always had that in my head since then. Being neurodivergent is like you’re running on a COMPLETELY different system than everyone is and it’s SUPER HARD to understand people sometimes! And to get them to understand you even just a little! That’s why I use a lot of metaphors, analogies etc to help people understand what I’m trying to say. I find that helps more than not most of the time.
Unfortunately there are still going to be people who refuse to accept you as you are now, refuse to even try to understand you and will be downright mean, hateful and rude because they don’t want to take the time to try and understand so they just blame you for everything or try to make you feel like there’s something wrong with you when there really isn’t. I had that experience at a previous job. The manager was totally fine with hiring me, being friendly and nice to me, until they found I was autistic because I had had a complete autistic shutdown the week before from overstimulation. Author: @MicrowavedAlastair5390
Content:
Sir, as a person on the spectrum, this surprises me none. I'm verbal, though somewhat less social. I also have a laundry list of things that happen with my body that I describe as a medical comedy.

Why would I never say anything? I don't have the same capacity to sort people into the same categories that a lot of other people do. This is the also part of the reason I'm not quite capable of wrapping my head around discrimination- Everyone is just people to me. People prove themselves through their actions towards me, not through arbitrary categories. The other reason is trauma. Can't discriminate if your brain thinks EVERYTHING is a threat, including, but not limited to:  people, sudden noises, fireworks five miles away, and my own damn shadow.

There's also a fun conversation to have about "person on the spectrum" vs. "person with autism" vs. "autistic person" vs "autistic".  I personally prefer the first because it is person-first without implying a struggle. I don't struggle with autism. The more accurate description is that other people struggle with me because I am on the spectrum. It does ultimately come down to a matter of preference though- pick whatever feels right in the moment.

In any case, it's good to have people come out and talk about it.

3:30 YEP! I have all of those too Sean! The anxiety and depression got diagnosed first, I’ve always had asthma, the joint issues didn’t show up until late 2018, I just got diagnosed late last year/earlier this year with level 1 EDS hypermobility and then the Autism diagnosis was the icing on the cupcake. This whole time over the last 20 years have felt like doing a puzzle but you’re only given one piece at a time and you have NO IDEA what the puzzle even looks like!

I do that. I don’t like that either. Yes, I’m very picky like that.” and so on thru the whole movie! I told my mom and my sister I thought I was autistic and they both just said “Yeah we know” like it wasn’t a big surprise to them. Certainly was for me!
Then trying to find an adult testing center that didn’t cost thousands of dollars to get an appointment took a very long time. We didn’t find one until my psychiatrist recommended a place last year after we brought up wanting to get tested but not being able to find a place. So we went to the place and they were extremely helpful, very nice, the testing was easy enough for us, filling out some medical history/social history/early life history my mom had to fill out, a few in person appointments and boom! Autism.
I’m still not sure how I’m supposed to feel about that or how I’m supposed to function now as an autistic person. I still mask heavily but not as all front facing and intense masking as I used to growing up, going thru puberty, having all these mental health challenges, which is good for me I’ve been told.

Author: @PotterFreak22
Content:
0:40 That is the masking front of autism. Making people think you’re totally normal just like them! Pretty much EVERY neurodivergent person I know has spent time figuring how to “be normal” by studying neurotypical behavior and learning how to do that all the time, for years and even decades in my case at least. I guess it’s a defense mechanism of our brains to protect ourselves from being bullied, being shamed, feeling threatened by other people. And trying to crack that mask is and will be the toughest time for all of us. It’s like trying to crack at cement with a tiny pickaxe some days, other times, you’re able to get a huge chunk out and you can finally show your real self! But sometimes your brain says “No, we’re still too scared to show our real selves” and slowly starts filling in that hole in the mask. The real task is to just keep chipping away at that mask, one day at a time, and to know when to stop and take a break.
2:16 Oh yes! That was EXACTLY me growing up in the 90s! In a super small town that only cared about farming and football, mental healthcare was non existent, you didn’t talk about that even with other family members, you just kept it all to yourself and pretended to be normal. I was the child who was always in the “fantasy” section of our elementary school library reading about Dracula, the Wolfman, the Mummy, the Loch Ness monster, the Creature from the Black Lagoon, the Invisible Man! Anything I could get my hands on I would read over and over again! Video games were a HUGE staple growing up and we played ALL THE TIME! Of course, my parents set limits on how much we could play before we had to go outside and play or do homework or go read a book. Internet WAS NOT A THING growing up so it was either games, books, cartoons, movies. I was also the kid that got shunned by every other kid because I was “too weird” for them and even had friends that I thought were friends stop being friends with me because their other friends didn’t like me! Growing up knowing you’re different than everyone else but not knowing why was really hard on my brain and I tried for ages to be more “normal” and try to be whatever anyone else wanted just to have a friend. 9 out 10 times it never worked, I’d get tossed to the side like garbage once the person who was supposed to be my friend got whatever they wanted from me. Be that money, Pokémon or YuGiOh cards, pens, whatever. I changed myself so many times that I didn’t even know who I was anymore! Which just made things worse.

My mom never had the perception you did, unfortunately. Autism was just a word for her. The only time she used it was when it suited her narrative. Like when she called the police on me because I would get mad at her for being dismissive. That led me in a mental hospital more times than I can count. The hypocrisy was the constant and strongest factor.

At seventeen, my mom dropped me off at my dad and stepmom's porch, just like that. My weekend visits with them haven't been the best when I was five all the way to fourteen. They were dealing with personal issues at the time. My mom forbid me from seeing them and once again, she suited narratives only for her of how my dad wasn't there for me and how my stepmom was just as bad because of her skin color. I haven't seen them in three years. I didn't know how they would react to seeing me again. I was so scared. 

I knocked on their door, my dad answered and was confused. She didn't even tell them about dropping me off their porch. It wouldn't take long for him to let me in. My stepmom was just as confused. I would explain to them what happened. After a lot of consideration, they took me in. They gave me all the care my life needed. I got food on the table, a roof over my head, clothes on my back, access to education, and most importantly, guidance. Here I am nineteen years old who graduated high school while recently getting my first job at retail. I would never be in this position without them.

On behalf of the people who have this diagnosis, thank you.

Author: @dafroakie9984
Content:
Yo Sean, as an autistic person it’s great to hear you figuring out this part of yourself, and doing so with the mindset of breaking negative stigmatism. However, I did want to add that if you’re looking to present this in a non-negative light, I’d recommend switching to identity-first language. Some people will say they “have autism” because they don’t want it to define them, however the majority of autistic people prefer to be called just that: autistic. The truth is that autism is, by definition, an inseparable part of us that defines who we are and how we think at a fundamental level. By describing it as having autism, it paints it as something like a disease, something that can be cured. This notion is the driving force of many harmful organizations like Autism Speaks and anti-vax conspiracy freaks. 

In short, the best next step to take towards normalizing autism is to use identity-first language. We do not have autism because we are never without it.

Author: @LordInvictus-yt
Content:
The argument that autism is overdiagnosed is compelling and grounded in significant changes to diagnostic criteria and increased awareness, rather than a genuine rise in prevalence. The broadening of the autism spectrum has resulted in more individuals being classified as autistic. Research shows that changes in diagnostic practices account for a substantial portion of the increase in diagnoses since the 1980s, indicating that many cases now labeled as autism were previously classified differently or not diagnosed at all.

Furthermore, autism diagnosis is based on consensus among mental health professionals rather than objective neurological testing. The criteria in the DSM are established through a voting process and lack direct neurological evidence. This reliance on observed behaviors and reported symptoms can lead to subjective interpretations that vary widely among practitioners.

As a result, the diagnosis of autism is inherently culturally informed. Behaviors deemed indicative of autism can differ significantly across cultures, leading to inconsistencies in diagnosis rates. This cultural influence strongly supports the assertion that many cases are overdiagnosed, as what is considered atypical behavior in one culture may be regarded as normal in another.

I struggle with socializing, paying attention, having energy and motivation to do tasks, easily overstimulated, not knowing how to react in certain situations, my diet is weird/repetitive, I like some routine and some chaos. My niece is diagnosed. I've self diagnosed myself AuDHD and self diagnosis is valid. It's nice to know that despite the problems of the healthcare system across the pond that adult autism is more widely recognized. We have programs here that help children function more normally but not much support for adults unless severe needing constant care.

Author: @necroarcanistxiii
Content: I was diagnosed with Asperger's Syndrome at the age of 5, my partner was diagnosed with ADHD, we're both 26 now. We have a lot of traits that are obviously those conditions, but we found that a lot of our traits that our diagnoses didn't explain, could be explained if we also had the other diagnosis, so I'm trying to get a reassessment to see if there's more to it, but it sucks as I live in a more rural area, and it's a 2 hour drive to the closest facility where I can talk to a professional. I don't drive, and am crippled with social anxiety, executive dysfunction (decision paralysis), and chronic procrastination, due to how severely I was bullied as a kid. I was doing great when I was holding down a job, but when the circumstances changed, and my physical health took a few hits post-COVID, I mentally regressed partially and still cannot keep up with my day to day tasks. They say the longer you take to get diagnosed makes it harder to come to terms with yourself, and that's true, my mother was diagnosed at the same time that I was, and a lot of it clicked for her. But also, I wasn't provided a lot of the support I should have been during my school years and so a lot of things people can just go and do seem foreign to me, it's like I'm playing a game but wasn't given the tutorial, and I'm just trying to figure out the controls with a controller with joystick drift and buttons that stick and don't always do what I want them to, so I'm masking and pretending like I'm normal, which lasts until I open my mouth and go on a hyperfixated rant, like how I'm posting this now. Then you've got all the sensory issues, which often activates my fight-or-flight due to my past bullying having practically primed that response towards fight, so I have a short fuse toward stress, and I can get aggressive rapidly. My fuse can't just deplete once I take a second to calm down, it just slowly regenerates, and a lot of small annoyances can burn it faster than a single large disaster. It can be really brutal trying to cope with my self-depression, self-loathing etc, when I'm having an emotional week. Thank god for my partner, they've really helped me over the last 15 months or so we've been together, and I've been there for them just the same. It's good that we've found each other, we bring out the best in each other.

Content:
I am also ADHD and an extrovert despite very slightly being on the spectrum. I am quite socially conscious and resist a lot of my autistic tendencies. My major symptoms of ADHD/autism is that I get pretty obsessed with ideas, subjects, or anything of the sort. I don’t love trains and sonic though. 😂 If I’m not careful I can be pretty annoying.

ADHD has less of a stigma associated with it, so sometimes I casually mention it. Most people are surprised when I say I’m not just ADHD, but I am also on the spectrum.

We are not alone. Many celebrities have come out autistic too including some of the richest men throughout history. I’ve come to be proud of parts of my autistic nature that I believe have helped me succeed in some areas of my life such as science, music, and a wide variety of talents.
