Author: @Love_tastic2
Content:
Just wanted to say, thank you so much for this video. 

Your point about spreading awareness is what I was really hoping for out of you.

I’ve been watching you since I’m young, I had friends that liked markiplier more, but I felt like I couldn’t connect with him. But seeing you and your videos, the raw energy, just made me feel at home. I was diagnosed with adhd at 11 and asd at 13, and just like you I was so happy with the autism diagnosis. I was bullied and socially isolated because I was different and I bragged about it thinking that people would be kinder to me. (They weren’t hahaha). And after being loud about being autistic, and still being harassed, I shut myself down, and became quiet. And the bullying stopped. Except, I became my own bully. I hate myself because I’m autistic. I hate that part of me. And my generation (gen z) is some of the most ableist assholes to exist, because they’re aware, they know how to make someone’s life hell and get away with it, and to gaslight the persons experience. And seeing my childhood fave YouTuber admit and talk about being autistic, it fills me with such warmth. The fact someone with such a large reach is openly having this conversation that has NEEDED to be spoken about for so long, I appreciate so goddamned much you have no idea.

The funny thing is as I grew up and became less hyperactive, you in your videos kinda matched that. I mean I’ll be 17 in a month which is crazy to think about, especially since I’ve been watching you since I was like, idk 8 or 9? I knew you had audhd, but I didn’t want to say anything about it because telling someone they’re autistic, from experience, doesn’t get a good reaction, especially when you’re not a doctor. (As well as the fact I knew you’d never see my comment lmfaoooo.) Btw I know you’re your own person behind the screen, so I’m not saying I know you. But the fact that I had someone to look up to, who was giving the same energy out in the world. And people liked it!? It genuinely gave me hope. It’s nice seeing someone who seems so ‘normal’ to most ppl talking about it, normalising it. 

Autism isn’t this scary thing, it’s not like we think and feel any different. We’re still people! Getting diagnosed doesn’t mean you’re suddenly different. And I think that’s why people think so little of autistic people. They don’t see that we’re just like them. And with new technology and research on females with asd, they kinda realised that so many men and women are autistic than originally thought. So the reality is, the amount of autistic people to neurotypical people is actually pretty similar, it’s just so many people aren’t diagnosed. And because of stigma, people won’t get diagnosed because people treat us with the diagnosis differently. But if more people who aren’t stereotypical get diagnosed, and spread the truth of what it means to be autistic, then maybe society will realise that we aren’t so different.

So thank you Sean, you have such a great impact on this world, and on me. Even if you only changed a few peoples ideas of what autism is, then that’s still a step forward. Keep doing what you love, and again thank you so much. ❤❤❤❤

Author: @TwoCentReview
Content:
I’m glad that he got tested and I’m honored that he shared it with us. He really didn’t have to, but him sharing will encourage others to get tested and learn more about themselves and live better lives. It’s always a good thing to know more about yourself.

I’m Autistic, as well. It helped me a lot to get diagnosed in second grade, because I could make adjustments and figure out how to work with my weaknesses and strengths. What happens with me is that I’m very focused on certain interests and I have sensitivity to sound. I have no sound filter, so I can’t ignore sounds and I can’t really “zero in” on things in certain things like conversations. I’ve learned to tell people that I “have weird hearing” and they usually accommodate. I learned that saying “bad hearing” would make them think that I’m partially deaf, which is sort of the opposite of what I have going on.

Jack has a great attitude about this and I know that this has helped a lot of people feel seen and reassured that they can find a place to learn and thrive.

Thanks so much, Jack.


(Also, I feel like Gawr Gura is definitely on the spectrum and I know that I’m not the only one)

(And Chibidoki. I know that these are probably the two easiest ones to talk about, but it says a lot that I can vibe with Chibidoki’s chaotic energy, while I usually can’t keep up with that kind of stuff. See also, dancing dinosaur and her milk shake story. Fair warning, the milkshake story is very inappropriate and devastating.)

Thank you. Thank you Thank you thank you. I can't fully express just how much this matters. The community is so tired having to advocate for itself when we are constantly being discriminated against and silenced, or the general public is fed an extremely unrealistic and unhealthy narrative that autism is a "disease" or immediately equals "stupid" and "an overly sensitive special snowflake". It's extremely important our voices are heard, both high masking and low masking, AND those who have other conditions intertwined like intellectual disabilities.  

Please keep being yourself, and do what makes you happy. We love you :)

Author: @Jamie-is5rm
Content:
As a fellow 'tism creature, the "I like trains" at the begining was a beautiful touch xDD You already have the autism jokes down to a T xD
*ONE OF US!*

Okay but seriously THANK YOU for talking about this, because as a low-need high-masking "high-functioning" autistic person (ew I hate the functioning labels), I also get coments like "But you seem so social!" "You don't seem autistic" and it's SO FRUSTRATING!!! The comments I got the most when I was younger, because I have really bad sensory issues when it comes to food (like it's REALLY BAD, I can pretty much only eat bread and cheese. Getting protein in my diet is very difficult!!!). But whenever I told people about my sensory issues, they would make comments like "Oh you're just a picky eater" and try to give me cook books to try to help me. Like, dude, do you think my parents didn't try EVERYTHING to try to help me with food? Do you think we haven't tried this before? It's so frustrating! This Thanksgiving, I even got a snarky comment about my sensory issues from a family member of mine, implying that I just don't like eating green stuff and only like eating things that are white. 

Also like, this might sound really dumb, but I have what I call 'Internalized Ablism" - I validate other people a lot when it comes to their disabilities but when it comes to my own struggles, I get really hard on myself. And that's coming from someone whose been diagnosed for roughly ten years lol. So hearing you talk about your experience and how similar it is to mine helps a lot.  It's oddly reasurring and help me to validate my own experience, you know?

Thank you for sharing your experience because it needs to be normalized and humanized and VALIDATED. And I will vouch what Sean said - if any of you are thinking of getting tested and you have the finances and resources to do so, I highly recommend it. It will help you understand yourself so much, regardless of whether or not you are autistic.

PS: Also you are so right that about the connection between neurodivergancy and content creation. That is a theory I've had for years.

Author: @kierstenmills8377
Content:
Why are you telling my life story for me 😂 the process you shared about going through and leading up to your diagnosis is more or less what I went through to get mine. Diagnosed in 2019 with adhd, meds didn't really do anything, eventually I just kind of gave up on them cause they made me feel gross more than they helped. Brought it up to my psychiatrist (who was helping me through my recent BPD diagnosis as well) and asked out of curiosity how accurate the raads-r test was, as a friend had suggested I take it and I scored quite high. She looked into it, found that it's 99% accurate in diagnosing autism, and 100% accurate in disproving it. A couple of other tests and she's confident that I'm autistic. And like you said, it doesn't actually change anything, it doesn't have some massive turning point in life where everything will be different now. But knowing what's going on makes it easier to adapt to living with it. Now that you know what obstacles are formed because of autism, you can find better ways to get around them. I feel like a lot of people, especially neurotypicals, see a diagnosis like this as a bad thing, but I find it freeing in a way. Making the changes I need to in order to make life slightly better or easier has done so much for my mental health, and I sincerely hope it does the same for you!!

On that note, I sent a screenshot of the video title to my friend with a shocked Pikachu meme because you're one of us and we probably should have told you sooner since we all knew 😂😂😂

Author: @timothygooding9544
Content:
about the part of forgiving problems you've identified about yourself because they are part of neurodivergence

To many it can sound like its using the condition as an excuse, but instead its approaching those problems in a different way.
If you identify that "x" problem is, yes, a problem you want to change, it becomes easier to also say "this is part of my condition, directly taking it out is not what will solve it, I will instead take into account that I am prone to this and strategize around it."

Realizing some of the symptoms I have are not because I wasnt caring enough or was lazy, and that they will just pop up from time to time gave me the frame of mind to adjust my life around them and make actual change in months that hadnt happened in years.

Not formally diagnosed, but exploring the symptoms of neurodivergence and the ways people strategize around their own symptoms has been a major boon in my life

As autism and adhd get more wide as spectrums and even combine, its important to remember that the labels we use are a useful shorthand, not the full picture like describing a bacteria.

Content:
Lol as someone with ASD/Asperger this does not surprise me at all.
I was actually extremely social as well before you know life kicks you in the balls for being too kind and innocent.
Though I'd like to say that I have somewhat recovered despite being relatively more introverted still, one of my qualities is still conversation and verbal intelligence. Autism mostly just means I have Disharmonic IQ profile so I have like an IQ of 90 in somethings and an IQ of 140 or 180 in others so you're always being over or under estimated your whole life in every school system or anywhere really and additionally my Brain just works on "Autism logic" (which is obviously much more logical than all you typical brained people lol) though because of the Asperger part, I do at least have the ability to adapt pretty well at the expensive of "more energy drain" which is not even an option for a lot of other people with ASD, so obviously I'm thankful for that.
To be clear it doesn't make me less autistic, I'm just able to actively "translate" "normal people speak to autism speak for myself and translate my own autism thoughts into normal people speak" as you can imagine that takes it's toll on your "processor" though and it doesn't help I already have a chronic headache regardless.

To be clear ADHD or Dyslexia are not the same thing as Autism they are just in the same spectrum, so they give your brain an increased chance of probably running on Autism.exe it's like... idfk, if you have a smartphone that is function and price over form it's statistically more likely to run on Android than on iOS.
That's a bad example but I couldn't think of anything better right now, you get the point it's correlation not causation. 

But I guess for fun here's my list:
Autism: Yes
ADHD: No
Depression: Managed
Anxiety: Not really
Intestinal issues: HELL YEAH (Wheat and Lactose in particular but much more in reality)
Hyper Mobility: Not really a little

Bonus DLC:
Chronic Headache: Yes

Lucid Dreaming: Yes

9:40 the sensory thing is real though, partially I think for me this is also because I miss one of my senses (balance) which makes me more reliant on sight.

9:58 No I just "stop smelling" at that point no issue there, though when it comes to foods I am a 100 times worse not only do I have a better taste than most (not as a brag it's mostly annoying) I am also indeed very sensitive to texture and that can absolutely ruin food for me. Author: @taxiboi2523
Content:
this is a good video overall but for a video thats supposed to be shedding light on a misunderstood and often stigmatized condition such as autism it really sucks to see it perpetuate negative stereotypes about another condition, albeit, i presume, and hope, unintentionally.

at 6:05 jack compares the idea of Legacy to Egotism and Narcissism. for those unaware, "narcissism" refers to the name of a certain mental condition known as Narcissistic Personality Disorder or NPD.

npd is a condition heavily associated with trauma, though has a genetic factor, and is not something that can be "cured" or "fixed", nor is it something that should need to be

and it is heavily stigmatized, to the point where certain groups claim that narcissists are inherently abusive, despite the fact that people with npd, like other trauma survivors and nuerodivergent people, are statistically more likely to be (repeated) victims of abuse than to become abusers themselves.

npd is a condition that can make people seem "egotistical" from an outside perspective, (depending on the presentation), but in reality these traits stem from a lack of self worth and a need to feel appreciated or respected by others.

i find that its similar to the dopamine theory of adhd, which suggests that people with adhd dont produce as much/ a proportional amount of dopamine as nuerotypical people do, which makes completing hard tasks less fulfilling on their own than doing a bunch of quick and easy tasks.

similarly people with npd dont create as strong of an internal sense of self worth on their own as egotypical (people without personality disorders) do, and need outside confirmation in order to create it

though some people with npd may treat others poorly because of it, this is not inherent to the condition, rather usually a consequence of not having the right support system or the understanding to realize why they struggle regulating their self worth, or that that is the problem in the first place. 

and the stigmatization of NPD by society doesnt help, with people who would be helped by understanding they have npd and being offered the support they need being more likely to deny their condition because of the stigma, and those who otherwise live healthily with their npd feeling ostrasized and unwelcome from the rest if society.

even if you don't use the word "narcissist" with the intention to refer to people with npd, as the word does have a separate colloquial definition that predates the name of the disorder, it still causes harm. in the same way it is harmful to use "gay" or "autistic" as an insult, even though both words innitially had different definitions.

even though i know it certainly wasn't the intention, it really hurts seeing that kind of language used in this video, especially given the similarities in the linguistic history between NPD and Autism.

autism etymologically comes from latin auto: meaning self, and ism: signifying an action, practice, or state of being. and originally referred to an idea of "morbid self-absorption" . people who were too self obsessed within their own inner worlds that they were unable to connect to other people.

looking at the outward symptoms of autism, (especially the more explicit presentations) you could imagine how this idea came to be. 

sensitivities to certain sounds, textures, foods, can seem petty, that of someone who needs everything to go their way. 
nonverbality (or semiverbality) without any physical cause for their inability to speak can seem rude or spiteful. like its just a choice to not talk.
special interests appearing as someone too busy with their personal hobbies and obsessions rather than being communal or focusing on what they are "supposed" to.
from an outside perspective, without an understanding of the inner workings of the condition, people with autism may seem

 egotistical.

while egotism isnt the name of a mental disorder like narcissism is, i find it unhelpful to use it as an indicator of morality.

the thing about egotism is it is not an action. its a feeling. its a feeling that is not only harmless on its own, but important to have, and a big part of improving ones emotional health.
its self worth, self love, self respect, self absorption, whatever you want to call it. the ability to see value in oneself as a person.

some would say that egotism is only healthy in small amounts, but i find that a precarious idea at best. once again egotism is still just a feeling. egotism only becomes a problem when it is used as an excuse to hurt other people. when people say "because i have so much value other people deserve less than me"

but that goes for every emotion, there is nothing stopping someone with no ego from harming others to get what they want, and theres no amount of ego that necessitates someone to do harm.

and acting like there is hurts innocent people and ignores the actual problem.

i dont think theres anything wrong with wanting to have a legacy. being remembered after death is an important part of a lot of cultures and beliefs systems around the world. oral tradition, ancestry, ofrendas, folk tales, life lessons, advancing science, being a role model, an inspiration, a voice, helping people, making a difference, making the world a better place.

wanting a legacy is not bad on its own. egotistical sure, but thats not a bad thing. though i imagine most of the people jack was thinking about when he said this are the type of people who are willing to step on others in order to get that legacy.

but to have a legacy on its own doesn't mean you have to hurt others. and you, jacksepticeye, are proof of it. whether you like it or not you have built yourself a legacy, and for the most part, so far, its been a good one.

this type of misuse of the word narcissist isnt specific to sean here. it is something seen everywhere and as disheartening as it is most people dont even realize that NPD exists, nonetheless that what they say could be so harmful. its just that deeply ingrained into our culture most of us dont realize what we're saying.

so i don't think this language was used out of malice, i just hope that in the future, Jack, anyone else who may read this comment, and eventually everyone in the world, can do whats in their power to make ammends for past mistakes and to help make this world a better, more accepting place for nuerodivergent people of all kinds.

Yes, Sean... most of us were pretty sure you had Autism and were high masking. Nobody said anything because we assumed you knew (and it tends to be a personal thing). Content:
The PMA man himself! Wooo!

So happy to hear such a take on autism. It feels like the idea of it is so radical, either super smart or the opposite. I've had people react like I should be some genius or even apologize like, "I'm so sorry to hear that." Not to mention even weirder assumptions.

I've tried to explain that it's more like I'm like a computer somehow working with a different search-engine or a Playstation that's somehow got an Xbox controller plugged in. It's *weird* but all it means is that the configuration is a little different than usual. It doesn't mean I'm broken or helpless. Also doesn't mean I'm taking apart a radio and putting it back together. It's more complicated than smart or not.

The different aspects of Autism is less of a spectrum to me, and more akin to a massive tree. A network of branches and roots, two people with sensory issues will differ, one may be irritated by too much light, the other with too much sound, one branch splitting into 2 new branches. The third may not ever be irritated at all by sensory issues. A whole different branch. 
All connected to the trunk of "Autism" or neurodivergent-ness in general.


But I've found that people don't like complicated answers.

I don't know if this was a good comparison, but it's how I've come to see it.

Author: @therealbeyoungho
Content:
Hi Jack! I know you won't see this, but I just wanted to come on and say that I'm happy you could figure it out for yourself and get a diagnosis! Not many people are as open as you are, and I think it's amazing how open you are with mental health. I struggle with mental health, and I also struggle with toxic masculinity on myself, and while I definitely have a "man up" mentality, I agree that it's bs and being a real man isn't like Andrew Tate or any of those douchebags, it's people like you, people who are genuinely good people. 
Anyway, back to what I was originally saying... I'm medically recognized as having a dissociative disorder, specifically DID/OSDD, my therapist isn't quite sure which my symptoms match more, but either way I like to say that I have partial-dissociative identity disorder as I think the label fits my case best. People may know this diagnosis as "Multiple personality disorder" which is it's late term, now known as DID. I was diagnosed closer to 2 years ago now, and I've been doing so much work on myself. It was such a relieving feeling when my therapist pulled up the evaluation for DID, and I did some research into what it is, and everything clicked and the weight on my chest was gone, and I felt like I was no longer alone in this. 
I know how nice it feels to finally know what's up with your brain, and being so open about it is awesome! People come back me all the time when I occasionally mention I have DID, because they automatically think I'm faking it (courtesy of tiktok freaks) or they claim it's weird that I was only diagnosed once I saw a therapist who was specialized in these disorders (Not that weird. I saw her a year prior to opening up about symptoms, and it took a few sessions till she finally evaluated me for DID, but at first she thought it was just intrusive thoughts or anxiety, so it wasn't sudden whatsoever) And this really harmed me, even though they were just strangers on the internet that didn't know anything about me or my experience with having DID, but it hurt so much that I almost wanted to go into full denial and pretend like I don't have this disorder. Turns out, the reason my mind really gets into things, is because I may have OCD. I'm not diagnosed, but my therapist and I were talking about the possibility of me having OCD, and she evaluated me twice,  both came out highly likely, and she agreed that my symptoms align with OCD symptoms...however, she isn't focused on diagnosing it, and rather just treating my symptoms, so I guess I can say that I likely have OCD, which would explain why things like that happen. If someone says one little thing, my brains sets off into "panic" mode, words repeating in my head, and a full on plan made of pretending like everything isn't real, and that the random person who said something was completely right. 
So yeah, that's my mental health journey lol. It sucks. I have many issues, and I'm probably going to be in therapy for the next 20 years of my life, because it is what it is. Being open was very hard for me to do, and very scary, especially when I first started opening up about the DID symptoms I was experiencing, because I had no idea what they were, and I was afraid my therapist would tell me I have psychosis or schizophrenia, or that I looked insane, but she was very supportive and everything worked out amazing, and I feel so much more confident in myself now, and I'm becoming stronger as a person. I think some of you, or Jack, can relate to the relief of diagnosis, after wondering what the hell was going on for so long, and then everything clicks.

Content: There are some misconceptions here. Most of all, just because someone has symptoms of Autism doesn't mean they have Autism. Someone may be antisocial because that's the social behavior that was modelled for them growing up. That is a LEARNED behavior, not a neurotype. Some people have behaviors similar to Autism because of trauma they experienced growing up. That is acquired, not a neurotype. If you look at brain studies, ADHD and Autism are NOT the same. People make a lot of assumptions about Autism based on what they read online, but it's leading to misinformation.

Author: @only1one1me
Content:
Welcome to the club, man! One of us! One of us! This just confirms we really are just collecting some of the best people. Lol. I wasn't officially diagnosed until 2020, when I was 25. I suspected it since I was 18. 

I was diagnosed with ADHD in the first grade--though my teachers also suspected autism, but the doctors at the time reasoned I couldn't be autistic because I talked. A lot. When I was 16, I was diagnosed with anxiety and depression, and then finally autism at 25.  Got that Triple A with a D. I thought I escaped the gastrointestinal issues too, but alas, they hit me around age 28 (diagnosed with EoE). I've always been hypermobile as well. 
Getting diagnosed with autism was a relief. I'd always felt like an alien piloting a human meatsuit without a manual, and even though I didn't really know what was wrong when I was young, I was acutely aware something was. As a kid, I described it as an invisible wall between me and everyone else that I could see through but couldn't get around no matter how hard I tried. The harder I tried, the more damage it did to my emotional health, and I burned out in my 20's. I had to accept I was wired to be different and do feel/things differently, grieve the loss of the person I thought I could be if I just tried hard enough, and start doing things in a way that was kind to me. I can still do what everyone else can, for the most part. I just can't do it the same way, and that's okay.

Author: @Wilfoe
Content:
Welcome to the autism community! I haven't really watched you before. I didn't expect us to think so similarly! A lot of what you said in this video really resonated with me.

I was diagnosed with autism back in elementary school, sometime in the late 1990s. The superpowers are certainly fun. I've also been given eight misdiagnoses to date, all of which are associated with autism in some way. It's confusing all of the stigma that surrounds mental health, even in mental health systems, isn't it? Personally, I firmly believe my autism has helped me much more than it has hurt. I think Mom judges me for having it though...

Jack, no matter who you are or what you do, you will never please everybody. No matter what you do, there will always be people who like it and there will always be people who dislike it. There will always be people who like you and there will always be people who dislike you. That's the case with every single one of us. I figure that we all might as well just be ourselves. Outside of dangerous situations, it's never worth it to put on a mask and pretend to be somebody else to make other people happy. If you aren't your true self, the world is missing out on an incredible, unique human being who can do the things that only you can do. The number one regret people have on their death beds is that they weren't more true to themselves. I have no intention of having that regret and I don't think anybody else should have that regret either.

Author: @Dah_jeff
Content:
0:27 I hate it when people do this, since 
1. It throws shade onto autism 
2. They tend to act like they already know everything about autism. No you don’t. You should never EVER do this with any disorder, even the ones that seem like you already understand. ADHD? It doesn’t necessarily mean energetic, sometimes it can make people be extremely demotivated, lazy, and apathetic. Schizophrenia? It doesn’t necessarily mean that you have constant visual hallucinations, it can means that you occasionally start to hear voices telling you to follow an intrusive thought. Hell, even the very people who study autism (& the brain in general) haven’t figured it out entirely yet, so you should NEVER lock your definition of mental conditions to specific symptoms. If someone having a mental illness doesn’t make sense to you, try to figure out what is it that you’re missing, don’t just assume you’re right.
3. They’re doubting trained professionals, and implying that the doctors who diagnosed the condition can’t do their job properly. This ends up with me feeling offended for the doctor, especially if I got onto friendly terms with the doctor in question.
And there’s still a couple of other reasons that I’m too lazy to list.

Content: although i'm not involved in research in any capacity, i am a professional psychologist and work in the public healthcare in my country (brazil). i have an opinion about the apparent rise of autism diagnoses in the last years. first, yeah, there's the modification in the criteria. they are more inclusive than 20, 30 years ago. they are also more dimensional in their asessment, taking into account how prevalent the signs and symptoms are, instead of only checking if they are there or not. it is definitely good that more people who have issues in their day-to-day live, wether in work, school/college or social/family life are now being looked into and receiving the care they need. however, i worry about overdiagnosis, for a number of reasons. first, people who have difficulty on the daily lives may have those issues not simply because of something going on "inside" them, but because of things going on around them. working hours, internet and screen exposure, declining living standards, erosion of social security networks and community bonds, they all impact our health and behavior without being themselves medical issues. also, autism is not very well understood still. the diagnostical label includes such a variety of symptoms and levels of impairment that two people with wildly different needs receive the same  diagnosis (with the necessary notes to differentiate them, but, still it is the same icd / dsm code). i wonder for how long the diagnostic label will endure such variation in cases before it becomes too confusing and more of a hindrance than a useful tool. and there's the case of the causality. as of yet, it is not fully known, although some success has been observed in genetics research. how the relevant genes interact between themselves and with others during development, however, is something still to be observed, as far as i know. and it is possible that not all cases share the same basic causality (which would explain the different manifestations and strengthen the cause for different diagnostic labels). finally, catching up with the first reason i mentioned, i fear that, by treating individual cases, wether they are the result of overdiagnosis or not, we give only individual answers to questions that have an import social and political aspect to it. to be clear, it is innevitable to treat individuals individually, but those efforts should be organized having in mind a societal framework. if this fails to happen, i fear for a future of new, pathologic normalcy, where having trouble with living would be much more common place than in the past, and where the solution for it would be having medical treatment. again, i am completely positive for people having the treatment they need, but i fear for a future where having a diagnosis will be the the way people will avoid admiting that life is becoming shittier and shittier for most of humanity, and doing something about it. sorry for the bleak vision. good news are still good news

Author: @laurenbassett507
Content:
A little insight from a social worker graduate student for those who are curious:

That overlap is sometimes referred to as co-morbidity, co-occurance, or dual diagnosis. The DSM 5 (and I think the ICD 11) has sections that talk about common co-morbid conditions for each diagnosis. They also sometimes explain how to differentiate between diagnosies that have very similar symptoms and signs. There are also diagnostic trees that are used to figure out a possible diagnoses via symptoms.
Ultimately, all these manuals are very clear about them being guides and not absolutes. The patient, how they respond to treatment, and observation are really what confirms most mental health diagnoses. Some diagnoses also have months, or even years, long windows of symptoms as part of their criteria (usually there is a different and/or milder version of the diagnosis in this case that they are given first).
The purpose of a diagnosis is to help explain and guide treatment. It gives Mental Health professionals a place to start when trying to assist a client meet their psychological, and other basic, needs. It should never be used to pigeonhole someone into a 'role' or 'identity' that does not suit them. This usually causes more harm than good.
Ideally, when someone is diagnosed with multiple mental health disorders, they are examined and tested fully enough to fulfill the criteria for both conditions (otherwise, one condition would be used a symptom specifier for the other condition). Though for various reasons besides malice (like time contraints, funding, training, etc.), sometimes this isn't fully done.
So long as Sean feels like the diagnoses he's recieved are a fit and are helping him, then the diagnoses fit. I'm happy he seems to have found the answers to some questions about himself and his idiosyncrasies that he has been looking for. I hope the dual diagnosis will also open up better, or more focused, treatment options that will help him alleviate any symptoms that are bothering him.

Author: @felisconcolori
Content:
A lot of people who are older, from a time before autism was really acknowledged or a diagnosis, have developed different skills to successfully make it through a world that didn't know or didn't support such things. I've got masks for my masks and sometimes aren't sure what is a mask or what is real. I have not an autism diagnosis, although a psychiatrist I was seeing had suspicions.
I don't know that an official diagnosis would be helpful as I've already got tips and tricks to deal with many times where I'm not sure of the next step or didn't hear someone attempting to say something to me. Different periods of my life and choices I made have had a profound impact, and not all of that being good. I deliberately chose to get a job where I would meet hundreds to thousands of people in a month; after some upward mobility career-wise I found myself in a position where communication, small talk and interviewing, were the basis for much of what I did. I don't recommend trying to force yourself into change - but absolutely be aware of it and get help if you need to do so. I grew up in a "walk it off" era; it took 20+ years before I really reached out for help. If you need help, get it without setting excuses to avoid it.
Of course, with healthcare systems the way they are, that's a lot easier said than done.

Author: @Smittywerbenjegermanjensen
Content:
Low-high support needs is acceptable, but the Autism spectrum is radial, not linear. It’s not so much a matter of it being a matter of offending people, but it’s actually misleading to say mild-severe- most people would assume that someone who can’t speak has “severe” Autism, but they may function better in other areas than someone with “mild” Autism. Low-high support needs gives people a better idea of the question they probably want answered when they’re told that someone is Autistic. You can google an image of the radial Autism spectrum if you need a visual. 
Thanks for making this video! I’m very happy to see Autism becoming normalized so people aren’t making false assumptions based on their previous misconceptions about Autism as often as they used to. I often imagine what my life would have been like if I had been diagnosed as a kid and understood my brain better back then and I hope it’s getting better for kids today.

Author: @raelynvids
Content:
I was 40 when I figured out I was autistic and it quite literally turned my life upside down for a few months. I had more of this... sorta break down of HOW DID I NOT KNOW FOR 40 YEARS?! And I was more so felt like my parents had let me down because they were the type of boomers that would never had had me tested because autism had such a negative connotation when I was a child in the 80s. Females with autism were even more misunderstood then males at the time, so yea... they totally dropped the ball on that one. But it explains so much of my childhood and my way of interacting with people and I've realized just how much of my life was masking that it just became second nature. I've since done lots of research since then and realized HAD I been diagnosed, I would have been called AT THAT TIME a high functioning autistic which is probably why they just brushed off a lot of my "unusual" mannerisms and habits. It's why I kept to myself but could devour books and stories for months at a time. It's why I love reading and writing to this day and why I could spend literally hours excitedly sharing some hobby or fan-thing or another of mine. It's also why I have realized why some things bother me where they wouldn't bother other people - my high sense of justice and doing what's right and so much more. 

It's been almost 2 years and I'm STILL figuring things out, but I'm glad I know even if it feels like I have so much catching up to do.

Content:
The entire intro to this is exactly my experience when I started my journey on getting diagnosed with ADHD. And I also love figuring out what exactly is going on with me just like you, because it helps me understand the WHY and allows me to forgive myself and give myself grace. I still think I'm autistic but I haven't gotten into diagnosing that yet because I have other things I'm trying to focus on (currently going through a breakup... *the* breakup, the one that is destroying me).

I went through several different medications for ADHD myself. One worked-ish but gave me bad side effects, another did nothing AND gave me bad side effects, and adderall did absolutely nothing for me (even when I doubled the dose that my psychiatrist prescribed me). My biggest issues with ADHD are my motivation and energy. The medicine I take now that works for me is Vyvanse. It's the only thing that allows me to feel "awake", able to focus on work, and makes me feel able to do a task when I think of it (for the most part). It still doesn't feel "night and day" like the way I've heard other people experience either, but it helps me function, specifically at work. When I don't take it I can sleep all day and still be exhausted.

I'm happy that you found this out about yourself and I hope your journey brings you more answers and that you find medication that works. Don't give up! It takes a few tries and you may even need to find a new psychiatrist who can make a cocktail of meds that work best for you

Author: @giat1141
Content:
While we're on the topic of starting conversations about taboo topics! Lets open discussion about: meltdowns!

I feel like overall, people villainize these parts of autistic life. That or they use it as a "trap card" to prove "that you're not autistic"

Or they use it to justify treating autistic folk as lesser or infantilize them because "oh boo-hoo, poor baby heard too many sounds and is now throwing a temper tantrum" no. It's not a "temper tantrum", it's overstimulation. The world is literally too much and our nervous systems are going haywire as a consequence. It's not done out of a need for attention, it's done because we literally cannot hold it inside of ourselves.

In my personal experience, I have also had people think of me as selfish or violent because of my meltdowns, they have even compared me with S/A-ers because of them! And it hurt a whole lot because these were people I respected, proving to me that they do not respect me back. That they see me as a horrible goddam person, when I am just not that....

It is true, in the past I have allowed my meltdowns to cause actual real problems that could have been avoided, but I also didn't know any better at the time because nobody taught me any good ways of navigating them. It doesn't remove the things I did before but it also doesn't mean that people can hold me accountable for it for my entire life. Everything I learned about navigating my meltdowns safely, I learned on my own and I am still not done learning.

People also treat meltdowns as if it is only an inconvenience to them, like we are doing them out of malice, but its not true. Yeah, I broke a lamp in a meltdown, but in that same meltdown I hit my head repeatedly. It's not just the bystanders that are victims, it's also the autistic person who is currently going to an amount of mental turmoil that allistics will never be able to imagine.

Meltdowns are not fun, they are not quirky, they are painful and sometimes violent. But they are also a normal part of autistic life. And they are not in the person's control, do not villainize the person having a meltdown. Villainize the chain of events that caused the meltdown to begin with.

Thank you for listening to my ted talk

Author: @ReneSchickbauer
Content:
I'm autistic. Yes, it limits me in some ways, especially communicating with other people. But it also gives me the ability to have a razor sharp focus for many, many hours on end, blocking out everything else. For me, this is a superpower (of sorts) that i can use when designing and writing software.

I can only speak for me. But my life got considerably easier after my diagnosis, because i really started to accept who i am instead of trying to hide it. My social life is limited at best, but after my diagnosis i realized that the only reason i wanted to improve the situation is because other people expected me to have a "full" social life. Once i realized that i don't *feel* the need to socialize more but can instead live my life the way i want to, it was like a an elephant was lifted off my shoulders.

So i would recommend to just take life one day at a time and live it in a way that feels right for you.

Author: @leneaqgaming2755
Content:
I was diagnosed with Asperger’s Syndrome (which is now considered part of the Autism Spectrum) in middle school. Knowing how I’d react (because it was bad enough having PTSD from my first middle school), my parents didn’t tell me, I had to find out while we were getting ready to move at the end of my Junior year of High School. I was helping my mom in packing my parent’s room, and I found my medical file in the box of our important papers.

I was pretty upset, a military kid, constantly getting bullied (and in two cases, the assholes used the race card against ME when I tried defending myself, yet one of them did a racial gesture towards me on Cinco de Mayo), and barely passing my classes while others were almost getting into the Honor Roll. I hated myself even more than I did in middle school (borderline suicidal if I didn’t join JROTC in high school as a form of self help)

But, over the years after graduating, as I looked into it, I started understanding and accepting it. I was always a quiet child (the kind that gets bullied), preferring to play alone more than with friends. I like to stick to a routine, and got stressed at major changes. But even with these challenges, I have some friends that I care for, I have a YouTube channel playing games (even with double digit subscribers, I’m still proud of it), I voice act (and cowriting with one of my friends I voice for), and most importantly: I have a dog that I love like a daughter!

Author: @mceyebrows
Content: To anyone who may be thinking they have autism: Remember to not focus too hard on the results of test scores! They are generalized by commonalities. As an example, I (diagnosed as adult with ADD and Autism) did 2 tests at general psychiatry as a pre-evaluation before I was sent of to a neuropsychiatry who specializes. One showed no signs of autism, the other showed high signs. Your individual experience may not match up perfectly and you may not even be interpreting a question the same way that they do when "grading" which can throw it off. Don't be discouraged and focus on your life and how you feel!

I was diagnosed with Autism at 15 (my primary school suspected I had it but decided not to tell my parents) while they were doing my anxiety and depression testing. Along with the Anxiety, Depression and Autism I also have Asthma and Dyspraxia, so yeah its 'fun' but at 25 I'm used to it now even though I find it exhausting.
I am also "social" I guess in terms of I make eye contact, have normal conversations etc. Its just I don't like to seek out loads of socialisation because I find it tiring because like Jack I also mask a shit ton and constantly observe body language, tone of voice, look for inconsistencies, etc in both myself and others. 
Sensory wise I'm similar as well, the smell and texture of raw meat (walking past a butchers shop as a child was torture, could never go in so I would just stand outside gagging while I waited for my parents to finish in there), the smell of a lot of perfumes and deodorants smell awful to me and overpowering. The feeling of super fresh dry towels (hotel ones) when I get out the shower with pruney fingers makes me cringe. On top of that I am a super fussy eater (getting better as I get older but its like discovering I like 1 new food every 5 years) both taste wise and texture wise, and yeah just a load more sensory issues that make life difficult and always did growing up leading to some various traumatic memories that I'm slowly getting over.
I've never understood people not wanting to be diagnosed though or hiding their autism from others, but each to their own I guess. Anyway long story short thank you for the video Jack, its nice to have more representation for Autism that tends to fly under the radar generally

Content:
Let's face it. The term "Autism" is so broad, it doesn't have a lot of meaning anymore. The term now spans the symptoms of screaming and flailing in uncomfortable situations, to social nervousness. Like, I now know more people with autism than without. I'm still not convinced that (in a lot of cases, not all) we're not diagnosing a natural process of the mind. We aren't perfect. Our minds aren't supercomputers. Our minds are biological, evolutionary machines made to survive in a world we VERY MUCH don't live in anymore.

A lot of people who are diagnosed with autism? I'm not unconvinced they aren't just people with a strong focus or instinct that would have been fine in the natural world, but doesn't cope well in our modern one.

To be clear, I'm not trying to insult or belittle anyone here. I'm just saying the diagnosis for a lot of people seems to be more akin to diagnosing that someone has a non-dominant arm and calling it something. It isn't wrong, but it also isn't anything faulty. It's just the way most Humans are.

Author: @OnlyKarlos
Content:
I have autism too, diagnosed at 23.

I'd say it was quite the shock finding out but honestly I wasn't that surprised. I always felt like an outsider and that people didn't understand me or support me. I was picked on at school for being weird and a nerd, I had awful social anxiety and isolation in high school. I spent most of my life not being understood and not feeling loved because of it.

Only person that loved, cared about me and understood me hates me now, because I had depression and lacked the emotional maturity needed to make a relationship work and to support someone with what they're going with. Not having any support and being emotionally neglected all my life didn't give me much experience, but because of that relationship now I have a lot more anxiety and trust issues. I feel like the world's out to get me, and I have to pretend I'm neurotypical if I want to survive.

If you're reading this Sean, I'll tell you the most important thing I've learned about being autistic. You are loved, you are valid, you are different but different isn't bad. Everything that makes you unique makes you who are, and you are beautiful. Always remember that.

So... Watching this video has given me something to think about. I've been diagnosed ADHD at a young age, and it has held true forever. During my research I found two key points that didn't necessarily help my study but we're still impactfull enough for me to remember today. 1. ADHD commonly pairs with autism, 2. A large portion of trans individuals tend to be autistic/ADHD or a combination. I feel like I'm living evidence for the 2nd but I doubted the 1st initially. It was after watching Sean's video where he talked about being diagnosed with ADHD I felt suddenly more confident (for lack of better word) with my own self, he said plenty of things in that video that I very much so identified with like here is someone who knows the struggle of for example wanting to do so much but somehow being unable to bring yourself to do it. Knowing that imagine how I feel now after watching this video, once again Sean remains so incredibly relatable, and while I have questioned if I am AuDHD over the the past year and a half now I can confidently say I really want to get tested officially. Call it fate or coincidence, I prefer the latter, but just yesterday I received a call that my time on the mental health wait list is done and I have been scheduled to see a therapist. While I feel I've asked and answered a lot of questions about myself over the past year, this is now a very prevalent question.
I felt compelled to write this out of an emotional response. It's bold of me seeing I've never commented on a video before, but I guess it's my way of saying thank you, Sean, really. <3

Author: @albertosingsattimes
Content: I know I'll get a lot of hate for this, but we need to stop calling everyone either "autistic" or not. There needs to be more specific verbiage used. I think it's so harmful for people that genuinely struggle in a way that stops your functioning with society in a "normal" way from their autism to be considered the same as someone like jack. People like Jack still have the ability to socialize, and I understand that he has problems related to that and that maybe it's forced or unnatural and that he goes through hardships, but this needs to be distinguished heavily. You don't "have autism". You're on the spectrum. You do have mental health issues and it's important to acknowledge that, but not everything on the spectrum is Autism. What's alarming is when he says "It doesn't change anything, I still am who I am". With these diagnosis, it's important to assess the situation and do what you can to improve that instead of just be like "welp I have it so I can be this way". I'm hoping that he doesn't go that route, cuz it's so lame. People with genuine autism can't do much about it. I took care of a lot of Autistic and special needs kids when I was younger, and seeing their struggle in comparison to Jack makes me cringe in unbelievable ways. I feel that this adds to the diminishing of people that actually struggle with it.  Anyways, welcome haters. Carry on.

Author: @Macdadivali
Content:
On the very slim chance Sean might see this, what you mentioned at 1:22 ,there is actually a term used for that. They are both considered "comorbid" disorders (kinda like how it's not uncommon for someone with depression to also be diagnosed with anxiety). I'm not trying to come off like "um actually -" about it. I just wanted to share the knowledge since psychology was my major, and even without the degree, I personally have my own mental health struggles (the example I used earlier being one that applies to myself).
I really appreciate your positive mindset on being diagnosed with autism, since some people have a very negative reaction to that news, despite the fact getting diagnosed is just explaining why you are the way you are and always have been. Autism didn't just sneak up on you one day and manifest itself, that's just how your brain is, and a lot of people struggle with accepting that when they are diagnosed. 
I don't know if there are enough words for me to express just how grateful I am that you are using your platform to try and help positvely change the narrative on mental health. That it's something that shouldn't be treated like this dirty, little secret people have, but is a part of them. Interesting fact: one out of every two people in the world will develop a mental health disorder in their lifetime (I'm not pulling these statistics out of my ass, this is based on a Harvard study). That means basically there is a 50/50 chance the person you are talking to is, has, or will deal with some form of mental illness in their life. Yet, people are still afraid that talking about it is some sort of weakness. I can respect some people wanting to keep their personal information to themselves just because they don't like oversharing, but people shouldn't feel like they need to keep any mental health stuff hush hush because it will negatively impact them and make them a social leper.
Although I personally don't have autism, I have ADHD, treatment-resistant chronic major depression, and generalized anxiety, so I'm a fun mix of mental health diagnoses. The depression runs in my family, and I was diagnosed at roughly 6 years old. I'm not sure when I was diagnosed with anxiety, but I was 17, close to the end of my senior year in high school, when I got diagnosed with ADHD. It wasn't even something I remotely considered having, but my therapist at the time (who herself had ADHD) suggested it and I was like "sure, it couldn't hurt to find out". I didn't think I had it since I was never hyperactive as a child, but lo and behold it turns out I do (with the DSM 5 at the time being used, I was labeled as having "ADHD with prone to attention deficit" [basically had an earlier version of the DSM been used, I would have just gotten ADD before they just got rid of the separate diagnosis and gave ADHD subtypes or whatever they're called]). You would think already having been diagnosed already with other mental illnesses that I'd take it in stride. Unfortunately, I did not. I struggled a lot with the common "well if I have it, why wasn't it diagnosed sooner?", and felt like I couldn't have it, I mean, I was an A student and even taking college courses as a high schooler (my high school had this whole dual credit program with the local university where you could instead take certain college classes in place of the ones offered at the high school and it would count as both your high school class AND as a class on your college transcript  [so basically when I graduated high school, I had already accumulated enough college credits to make me a sophomore in college]) so obviously there had been some mistake, right? Nope, it was 100% correct and the more I payed attention to myself, the more I realized "oh, shit, I really do have ADHD"; however, there was still a part of me that felt almost like an imposter and wondered "am I just now acting/thinking this way because I feel I need to justify my diagnosis? (PSA to everyone, you should NEVER have to justify your mental health diagnoses to someone because you don't "act like it" or whatever. I've dead ass had someone, another patient at a residential treatment center, say to me "why are you even here? you don't seem depressed." Like, dude, just because I don't have some specific tragedy in my life like a number of people there did, doesn't make my depression any less valid. Sure, I might be high functioning [for context at this point I had both my bachelor's and master's degree], but that's because my fear of failure drives me even if I mentally feel like absolute shit and just want to lay in my bed and cry all day), or am I just now more conscientious about why I do the things I do?". It's been a number of years since getting diagnosed and by now I've accepted that I have ADHD (if going to my usual psychiatrist appointment with the intention of bringing up possibly starting back on ADHD meds [I had to quit taking them because they reacted badly with my other medication at the time and I would just feel incredibly dizzy], and completely forgetting until later that evening when on a discord call with some friends and they asked if I finally got new ADHD meds, isn't one of the most ADHD things ever, then I don't know what is) and accepting it has really helped with some of my depressive thoughts with the knowledge that, for example, "I'm not bad at ___ because I'm an idiot, I have ADHD which literally makes doing ___ much more difficult for me". Another shining example of my ADHD is this entire essay of a comment. I only meant to mention the comorbid disorder thing, but it got a tad bit out of hand as I just let my brain type out my stream of thoughts for so long my phone is now lagging when I type.
Anyways, tldr: Sean, if you actually see this disaster of a comment, I just want to say I appreciate everything you are doing to try and change the stigma of talking about mental health, and that I am glad getting diagnosed with autism has given you answers to things you might not even have  considered and is letting you feel more comfortable with yourself. To anyone else who suffered through my ramblings, remember to be kind to yourself because it's possible that whatever you might beat yourself up over is just how your brain works. If you already know you're neurospicey, still keep that in mind because sometimes we can forget why we are the way we are.

I'm 19 and got diagnosed with adhd earlier this year and with level 2 autism two weeks ago - I was selectively mute when I was little but the teachers and even doctors all brushed it off because I was both a woman, intellectually capable and would say a few words each day when absolutely necessary (pretty much exclusively to my parent and always whispered) it took ages to find people who'd listen and actually recognise what was going on because even if I wasn't a "mild" case I didnt fit the stereotype and even then it was ridiculously expensive (normally healthcare is free here - I'm australian) and I didn't really have the money for it but we had to because I have a host of physical disabilities that make it so I can't work but the government refuses to give people financial assistance for their disabilities here unless its reasonably treated and stabilised and its near impossible to prove my other conditions are stabilised so I needed the autism diagnosis to even be able to afford to get the diagnosis, purely because the public healthcare doctors had such stereotyped views of what autism had to be that they'd excuse anything i did that could fit autism as made up or just a coincidence because i wasn't the cookie cutter 5 year old boy thats obsessed with trains 
in the end one of the scored tests they did had a threshold of 65 for autism and i got 210 haha so safe to say i aced the test, i was in the 98th percentile of autistic people for another one of the tests and yet it still took 19 years for someone to listen and help

awareness about autism is super important and its really nice to see someone i grew up watching actually seek that out for themselves and then use it to try and help raise awareness for the rest of us and help shift the creator industry as a whole to something better

Author: @vickypedia1308
Content:
I work with disabled and special needs children, and I'm also neurodivergent (ADHD, and what I like to call "Schrödinger's Autism"). I have very low support needs, whereas a lot of the autistic children I work with are non-verbal, and/or have strong developmental delays, and require constant support. The spectrum is HUGE, to a point where it almost makes you wonder how all of these different versions of it could be the same diagnosis, but then you pay attention.

I *get* these children. We're on the same wavelength. I often mirror their stims, even if at a lower intensity and less frequent. I can interpret their non-verbal communication surprisingly well. They are drawn to me more than to my neurotypical co-workers. I can explain and instruct to them in ways they can understand, simply by phrasing things in a way *I* would understand. We are kin.

Author: @cdubbart
Content:
It’s a funny thing once you’re diagnosed… and you seem OK with it. It’s like it seems to dilute the effectiveness or validity of the condition for other ppl if you’re not automatically broken by it. The implication being autism is an awful thing that no sane person wants and therefore if your perception of autism doesn’t fit that narrative you’re either faking it or you must not be going through anything substantial enough to warrant empathy or concern.

I think what ppl with this mentality are missing is that it can be quite liberating & validating to receive a diagnosis… to receive an answer. Especially if you’re hyper sensitive, hyper analytical or hyper introspective. 

For me, being diagnosed opened a door to so many pathways to understand & forgive myself. It may be cliche, but imagine being a fish & being taught to climb a tree your entire life… when all along you really should’ve been swimming. The perspective shift can be unbelievable.

Content:
Really cool to see this sort of thing being talked about like this by somebody so big.

Personally, I think the dark side with this sort of thing as somebody who is a heavy masker (and sadly needs to be to simply survive in settings like at work), the response to disclosure isn't always positive or even neutral. I know I'm not alone in being met with comments denying my own diagnoses because apparently people can tell when you look ADHD, autistic or dyslexic somehow or because I don't openly display outdated stereotypical behaviours. 

At this point, I rarely disclose as professionally, it seems to work against me even though I work in education where neurodiversity is supposed to be properly supported and in my social life, people I give a crap about simply take me as I am which I don't think needs any diagnostic labels currently. Hopefully things change in the future as more prominent voices help to change public perceptions but for now, most people I meet will get a load of masking and camouflaging as society has quite clearly shown me that this is the safest way for me to operate - I'm kinda hoping we'll see what felt like an overnight shift with things like trans/gender openness but neurodiversity isn't quite there yet for me. 

Welcome to the super secret club which is so secret that some people don't even know they're a member yet Jack!

With everything said here, i wish i could sit down and have a conversation with you, there are so many things that i relate to, i just got Diagnosed about 6 months ago with Aspergers, and compared to a group i was put it, i feel you seem more similar to me.

Author: @EriahSylverstone
Content:
6:06 I disagree with this assessment, and here's why: Building a legacy really has nothing to do with your ego, or the world remembering you. A legacy is the mark you made on the world. It's the things you did that impacted people, that changed people. It's not about people remembering you. It's about people remembering the things you did. You, Sean, have a legacy. You made a mark on YouTube, and the internet as a whole. A lot of people will remember the things you've done over the past...decade, decade and a half. It's been a long time. And people will remember Jacksepticeye, but not because it's something feeding into your ego. The legacy you want to leave behind is one people will remember in a positive way. To know you did something good. There are good legacies and bad legacies. You've affected a lot of people in a positive way, thus you have a good legacy. I don't see it as boasting your ego. I see it as having made a difference. Having done some good in the world, meaningful things, things that people will look back on and be happy for. Remember and admire. That's what legacy is about. Building a legacy for the sake of building a legacy, yeah, that's selfish. Most don't want that. They want to say they did good. So that, by the time they die, their life meant something, and was worthwhile. And to be honest, no one should really just want to die and be forgotten.

You can die twice. First, when you draw your last breath. Second, when the world speaks your name for the last time. That second time is what most people are most afraid of.
Sure, this doesn't apply to everyone. Some people really just don't care at all about being remembered. Fine. But the people who do the work for it, the ones who genuinely want to make the world a better place, and make it last after they've gone, they should be able to do that and not be shamed for it. Maybe you weren't shaming those people, but it does come off as you only see legacy as something purely egotistical, or a mindset that people forced themselves into because of some social or personal issue, and it's not. Some just want to do the right thing and know they did the right thing, and see the effect it had on others. That's all. No problem in that.

Now, myself, I have aspergers. I've known I have aspergers since I was early teens. I never really cared that much. I work around my problems, I deal with what I can. What I can't, I don't sweat over. I just do what I can, be myself, and do the things I like. I run a tabletop. I write a story. It's what I like. Not everyone has to like or acknowledge it, but it's what makes me feel good, and what's fun for me. If I can share it with people, then great. I love expressing myself to people who care to listen. It makes me feel like my work, my lifelong hobby, is even more worthwhile, because I can actually be productive doing something I like. And yeah, I work a low end labor job to keep myself afloat so I can do the things I enjoy. What I'm doing on here doesn't make me a living income, but I'll keep doing it. Maybe someday it will, maybe it never will, but I'll keep going. It wouldn't be me not to. I've dedicated so much to this, and to drop it would effectively be suicide. That's why I try so hard. And if I can leave something for people to enjoy after I'm gone, then that's amazing. I'd like to. I might not, but it'd be nice to. Either way, I'm gonna keep doing what I love.

Author: @floofzykitty5072
Content:
When two different conditions are often present with each other it is called comorbidity. Psychologists know that autism and ADHD have a high comorbidity rate - roughly half of those with autism have been observed to also have ADHD - but these two conditions are in ways antithetical to each other and mask each other. This is also why psychologists aren't entirely sure what the exact rate of comorbidity is. 

A lot of people wonder how these two conditions with seemingly mutually exclusive symptoms can coexist, and the answer is simply "with great difficulty". I've been in situations where the autism side of my brain feels overstimulated and needs to go somewhere quiet to calm down, but at the same time my ADHD brain feels bored and agitated the moment I go somewhere too quiet. That being said, I'm sure it's easy to imagine how having autism and ADHD significantly increases the likelihood you also have depression and/or an anxiety disorder.

Author: @tatianaes3354
Content:
OVER-DIAGNOSING is a major issue.

You might want to consult with a different doctor. People get wrongly diagnosed with ADHD and Asperger’s/Autism all the time. Liking video games well into adulthood is not a symptom of autism whatsoever.

Overanalysing people during communication is not a symptom of autism, either. E.g. I do exactly the same thing, and there is no autism. Some people just naturally care about such things more than others. Being over-sensitive to smells and gagging from bad ones is also not autism, it is just your personal trait.

ADHD is often also not a thing. Sean is a long-time caffeine addict, and then he goes to get medication to fight its effects. Just fundamentally removing all of the coffee, tea and energy drinks would make his life much easer.

For most of my life I have mostly just done whatever's been on my mind and been happy, but as time went on I started to notice more and more how I was an outsider no matter where I was. Then last summer my mother came to me and told me straight to my face "Me and your father think you have autism." and I was in complete shock. At first I was devastated, because I realized that I wasn't "normal". And after that I tried to get a public diagnosis, which like Jack said, would have taken two years or more because my case wasn't "extreme" enough. I didn't do it privately because I couldn't afford it, but I still say that I have autism on the lower end of the spectrum so people understand the way I am.

Since then I have learned to accept this part of me and tried to be more aware of my words and actions, and even though it's not easy I haven't given up yet. And hey, knowing that one of my favorite Youtubers has it too makes me feel a bit better about myself. Thank you Jack, keep being awesome.

Author: @the_devilsadvocate91
Content:
There's nothing wrong with being autistic. I believe, and this is just my opinion, that autism could be an evolutionary leap or advantage.

For me, I have very niche interests, I research EVERYTHING I get into in order to have the most knowledge of it (MTG is a huge one for this) among my friends, and it's given me more heightened, acute senses with sound, smells, and touch. It's done more for me than being "normal" ever could. I've even found myself being very open-minded with things that would normally freak people out or be seen as spiritually insane.

Autism (or at least Aspberger's in my case) is 1000% a superpower and I think a lot of us on the spectrum are lucky to have the abilities we gain from it.

The only thing that should be avoided is using it as a crutch. It's not an excuse to be a jerk to people. The autistic spectrum is nothing more than an altered way of thinking and interpreting the world, and it's more than possible for anyone with that "disorder" to master their own mind and be able to control it instead of letting it control them.

But this is just one man's opinion. 🤘

Content:
I just wanted to mention that autism is a spectrum and nearly every person you meet has a trait. It's whether it affects your life, personal relationships and prevents you from interacting with the world in a meaningful way is when it needs to get diagnosed.

I believe autism is fairly over diagnosed, I was diagnosed with it when I was younger because it was an easy answer to showcase why I was struggling at school. It wasn't until I learned and experienced at work that people with true autism are deeply affected by the environment, change and find it nearly impossible to communicate. Often smearing, stimming and engaging in repetitive behaviors that would even prevent you from playing sonic that people normally label as a link to autism.

I'm not saying jack is doing this either, but it's also important to mention that people label themselves with these terms because it can offer an escape from their own mediorcacy, or offer an escape from feeling stilled. and having autism distinguishes you from the crowd. Although nearly everyone I meet in college said "oh ma gawd, I totally have ADHD and BPD, like one moment I'm happy, the next I'm like, totally sad. I mean like WOW!"

I have written a lot, but I guess what I'm trying to say is that we are all unique, our minds our bound torture oneself. So suffer silence, because I or no one else wants to hear it.

Author: @DaydreamingArtist322
Content:
Thank you for this video. This one deserves 5 stars, too.
1:36-1:46, 1:49-2:04, 2:43-2:55, 3:19-3:23, 3:30-3:36, 3:54-4:31, 8:41-8:57, 9:00-9:12, 9:32-10:06, 12:04-12:21, & 15:08-15:15: These are common for people with Asperger's and Autism.
Tbh, the Venn diagram description is more accurate than saying that ADHD is the same thing as Asperger's Syndrome or Autism. Also, there's a LOT of variation in the qualities (both number and intensity) that a person on this spectrum can have. To quote Tony Attwood, "If you've seen one [person with Asperger's], you've seen one [person with Asperger's]." Come to think of it, have you heard of Asperger's Syndrome? There's quite a lot of overlap between it and Autism (technically, it _is_ part of the Autism Spectrum). The DSM4 included both of them. But the DSM5 reclassified Asperger's as "high-functioning autism" (yes, that's the actual term they used). Some of the biggest differences between Asperger's Syndrome and Autism are: the age at which people reach milestones, effects on IQ, and the scores you mentioned. People with Asperger's often reach developmental milestones (such as when a child starts to walk, talk, or read) on time or early. People with Autism often reach these milestones late. In extreme cases, they may not reach them at all. Although there's a chance of both people with Asperger's Syndrome and people with Autism having IQ's that are higher than average, the odds aren't exactly the same. Sometimes–in extreme cases–Autism may cause a decrease in IQ. When a person with Asperger's Syndrome takes a graded assessment to determine whether they're on the Spectrum, they're more likely to have a relatively low score. People with Autism are more likely to have a high score. Based on this, you *might* have Asperger's Syndrome (but I don't know you well enough to say for sure). Please note: this is NOT meant to degrade people with Autism. There is NOT a better or worse Autism Spectrum diagnosis. The syndromes differ a little, but the value of the people who have them DOES NOT. Blue isn't the exact same color as indigo, but that doesn't make one better than the other.

Author: @CherryGryffon
Content:
As the wife, mother, sister, aunt and grandmother to folks with Autism... We don't bring it up, because it doesn't /matter/. It looks different for everyone, just the same as everything else. I also have OCD and Anxiety, both hereditary, and it was never something that we had to SAY. We simply adapted. My mom and I were the two that had it in the same house growing up, and while some things like our Crayons being OURS and no one else could touch them, there were also a lot of things that didn't overlap. If we had a "quirk" we just adapted, and moved forward lol. My granddaughter is "nonverbal" but she still TALKS. "Hi *name*!" I say over the phone, and you hear an echoed "Hello hi" in the back. Randomly you'll hear her say "Shit!" even though she absolutely shouldn't. My daughter said Happy Thanksgiving to her father over the phone, and teased him for being old. My granddaughter, in the back, pipes up "old!!" and then giggles. She's fully sentient, she's not an idiot, and even nonverbal as a label means fuck all bc she's NOT nonverbal. She's vocalizing ALL DAMN DAY LONG, including several words (She IS 3 after all). 

So, yeah, anyway, congrats on the diagnosis and I do hope it helps, but also... It doesn't make you any more different than any of the rest of us are tbh. It's just another hashtag on the page called Jack :)

Content:
I was diagnosed with autism as an adult. The twist was that I didn't even know what it was. No knowledge, no biases, no expectations or understanding. I just wanted to know why I couldn't pass through university as easily as high school...

So basically, imagine me: I now had this label that I stared at with slight apathy and vague confusion, trying to figure it out and if the accessibility options now open to me could truly help me pass my classes or not. Meanwhile my Mum acted really weird - "I never knew! I should've looked into it earlier! Here's some resources!" And like... I didn't care or blame her or whatever reaction she thought I might have, because I was still just me, and Autism was still just a label I'd recieved.

It took me five years to take an interest in and finally feel like I understood Autism before I began to accept the it was a word relevant to me as a person. Even with the dual diagnosis, it was only then that I decided "yes, that fits, actually". I am Autistic, I've always had Autistic traits. It's just another (actually quite major) indicator flag put into the excavation site that is me, another thing discovered and named that explains part of how I am as a whole.

I don't know why anyone treats Autism as more than that, as if it's scary or world shattering to find out you have it, or to birth a child or meet someone who has it. I don't understand the fear mongering and the negative reactions some people have to it and I never will. But that's just my unique experience and journey, which will obviously be very different from everyone else's experiences and journeys.

Author: @Nebbed
Content:
It's relieving to hear you talk about this. I'm 22 and I learnt only two years ago that I was diagnosed with Autism when I was three years old. But it was kept from me by family and friends because they feared that it would shatter my self-worth and self-confidence. It was kept from me by everyone in my life, the only person that didn't know was myself. But as you pointed out with your experience learning about it, it brought so much clarity into my life, it helped me re-evaluate my past experiences, and helped me re-evaluate how I view myself for the better. It also helped me realise truths, and break away from the unhealthy & toxic friendships that I had since childhood. I realised I'd spent years in a toxic friend group, and it got to a point after I learnt about it, where I had to withdraw myself from them.

It was a painful experience, but one I needed to go through to learn and grow as a person. It's been a year since everything happened, and I now have new people in my life who care and value me for who I am, beyond the mere fact that I'm Autistic. The important thing people need to realise is that ADHD/Autism (AuDHD) doesn't define who you are as a person. It makes you different, sure. But really, we're all different one way or another. And we should be embracing people, instead of rejecting people because of what makes them different. 

People should stop treating being diagnosed, or knowing someone that gets diagnosed like it's something that should be feared. Because really, it isn't. Thank you for talking about this, while it's been a long time since I last followed your work. But I must say, I have a new found respect for you...

Self-analysis, forcing yourself to put yourself in someone else's shoes, stepping away from politics, and being critical on yourself are the keys to you finally getting help Jack. Consider the scenario that you're wrong in a lot of views in life. Force yourself to take the opposite mindset from people you hate. Eventually you'll reach back the center of the two conflicting views, which is probably where reality and truth is.

Unfortunately there's no medication for autism so this next step is all on you. Switch therapists is my recommendation, set goals, and learn to improve yourself. Stop coming up with excuses, criticizing others for different views, and Just work on achieving your goal is one by one. You realize happiness will come eventually, and pretty quick if you do it right.
