Author: @bythelee
Content:
I'm definitely autistic, but remain undiagnosed. Not for lack of trying, but the endless fobbing off and disinterest of "professionals". I was always different. Weird, if you like. But only worked out it was a high-functioning autism (aka Aspergers) circa 2008 in my 40's. Suddenly ALL of the incidents throughout my life had a perfect and neat explanation. I remember moments from when I was 2, btw. Not many, but they are ALL "stress moments" when I was freaking out. Analysing myself and my experiences in hindsight, make it screamingly obvious I'm autistic. But my parents buried their heads in the sand. "He's painfully shy" said my Mom, when my first primary school teacher was in tears that I had not said one word to her in six months... (I was 4).

I have tried sharing my autism with others, like my new neighbours. The sooner they know, the better, I reckoned. Given how past neighbours have mostly been distant and cold-shouldering, no matter how hard I tried to be nice. This time would be different, I hoped. Well, yes, it was. But not in the way I hoped. 

I have never yet had a positive reaction to such sharing. The usual question is an angry "Why tell me?" followed by years of awkward, uncomfortable encounters that would not have been like that, if only they had bothered to listen to what I had told them about my autism and how it makes me behave. 
Despite all the fashionable lip service about inclusivity, nobody cares, and nobody is interested in what makes you YOU. Hearing someone say they are autistic has become a kind of "I'm special too" claim for fame, to have something that makes them stand out from a crowd. And the vast majority of people judge and condemn you for being a drama queen, because they don't want to have to make any special effort to accommodate your special needs. 
They want to do their thing and not feel uncomfortable that they might be triggering your nuclear red buttons while they do it. 

In other words, telling anyone about your autism needs to be carefully considered. I was deeply shocked to see and hear Jack readily telling the world here. But the general positive reaction in the comments explains why. Nothing to fear, because the followers all knew him well enough already. They LIKE his quirks - that's why they are here. Which gives a safety net that nearly all of the rest of us do not have. 

Once the autism genie is out of the bottle, there is no way to put it back in. So choose carefully and wisely, and don't just blurt it out to everyone. Save it for when there has been an ugly incident, when sharing the truth can help defuse the situation. Because, quite frankly, it has become clear to me that sharing this knowledge prematurely does not help at all, and quite possibly makes things worse. Life is not fair. Having autism is already a lifetime sentence. But people are people. You might be lucky enough to have parents and siblings that understand and care (mine did not) or extremely lucky to have actual friends that enjoy your company. But the vast majority of people, including professional doctors who should know better, still react instinctively to "you're weirdly different" and avoid you with a long barge pole. Everybody wishes you would just go away and be somebody else's problem. (Which added a distinct mark of absolute genius to Douglas Adam's SEP field in The Hitchhikers Guide to the Galaxy series.) I've experienced this for 6 decades. And it won't change anytime soon. 

For me, sharing this knowledge about myself, and my accompanying idiosyncracies and behaviors, only results in instant rejection and avoidance. 
Instead of a long period of difficult interaction first, before the ultimate unavoidable rejection. That's how it was for 40 years. Now I get to feel the rejection instantly, instead of prolonged agony beforehand. 

For all of Jack's followers and their positive reactions, there will be many more that have watched and moved on. The best part about a Youtube channel, is that only people that like and enjoy what you do will stick around. But everyone has a chance to see it. 

My neighbors are a very limited and select group. And I am stuck with them. Thankfully our houses are far enough apart (because I specifically chose a house that had nobody else living within half a mile of me) that we can get by without having to talk to each other. 
4 years on, one of them has finally seen the light, grasping that what I told him 4 years ago was exactly true. He didn't apologize for all the grief he's given me, during the time he ignored my issues and pressed my nuclear buttons. He doesn't see the irony that him behaving exactly as he pleases causes me grief, while he complains that me doing what I am COMPELLED to do is "unwanted". Yeah, I'm not even allowed to be myself in his company, while he demands the absolute right to be himself, as difficult and cantankerous as he can be. 

I don't believe that everything in the future will be peachy, either. He's only just realised that what I told him meant something. He has yet to comprehend what it actually means. So at that rate, one of us will die of old age before any actual understanding develops... 

Thanks for reading. 
I hope you realise that my intentions here were just to urge caution to anyone that thinks they should shout out to the world about their own condition. 
It does not go well for the vast majority, because the "normal" folk don't want to be bothered with your quirks and needs. Best to just be yourself, and let them move on and reject you if they wish. Because, those that stick around, enjoying your company, WITHOUT knowing this truth about you, are the true friends that will be cherished more than they can ever know.

I do see autism for me personally as a mental disability as it affects my ability to basically… do what neurotypical people can do without really thinking about it. Like I’m more prone to social and work burnout and I get irritated a lot easier by noises, behaviours etc, amongst a bunch of other stuff. Hyper-fixating on things is a huge thing for me but I like that I got that passion. I feel autism as a general term has definitely been overused and almost glamorised or “meme-ified” which can be frustrating but in some instances also comforting, it’s nice to see relatable memes about  it! I do think people should be professionally diagnosed before labelling stuff they do as “oh it’s because I’m autistic”. It can muddy the water when people start using it wrongly… like I don’t want to be seen as a joke or not taken seriously because of how autism is talked about online now. 

Thanks for being so vulnerable and open with your journey, wishing you all the best! You have my whole support and I can see a lot of others also supporting you. Take care!

Content:
General piece of advice to anyone that is a bit different: Don't be ashamed of who you are, just accept yourself, you'll feel so much better.

I have autism, diagnosed at 10 and have always been a little different. When I was diagnosed at 10, it finally explained all of it. Especially to my mum, who had fought for my diagnosis as she really just wanted validation that I was not a "problem child". Luckily that wasn't the case.

When I got to high school, I was bullied for 2 years, and what did I try to do? Blend in. Big mistake as I ended up getting even more bullied. I also didn't talk to the staff as my communication skills were (and still can be) rubbish. It was probably the worst time in my life, as I had more bullies than friends. 

But I was always told by my keyworker to just be myself. So one day, I tried it, and while the bullying persisted, I felt more open and free to express. I even got a few more friends who accepted me and my quirks and autism. Now, come next year, I'm graduating university with a degree. And it's all because I just acted like myself.

Author: @MiriamTV2
Content:
My story is I basically broke down at 30, tried to get up again, but got accepted to an evaluation when it got to a point where I couldn't see myself go on at 31 unless I could find answers to why I am the way I am, which is "wrong" when it comes to functioning in today's society. Had to wait 2+ years, and then I finally get diagnosed with AuDHD, right before covid. I live in a small town, resources are sh*t. Someone with no education on neuropsychiatric diagnoses was put in charge of my rehab and drove me to a nervous breakdown. I can speak for myself, I can behave, so no one understands what it's like inside my head, how much I work every day to not let the self-hatred win, it takes so much energy. I want structure, but I feel like no job would want me. I have worked before, and I know I can do good work, just not full-time, just not with extreme stress and rude customers.... I'd like to find a way back, but have so little hope. 
Oh yea, I did raise concerns that I was sure I had Asperger to my CBT therapist when I was 23, but was told that "you're a smart girl, you'll get through this", so boy did I continue to blame myself every time an employment or endeavour would fail. 
TMI overshare, but that's what we do. The message between the lines is probably: "Halp plz, any advice?:/". Thank you for sharing, Sean. I like Japanese trains, they're quiet and on time. XD

Author: @BlameItOnTheADD
Content:
I was diagnosed ADHD back in 2009, even with medication I always felt different and couldn't fit in however hard I tried. 
I kept saying my ADHD is just you know, losing my keys every day, oopsie there's me distracted again by a squirrel ort something to downplay it to everyone else - I basically ended up gaslighting myself for 10 years to think "everyone else have these struggles right, I don't need adjustments for me". 

I didn't realise up until 2020, how much I masked. And by the end of 2019 I was suffering Burnout, which I now believe was autistic Burnout. 
Before 2020 I needed "Time outs" and non verbal days because I was just so exhausted from being... not me.

2020 allowed me to suddenly not have to mask, not having to go places I didn't want to go, be social when I didn't want to - make the noises and arm movements I wasn't "allowed to" before. I realised how much sound drained me, how much lights affected me. 
I was allowed to pursue my special interests, I would deep dive into art that I hadn't done since childhood. 
I'm still recovering my burnout, but now I'm self-employed. Although I'm just barely scraping by, I'm loving doing what I LOVE to do, and what interests me. 
I've got about 11-20 weeks waiting until my Autism assessment. 

I'm hoping to get the same peace of mind as you do <3

Author: @ENDERSTIXgaming
Content:
autistic ppl (like me) usually like to just KNOW things as fact. it's frustrating to hear that things aren't fully known/ understood. for example. we do not have a full understanding of autism/ adhd/ etc. our understanding grows every day HOPEFULLY towards the better. adhd and autism tend to have all these other disorders/ neurotypical thingamajigs because your brain is hardwired DIFFERENT and it's never the same as anyone else. there's overlaps which make it easier for psychologists to say "this means you are like this" when really you are YOU. and no matter how many boxes you fill you will never quite FULLY understand your own brain. it's unique and constantly adapting to it's environment. if anyone reading this is questioning if they are autistic or adhd etc... just ask ur friends if they are, then ask them if they think you are. most adhd/autistic etc tend to accidentally attract eachother into groups so if ur friend is adhd there's a chance you are too. not the SAME symptoms but likely have ones in common. IMO that is a more valid confirmation than going to the doctor and asking cause 1 went to school years ago and tried really hard to understand it... and the other has lived it every day of their life. u get 2 adhd/autistic ppl that both say yes then it's not even a question.
anyone saying "oh everyone is adhd or autistic blah blah blah"... yeah... no one's brain is exactly the same and the symptoms are VERY broad. so likely you also experience symptoms. whether you are masking them or not. also not THAT long ago adhd and autism were Taboo. so even if you WERE adhd no one talked about it so you wouldn't know. these days it's less Taboo so more ppl are learning about it and discovering they ARE it. like how left handed ppl were so uncommon then after it wasn't as Taboo it surged. it'll level out at some point but we don't know when

Author: @CassianGray
Content:
Jack, this is why you're one of my top youtubers; you're authentic and grounded, and also neurodivergent like me!!  I'm so happy for you that you have more answers to your questions of "why tf is my brain like this", which I can relate to.  I hope that you are able to make more accommodations for yourself and focus on what brings you peace and comfort.  Evelien seems like the perfect partner to have alongside you on this path.  My love and admiration to you both!

I got diagnosed with autism a couple years ago, and that was a shock to my system of both relief and dismay.  I'm still adjusting to my new POV on life and figuring out what I want to do with myself from here on.  I really like how you phrased it as "being kinder to myself", because that's what I'm doing (but my parents call it laziness).  I am spending more time on my hobbies and with my friends, and my day-to-day demands are usually low.  I'm overall happier than when I was stressed af in college and while working customer service.  I didn't/don't want to be in public much, and I realized it wasn't social anxiety, it was autistic sensory overload.

The way my autism manifests is I'm book-smart and good at learning (graduated college with a 4.0 GPA), but I suck at social stuff.  That's why I love video games; socialization is so much simpler and straightforward.  I got the sensory sensitivities, too: light and sound and touch are my biggest triggers.  Again, all things I can control while gaming!  I'm so grateful for my friend group of gamers, who I wouldn't survive without.

Author: @ModifiedRabbit
Content:
I got diagnosed with autism a few years ago and tbh the way people treat me when I tell them is usually BETTER because now they understand some of the things that they thought were weird or a tad annoying, and its helped them know that im not doing certain things on purpose and I get a bit more understanding from them. 
Yeah, some people are like "Well EVERYONE has autism nowadays", which is kinda rude as it kind of makes it out like my struggles I have with my autism are nothing, BUT they tend to change their tune once they are forced to see some of those actual harder struggles that I cant deal with much. 
Mainly various sensory issues and such or they see me stimming or have some sort of small meltdown because I got overstimulated etc. 

People dont understand how much autism affects your life even if youre on the end that is 'high functioning' (for lack of a better phrase for it). 
My coordination is affected and, for the life of me, I cant really hammer in a dang nail very well or handle tools well. I stumble around and tip over a lot so I get a lot of bruises or have fallen down the stairs a good bit in my life, compared to most people.  

Ive had awful constipation issues my whole life, which have caused other issues that suck. 
I can smell and hear things really well which can be nifty BUT also can be awful... My dog and I smelled out a dead mouse in the house while my partner had no idea at all cause to me, it smelled so absolutely awful that I couldnt think of anything else, which is also why he cleans the litter box and not me.  lol   
I also get nasty migraines and headaches from light sensitivity and stuff from sound. I cant sit listening to music with heavy base because it gives me massive anxiety and I cant breath. I cant eat things like yogurt or angel hair pasta because it makes me wanna vomit, no matter how much I like the taste. The texture just is a nope for me. Same with touch. 
With MANY things, it feels like im rubbing my hands on carpet. Especially after a shower. 
The only good touch stuff for me is that super soft fabric that they often use in baby blankets and toys. 

As for behavioral, I have rejection sensitivity so In order to help with that, Ive found certain ways to tell friends to deal with me if im being obnoxious. Like if I end up talking over them (which I do a lot sadly) I tell them, just keep talking over me in return. It wont take long that ill pick up on the fact that I need to shut up. It doesnt trigger my rejection sensitivity nearly as much as being flat out called out in front of everyone over it. 
I cant look people in the eyes. It weirds me out. 
I love people watching but I dont like being in crowded places so Ill find a spot in the corner at parties or gatherings and have to have an 'escape room' where its quiet and I can calm down and decompress.  
I tend to have no middle ground. 
Its 0 or 100 with how talkative I am and that depends on the topic. If its a hyperfocus of mine, youre getting 100. If not, I likely wont talk much at all. 
And I absolutely cannot stand up and do stuff in front of a bunch of people. 
Doing stuff on camera is MUCH easier. 

Im glad you got your diagnosis. It DOES feel better to know whats going on with you, BUT at the same time (At least from my experience), its annoying because you know that many of these things cant be 'cured' and some cant even really be treated and those things tend to be the biggest things that make your life hard. 
Like, while I love my autism when it comes to creative endeavors, I HATE it for everything else like every day life, social situations, and even physical health (intestinal issues and coordination etc) and at those times I am constantly wishing autism were curable. 
I wish I could make friends easier, keep friends easier, have a normal functioning body so I could do things like work with the tools in our garage to make stuff without help, be able to hold down a normal job, be able to sleep without meds cause my brain wont shut up, not absolutely NEED someone to come in and basically parent me into a proper routine. 
Once I get into one its great and I can easily stick to it but its getting into one thats hard to do alone.

Whats worse is if you get your diagnosis as an adult over being a kid when you get it. 
There are a LOT of programs out there to help kids and its easier to get the medication you need etc. 
As an adult there are pretty much no programs and its so hard to get onto certain medications because youre just assumed to be drug seeking if you even ask about them once. 

I hope your diagnosis helps you a lot and you get any help where you need it and such.

Author: @Lowellia
Content:
I sort of wanted to open up a sub-conversation about getting diagnosed for adults. I was surprised when Sean said that he could go and get tested for autism, because that's not really a thing where I come from, and I'm sure that for some of you guys the availability might not be there as well. I'm from Latvia, where spectrum disorders in adults aren't really talked about. In fact, the general sentiment is that adults don't have it and are simply seeking attention if they speak out about their struggles. 

I've been formally diagnosed twice with bipolar disorder and social anxiety. But having reflected on my childhood, as well as my difficulties now as an adult, I find that there are way too many things that don't fit into the equation. Like my light and sound sensitivity, issues regulating the volume of my voice (either I'm too loud or too soft-spoken), difficulties relating to most people I meet, my love for MS Excel and complete inability to focus on anything else while OSRS Leagues event is happening (although that could be a general effect of that event, lol), and the list goes on.

I'm sure I'm not gonna get diagnosed anytime soon but I do have a great support system from the people around me and I've learned to manage my difficulties. Seeing Sean speaking out about his diagnosis and embracing it is incredibly encouraging. ❤

I love my autistic brain, it’s incredible at what it does, but unfortunately the world we live in was not designed with me in mind so I burned out six or seven times over the course of my life and currently I’m struggling so hard mentally that I’m not able to work. The stress has physically shut down my body. 
Thanks for everything you’ve done, I’m so grateful for all the effort you’ve put in over the years to make YouTube a more positive and kind environment. Sometimes it’s hard to hold on to hope, so you genuinely make the internet more bearable.

Content:
I'm so happy that you finally have additional answers on yourself and now can find new strategies to navigate your life to best manage it.

Warning for a long, potentially nonsensical life story because I need advice:

Growing up, I was badly bullied in school and teachers tried to get me falsely labelled with Autism, ADHD etc trying to blame it on me being completely different. Though, I was evaluated by several people including someone from social services and from their reports, I just had the mark of an extremely traumatised person.

Author: @neurodivergent_aussie
Content:
As another adult diagnosed in my 30s - it's pretty rough. Adhd diagnosis came a few weeks before 30, asd at 34. Now I've just finished my placement in my Education Support Worker course to help kids with additional needs in the classroom to help them in whatever way they need. Helping autistic kids and adhd kids is also healing my inner child who was labelled as lazy or stupid because I was undiagnosed and had no support. My own two kids with additional needs are supported and getting through at their own pace in a way I never would have been capable of in my own childhood. 

My autism diagnosis didn't change much, exactly, but it totally made me feel way better about myself. I am kinder to myself. I actually like who I am and am proud of what I have achieved with all odds stacked against me and 3 decades of struggling alone. So I've turned it into stopping other kids from going through that labelling and pressure to perform at a neurotypical level of expectations and requirements. We're valid. We need all types of people to make the world go around. 

Thanks for your openness. I hope this helps people see what they taught me during my certificate: "if you meet someone with autism, you've met one person with autism." We're all different.

Hi Jack, congratulations on your diagnosis! 

I just wanted to share that even as I am considered extremely neurodivergent on paper (diagnosed with Autism, ADHD, Tourette's Syndrome, Visual Snow Syndrome, Synesthesia, and the list goes on far beyond just that,) upon taking a traditional/conventional autism test, like those you find online or elsewhere, even I do not receive a score indicative of strong likelihood.

When I was first diagnosed with ASD, and later ADHD (as someone who performed really well in school *prior to year 8*), I felt really broken. Like 'wow, this is why people would tease me, everyone knew at school except me'. And now after so many years, it's really nice to just understand how and why I think the way I do. Author: @ceekay3143
Content:
Congratulations on learning more about yourself, Sean. 

I suspect that I might be a high masking autistic female. I haven't sought a diagnosis because I seem too "functional" to be taken seriously in a space where there is still a gender bias and under-diagnosis.
But, it also opens up trauma issues around emotional neglect and how little my loved ones really understand and accept me. Like, how little did somebody notice me and my suffering and/or care about me that they didn't get me tested when I was younger? That because I was a people pleasing nerd, they thought I was okay and didn't need any comfort or support? 

I have diagnoses in anxiety and depression, and my autistic friends claim me as One Of Us. But I'm also a Science teacher who has personal interests in learning about all the things, including how to people/psychology. If my phone dies or the internet is down, I miss the ability to search anything I can think of, more than I miss being able to communicate with others (though people kinda suck at communicating). Sorting things soothes my soul, noise overstimulates me, and I really enjoy doing tests for fun (yes I spent most of my 20s doing Buzzfeed quizzes and allll the "Am I Autistic?" type quizzes). 

I would identify myself as a Highly Sensitive Person and definitely feel the sensory issues. I definitely notice the little things that tell me what someone else is feeling, and I start to feel that way too. Though some experts say that is just from hyper alert trauma things; knowing who is coming down the hall and what their mood is just by the sound of their footsteps is a particular skill some of us needed to survive. I'm glad I only have a couple of weeks left at my current work, because the feeling of everybody else's stress and burnout is super draining on me, on top of the noise.

Sometimes it's hard to even unmask to yourself. Noticing and allowing all the little things you do and think as part of being what some people call Neurospicy (which covers ASD ADHD etc as well as PTSD, BPD and other trauma based different brains). 
Do you sing when you're vacuuming because nobody can hear you and complain about your voice, because it counteracts the sensory discomfort, or because you just like to sing while cleaning like you're a Disney princess? 
Have you developed little rituals that others don't notice or think are "weird", but are actually self-stimulating or self-soothing behaviours? E.g. lifting your toes up in your shoes when the car goes past a cross-street, so you have some movement and a "game" to play when you were told you aren't allowed to move or express yourself in the car? Use your fingernail to push back your wicks because it makes your nails look nicer/healthier, but also gives your anxiety something to work through?

...Do you practise writing novels in the comments of Youtube videos because you genuinely don't know how to keep friends, and don't have enough people to communicate with to "get your words out" for the day? Knowing that there's over 20,000 other comments on here already, so it's almost like screaming into the void?

Content:
Welcome to the club bud. Cant say im shocked. Youre pretty damn weird. Like me. And being social doesnt mean anything. Im social, im just weird.

And yes. There is a spectrum Autism on one side, normal in the middle, add and adhd on the other side. So theyre opposites, but they both differ from normal people for the same reason. Infants all become autistic for a few weeks. Its too help them learn about and understand the world around them you become autistic when your brain does not revert back to normal function. Adhd is when it reverts and then some. And people say you can have both, which you cant, theyre literally opposites. Symptoms... Symptoms overlap. Content:
I’m somewhere under the neurodivergent umbrella. I was diagnosed with ADD when I was around 8, then around 10 I was diagnosed with Asperger’s.

In my late teens, I decided to get reevaluated. I was exhausted as I’d just finished school and had only slept for 5 hours and had only eaten half an apple that day, and the guy kept telling the same stupid joke over and over again to try to get me to laugh. At the end, he told me it was clear that I had autism because I wouldn’t stroke his ego by laughing at his stupid joke.

He also said I didn’t have ADHD. I asked him why I had been having worsening memory issues for the past year, and he said it was because I didn’t care about anything besides my specific interests. I was forgetting stuff I was talking about midsentence, was forgetting what to call my parents (I would forget what my dad was called, so I’d call him “Bald Mom”), etc. My memory had gotten so bad that one day when I saw one of my pets, I had no clue who they were, as though they were a complete stranger. He said that, due to autism, I wasn’t actually interested in any of the things I was having memory issues with (my parents, my pet, school work, hobbies, etc.). He wouldn’t take my concerns seriously, despite the fact that I now think they were due to severe insomnia and worsening anxiety.

Author: @ShadeNightstepD24
Content:
I'm going to be completely honest here: I haven't really casually engaged with Sean's content in years, but I have always respected him and without a doubt he is one of the few content creators who, in my opinion, has done a good job of being genuine and maintaining a respectable level of integrity. With that said, as someone who watched you during my younger years, who grew up with such good role models in the 'neuro-divergent' space (both, youtubers like Mark and Jack, as well as close friends and family), and who has grown up to study psychology, This video *still* took me by surprise.

I am going through my own struggle with trying to get my mental health sorted out (after a series of- fairly large failed projects due to me NOT having it figured out.) I was going through the same feelings of disconnect, feeling like the outsider, even as I got certain diagnosis and treatments figured out. While I know better than to self diagnose, the possibility that I could have autism never even crossed my mind (not in any manner that was serious, anyways). 

I know this is anecdotal, but I really do think that my experience isn't an isolated one, *even* as someone who has *heavy* roots in psychology and mental health, with an open mind and genuine deep curiosity, I *still* fell victim to the incorrect and limiting belief of what autism looks like, which to me highlights how *important* it is for people like Sean to be open and vocal about their own experiences, to help bring attention to what the *full* spectrum of mental health can look like. Not only for autism, but for all manner of mental health, I have seen so many people who aren't the "Extreme very-obviously-not-normal" end of a disorder/condition feel like they can't possibly have anything because they aren't "that bad", and thus they end up being way harder on themselves than they should be, because they never recognize and validate their own struggles (and strengths!)

Thank you for this video, thank you for your honesty, and thank you for just being your best, we all appreciate you <3

(and thank you to anyone for reading this comment, if the video hasn't convinced you to already, I urge you to challenge your beliefs of what mental health can look like, seeing is the first and most vital step to improving! both in yourself, and in others!)

Author: @WinterRoseASFR1
Content:
Diagnosed at 50, started to suspect in my early to mid 40's.  And looking through that lens explained so much.  Going from gifted classes to special ed classes as I progressed from school to school in the 1970's and 80's because they still didn't REALLY know what to do with Autistic kids or ADHD kids other than flatten them with lithium.  I got off light in that regard most likely.  I'm also told I'm quite well spoken and communicative.  Most folk seem to think I learned to mask quite well.  I'm a voice and stage actor, so that kind of lines up?  I don't know myself.  However well, I may have masked, I was still the weird kid.  The one that never fit in.  The one that was just 'off' to most people around me.  Social situations full of shyness and awkwardness through the lens of my own diagnosis... The simile I use is like finding out I've been playing a game without instructions on hard mode without knowing it my entire life.  50 years, wondering what was 'wrong' with me with no context.  

I'm regretful I didn't have the insight or context for so long, but as you say, extremely pleased to have that lens to recontextualize both my life and myself.  I got medications (Methylphenidate 54 mg and Trintellix) for the ND cocktail I seem to have in my own spectrum.  Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria, Depression, ADHD and Autism,   Partial Aphantasia.  Context based attention that varied based on whatever topic I was experiencing.  

There's actually something of a low key movement to reject the idea of Attention Deficit Hyperactive Disorder as a descriptor altogether.  A rejection of the idea of theidea that it's a disorder of any kind at all, but merely a trait of a variant human.  The Acronym VAST seems a LOT kinder and positive.  (Variable Attention Stimulus Trait)  I still haven't found the peace I hoped for, even 3 years later as the rediscovery of myself is an ongoing thing.  But I have indeed found that I treat myself with more kindness and understandting.  I always celebrated my weirdness and owned it.  I can remember proudly claiming the term weird to my classmates at the age of 5.  But it was hard.  It still is hard.  But I am determined to live for myself and my loved ones unashamed of who I am and what I am.  As you said.  I'm still me.  I'm just me with clarity I lacked for so long.  And while I still don't have the instructions to the hard mode game life is?  I find that I don't have to try to play that game on neurotypical mode any longer.  I got my own game now.  And I can be fantastic at that.

Author: @nobody.of.importance
Content:
This was a really nice video, and it's cool that many of my favorite YouTubers are on the spectrum like I am. Arin of Game Grumps and Rubber Ross are ADHD, Kyle Hill is autistic, MrBeast, and Mark Rober’s child. Given the genetic component, it’s possible Mark is on the spectrum too. Glad to see we're getting more public figures representing us and speaking up on the subject. A diagnosis can feel very cathartic, like you finally have a name to put to your more unusual traits that finally connect all the dots. I'm glad you're happy about it. Love you, Sean <3 Platonically, of course.

As someone who's really curious about neuropsychiatry, I like trying to figure out how alterations to the physical structure of the brain affect personality. I'm left-handed, trans, and autistic, and I often ask myself, "What makes me these things, physically?" After years of searching, I've come up with some interesting bits that might be familiar to others on the spectrum.

The biggest difference I've noticed between us and neurotypicals is that their brains seem to have a stronger ability to filter out background information—like sights, sounds, and smells—automatically. For us, it's not as strict and allows more of that background noise through, which then takes up conscious effort to process. I've heard it described as a buzzer turning on in the brain, and if it persists but isn’t important, neurotypicals can sort of turn the volume down. Autistic people can’t do that to the same degree. It’s a double-edged sword: we can get overwhelmed by the flood of data, but we’re also better at noticing small details that others might unconsciously filter out. From an evolutionary standpoint, we’re like the tribe’s lookouts—really good at catching things others miss. This idea is part of the Intense World Hypothesis, which suggests that our brains experience more sensory and emotional input than normal, leading to both heightened awareness and a greater susceptibility to meltdowns and shutdowns. This can also make it more difficult for us to learn in typical classroom settings.

A metaphor I like to use to describe autism as a spectrum is to compare the mind to an equalizer on a music player. Instead of adjusting sound frequencies, the sliders represent different mental functions: social confidence, coordination, planning, mathematical ability, etc. Most people have sliders relatively close to the baseline, with one or two slightly higher. Autistic people, on the other hand, tend to have more extreme slider values. Someone might be incredible at math but struggle with fine motor skills, while another might be extremely socially adept but highly disorganized. This is why you often hear, “If you’ve met one autistic person, you’ve met one autistic person.” Each of us is unique, and autism presents in so many different and beautiful ways. In this way, autism isn’t about deficits—it’s about diversity. Each mind operates on its own unique settings, offering different strengths and challenges.

Author: @FlfyCats17
Content: I have an autism diagnosis, and as you can also see, my profile picture is a furry. When I have sensory issues (voices sound louder than they do, faces are difficult to look at, food feels bad etc.) the one thing that calms me down most is things that are soft and fluffy. Wearing a hoodie indoors makes me feel safer in general, and throwing a blanket on at my home office helps me focus. The texture of warm and fluffy is my brain's version of some kids feeling good when they look at a fidget spinner. BUT HEY, YOU KNOW WHAT THAT MEANS? Since another problem I have is that HUMAN FACES are too difficult to look at; you know what's fluffy, soft, and not as ugly as a human to look at? FURRIES!!!! Furries are my sensory paradise. This not only puts me into the category of autistics who love Sonic, but also the category of people who never outgrew soft fluffy things like cute cartoons and stuffed plushies. As someone who's constantly overwhelmed with negative sensory inputs that can't even be described in English, furries are one of the few things that give my life meaning.

Author: @Andrew-zc4qo
Content:
As someone who's worked with the disability community for 26 years (since I was 12), it honestly annoys me how much terminologies have changed over the decades. Now "Autism" is used to describe anyone who's slightly outside "the norm". With billions of people on earth, that margine is widening. 

I have ADHD, diagnosed at age 22. My dad always struggled with social cues like a conversation ending etc. My family all thought he had Asbergers, which is now part of autism. When he was in his 60s he randomly said to us that he thought he was "on the spectrum". We laughed saying we know! But that was just dad, ya know.

All this is to say, TLDR: that this conversation of needing to label people who dont perfectly fit the mold societies have formed, is the new "barbie doll". Weve gone from body image issues to mental health issues. Everyone is different and we just need to put loving others first as our priority as Jesus taught! 

(Imo) Being obsessed with having to put everyone in a neatly labeled box, put on the society shelf to be monitored and classified, devalues people. Just because someone is a little different shouldn't effect how we view their value. By labeling people, we create stereotyping, which can be toxic. So us "on the spectrum" folk have to be careful to not let ourselves be put into a box, or scrutinized by society for our personal world views. Individuality is even more important today than ever before! 

Sean, if you happen to read this, I agree with so much of this video! I relate man! But please dont be fooled into trapping yourself into the definitions society creates.. I've taken many personality tests from lots of cultures and views to understand more and learn more about myself. But I'll never let one measurement define who I am! 

Just wanted to pass these thoughts onto the wider internet, hopefully it helps some..

Author: @Wildcat_Media
Content:
Oh, Jack. This makes me so happy for you. To be able to put a name and an explanation to what you face - it makes a world of difference!

For the first few years of my son’s life, he showed some hints of autism but I dismissed them because he was such a loving and affectionate kid. He loves giving hugs and seeing his family. In my mind, autism means you don’t like hugs or physical contact. So there was *no way* he had it.

But one day we were at a parade and the fire trucks blared their horns, and my son just flipped out. I had never seen him so upset and scared. I had to go sit in the car with him before he calmed down. And that’s when I decided to get him tested - just to be sure. And, indeed, he has autism.

Because autism hasn’t been so frankly discussed or understood until somewhat recently, a lot of people have incorrect ideas about it. So many adults went through their whole lives thinking there was something wrong with them, but in reality, the explanation isn’t that hard to figure out.

This may sound weird or insulting, but I don’t mean it to be at all. I am grateful for the people who went through that because it means my little boy could get diagnosed early and he can get the help and support he needs. The more we can understand and communicate what autism (or any other mental or physical condition someone may have), the more everyone can better know how to interact with someone who might be different. Now my son is in elementary school and he has had the most wonderful teachers and therapists - they’ve helped him and us as his parents. Those things weren’t as commonplace when I was growing up. But they are now, and I am grateful for that.

All the best to you, Jack! ❤

Author: @evanschulz9704
Content:
I've been diagnosed since I was around 4 years old. And I have years of experience when it comes to Autism, ADHD and what have you. So right now while you're still new to understanding the disorder. I want to give you my best advice I can give to people on the spectrum *Don't attach every problem you have to autism*
This is a mental trapping I've seen first hand how detrimental doing this on a consistent basis.

What I mean is; when you say you can't pick up BB's crap off the ground, Because you'll get a sensory overload. You immediately attached your autism to that exact problem. So you get into this bad habit of chain balling all your problems to autism. Where you may go "BB's crap stinks, *And because of my autism I notice it more*" You attach any and all problems you have to autism. And you convince yourself that your autism is the problem, and due to the disorder being uncurable. You basically have the feeling that you're eternally flawed, and that there's nothing you can do about it.

This is a horrible mindset that I see so many people under the spectrum fall for. My dad is heavily autistic yet never diagnosed himself. And he had all the negative mindsets I've listed off here. He became a broken man, a man without the constant struggle of his own personal failures. And if you think this story has a happy ending, I am sorry to disappoint. But My mum had divorced him a couple months ago because he was just such a broken man.

Now to uplift this conversation, I do want to say there is still a positive to my argument. I've gone under the habit of just feeling my emotions, rather than categorising them. Which has not put me in a situation where I blame my disability on inconsequential problems. If I encounter a place with loud noise, I think "I don't like this" instead of "My autism is killing me"

Author: @mushiiluvs
Content:
Genuinely? Undiagnosed adult here. It makes me glad people are still able to get diagnosed professionally, and that people I relate and look up to can relate to me that way. 

Only reasons I can't get diagnosed tbh, are probably the facts that insurance in the USA sucks, and also the fact that like you said, the waiting lists suck. I've been tested ONCE, in 8th grade during a time where I genuinely wasn't in the right headspace and in a, frankly, traumatizing psych ward. I didn't even KNOW I was being tested. They just asked me questions that I didn't answer honestly to bc both that I was insanely masking to both leave, and yknow, they didn't tell me it's what the questions were for. I thought it was my exit questions. And now all the psych doctors around me are like "well they didn't see it in (time frame)"... The system here sucks. Legit everyone close to me can tell but I've just given up on being officially diagnosed unless its gonna need to be something I need formally. I mean, I basically already know I am, but I genuinely wish the support system for this was better. I want to be myself without the fear that people will both be misogynistic and judgemental as hell. Bc my brother, *is* diagnosed. And an officer who had to come here once (that's a whole other story)? Literally laughed about it to our faces, and it's terrifying that if I get diagnosed officially that that's how I'd get treated here. 🥲

Long comment rant, I know. You probably wont see this Sean, but fr? Thank you, it gives me some hope that things are progressing, if just slowly. 💕 I'm glad you got to figure it out.

Content: 1:03 Ppl are still surprised I’m autistic as well because I am very extroverted and social… until they see me during a busy holiday or in a crowd and I experience shutdowns, nonverbal episodes, and do need stims. Author: @foxroddraws
Content:
"Jack why do you talk about these things, it's not like you have cancer"

Honestly, I love these kinds of videos where content creators start opening up to their audience about certain life things that have happened, whether it's about family or mental health or recent diagnostics, it makes them feel more human and that's something people really need to start doing is treating those that we look up to in entertainment as regular people with relatable situations

I am also AuDHD, both undiagnosed simply because 1. It's very difficult to get a diagnosis, let alone a proper one in the US and it can be extremely pricey based on how detail of a test you get, your provider, your insurance, not to mention how long it takes to even get to that point.

2. For myself, I am unfortunately not in a safe place to willingly get an official diagnosis. I have family who is very pessimistic and very judgemental when it comes to mental health and things like this. They believe if you're depressed you're either looking for attention or suicidal all the time, gosh forbid I tell them I want to get tested for autism 🫠

But doing the research myself, talking with mutuals, seeing strangers experience the same things I go through and then explaining it from their perspective has been such an eye opening thing. Like Sean said, it gives me that satisfaction and understanding of "oh okay, this is why I am the way I am, I kinda know how to deal with that or work around it or just know it's not me having an issue" instead of just thinking I was being a problem and a nuisance to myself and others

I am really happy that Sean spoke up and shared about this, it does bring me comfortable hearing about similar experiences and something no one should be ashamed to talk about. It's hard enough dealing with the stereotype accusations.

Author: @foggy922
Content:
I hope people can understand that being autistic isn't inherently bad. Being autistic is like having ADHD or Dyslexia; you can learn how to live life relatively comfortably by playing into your strengths and accepting your weaknesses, and in most cases autistic people are capable of making a good life for ourselves independently — this is partly why most autistic people remain undiagnosed and showcases that being autistic does not mean you are doomed to fail.

I discovered that I am autistic when I was 15. I remember feeling like a normal person until my later school years, where other teenagers resorted to endless bullying and rejection. I managed to integrate and be accepted socially until my mid teenage years, where everything suddenly began to fall apart. From talking to and knowing other autistic people, this seems to be a common experience. There are multiple social stages in life; when you're younger and surrounded by other young children, your peers tend to be more accepting and less judgemental, but when you get into your teenage years people seem to shift into having a strong hatred for difference and diversity — this is where I believe a lot of autistic people are failed by society and blamed for being different, when it is in fact a problem with other people.

There is no worse feeling than going from having a decent social life to suddenly being hated by everyone because they see you being different as a threat. It is life ruining and plays a primary role in why autistic people are significantly more likely to commit suicide. It is completely unfair and unjustified to persecute someone for being harmlessly different; it is pathetic and anger-inducing. As autistic people, I hope we can learn to love ourselves more and understand that we are not inherently broken because other people treat us poorly.

Me, my siblings, one of my parents, one of my grandparents, and most of my friends are autistic. The only time I feel at ease and comfortable about my autistic self is when I surround myself with them. A lot of us have immediate relatives that are autistic, and this is how we find peace in being comfortable with our own tribe. I suspect the same goes for many other autistic people out there as well.

*A message to Jack:* Please do not ever let anyone tell you that you are broken because you are autistic. You have provided your audience with countless hours of entertainment with your unique personality and energy, which is likely in part fuelled by autism. You have managed to successfully leverage your strengths by providing content that gives people happiness. I personally remember watching you when I was younger and you pulled me out of the deepest pits of depression and suicidality with your incredibly energetic and upbeat personality — you deserve nothing but the best in life and to be proud of who you are. Thank you for everything.

Author: @CraftyMaelyss
Content:
I've said this for the longest time:
Autism is not a disease. It's just a different operating system.
Saying Autism needs to be cured is like saying Linux or Max is a virus because it's not Windows.

We learn things differently, if you put C# in Python, you'll get errors because it's not compatible and that's just like us:
We can't do things the 'standard' way, because we're running on a different system. It may take a while because we have to convert things into something that we *do* understand but that takes time and a lot of mental effort. That's why a lot of Autistic people like us can get frustrated really easy, because of this factor of everyone using Python and Windows, but we're trying to figure out how to write this down in C# so it works on Linux or Mac.

That's how I always explain autism to anyone who asks or says I don't look autistic, because of the stereotype that's been around for a very long time. I was very lucky to get diagnosed when I was young, but not a lot of people get that luck, especially since I was diagnosed in the late 90's too.

To anyone who's struggling:
You're doing amazing, you're working with what you have and you're going to be okay, just be extra kind to yourself- you have nothing to prove to anyone :)

Author: @IWashWithSope
Content: I made a comment on this video when I was watching the beginning of it, and now I'm at the part where Seán is discussing terminology and how most of it is outdated. For example, high functioning and low functioning. A better, less degrading way of describing this is by saying low or high support needs. Sometimes autistic people need more help, and sometimes others are extremely independent; and that works well for them. I would also like to point out that autism is a spectrum in more ways than one. For example, an autistic person's ability to function according to how society expects them to, is entirely dependent on how they are affected by their surroundings. What I essentially mean by this is that someone who might seem like they would be a low support needs autistic person (they function in accordance to most societal expectations and can communicate quite well), can have all of that thrown out the window if they get extremely overwhelmed or overstimulated. That level of functioning can regress. It is completely normal and should be treated with patience and understanding.

- *lets me rest and recover by myself after social events*
- etc

Author: @LordPichuPal
Content:
The opening line of "Apparently everyone knew I was autistic and didn't tell me" has been my whole life, too. All throughout childhood and teenage life I was clearly lagging behind everyone else mentally, had issues focusing, didn't understand social cues, didn't communicate well or engage with people, obsessed over things. I even got into Pokemon late and when everyone else moved on from it, I still was hooked on it and always trying to talk about it. And yet nobody ever once stopped to consider maybe something was up and should get tested to find out. My parents just would tell me "it's a phase, you'll grow out of it" and act like it's a normal thing.

Wasn't until I was an adult that I heard a friend talking about how he was autistic and I'd never heard of it before, so I looked up what it was because I didn't want to seem dumb asking about it. Came to realize the more I read about it and read about ADHD, all of it hit the neurons in my brain to be like "wait a second, these all identify and align perfectly with what I've been struggling with." While I have not been diagnosed officially, even just coming to find out on my own and doing tests online about it have helped me better understand this is what I'm dealing with and there is that sense of relief knowing. It helps explain what's "wrong" exactly so that others can better understand and adjust. It's not a free pass to do whatever, but it does make explaining how you feel and act easier. I'd love to have seen how much differently my life could've been had I known sooner, because unchecked autism definitely made my whole school life much more difficult than it needed to be, and I really wish I could've had the help to tackle it. At least now more people are becoming aware of mental health and these types of disorders, and are more accepting about it and supportive.

I wouldn’t say that ADHD and autism are “part of the same spectrum” or really THAT similar. It’s more that they have a lot of symptoms that can look similar to an observer but ultimately have totally different reasons behind them.
Someone with ADHD may interrupt you during conversation because of a lack of impulse control, whereas an autistic person doing that is probably struggling to tell when it’s their turn to speak. It looks the same, it’s the same action, but the reason is different. Many of the overlapping symptoms are this way

Author: @Afterrdusk
Content:
I hate that so many negative people have turned autism into a category of certain traits and now it feels taboo to be open and accepting of your diagnosis. When you are high functioning you are always introduced with “oh yeah they have autism…but you could never tell” or “they’re autistic but they are chill I swear”or even “they don’t act like THOSE autistic people” Or they use autism as a joke and anyone who behaves differently or “weirdly”online is met with the same boring jokes about how they have autism or are special. Having autism isn’t something to hide or belittle, we are just people living in the same world as everybody else trying to go through our day to day the best we can. An autism diagnosis isn’t a disease that needs to be whispered about, but I also don’t think others should bring it up as the very first thing they mention about someone because it DOES change others mindset about you and it’s not the only thing that defines you. It’s just one part of you. Sadly people avoid you once they find out, like you have some sort of virus that changes you. Our minds just function a little bit differently, we’ve always been this way and that’s okay! A diagnosis isn’t FOR them.

A diagnosis never changes who we are, just gives us clarity on why we are the way we are. Questions are answered and we start to feel comfortable with our identity. And I think everyone deserves that kind of clarity.

Author: @risingdragon5306
Content:
You know, Jack, this was the first time I was very disappointed with a video of yours. I'm a doctor that works in the mental health field, and I believe you've done a great disservice by talking about a disorder which you have no training to talk about, we see a very problematic pattern in the behaviours that patients adopt when in trying to figure out what they have, instead of consulting a professional, they inform themselves on tiktok/unreliable sources, and affirm a belief in their minds that they must surely have a certain pathology (a belief that can create suffering), in this regard, I see your video as contributing to the suffering of non-pathological traits and behaviours.
Other examples such as never even been examined to maybe having a differential diagnosis, such as a very commonly ignored possibility of a Personality Disorder, in which they use whatever other disorder they may think about having as a crutch, to justify pathological behaviours that they shouldn't be having, especially because they don't have that pathology they claim to have.

Mental Health disorders are a very serious business, think twice before talking about it again without carefully planning what you are going to say when it extends beyond just your personal experience, in the chance you might misinform or promote a way of thinking about disorders in which they become a certain kind of crutch to the individual, that can justify behaviours that should be treated, independently of having a certain diagnosis or not, and traits that shouldn't be pathologized when they bring no suffering to the individual.

Content:
As an AuDHD person too, I'm surprised to hear this for you, Sean! I was thinking the same things you quoted at the start. "But you seem so social." But it also makes a lot of sense. "Autism is a spectrum" means that you can have any number, and any severity, of dozens of symptoms that all fall under the umbrella of ASD. Someone who is high-functioning/level 1 does have the same neurodivergency as someone who is nonverbal/level 3, just not to the same severity.

Even though I initially felt frustration being diagnosed with autism and had a momentary identity crisis, it's also been really helpful and enlightening. I have sooooo many symptoms that are explained by autism. Sensory issues to sound and lights (used to be unable to wear jeans til I was a teen), disliking changes and spontaneity, poor coordination (both fine and gross motor skills), low energy levels and preferring sedentary activities, issues with digestion AND sleep... It's just like wow, no matter I struggle so much. I'm literally, legally handicapped!

Hope this makes life easier for you moving forward :)

Content:
Just to inform. The term 'High Functioning' is criticised for how it defines an autistic individual. It focuses on how well the individual 'performs' by neurotypical standards. Which is why it's since been replaced with modes of support needs! 

Low support needs, medium support needs and high support needs are better terms as rather than define the individual by how well they act, it focuses on what the autistic individual needs. The different terms just help in restoring a bit of autonomy and independence that  honestly the entire disabled community struggle with getting mostly due to how other abled people treat us.  

'High functioning' would qualify you as low support needs.

Content:
I have ADHD. Hell, I may even have Autism for all that I know. I wouldn't be surprised. Funny enough, I got rediagnosed for ADHD a few years ago. I was originally diagnosed when I was 12, took medication for a few years, then got out of it. As time went on, I was doing okay without meds, but school was harder to get through. It took me about eight years for me to get my BA in college. Post-Covid, I felt like I wasn't doing mentally well. I ended up going through therapy and seeing a psychiatrist, and both of them helped me wrapped my brain around to know what's going on with me. At the moment, I am managing well without any medication. If anything, I'm hyperanalyzing myself on what I'm doing so I don't go overboard. I'm a lot more open with my close friends and somehow became a lot more social. I feel a lot more comfortable with myself has a human being and don't make my ADHD as my personality, it's just something that I have. 

In terms of being a neurodivergent, there are always different levels of ADHD, Austism, or anything involving the neurodivergent brain and how one manages it before and after being diagnosed. You can be the smartest person in the world and be neurodivergent. You can be the shittiest person and be neurodivergent. Being neurodivergent is something that is underdiagnosed and I always try to advocate people getting the help that they need.

Author: @yesterdaze2375
Content:
I'm no expert, but culture - the desire to fit in, the subsequent need to conform - has a pretty terrifying way of affecting us humans. What we don't understand intuitively becomes something "other," and with enough pressure we "other" each other. The stigma and discrimination against Autism is just one of the many, many ways in which that trend has manifested. In that way, it isn't a "good" thing: those who have it will have to face that discrimination, that othering.

But a diagnosis is also liberating. It opens doors to tools, strategies, and knowledge cultivated across decades by people who have gone through what you are and know how to guide you to the other side of the worst of it. It gives you the language necessary to talk about and address the issues and peculiarities of what you experience, and express them to others. At times, it's even a reason for bonding with those who share those experiences. For all these reasons, it's not at all a "bad" thing either.

So if it's not good, and it's not bad, what is it? It's beyond all that. My mother once told me that she thought that the term "disorder" for such things was a bit of a misnomer: there is no "right" way to think, just the ways in which we do think, function, and live. Those peculiarities will make it hard for some of us to navigate this world humanity has built for itself, true, but we nonetheless all have something to offer to it - some way and means in which we'll be more than able to live and thrive. I hope you'll continue to be an example of that aspiration, Sean.

Content: Hey Jack, I actually worked in ABA therapy for a bit (thankfully an ethical clinic) which stands for Applied Behavioral Analysis and is a common treatment for individuals with autism and have my degree in psychology. Autism more often than not is accompanied by other diagnosis’ (ADHD, OCD, SPD, various anxiety disorders, etc.) but it’s important to distinguish between the ASD and other diagnosis’ as not everyone w ADHD, OCD etc. has autism and vice versa. A good way to view the autism spectrum is not like a linear sliding scale but a color wheel, autism can look extremely different in some people vs others. If you’re curious and want some more in depth explanations of autism and other diagnosis’ I’d encourage you to look into buying a copy of the DSM-5. BUT it’s very common for people to begin to self diagnosis when reading the DSM-5 which can be dangerous. It is by no means wrong to be curious about whether or not you might have something, but absolutely ask your therapist or other professionals first. In my opinion I’d say Autism Spectrum Disorder  is probably one of if not the most misunderstood disorders, and I’d encourage you and anyone else out there to research it. Love what you do, keep up the good work and I hope you’re enjoying the new Kendrick album🙏❤️

Author: @LexAnnalyn
Content:
Fellow AuDHDer! I was diagnosed with autism this year, too! In February. Turned 31 this year, so diagnosed rather late myself. I relate to much of what you say in this video. My ADHD diagnosis explained and helped a fair amount, as did my anxiety. But neither really covered it, and I repeatedly felt that my doc was missing something when she treated my “anxiety attacks” the way she did. I now think my experiences are better described as meltdowns triggered by overstimulation. And neither generalized nor social anxiety fully explained my apprehension about peoply events. (I wasn’t anxious at  big gatherings because I was shy, or at least not mainly. I was on edge because NOISE. Energy-sucking human interaction! Ensuring I understand the event and what’s expected of me!) And ADHD didn’t explain why I was so slow at processing things people with similar smarts did three times as quickly.

The expert who diagnosed me had autism as my main diagnosis, with ADHD and unspecified anxiety as secondary diagnoses. It’s SO affirming. I didn’t realize I needed further “permission” to accommodate my own needs. I thought I was already good at being kind to myself in that way. But I did.

Glad you got your diagnosis and that it’s already helping you, too. ^_^

Author: @theTruthlessRecluse
Content:
Omg, but... at 0:34 my communication is EXCELLENT. Well, online anyway. I stutter a lot due to nervousness and anxiety, not because I'm Autistic. If I weren't nervous, anxious, or afraid of judgement, I'd be extremely good at speaking.

I've met only one person in my life, irl, who had the non-verbal, "can't think for themselves" side of the Autism Spectrum. Everyone else I ever met, not irl, and has claimed to be Autistic, never showed any symptoms (which is obvious. They can't fuction on the internet if they're non-verbal and can't think for themselves. However I'm not aware of a non-verbal autistic person who's smart enough to write long paragraphs and etc. They could be a selective mute, but I doubt that there's a non-verbal autistic person.)

1:51 is relatable by A LOT. People would judge me constantly, question why I was so quiet or ugly, or why I preferred things that people wouldn't prefer because they think "mature is better." At least online, I can't see judging faces. I'm very much an outsider, even now, around other autistic people and around other people who have the same problems as me. (3:48 is something I hate irl. I don't like other people irl to know I'm Autistic. Like I said, I don't like being judged in person, so I try my best not to let my classmates know, not even those I considered best friends.)

As an Autistic person, I'm not the stereotypical kind who likes horses or trains. I'm not like the boys who obsess over trains or the girls who adore horses. In fact, I prefer spaceships and ferrys, giraffes, llamas/alpacas, goats, and wolves. I don't know an autistic person who loves the animals I like, but I'm aware of autistic people who obsses over space, like me. I learn things a lot faster than others, yet people think all autistic people learn at a slower pace. It's called a spectrum for a reason, and it's why I hate stereotypes regarding Autism.
7:47 makes sense to me, as I've noticed more and more content creators are coming out as being diagnosed with ADHD. Take JaidenAnimations for example. It's actually a bit too obvious that she's AuADHD. And, someone like, well, SmallAnt (mentioning him because he's one of the creators I watch constantly), it makes sense that he has AuADHD. A perfect example is his dedication to focus on a project because he's interested in it. Not because he has to, but because he's interested. I think another perfect example of that dedication is beating Pokémon nuzlockes easily. I feel like anyone who is dedicated enough to a project to study, work, and perfect something probably, and I say probably, has AuADHD. I'm a very dedicated person, however I'm only diagnosed with Autism, so I can't claim that I have ADHD as well. But I'm sure I have it. I just can't get diagnosed. Too poor, no therapist, and no way to drive. :(
8:47 is me. I do in fact overanalyze everything, mainly due to doubting myself. My friend, who doesn't have Autism, thinks it's something I can fix with therapy. I doubt it because it's a part of who I am. And even if I could, therapy couldn't fix me.
9:54 is something I experience too, however I never sensed it as a sensory issue. I thought that everyone gagged to death when picking up poop, I had no idea it was related to Autism.

You've earned a new subscriber, even if I've known you since 2017. I never really liked you because I felt uncomfortable with the weirdo fangirls/fanboys, but I know it was NOT your fault that they did their weird shipping. I respect you, and I have been watch youtubers who have been diagnosed with Autism lately, because I want to understand their experiences, just so I can find ways to tell people that Autism isn't just a few simple symptoms, but that it's a really huge spectrum. (Also, I'm probably not going to watch any horror content because it scares me...)
I'd like to mention, every youtuber getting diagnosed makes me want to get rediagnosed, just to see if I've gotten worse, or I've been the same the whole time. They diagnosed me with "mild autism", not to my face, but that's what my mother said. I was 7 at the time. However it'd be nice to see if I had more than just Autism. I'd love to see what else I have, but I'm afraid I'd get diagnosed with what my mother degrades me for. (She says I'm paranoid, which I am, so I'm afraid to get diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia, or bipolar disorder because my mother is definitely two-faced.)

Also at 13:58 I hope those people suffer (as in their terms, get diagnosed with Autism.)

Author: @firefly313
Content:
I have diagnosed ADHD and am finishing up a master of social work program to become a psychotherapist -- I think it's important to clarify for your audience that while ADHD and autism have a number of overlapping characteristics, and many people have both, they ARE distinct concepts and diagnoses! They're both forms of neurodivergence (or 'neurodevelopmental disorders'), but they're not actually the same thing or on the same spectrum.

That being said, the high overlap of possible symptoms/traits can be very confusing! I have a lot of sensory hypersensitivities (can't stand loud noises or most scented products) and I hyperfocus on things in a very 'special interest' type of way, but I don't think I have any of the social traits and thus don't think I'm autistic. A lot of people don't know that sensory issues and hyperfocus can also be ADHD traits! (This is not to challenge your diagnosis at all, just to add more detail on how ADHD and autism can show up in general)

Author: @wl9162
Content:
I could be wrong about this (I have BPD, so anyone who's non-neurodivergent, pls step in if I got this wrong), but the reason a lot of neurotypical ppl don't say anything to autistic ppl about them being autistic is because 1) They think you're either already self-aware of it and/or 2) they're simply not mentioning it because of the stigma surrounding it.  Basically, they're projecting their own biased viewpoints onto you (they think you're not mentioning it because you must be ashamed of it, because -- and this sucks -- THEY would be ashamed, usually since they're not particularly educated about the subject). 

And the stigma surrounding autism is pretty brutal. But it shouldn't be. If non-autistic people had half as much emotional empathy and compassion as many autistic people do, they'd understand you better.  You've been making room at the table for them (that's often what masking is). Now THEY can make some actual room for you.

***Edit: Also, a lot of society sees the word "autism" as a synonym for the r-slur (which it isn't -- I mean, I'm not throwing ppl with intellectual disabilities under the bus here, but autism just literally isn't that).

I think things like autism and ADHD are being over-diagnosed due to social political interference. I think 99% of people who are diagnosed with these things in the modern day likely do not have the condition they were diagnosed with. Author: @clwilliams9276
Content:
The autism diagnosis is important to know and important to talk about for so many reasons. It helps u understand urself better cuz it gives u something to actually pay more attention to. My self awareness is heavily limited due to a multitude of both mental and physical conditions so having a focus point always helps me understand better. It also helps me to EXPLAIN it better. N yeah, going easier on urself.

Some very unnecessary personal context that I typed up, realized was unneeded, but decided not to delete anyway:
My mom self diagnosed me with autism when I was 8 cuz her friend had an adult autistic son n I seemed a bit too similar. She didn't think it before even tho I had a diagnosed autistic cousin cuz we were never really similar. But, like, I was absolutely obsessed with Dora until I was 8. Literally to the point that I brought my Dora flip phone to an acting thing unironically. N my favorite toy was Fairy Dora. Favorite pillow was a very large dora pillow. Even had the dora hair cut for awhile. Etc. Was diagnosed when I was 14 n it was actually a pretty quick assessment. This is entirely because I was sent to a psychiatrist that does diagnoses for the charter school I was about to start attending that gets money for having disabled students. N autism counts as a disability for that measure. Seriously, I literally had a few attempts at unaliving myself, told him, n the only thing he said about it is that "her mother says she is depressed" 😑. He existed to give me a diagnosis that could get them money without doing anything to help me. Depression would require them doing something. Hell, he said "unspecified learning disability" rather than dislexia or discalcula so they couldn't pinpoint something to help me with. I finally saw an actual legitimate psychiatrist starting at the end of 2020 and got a multitude of diagnoses as well as meds. I'm on a med combo that works to treat all the major bs, the minor bs is now my bigger problem because of that. Mental: AuDHD, unspecified mood disorder (didn't qualify for bipolar but bad enough for meds to be needed. Btw I also informed that og psych that I was having hallucinations n he didn't even reference that in the diagnostic report. Should be fired.), SAD, Depression, learning disabilities, insomnia, gender dysphoria (aka, am trans), binge eating disorder, anxiety, (mild) ocd, and ptsd. Might be forgetting something. Some of those things r not officially in my records cuz if they were, no doctor would believe i had any of them, nevermind all of them. Especially those docs that don't think someone can have both anxiety and OCD separately. Physically, I have quite the lineup as well: Small Fiber Neuropathy (sfn. Look it up if u want. Too much is part of it for me to list it all off), type 2 diabetes, asthma, hemmeroids, lactose intolerance (worse than the rest of my family. Normal milk is a death sentence for my GI tract), a fair bit of allergies (take meds for em cuz they r too constant with too many symptoms for me to reasonably deal with without meds), and eye problems (pretty sure lazy eye but honestly, could be something else entirely lol). Ok so not that long of a list but SFN is complex with no treatment that covers all its symptoms resulting in my physical diagnosis chart including the major aspects of SFN that cause me problems. Such as PAIN, balance issues (i use a cane even tho I'm 22), frequent constipation (no med ever ended up working to treat it), near constant acid reflux (got a med for that. Supposed to be taken for 1-2 years max but my reflux is far too bad for that. So instead I just get yearly magnesium level checks to make sure i haven't taken too much for my body to handle), restless leg syndrome (my legs remind me I have that so fricken often).

Anyway, i'm glad u got ur diagnosis n yeah, one of those "makes a lot of sense" moments for sure. Stay safe tomorrow if u go out, given tomorrow's Black Friday. Dangerous.

Author: @kashsystemDID
Content:
From my experience as an AuDHDer, people don't like being told they're autistic. I have a keen neurodivergent radar. I picked up on my kid having at least ADHD by the time he was 2, and by the time he was 5 I knew he had autism. It's genetic, and 70% of people with ADHD have ASD. 

Additionally, most neurodivergent people are really good at masking, playing the part so to speak. The thing is, when you're alone, not in public, that's when the mask comes off. Hence the fatigue that comes with socializing and being in a work environment, even just going shopping etc. We get good at "fitting in" on the outside. 

It's like a survival mechanism. It really is a super power too! I love my spicy brain and the amazing things it allows me to do in spite of the hurdles I have to overcome. 

Congratulations Sean! Part of the ship, part of the crew! Me and my neurospicy family will be at the evening Thankmas show!! Driving to LA from chilly Las Vegas lol. 🎉🎉🎉

I learned I have Asperger's when I was 10/11. I had to go to social skills classes to learn to fake interacting with people better because I was HORRIBLY socially awkward. I still am, I'm just mich better at hiding it now. But it's funny, the list of things he said you probably have if you have autism, I have.......none of those things. Like not even close. Before I got diagnosed, one therapist thought I might have ADHD and then they asked what my grades were and my mom said straight As and they went "Oh no. People with ADHD don't get straight As with no help. She DEFINITELY doesn't have that." But it's funny to me that I have none of those other things he listed either because the man who diagnosed me was a brilliant psychiatrist and he told my mom "I know no one is 'normal' but for lack of a better term, your daughter is sooooo close to being normal. She's the most well-adjusted autistic person I've ever met, what did you DO to her?" And the answer was honestly a lot of tough love. She pushed me to do things I had to do like get a driver's license and put up with doctor's appointments. And she didn't fight me on things that we're worth fighting about like that fact that I was a picky eater. I ate enough kinds of food to get nutrition, what skin was it off her nose if I made the same thing for dinner 5 nights a week?

Anyway, I'm glad you're happy Sean, learning I had autism answered a lot of questions for me and helped my mom learn how to raise me better. I hope this news helps you too.

Author: @AussieMarshmallow
Content: I was diagnosed ADHD as a teenager, but struggled with medications long into adulthood. But I didn't get an Autism diagnosis until my mid-30s. And have also struggled with life-long anxiety, depression, insomnia ( and even asthma! I heard you listing off your umbrella and thinking "Yep, sounds about right"). I am 39 years old. I feel like my life could have turned out so much different if I had just known from the beginning, but even then... Autism support in the 80s and 90s was not great. Hell, during the 90s doctors weren't allowed to diagnose a person with both ADHD and Autism, you could only have one or the other until new studies came out around 2013. So often enough, kids like me were handed the "less severe" diagnosis of ADHD, and then had to struggle through life wondering what the hell was wrong with us. But at least I know now, and have made efforts to learn as much as I can about Autism and try to unlearn what I now know were unhealthy coping mechanisms. Knowing is half the battle, and I am happy for you to have found out about this missing piece of yourself. Read, learn, talk to others who share your story. We support you :) Best wishes from Aus
