Author: @ImpulsiveLimbo
Content:
I work with children with ASD it's now based on levels (1, 2, and 3)

Level 1 ASD may need minimal support to manage daily activities. They may have difficulty with social interactions and communication, and may experience social anxiety.

Level 2 ASD require substantial support. They may have trouble with verbal communication, have very restricted interests, and exhibit frequent, repetitive behaviors.

Level 3 ASD require very substantial support. They may have limited ability to communicate and interact socially with others. They may also face significant challenges in daily living tasks. 


Wait-list for diagnosis is long across the world sadly 2 years minimum. Private pay in the US can be $400+.

Author: @awkwardukulele
Content:
I had a VERY similar story with my ADHD diagnosis a few years back.  I was always told by everyone I knew as a kid that I "Couldn't possibly have adhd" or "There's no way you're autistic!" because I didn't quite fit the stereotype in everyone's heads of what a neurodivergent kid looked like.  

Then, I had to redo my last semester of college due to missed hours and assignments, and i was at the end of my rope and thought what the hell, lemme see if there's some other reason I'm so bad at school.  When I finished my appointment, the doctor who diagnosed me with ADHD told me straight up, "You've got almost every point on this test, _how_ have you not gotten diagnosed sooner?!"  And the absolute WAVE of relief I felt hearing those words is beyond description.  Every adult i had trusted and asked for help from had been saying the same thing, how there's no way my brain works differently, I'm just lazy and don't want to try anything.  After decades of trying as hard as I possibly could, and even harder after that, having someone look me in the eye and tell me i had a problem was the best feeling in the world.  

I'm currently trying to get an autism diagnosis, although I already know I have it as well.  It's more for my peace of mind, and frankly so that if anyone ever tries to tell me I'm not what I am I'll actually have scientific proof that they're just spouting nonsense!  I am SO grateful there's folks like Sean who have enough social standing to make a difference and start bringing awareness to what neurodivergence looks like in different people.

Author: @takendruid
Content:
1:17 I want to really quickly clear up something about ADHD and autism because I have done a ton of research into this. But also there’s a reason they’re diagnosed as separate things because if they were “basically the same”, they wouldn’t be completely different diagnoses and conditions… would they now…

Autism and ADHD have extremely few overlapping symptoms! They don’t share a lot of symptoms. HOWEVER!! They are extremely and highly comorbid, which means you’re more likely to have one if you have the other. I think the comorbidity rate might be like 50% or something but don’t quote me on that. But because they’re so highly comorbid, something got mixed up and people started to think that autism shared ADHD symptoms and ADHD shared autism symptoms. And when people are trying to get diagnosed for autism (because of the very strict and dumb diagnostic criteria for autism), they will often get told they have ADHD instead. When they, in most cases, actually have both and the combination of the highly specific set of criteria you have to meet to be diagnosed for a SPECTRUM CONDITION meaning EVERY EXPERIENCE IS DIFFERENT, and also that the belief ADHD and autism share a lot of symptoms, means they and a lot of other people (usually women or afab people) either get misdiagnosed, or only diagnosed with ADHD when they actually have both. This is a thousand times more common for women or afab people because of the way ADHD usually presents in afab people.

ADHD and autism also both have symptoms that look the same on the surface, but are actually different when you look further into it. “ADHD and autism affect people’s ability to socialise” “ADHD and autism both have sensory problems, and can have sensory overloads” “people with ADHD or autism can have intense interests” are all things that look the same, but are very very different once you actually look into them. Autism is quite literally classed as a social and sensory disorder, if I remember correctly, and ADHD is classed as a developmental disorder like dyslexia (again, if I remembered correctly). “ADHD and autism share symptoms” make sense on the surface, until you actually start to think about it and start doing proper research into them.

I really hope this helps clear up some things because the phrase “autism and adhd share a lot of symptoms” gets under my skin as someone with both. They have a lot in common on the surface, but they don’t share a lot of symptoms.

Author: @TooHazie
Content:
The whole "I have autism" "We knew" "Why didn't you tell me?!" interaction is basically a late diagnosis staple at this point. I was gently pushed to get tested by two of my closest friends at the time who were both autistic after they found out I didn't know I was. Because that's usually the thing - and it develops more the longer you have your diagnosis - for autistic people that know they are autistic it becomes SO OBVIOUS to us when someone else is that it's easy to forget that not everyone knows that about themselves. I had no clue because to me I was just me and that's how I was. I also figured that a lot of what I was experiencing was normal because I wound up hanging out with other autistic people and for some reason it never clicked that I was likely hanging out with them and not allistic (non-autistic) people because I could relate more. In fact, it never even occurred to me that I had more autistic friends than not - often, again, because people usually either don't know and thus don't see it or they DO know and can spot autism a mile away and forget that undiagnosed people usually can't so they don't think to mention it. I usually wind up trying to mention it to people I pick autism vibes up from because of this and because of how much my diagnosis helped me and it's been pretty much the same reaction every time: relief and gentler self-treatment.

Turns out, a condition that affects communication can make communicating about it pretty tricky. Who'd'a Thunk?

Author: @collymonster
Content:
I'm undiagnosed ADHD, been on the NHS waiting list for 2 years already, could be waiting at least another 4, no idea how i will manage because I can't afford to go private.
I'm 35, i joked a lot over the last 15 years about being ADHD but never once did I think I actually was, then along came tik tok and one day the algorithm started showing me ADHD tiktoks and I suddenly felt so heard, everything all made sense, the way I was growing up, the struggles I had in school academically, leaving everything to the last minute because it was like a block in my brain that refused to let me do anything in good time, the disorganisation, loosing everything and yet being able to work very well under immense pressure (I was a chef before I had kids) and it just clicked.
My mum took a bit of convincing when I told her but she believes me now when she looks back on my childhood. you see it really wasn't properly understood in the 90's especially for us women, I dont have the physical hyperactivity that typically presents in boys but the mental chatter is unreal, and I thought that was normal!
I have 2 kids now and my eldest (7F) absolutely has ADHD, she is so much like me as a kid it's honestly a shock that it was never picked up on - I was just labelled as naughty.

I seriously look forward to the day that a doctor can look at me and confirm what I now know, because it really will be a huge relief and a massive weight off my shoulders and will finally confirm to me that I'm not useless, i'm not lazy or rude or any of the things i've been labelled over the years and that there is a genuine reason behind it all.

I know you wont see this Sean but honestly I'm really genuinely very happy for you, please be kinder to yourself, all those negative thoughts you have about yourself are more than likely caused by Rejection Sensitivity Dysphoria which is unfortunately a part of the Neurodivergency package that you have installed!

Author: @takendruid
Content:
I noticed a huge distinction about myself from other autistic people and it’s just that I have some physical inability to be friends with non-autistic people. Can I het along with allistics? Sure! But have I ever made a single allistic friend? No, I don’t think I have. Every single friend I’ve made in my life is either diagnosed, self-diagnosed (which is valid btw), or partially suspected to have autism. Even all my ex-friends are autistic I’m pretty sure. Hell, even my entire adoptive family is autistic (I share a lot more in common with my adoptive family than I do my blood family, it’s weird).

Now this doesn’t mean every autistic person I meet is automatically my friend outside of me having ex-friends, it’s just that everyone I ended up being friends with are autistic… and usually also have ADHD! Like me! And I have no idea why this is, I’m going to be so real, but it might be to do with the fact I can’t and don’t mask.

My adoptive nan realised I was autistic when she first met me because I was exactly like her son, now my uncle, who was diagnosed with Asperger’s. I found out from them I am autistic when I was 13. Unfortunately due to circumstances out of my control and massive medical neglect, I have not been diagnosed, and I am currently even unable to get referred for a diagnosis because of stupid fucking decisions made by the council in/for my area making it so my GP cannot refer adult patients (but when I was a minor, they couldn’t refer child patients. And I missed the very small window to be able to get referred). But anyway!

Because of that, I will never and would never have a “you’re autistic? I never would have guessed” moment if I told anyone close to me that I am autistic if I found out later in life. I am so painfully and obviously autistic to autistic people, and allistic to allistic people with their fucking eyes closed (*cough* my first high school). Out of my friend group, I also have the worst sensory issues even if I wouldn’t be considered the “most autistic” (even though that doesn’t exist).

But yeah, the whole thing about “you’re autistic? But you’re so XYZ” made me think of the fact that I would never have that because everyone in my personal life is also autistic

Content:
I don't even watch your videos that often, and I am not surprised by this. XD

Autism presents itself so differently in folks that it's looks different in two people who have it. Some are very socialable. Others have a hard time socializing. You are very straight forward, get excited playing games, have a focus on video games, and are loud. That can always just be personally traits, but that stuff is also common in Autistics.

Being Autistic isn't bad. It's mostly an explanation for personality quirks! But, one thing I will say is knowing helps Autistics learn how to cope with some of the symptoms that aren't great. Louds noises, over stimulation, not reading social ques well, rough communication, and other things are more easily managed and helped just by knowing you have to deal with them. And knowing means finding help for these things!

Autisim isn't bad, it's just you.

Content: Well, glad to see someone talk about it. The last year, I have been trying to let more people in on a request I got from a friend that passed away a few years ago to let more people in and remove the masks. I can't get tested for this stuff, as I believe I have a fear of hospitals and medications. I know I'm introverted, and I overthink everything a lot. I do say I don't like people, but if someone asks for help, I will move mountains to help them out. I think the fear started 23 years ago. I was surrounded by psychiatrists, and something broke, or my mind went on a lockdown, not allowing anyone in. used to be a completely different person before that but was afraid of a lot more things. After the lockdown of my mind, most of the fears went away, but new ones popped up, like hospitals and meds. To such a point I haven't walked into a hospital or pharmacy in over 20 years. I freeze in front of the door or gate and can't move closer. So now I have these masks, each one for a different thing, and in all these years, only one person has been allowed to see me without the mask, and it feels peaceful. I never knew why I did not need the mask around this person; maybe it's due to the fact it won't work, or I trust the person well enough. It's also hard to say, as there was never a mask around this person from the first 5 seconds of meeting.

Author: @jessykak2399
Content:
At 31 I also got diagnosed with both and am in the AuDHD club myself. I was the same, I just wanted answers. I wanted to know why I was the gifted child growing up but as I got older I just struggled more and more. I got diagnosed with a bunch of chronic illnesses and things still got worse. Finally realised there was more than just anxiety and depression going on. It also allows me to go a bit easier on myself. It also helped me begin to move out of the mindset that I was a failure or broken or that there was something wrong with me. I said the same thing to those close to me in my life, I'm still the same person, it doesn't change that, it just gives me a better understanding of myself and my struggles. But just a heads up and forewarning, you start to realise it affects everything. Looking back on stuff, sure, there were definitely signs (especially sensory ones) but you also start to realise it affects every part of yourself and the way you do and respond to things. I know that seems obvious but it hit me harder than I thought it would of. But that also makes sense because it's a brain type, so of course it affects everything. 
I'm glad you've gotten some answers now. 
And also just a little note to any other neurodivergents out there, you're not broken or wrong and you don't need to be 'cured' either. I know it's what hurt the most hearing from my family (they asked if the doctors could cure me now they knew it was autism) so I wanted to let others that may need to hear it too. It's hard, for sure, but you are the way you're supposed to be, it's just now time to try and accept yourself and that you are NOT alone.

Author: @trentonloomis9565
Content:
Only just saw this so I thought I'd talk about myself a bit.

Autism is prevalent in my family, I have at least 3 family members on the spectrum, so chances are very well could be.

Do I care? No. Am I getting tested for it? No. Because it would change literally nothing about my life.

There are a lot of things Jack has mentioned now and in the past that I... just can't agree with. I don't hold anything against him, that would be stupid.

I'm nearing the age where I can no longer use my age as an excuse for being unproductive. When Jack talks about inherent ridiculousness of "people remembering you after you die" and how narcissistic it may seem. I feel like anything less would be self-hatred or degradation.

I... can't see it that way. I've spent the first 18 years of my life being unproductive, that's enough. I don't see it as being remembered, I see it as affecting HOW you are remembered.

I don't want to be the guy who reached his goal, and got comfortable, and stopped reaching for anything new. I WANT to overwork myself. I WANT to be remembered as the guy who reached his dreams, then found more and reached those. I want to be a role model, an inspiration to those around me as the guy who pushes through any sort of doubt or hesitation he has.

A lot of what he says regarding mental health is really intelligent and is perfectly valid, but I don't see life that way in that specific regard.

Author: @BloodsireArchitectGM
Content:
Was diagnosed 4 months ago through a friends connection, i was so happy to be diagnosed with AUDHD as now there was a reason why i act the way i do, i had good social skills through out my life by reading body language and using particular tones and word choice and try not to irritate people or just to leave a conversation without any drama but i did not know that it was still something caused by my Autism,. For awhile i just assumed that was because i was an Introvert but if you had any social skills you cannot have Autism because Autism back in the day was treated as just the High Functioning or low Functioning types, i did not study the term Introvert i just heard it in passing and assumed it ment you dont like hanging out socially and so i labeled myself an introvert. Next when ive been unable to focus i was unaware that it was my ADHD but instead thought that i was just Stupid and lazy then immediately feeling upset that im unable to hit any of my goals, it did not help that i had a weird and rough family life and school life. My parents just told me to do better when i was bad in school and i had the oldschool dad who would bring out the belt for discipline. Looking back my parents partied alot and i can see the signs my parents may have had the same Mental Divergence as well expecially when the doc told me during my Diagnosis that alot of folks with Autism and ADHD and both often get it geneticly but they are gone now and so ill never know. Anyway before i Rant even more i felt alot of things were wrong with me or rather just different, theres no way i was just incompetent all the time and unable to feel like a normal person i always called myself lazy but having so much self hate youde think would motivate myself to action, it sometimes does but in short bursts and not for the long run ive now spent so much of my life just surviving off coping habits and barely getting by even though there are dreams of being a TTRPG channel maker or a Video game designer ive felt lost all the time even when trying to begin working on something i know i like and i hope soon i can get some progress towards my happiness and anytime people told me just work on yourself ive always thought thats what im trying to do but its not working..... When i was diagnosed i felt better i was releived there was something to call what i had, now of course it does not stop the Autistic or ADHD symptoms and habits but it does help to know so that way if you know what your struggling with you can be a little easier on yourself as Sean said and also find not a solution as there is no 1 trick pony or 1 quick fix but a way to make it comfortable and work alongside your daily plans. This part im still working on but it does give me hope that my work will pay off someday maybe. I now have a few more ideas in how to make my life a little easier.

I know not every one will be able to get a diagnosis its either expensive or has long wait lists expecially if you dont have insurance, but just dont be so hard on yourself, do some honest look into your mental and physical habits and do some research and try your best and if you can see someone because you really want to know and want to take steps but if you believe you are on the spectrum take small little steps to help yourself. Author: @senatorpalpabean2638
Content:
I highly suspect that I've got AuDHD, so seeing this video and hearing the perspective of someone with both diagnoses is really helpful! I relate to just about everything you've said here. I should really get tested... Once I get insurance, I'm going to get that checked out. I used to have an ADD diagnosis (back when that was a label that was used), but they revoked it when I reacted poorly to Adderall. As a child. On a high dose. Lots of kids get hyperactive symptoms from Adderall in that situation.

I especially relate to the communication thing! Every conversation follows a script in my mind, and if something is off-script, then I switch to the "other script" to keep going. It's like a dialogue tree and I have to respond appropriately according to the option's proper answer. I've memorized the scripts for all sorts of small-talk to get me through. But the scripts also depend on their body language and tone- both of which I'm CONSTANTLY overanalyzing to figure out whether or not I'm boring them with my rambles or if I've said something wrong. My mind is constantly racing with all the things I have to do in order to hold a normal conversation: the script, how to position/hold myself, what my face is doing, what their face is doing, how they're holding themselves, tone and volume of myself and the person I'm talking to, telling myself LOOK THEM IN THE EYES DO IT LOOK THEM IN THE EYES IT'S UNCOMFORTABLE BUT YOU GOTTA DO IT!!! And also all the surrounding stimuli that I'm trying to process at the same time!! Horrible, hate it, 0/10 but I'm apparently fairly decent at it as far as anyone else is concerned. 

And the sensory issues!! I was diagnosed with misophonia, but it's more than just sound processing issues. I can't touch certain textures, I can't eat foods with certain textures (looking at you, mushrooms), I can't be around smelly stuff,  and I CAN'T do chores that involve vomit/feces, old/wet food, etc. We've got two cats in my family house, and it upsets everyone that I CAN'T do the litter box, and it's so hard to explain why that is.

And just... everything else! Developmental delays, "childish" interests when I "should have grown out of them," extreme emotions/sense of justice, the executive dysfunction and overstimulation, depression, anxiety, and so many other things that I'm just too lazy to list (I've typed enough already, lmao).

I was diagnosed with Asperger's back when that was a diagnosis.  A lot of people said I didn't seem autistic to them, I seemed "normal".  That proved to be the worst part. Author: @FSE-Star
Content:
Sean, you are my heart and soul. I have been watching your content for a full decade now (a friend on Tumblr of all places got me hooked on you), and while I don't typically reach out and leave comments (I'm a "quietly show them love with a like" type) I just had to tell you how much you mean to me. 

I cannot name a single creator I've kept up with for more than a year or two. I feel like I lose connection with the person, their work, etc. and move on. I've always been like that- socially a nomad, never staying anywhere or with anyone for too long. But I've been with you, watching all of your videos for the last 10 years. Even though I'm not interested in two thirds of the games you play, I've always felt so strongly about you. I knew you were different from others, like how I'm different. You're sensitive, thoughtful, kind, straightforward, and you try so hard to help others. In a world where people are so self involved, where everyone seems so wrapped up in themselves, you were genuine and selfless. I have always admired you. But there was something more, I just knew it. We were like kindred souls. 

The day you told the world you had ADHD, I began to wonder if maybe I had it too. I have a little bit of psychology under my belt, and I guess I already kind of suspected it. But seeing you go out there and get diagnosed lit a fire under me. I went and saw a medical professional for the first time since I graduated high school- in 2010. While I was at it, I had them do the test for ASD, as several members of my family are Autistic, and I am very much like them. May of this year, right after my 32nd birthday, I was diagnosed as Autistic. Everything made sense after I got my diagnosis. And now, even the kinship I felt with you makes sense to me. ASD people can often have a strong sense of right and wrong, and be very giving, helpful, and kind. I think there's an unspoken connection between us Neruodivergent people. And I know I'm younger than you, but I'm taller, so the other day when you said you were always looking for an older sibling type- I want you to know that I nearly punched my way through the internet to give you a big old bear hug, ask you about your day, and make you dinner. Take care of yourself. I'm so happy for you, and I hope your diagnosis can help you find skills and therapy to help you live a better, happier life. I love you, lil' broski. 

Also, I too struggle a lot with textures- especially in food. I was always the "weird and picky," eater. And I'm very sensitive to scent. I love strong, good smells. I'm addicted to cologne and perfume. But, like you, I can smell shite a mile away. And I am very introspective and tend to overthink things as well. Happy Thankmas, hope you have a good show. And stay safe!! I'm proud of the work you do!

Author: @darlthris
Content:
Autism is something that isn't considered rare anymore. So many people are told they have some form of mental difference. It isn't something to consider a disability outright, more like a means to approach it differently, especially when it comes to learning. I HAVE Autism and I couldn't care less. Even when I was told I had Autism in middle school two decades ago, I shrugged to myself. Why did that matter?  They told me I may be socially awkward, I may learn things not the same way as most people do. And I can agree to that, just not to me. I can SEE how they think I may be that way, I won't deny I could be a introvert, I could like certain things. When I think more about myself, I am actually not a people person and if a stranger came to me negatively, I'm gonna react in kind. If I am going to be taught something, I am going to ask "How" to do it, just don't tell me and expect that words alone is enough, SHOW ME how it is done. Most of my experience for being a person with Autism is a WIDE spectrum, and depending on it, it can be managed. And if they don't have a way to do it, they are failing you and you're often left to deal with it yourself. I had to overcome my ability to learn English when it comes to spelling, grammar, anything in that category and that happened well after high school. They FAILED me because they couldn't teach me even when I asked.

Autism could be anything and some will have a harder time with others who may or may not realize you or someone has it, let alone which kind. And like you came around stating, it may not even be important but comes down to what makes you tick ultimately and you end up having more insight and realizing what caused your past events to happen, and reinforces your future to overcome it. Autism is something that goes downright undiagnosed and we may have lived our lives without realizing it, imagine so many adults who are 10-50 farther than our age and if you told them to get checked and they come back being Autistic, they'll be surprised and thought they were just 'weird' or originally and primarily diagnosed with ADHD or something else. Those people tend to be as "Normal" as anyone else, me included but I don't live a life knowing this, I just...live not caring I do, I just approach things differently and some people may not see or think the same way as I do.

That said, Autism or not, whether it be me, you, or anybody else in this comment section, we just have to realize this is a 'thing' now apparently.

I was very much was the same in terms of “peace of mind” everyone around me was like “he’ll grow out of it” or “aren’t you a bit too old to like this?”

Asthma? Check! 
Hyper mobility? Check! 
Anxiety , depression? Check! 
Digestinal problems? Check! 

I asked why I was diagnosed younger when it was “obvious” and was told “it wasn’t thing really” 

But also people say stuff like “oh you want a diagnoses just for an excuse!” - no… I wanted answers for myself, the pieces all coming together and that I was just me?! 

Having people view autism as a bad thing when you tell them is such a disheartening thing… we need more awareness. People need to be educated on what autism is and how it differs.

Author: @blu5018
Content:
Adhd and autism aren't the same thing. They have a lot of similar symptoms and they're both processing disorders but they absolutely are not on the same spectrum. 

It's very common that people with ADHD have autism. ADHD can not quite cause but you can get Depression, Anxiety, etc as a result of not managing ADHD symptoms.

They organize autism into levels based on how much it affects your life now because autism/aspergers didn't work and you can't categorize based solely on the drive to communicate. 

When people say that they don't notice you're bad at socializing its because we mask. It feels like everyone else got a handbook to socializing that you never got and you basically make your own. You find human behavior fascinating because you don't understand and other people work differently and then you notice that it was actually you that worked differently. You sit there and ask questions about why other people do the things they do and then you ask those questions about yourself. 

You learn empathy faster than other people with autism because you see that you're different and you feel different and you feel alone. You become the person you wish you had because you know how terrible it was. 

People that are drawn to art have something to say. It makes the best art and it makes sense that people who feel like they aren't understood would seek to be understood through art. 

I can't remember where I read it but there's something that happens when kids get older where they lose the hypersensitivity they have as kids but people with ADHD and Autism don't. I think it was neurons but its how kids grow quickly as babies and partially why they're so sensitive to everything. 

The reason I don't get an official diagnosis is because you can be denied life saving organ transplants because people believe that people with autism and downs syndrome are less worthy. It can affect your ability to adopt kids and legally jobs can pay you less because of your disability.

3:03 don't think those things are likely. It's or not likely aaalllll of them. They are just more likely then without ASD people. 
6:05 legacy is the same as ego/narcissism. What? Aren't you the one doing charity each year. That's part of your legacy bro. You don't have to have a big ego to do it. Just a big heart. You have that. Just don't confuse the two.

10:20 ""no I am just introverted". You are probably just autistic" sorry what? That not how it works. Author: @AllahWhoSnackBar-is9dg
Content: Hi Jack. I really appreciate what you had to say in this video. I'm really proud of what you're doing with raising awareness and making this the focus for thankmas. A few years ago, I wanted to get tested for autism. I felt very concerned that if I didn't that it would hold me back in life if I didn't have the answers. I never wanted to be tested just to be able to blame random things on having autism but I just felt like it would serve to me as a bit of clarity. I never did get tested. But as you said, I'm still the same person exactly where I am in life, no better no worse. Thing is, I probably do have autism (as my sister has ADHD and austism and apparently if you have a sibling with ADHD/autism you are highly likely to have it too). I'm not too good with loud and unexpected sounds. I have an insatiable fixation and passion for cars and everything about them. I hyperanalyse everything I see, say and do, especially during conversations with others. When I talk with other people, sometimes they say that I'm really good at relating to them or just understanding how they feel, and they'll tell me that I'm like a therapist/psychologist. I'm not. So while I might show strong indication for having autism, I'll never know because I won't bother to be tested. Whether I have it or I don't I too like to think of it as my superpower. My passion for cars gives me direction in my life, as I plan to become a mechanical engineer working for Porsche building 911 GT3 race cars. Along with that, I like to think that my ability to relate to other people and have deep conversations with them about their emotions or whatever it is we're talking about helps other people feel seen with their experiences even if I haven't had the exact same experience as them. My point is, thank you. Thank you for being vulnerable and by extension helping other people feel comfortable with themselves and seeing their so called "mental disorder" as a superpower to have a positive impact on this world even if it is a small one. Take care of yourself.

Author: @eyy_its_danny7584
Content:
It might sound weird to say this but congrats on the diagnosis. I also have AUADHD, I was somewhat late diagnosed, so I somewhat understand. The mix of autism and ADHD can be a bit of a "fun mix", please try not to obsess around the ADHD medication side of things, in my experience it won't work the same way it does with solely adhd people, it is an assistant,t not a fix. If you need to concentrate try experimenting with what can keep you focused, I tend to watch documentaries and podcasts as background noise to concentrate, others need to be using their hands, and I can't do something without having something else to do.
I completely agree with the perception of autism, people don't believe someone is autistic unless they are the non-verbal "low functioning" type, I think people don't realise that people who are late diagnosed usually have to "train" themselves how to fit in, masking is a massive thing that can happen without realising that you are doing it, it can be hard to get diagnosed because not realising you are masking can mean you don't know how to stop masking, therefore, it can be hard even for professionals to recognise.
If you can try to find therapists that have experience with autistic people because our mental health can present differently.

And it can be almost impossible to see, autism deserves awareness as it affects us day to day and some people dont realise it, some day if someone ends up getting diagnosed they will realise how much knowing what you have does help, and gives you so many helping hands with moving through your day, thanks jack

Author: @TheOneMagpie
Content:
"I've always said I have a really good judge of character" is honestly a recurring phrase I hear from autistics, including myself. I think, between your reason, another massive reason is that your judge of character is skewed to seek comfort in people who match your communicative wavelength, which for the longest time you likely weren't realising was due to your autistic pattern of thinking needing people who act and communicate in a certain way that makes them easier to read (such as traits like honesty, deeper discussion, etc.)

It's no surprise that there's a domino effect when one person gets diagnosed with ADHD or autism, that their friends start going "wait a minute... am I, too?". Your 'judge of character' is bound to attract people that are like yourself, and in turn those people will more likely reciprocate you because they're seeking that same sort of communication often due to their own autistic traits.

Content:
I can't imagine someone as beloved as Jack saying they ever felt like an outsider.



Once, in Creative Writing class, we were talking about what high school movie stereotypes we would be. I made the silly choice of asking what I am. Teacher answered immediately.

The Loner.

No duh. When are you really given time, or incentive, to interact? Especially if you're an introvert who needs alone time to decompress, or live far from the school and need an hour+ to get home. Only if you're just straight up slacking, or doing something that doesn't require writing (writing is about 95% of the workload there) can you work and talk at the same time. And they put so much weight on your performance in school, the shame of being A Failure outweighs the desire to... be... known, even.

The school system is awful. Especially in rural areas, where everyone who lives there do so because they're old and hateful.

Author: @overthinkinggamer7377
Content: I am so glad you figured this out and it is such a good thing for you, as it sounds like. A couple years ago I looked into having ADHD and finally got on medication in my mid 20s (im 28 now), and i remember the feeling of "oh I can actually organize my thoughts more and not spiral into disassociation because I can't focus on how to do one thing at a time. It was always "well, I have to do this to do this and then I'll have to do this," and it just never ended. And when I took meds for the first time, I remember actually starting to organize my home for the first time and being able to actually keep things mostly organized and not as messy. For me, it definitely felt like a huge change in my brain. And, only now am I beginning to reprogram my brain into understanding that I have this disorder and it makes my life harder, so I can't necessarily always do what I think I should be doing or what others are doing, and "going easy on myself." I also had a rough time at college, dropping out after two years and for a long time I did not understand why. I felt like a complete failure and have struggled with that for a long time. The major thing I still struggle with the most is how much time I feel was "wasted" as a result of having this disorder and never knowing about it. Like, where could I be now if I had known about this years ago. Remembering that those years weren't wasted, and sort of "forgiving" (not that I necessarily caused it or anything) and being ok with your past self is definitely a hard part of the healing process. I also didn't know that Autism and ADHD were kind of the same thing and you can have both until one of my friends was also diagnosed with both. And, it's interesting kind of learning about the parallels between both as well as the differences. Thank you for trying to normalize this stuff because for over twenty years I thought ADHD was just the stereotypical kid who can't sit still and talks all the time. And, then when I heard the way ADHD people's brains actually work, so much made sense. I remember feeling like "OH MY GOD, I'M NOT JUST A LAZY PIECE OF GARBAGE. I'M LITERALLY CARRYING AROUND THIS DISORDER (and more), AND IT MAKES MY LIFE 100x HARDER THAN THE AVERAGE PERSON." So, yes, thank you for talking about this because without people talking about it, I may still never have known and would still be struggling to just get up in the morning. 🖤🖤🖤

Author: @HeavensMemory
Content:
It's nice to see people talking openly about neurodivergents and mental health. 
Problem with the ADHD-Autism-combo is, from what I've heard, that certain aspects of them can interfere with one another in a way that makes diagnosing both of them at the same time really hard. People look at you and see your ADHD-aspects, that don't fit in with an autism diagnosis, so they assume you aren't autistic and the other way around. Also many people believe the "non-verbal" aspect of autism to be universal but the fact is, its more like general abnormalities and difficulties in communication. Analysing body language, tone, setting and everything else is usually mostly on auto-pilot but with autism you have to do all those things manually. So autistic people can appear to be rude or act inappropiatly, not because they want to,  but because they misjudge a situation (based on lack of information or missreading the room) or the impact their action will have. Getting a diagnosis can mean so much to people, who struggled with social interaction and other aspects of life for as long as they can think. Life won't be easier all of a sudden, but at least now you know what you are dealing with and can adjust to it in a fitting way.

Author: @TheSuperEmily
Content:
I also just got my autism diagnosis (yesterday)! 

I had to go the public way, so it's been a 2 year waiting time for me, which was awful. To anyone who's out there with a hunch that they could have autism, and considering getting it diagnosed: trust your gut and go get it assessed! My boyfriend was the ONLY person who believed that I could be autistic, and it was so mentally taxing to keep being told that I'm "normal" and "everyone struggles with that". 

If you are struggling, that's okay and there's help to get. If you can't afford getting an assessment, self-diagnosing is okay, if it will help you mentally and in your daily life. It is not embarrassing to have a diagnosis, but it is really frekking cool to be brave and stand up for yourself. 

Thank you Seán for speaking out about this. The internet helped me realise I have autism, and I'm sure you spreading awareness is also going to help someone.

Author: @EmillyOrr
Content:
See, this is part of the problem. At least in the US, researchers are finding that ADHD quite often pairs with autism, and as you said, can be *the same exact thing*--but Autism Speaks and a couple generations of anti-vaxxers have created this monolithic cultural understanding: Autism means your kid is broken. Autism means your kid is irreparably harmed. Autism means have the funeral now and mourn BIG for the loss of your child...who is STANDING RIGHT THERE. 

Even when we're talking the "classic" perception of autism--a completely non-verbal kid that has to wear a helmet all the time, can't meat their parents; eyes, just rocks in the corner, will never go to college and fulfill their parents' Harvard dreams--guess what? We HAVE technology now. The sheer TONNAGE of folks who got handed a tablet or a keyboard, and realized they can communicate with the folks who ignore them because they're "damaged"...

They'rre not damaged. It's a different way brains are wired. Get over it.

(sorry for the rant, but my gods, it's not a death sentence. It's never been a death sentence. It just requires adaptive tools, and understanding.)

It took getting chronically ill for me to realise that it might not be just anxiety I was experiencing. It's gonna be a long wait but it'll be worth it for me. People also asked me why I would want to know and well, I want validation and answers. I got the depression and hypermobility and I beat myself up for years as to why I found everything so much harder than my peers, why people would just disappear on me, why I felt ill when I'd have to go into school/work every day.

I'm about the same age as you, so yeah, I was a bit shook when I realised I probably am one or both because I was just the shy, quiet kid who kept to themselves and nobody looked deeper than that (I didn't even know what anxiety was). I kept my interests to myself because I realised most people would think it's odd. Nowadays it's all the rage but I had to hide my love for Naruto, Zelda, Final Fantasy and my fantasy books for fear of being bullied. I tried so hard to be someone I'm not to try and be successful and I ended up disabled and ill for all my efforts. It was a hard pill to swallow and I wish I'd known sooner and been truer to myself. I'm trying to find myself again and have got back into my art and am following creative pursuits.

I'm happy you've got your diagnosis Sean, try to be a little easier on yourself ❤

Author: @aodhancampbell7507
Content:
Hi Seán (idk if the accent is important to you for people to remember but as an Aodhán I know I appreciate it), fellow autistic here. 

I’m really happy to hear about how you’re handling it, because like you, I also didn’t get diagnosed until adulthood, even though I seem like (I think, at least) a person with their shit somewhat together. 

Autism is what you make of it, and if other people want to make something bad of it, that’s on them. Just know that if you play to your strengths, and yes, autism often comes with those, too, very few people will be able to do what you love like you can. 

You also don’t have to embrace it like an identity; like you said, it doesn’t have to change things. But there are some things, if you’re interested in this sphere of conversation, that I recommend you look into. Like the dehumanising, ableist principles Autism Speaks operates on. Or the Judge Rotenberg Educational Centre, which “treats” autism in children with electroshock therapy. Trigger warning for the latter, some of the documented abuses are really sick stuff. Both are issues of great importance to much of the autistic community, and both operate on U.S. soil. A platform like yours could be seriously helpful for taking the conversation, which has been the same for years and which doesn’t even really CONSULT autistics, to new and valuable places.

Content:
Congratulations! Welcome to the late Diagnosis AuDHD gang! 

As someone who also got diagnosed earlier this year, I can relate heavily to what you were talking about with the over analysing everything and everyone in social situations. When I was talking about it with my doctor she called it my Decision Tree. If I see this person doing this thing with their body language it means this thing, thus they are feeling this emotion, thus I should react in this way and say this thing in order to get the desired outcome of this conversation. And of course sometimes I get it wrong because I'm analysing things from a logical standpoint based on what I've learned or been told about human psychology and behavioural patterns and I don't have that innate understanding that neurotypical people do. 

A big part of unmasking for me has been trying to relax and stop analysing everything all the time and just reacting naturally to things instead. Not watching everyone for a reaction at all times and just responding with what I really think and feel rather than what I think they want me to say. This is of course much easier said than done and it's not the kind of thing I can do just anywhere with anyone but around my friends and people that I trust I've been trying to unmask and relax so I don't end up so tired and burnt out all the time.

Author: @EzraPlutoCharles
Content:
As a fellow AuDHDer who also struggles with all of the other mental and physical health issues that you listed as commonly occurring with AuDHD, mental health and neurodivergence are some of my special interests. I find it extremely fascinating how much overlap there is. Co-morbidity is so common.
I was technically tested when I was 4 but never told what the results were til I was later, but I still didn't know what my results meant as they never said the word in the document I was given, but they do outline my symptoms. I didn't know what Autism actually was until I was 21 and my therapist at the time told me that he suspects I have it. Then I researched and found what info I had been missing my whole life.
I know a lot of times, parents may not want their child to know they are autistic or neurodivergent in general as they believe the lack of a label would prevent them from being bullied for it. Well, news flash. Most kids will still get bullied for their autistic traits regardless of whether they know they are autistic. That was my experience. Tons from Grade 1-9, and it followed me into adulthood. If I had known I am autistic a lot earlier, and could comprehend what it actually is, then at least I would have known WHY the other kids didn't like me.

Author: @agoodwasteoftime
Content:
To correct a little misinformation: adhd and autism are not “on the same spectrum” or “one and the same”, that idea was spread around a lot a little while ago, but there’s not much truth to it. They’re just soo commonly comorbid that people are led on to believe so, but most who have both can tell, because they sort of fight each other. Like the adhd in me wants to be spontaneous and wants change but the autism wants everything to stay the same and gets uncomfortable with change. And for me, the hyperactive adhd part is all in my head. My head goes 10000mph, but to everyone else i probably look a little lost, very quiet, never has much to say.

For me, communication is probably the biggest way autism affects me. I really struggle with it. It’s why I’m a writer: my thoughts are so much clearer and concise when I write, as opposed to getting scattered, or just not coming out at all, verbally. I’m not a great masker. I can force eye contact to a certain extent but then it starts to hurt. I can hide stims, but I can’t force myself to be talkative and have things to say. I forget to ask questions in conversations, so they end quickly and I think I come off as rude to people. I think it takes someone patient and also someone chatty who’s happy to be listened to, to be friends with me. As a result I don’t have many friends, not in person. But I have lots of lovely online friends and they’re my best friends and I wouldn’t change them for the world. 

Anyway, welcome to the club, Sean! Enjoy all the moments of “ohhhhhh that was autismmmmm” and “oh wait fuck am I autistic? What if I’m not? What if this is all a lie? What if I’ve just been a master manipulator and convinced the assessor and myself that I’m autistic when I’m not?!!?!??” 

Yay so fun. /s

Content:

Content:
Oh boy, welcome to the club. The social anxiety, eye contact avoidance (in my case) the rambling, the sensory issues, nonexistent attention span, gastrointestinal, I have it all It feels so validating to learn why your mind functions the way it does. Author: @Vesper_Eveningstar
Content:
Fellow AuDHDer here. I just want to say a few things to hopefully provide some insight both into the community and just about autism in general. But first of all, I just want to say that we all love and support you. ❤

One of the things you mentioned was that ADHD meds haven’t felt like they’ve helped you much compared to others. I also recently started meds and they’ve definitely helped me, but it’s still a struggle. One thing myself and fellow AuDHDers have noticed, is that for us, when we take meds it also accentuates the autistic traits a bit more, possibly bcs often times ADHD and autistic traits cancel each other out a bit, so that could be a potential factor in meds for you.

Another thing you touched on briefly was that stuff like mild, severe, and high/low functioning is language that we don’t really use more. And like you said, part of that is bcs it’s derogatory. But I also just want to provide some more information on why, cuz that’s just one piece of it. One of the other big pieces is that it’s simply inaccurate. That language tends to insinuate that the spectrum is a line that you fall somewhere on, but it’s not a line. One analogy ppl like to use is that it’s like a sound board, with each dial representing a different autistic trait and that each one varies. But that also the dials can change throughout time, whether over a few years or even throughout the day. The language that we tend towards is high/low support needs, with ppl like you and me being low support needs bcs we’re able to generally navigate the world on our own, whereas high support needs autistics need day to day support. I like what one person said on TT of the differentiation. Is that low support needs autistics are able to adapt/mask to be able to get through life, whereas high support needs autistics can’t do that.

And yes I love how you want to change the industry! I wholeheartedly agree. I think it’s so important to be open (when safe to do so) so that ppl can learn and hopefully change the world for the better.

This is more on the ADHD side, but one thing that ppl with ADHD often experience is rejection sensitive dysphoria (RSD). I mentioned this to a few of my friends and they were like “Oh my god, that’s exactly how it feels, thank you for the language to express what it feels like” so I wanted to bring it up in case it’ll do the same for you. And that’s what RSD feels like (at least for me, it might feel different for others) is that it feels like a wave of depression just comes over my body when someone tells me no. Even simple things that make sense to say no to, it still feels awful. And it’s a tough thing to balance cuz I don’t want others to feel pressured to say yes just so that I don’t feel bad.

I wish you the best of luck in your journey as you continue to discover things about how autism looks for you and how you can better navigate it while also working towards being your authentic self. Again, we love you Sean.

Author: @thecommander9137
Content:
Hi Jack, Fellow Autist here. Now, I won't tell you that exactly how yours differs from mine, but as far as I know (I've only been diagnosed for 7 years, and I'm now 25, so it's likely that I'm missing some elements).

There's little to no physical identifiers to Autism, most physical obviously relate to non-verbal communication, like intense staring, or avoiding eye contact, lack of gestures, lack of facial expressions or inappropriate facial expressions (meaning it doesn't fit the situation, not the type of inappropriate). Something like Astma is more genetic than mental, which is where Autism comes from.

We are Neurodivergent, meaning our brains are wired differently to people who are neurotypical or NT's (or as like to call it, "Normal thinking"). A good way to think of it, as I've understood after a hard fight is we autists drive on a train tracks (we need order and system on everything, and can't really diverge from our tracks) and NT's drive cars (much more flexible, can diverge on plans or ways of thinking) this causes autists to generally be bad at communication as we can't truly put ourselves into other people's minds. 
NT's sees the forest and then the trees, we with Autism see the trees then the forest. And while ADHD and Autism does overlap, it's not necessary, if you have ADHD you might not have Autism, but if you have Autism you are very likely to also have ADHD, there's a reason why both can be diagnosed independently of each other. 

Quick note: and trust me here, you will fight the Diagnosis, I also thought I were happy with getting the Diagnosis and that it would give me answers, but turns out I fought against my Psychologist as I wouldn't believe it to be true. 
Then there's also differences in how we think, I generally went through college without problems (though I never did my homework, why should I? We would get the answers the following day) I simply don't have the ability to study anymore, at least not on university levels, as I pass college, first one to do so where I live, allegedly.

Regarding legacy and ambition, if anything this shows your Autism, as Autists like order and routine, we are generally fine with status quo. To autists, (again I can't speak for all and primarily use my experience, and I've learned), as long as the day still works we are happy, as long as routine isn't broken we go to bed happy. Normal thinking people, don't think like that, they think more in doing something, Society we have build caters to Normal people (and psychopaths), Autists, don't fit in therefore Autism is a handicap.

You are correct"ish", that content creators might or could have ADHD, though Autism? No! We don't generally make good content creators due to our mental problems. Also, as far as we know, ~1.7% of the world's population might have autism, there are too many content creators for that statistic to be correct.

I didn't finish the Video yet, but I'm certain I don't have more to offer.

Author: @jurtle999
Content:
Tysm for having this conversation and helping normalize Autism!! 💖💖 I strongly believe there's a high number of "high masking" Autistic people out there who have no idea, the more visibility the better. Also we're subconsciously drawn together, diagnosed/aware of ASD or not. The amount of my old friends I've realized are probably also Autistic. Or that are realizing it themselves now. We're just on similar wavelengths 😂

I realized my AuDHD soon after starting therapy and it was so world changing. I ended up getting a diagnosis, partially as a middle finger to those that didn't believe me, also hoping I could get employment accomodations as that's somewhere I've struggled the most. It took a while to be comfortable and confident in my validity and differences, and I'm still healing and learning to unmask. That shit is SO draining and most ppl don't realize how much energy it takes, just existing around other people 😅 

In car terms, it's like living life in manual mode whereas non-ND people cruise through on automatic, sometimes even cruise control. Like we have to think about. Every. Fucking. Thing. We. Have. To. Do. Like showering? Most people say "yeah I just shower." It's autopilot mode for them. For me, showering is "set up skin/haircare on counter, undress, turn on the water to the right temp, get in, wash hands, wet hair, shampoo, rinse, conditioner (let it sit!), wash body in this specific order, and etc" I'm not writing it all 😂 Along with what feels like at least 3 different conversations going on in my head while doing each task. Basic tasks feel like mountains. And we have to do it all again the next day 😂😭 

What really matters is that I understand myself better, and am learning to take care of myself in ways that actually work for me. Learning that my sensitivities aren't character flaws and deserve to be respected. I found that family didn't take me seriously bc they related too much to the symptoms I talked about, and they reacted with "that's normal, suck it up like I did, you're not special for that or deserve special treatment ((aka basic understanding/decency/accomodations))". I've learned to view their perspectives more objectively and I don't take their opinions to heart anymore. I'm learning to love myself and deserve support, as we all do ❤️‍🩹

Also the amount of ND people who end up in psychology fields is wild 😂 it's a form of masking, we seek to understand how people think/act, so in theory interactions should be more predictable and maneuverable right? Or maybe we can figure out why we feel so different?

Author: @Kewlausgirl
Content:
auADHDer here. I was diagnosed with ADHD in 2021 (at 36 years) and this year I was diagnosed with Autism. For me, I resonated so much more with ADHD than Autism. But what I've learnt now is Autism is there in the background..
I only started looking into it when my ADHD meds were triggering my sensitivities coz I can't handle sweat lol. Yay. And then my partner and I were noticing that I just couldn't let go of things. Or I became even more blank in my expressions at times. Or couldn't tell how I was masking lol. 

Turns out, when I did my autism assessment that I have low self awareness. And it was also a huge pain to go through the autism assessment - not for me - but my parents couldn't remember half the stuff I did as a kid. They couldn't remember the struggles where I couldn't process things or couldn't comprehend why people were angry with me or what I said wrong when .. It was right??
Or they just were in huge denial - still are. But luckily I found out through my older cousins (I'm the baby on both sides of my family lol) their kids have all been diagnosed with ADHD or Autism lol 
And one of my cousin's kids who we both resonated with each other so much when I was in my 20s and she was a kid .... She was diagnosed with ADHD and Autism. 
And I'm like WTF. Why did no one tell me earlier lol. 😅 

Anyhow, Jack and everyone here... I'm so glad there's a community here lol. No wonder I still keep coming back to Jack lol some people you stop watching or whatever, and I do have gaps but I keep coming back lol. 😂❤ You are amazing, Jack!!

Ooh and yeah for that are in the precipice and wondering if they have both ADHD and Autism, then think about how you are with your meds. It helps ADHD? Yes....
But what is suddenly harder for you? 
For me it was sounds were suddenly unable to drown out, became way more hyperfocused a lot of the time on small things than I did before. Sensitivities were harder to ignore. Normally it's only once it's super humid that i couldn't stand hair on my face or neck, but now especially with the sweating side effects, I couldn't cope. I had to dry myself down and just work through it. 
And sounds are so much more intense now. 

I used to power through things and ignore it with my ADHD until I melted down and couldn't figure out why I was melting down. It was awful at times. And I was always trying to process everything. What went wrong. Why. How. Who. Everything. And this is something I'm still trying to get the hang of and I'm learning to try and internalize it coz my partner gets the blunt end of it. 

And that, I used to get told I was complaining or something or nagging when I pointed something out but it was just me literally pointing it out to them because I don't know if they were aware of it. And then mix in ADHD where you constantly forget you told someone lolol 😅😂

The other side is that I'm not sure if it is the same for Jack, is the internal struggle in your mind. 
For me, I want to do things in a certain way or a certain order. But my ADHD mind is like nope, impulse time. Then my autism side suffers.
And cleaning or organising, put it off until it's eating at my insides and I go on a huge cleaning spree and organise everything until it's all done. And I find it hard to stop, I become anxious because if I don't finish it, I might never get back to it lol but I also have that need from the Autism side that wants everything to be out of the way, to be in its place. 

Anyhow there are some great YouTube videos out there that mention the struggles between ADHD and Autism... So hopefully that can help you guys!!
😊

Author: @hlh-os8lc
Content:
I am undiagnosed, but I am sure sure I'm on the autism spectrum and potentially AuDHD, I also suspect that most of my family is on the autistic spectrum as well. I grew up believing something was "wrong" with me, I was given so many labels such as: 'slow', 'weird', 'freak', 'cack-handed', 'stupid', 'shy', when in actual fact, everyone around me was blinded by ignorance and had absolutely no education on what autism is.

The way autism affects me is my brain goes completely blank in social situations, like I genuinely can't think of what to say next in conversations, my socialising has gotten better over time but no one really goes out of their way to talk to me or be my friend, a lot of the time I am very lonely. I feel like everyone around me is in on some inside joke that I'm not cool enough to understand. I am often infantilised (treated like a child) or treated like I'm stupid, however I've also been described as bright and intelligent. I struggled massively in school, I was constantly getting into trouble and I was very slow at processing information. I have sensory issues when it comes to sound and I have Misophonia, I often behave in 'strange' ways when I don't like the sensation of something or I contort myself if my clothes don't feel right. I used to walk on tip toes all the time as a kid which I only found out recently is a common autistic trait.

The ways autism has positively affected my life is that it's made me very creative and inquisitive about the world around me, I love nature, dinosaurs, video games, painting, Pokemon etc, I am a very authentic, laid back person, I don't really care that much about what people think about me or societal expectations and I think its made me a happier person in the long run.

But yeah, to cut a long story short I have many typical signs of autism and other peoples ignorance towards the subject has made my life considerably more unpleasant than it needed to be. I am glad you're bringing this subject to light as many autistic people feel invisible and invalidated by modern society.

Autism isn't a curse, it's a superpower :)

Author: @angelofdusk13
Content: Welcome, Sean! :D I'm 33, and didn't start suspecting I was autistic until a few years ago. I struggled sooooooo much as a kid because I was (and still am!) so weird, and social situations were borderline traumatic. But I worked customer service for a decade, so I learned to mask very well, and I know EXACTLY what you're talking about! When I talk with a stranger or acquaintance, I'm constantly watching their facial expressions and body language to figure out how they're feeling and responding to me, I'm constantly purposefully making eye contact (it's SOOOO uncomfortable), I'm constantly adjusting my facial expression according to what I think the other person expects because I don't naturally emote that way. It's incredibly exhausting and I usually need a whole day to myself to recover lol. And I have so many sensory issues around bright lights, loud noises, clothing, and food--I have so many weird eating habits all because of my texture sensory issues. Thank you so much for sharing with us, and while I'm sorry that you have to deal with the many struggles that comes with being AuDHD, I'm very happy to welcome you into the autistic community. We love you, and we're proud to call you one of us ❤

Content:
Yup, same here (adult diagnosed as AuDHD/OCD with depression/anxiety).  A lot of folks struggle with understanding why we'd want to check with a specialist to see if we're on the spectrum, and while answers vary for each individual the validation I got was so relieving. Author: @troller9838
Content:
I also have Autism and ADHD. Got diagnosed when I was a kid.

Downsides like social anxiety, overthinking things, not liking specific textures of clothing and food can be annoying sometimes, but the upsides of autism can be good. 

I am a highly suspicious person due to my autism, I overanalyse everything, especially people. For example I can tell who's untrustworthy, trying to use me or just a general waste of time to interact with very quickly, much faster then the average person, I notice all their facial expressions, weather they're genuine or fake, as well as how they talk and what they're saying. I am like a human BS detector.

Another advantage is being able to learn stuff quickly, like a sponge soaking up the information, this is very useful, however this only works on stuff that I find interesting. Boring stuff takes longer to learn.

There's good and bad sides of being a high functioning autist, so don't worry about it much jack, in fact it's best to ignore it, that's what I do generally, I don't sit around thinking "Oh I'm autistic" I think of it more as a more as introvertism rather then autism, since I don't really like being around a lot of people all at once, much prefer smaller groups of friends and family.

In public I don't talk to anyone I don't know or have to talk to, I only talk to people I have to, like cashiers for example, but I won't start a conversation with random people in the street, which is what some extroverted people I know sometimes do, which just seems awkward and a waste of time generally. 

However this changes in online games, I will talk to just about anyone in an online game, especially if they're interesting to talk to or share similar humour to mine.

Anyway, you don't need to do anything now you have been diagnosed, it's actually a bad idea to try and alter your behavior since your already well adjusted and such a nice guy already. Just be yourself.

Author: @Leathurkatt
Content:
As a "female" Gen-Xer born in '74, I was literally always the outsider even among outcasts.  I'm an old school Goth Metal Head Thrasher, and of course, because of the Satanic Panic of the '80's, I ended up in Adolescent Hospitals 5 different times (and a Christian Children's Ranch for 16 months, spent my 12th and 13th birthdays there), dealt with multiple different doctors, and given the flavor-of-the-month diagnosis from age 11 to age 16 because "there's something wrong with you but only boys have autism" because I don't fit the narrow-minded fundamentalist evangelical idea of a normal girly girl (I'm generally Androgynous).  I have Hypermobility joint issues, a history of "Falling Seizures" (Petit Mal Seizures), cPTSD, Anxiety, issues with certain textures, sensory sensitivity, I'm an unconscious mimic (I mimic accents and such without realizing it), and hyperfixate on science, puzzles, and arts-and-crafts (drawing, painting, miniatures, chain mail, wire wrapping, jewelry, etc).  I have a hard time getting into video games because I figure them out too easily and get bored with them, unless they're puzzles...  But I really enjoy Tabletop RPGs...  🤷‍♀️  So yeah... that's a thing...

Imagine my surprise when a friend of mine I've known since 1995 tells me she's known I was an Aspie (ASD) for literally years, and in doing research, the more I learn, the more obvious it is that I am DEFINITELY on the Autism spectrum, but can't get a diagnosis because "you're a girl" and "you're too old"...  🤦‍♀️  And yet, my son (currently 23 years old) has been diagnosed by MULTIPLE doctors as being Autistic, yet literally no one bothered to tell me...  He didn't even find out he was diagnosed Autistic until he finally got ahold of his medical records and saw the diagnosis going back to when he was a toddler (and then told me).  Yeah...

Author: @LokiCriwall
Content:
Something very important that you bring up here, is the fact that you are going easier on yourself is exactly what a lot of neurodivergent people need to learn to do to themselves. One thing I've learned when I was diagnosed, like you said, was that I was measuring myself up to a neurotypical standard that just doesn't work with my disorders, something every neurodivergent person can learn from. 

That doesn't mean that one's disorder should be a crutch or an excuse to use for bad behaviour as some unfortunately do (tho tbf it's usually the neurotypical people surrounding the neurospicy person that does this only to condemn them in the same sentence..), but it does tell you to just slow down and do things in your own tempo, at your own speed.

I personally have Schizotypal Personality disorder, which include AuDHD, plus depression and anxiety, I also have asthma and I got operated for an intestine problem in my early twenties related to all of this. So I can definitely relate to this, Seán. Many of us do in fact!

Thank you for talking about your experience with getting your Autism (and by extension AuDHD) diagnosis, the social stigma surrounding mental health, as well as the process of continuing to figure out yourself when stuff doesn't quite make sense even during your initial diagnosis of ADHD!

Author: @0r1g1n4l_
Content:
I'm really glad that you talk about these topics, Jack. I raised the question myself to my designated care facility and got a brief assessment conducted there by a psychiatrist. They aren't allowed to do a proper assessment and give a diagnosis though. They sent a referral along with their assessment to our local psychologist clinic, but they denied it with their conclusion being that I didn't seem to be affected enough for them to assess me. It's worth noting that the wait time for a diagnosis can go up to years here so, they have to narrow down who they put their time into. I respect that, but it still hurts to be rejected when you've already realised that you relate to the experiences of so many people with ADHD and autism. I still believe I have inattentive ADHD and mild autism, but apparently it isn't disruptive enough in my day to day according to them. I'd likely have to go to a private psychologist clinic if I hope to get diagnosed at this point, but I can't afford that.

Having had my eyes opened to likely having both I can at least look for ways to lessen some of my symptoms myself now, contrary to when I was oblivious to it, since I don't show like the more common stereotype.

If you read this far, thank you.
I appreciate you and I hope you get the help you need, if you need help, to lead a truly fulfilling life. Sending you lots of love! ❤

A doctoral researcher and long term Jacksepticeye fan making his first YouTube comment here! I've watched this video multiple times now and I can definitely say Sean sums up a lot of challenges reported to me by autistic college students. 

Autistic students have a really tough time in higher education for a variety of reasons and the majority report negative feelings and mental health issues.

What struck me as even more was Sean pointing out that autistic people often wish to distance themselves from  their autism diagnosis. And that brings me to the reason I'm making this comment. 👇

TLDR: Autistic people should not distance themselves from their diagnosis and instead engage with it to better understand themselves and help their community (sort of what is going on in this very comments section) 

My current research field focuses on harnessing digital technologies to improve the mental and physical health of autistic adults (i.e. everything from social media and YouTube, to conversational artifical intelligence). Exciting stuff! 

I'm passionate about the health of the growing population of autistic people but I really struggle with recruiting members of this population for my research due to some of the reasons Sean mentions on this video!

Understandably, people don't wish to be defined by an autism diagnosis but by trying to avoid addressing it they will be unable to contribute to initiatives that seek to help autistic people.

Recruiting has and continues to be an issue for my research so here is my main message to whoever is kind enough to read all of this: My own research aside, please consider contributing to any initiatives or projects that seek to improve the health of autistic populations.

Thanks to Sean for speaking so openly about his autism diagnosis in his own way. 🚂 You can see the benefit of it as you continue scrolling through these comments. 😊 And thanks to you for hearing a neurotypical casual out in an very long comment!

Author: @reyelkhaert
Content:
Finally receiving my diagnosis last year was such a weight off my shoulders. I'd been dealing with particularly aggressive anxiety and depression from a young age, and even after years of treatment something was just... Wrong. I could feel that something was still off. Something that wasn't being addressed that really, really needed to. 

The Internet and social media can absolutely be a cesspool, but tiktok slowly began feeding me content about being autistic and it began to dawn on me that a lot of what these autistic people were experiencing, i was experiencing as well. Thank you for talking about it, because a lot of people, especially afab people, are looked over because they don't fit what a lot of people perceive as autistic. 

People likely will treat you differently after finding out. People will infantilize you, including medical professionals. People will say you aren't autistic because you don't act like their 7 year old cousin with autism. And you know what? Those people just made it really easy to avoid. They have made you aware that they aren't worth bothering with. 

Being autistic is a disability. There are things about it that are good, but there are definitely things that are bad. 78% of us are unemployed. The world is not built for us (Seán basically said as much himself), and we face a lot of difficulties. 

Being diagnosed as autistic doesn't change who you are. You were always autistic before your diagnosis. But "autistic" is a far kinder answer to "what's wrong with me" than "you're lazy" or "you're stupid" or "you're just 'off'". Realizing you're autistic allows you to be more gentle with yourself. To be more understanding of your needs and differences. To seek out things that may help you cope with the world better, and if you're privileged enough to afford or access it, professionals who understand neurodivergence and who can help you navigate the world a little better.

Being autistic is nothing to be ashamed of, and anyone who says otherwise is not worth your time. I'm so happy Seán was able to receive a diagnosis. It is a privilege to be diagnosed when so many of us can't. I was self diagnosed for two years before my official diagnosis. You're not hurting anyone to be self diagnosed. You aren't taking anything away from people who are "actually autistic". There's practically no resources for adult autistic people anyway. A diagnosis gets you no special treatment (unless you count being treated like a child or like you're stupid) and a self diagnosis is all most of us will ever be able to access. 

All this yappin just to say I'm so happy for you. There's a lot of us out here (and in your audience, we tend to unknowingly be drawn to each other) and you're not alone, and there's nothing "wrong" with you. Being autistic does make your life more difficult, but it's nothing to be ashamed of, just like any other disability. Through self reflection, a lot of things will continue to click into place. A diagnosis does not make you autistic, you've always been autistic, and your life will not drastically change all of a sudden. You'll just have more answers, and ideally be a little more gentle with yourself.

Be gentle with yourself guys. The world is cruel enough on it's own.

Author: @Circletwice
Content: Bro. 32 yo here. Only just begun to look into autism and ADHD for myself, and finally everything is clicking into place and making sense. I've spent 32 years or my life trying, failing, stuggling, all-effort-spent to figure myself out, slowly trying out and figuring out how to make normal every-day-life stuff more effiicient and low-effort to make it all somewhat functional for me... And it's cool that I've whipped myself into somewhat well-figured out shape and that I know how I funtion somewhat, how to recognize and brace for the burnout storms, how to keep things more organized, even without the diagnosis... But oh my GOD, how many years I would have saved if only I could have been sat down 20 years ago and be told "look, this is what you have, when x happens, it's because of y, people with autism/ADHD often struggle with z, they cope well by doing æ" etc. In stead of me having to blindly feel around through trial and error all my life! Been through some pretty hellish experiences with public health, too... I'm glad to finally know (not diagnosed yet, but now that I know, it's painfully obvious and I'm seeking out private places to get tested), but oh my god... Knowledge could have been power. I'm happy for you that you've finally gotten your answers, too. Even if life won't change dramatically, at least it's nice to *know* what's actually going on when you experience x y z. Keep on keeping on.
