Content:
Had a similar with with my ADHD spectrum. ADHD is already more difficult to diagnose in women but I myself was also in denial because it kinda became a trend amongst my age group. And I kept thinking "Hey I'm actually not as hyper active or focused or struggled too much with focus."
But after getting my Depression and Social Anxiety diagnosed my sister threw in the idea that ADHD often leads towards depression for women. So I asked my therapist and when they laid out the symptoms for women, my head just clicked: "Oh... MY LIFE SO FAR MAKES SENSE NOW!" It was like getting the answer I've been subconciously looking for why I am so different from what others described as the "norm". I have never felt so liberated and happy.
I now feel less bad for using the methods others deem wrong or unorthodox to achieve what I want (like listening to music while typing or studying)
And yet many people still look at me amd go: You don't look like someone with ADHD/Depression/Social Anxiety. You can be so quiet and well behaved and have a healthy focus. You actually look geniunely happy! You make plans and talk so relaxingly about your Depression! You are so outward going and social and really conversational even with strangers! And why would you say all this proudly out loud?!
Well... Surprise! 
There are millions of us. We all deal with things differently. We all experience different things. You don't notice anything on me is because women have been sociataly conditioned to hide and pretend. And many others are being shamed for having these. No. You only say that I don't "look like the part" is because I am not acting what you expect the part to be. I am happily proclaiming that I have been in a dark place and in certain moments still am. But admitting it and talking to others about it helps me cope. And also helps others understand.

Author: @WidgetWitch
Content:
i am also an adhd and autism haver and was diagnosed in my mid-20s so im really feeling you on this. One thing i've found with meds is that i've discovered how much my adhd masks up my autism. Sometimes I take my meds and it feels like all it does is uncover how autistic i'm feeling that day. Where i might normally have gotten energy from being thrown into an unexpected social situation bc my brain is pleased by its novelty, instead I'm just exhausted and irritable from it. I feel way more frustration/anxiety when my plans and schedule are interrupted or i lose control of a situation when before I might have relished the opportunity to be receptive and adaptive. Its been a huge struggle to balance these seemingly disparate elements of my personality.

SUUUUPER relate to the "hyper-analysing" of other people in social situations tho bc that was one of the things that made me think i didn't have autism. It wasn't until i heard someone say "neurotypical people would never say 'oh yeah im good at observing social cues' because they dont observe social cues, they absorb them intuitively" that I realised I'd just put the pattern finding part of my autistic brain onto analysing social cues and trying to learn and intuit the next part of the sequence - which my adhd reactivity also responds well to. I feel like it synergises well with being v introspective bc im also someone who enjoys breaking my life down into building blocks and analysing them. Not in like a 2am regret way, but in like a "why did that person respond like that? What was I feeling at that time? Was it because x or y had just happened?" I found getting my diagnosis reframed a LOT of my life and i got very fixated on doing specifically that for months which annoyed the shit out of my partner lmaooo

Author: @Hari-Harmonies
Content:
Hey as someone who knew about their diagnosis for Asperger's Syndrome from the age of 11, and have subscribed to you ever since I got YouTube, you're awesome Sean! Please if any of you have any thoughts that you may not be neurotypical, please get tested, it is so helpful. You will find yourself in such a position that you begin to understand why you react to things in a certain way compared to neurotypicals, judge how much you're masking, understand where your limits lie and how to deal with it so you don't get so anxious or panicked. 

For those who don't know, the best way to describe it is trying to use 6 different monitors operating different systems at all times. You are always aware of what your clothes feel like as they touch your skin, how your tongue feels in your mouth and behind your teeth, what body language are you projecting, what cadence and tone you're talking at, how other people are doing that at the same time all the while trying to hear and listen what they're saying when there is a leaf or bird or motor or another conversation in the background that you feel is more interesting for no apparent reason. Why do I feel put on the spot and why do these people keep wanting to look in my eyes (masking to allow that to happen to maintain strong eye contact with someone even though it's filling your head with noise)? At the same time, your social awareness may often go out the window whenever you talk about a topic you're really interested in, whilst also at the same time that other people wish to speak about their own experiences and why should I or listen to that if there is no gain and time I won't get back?!

 Because that's how conversation works and in doing so you develop some incredible relationships with exceptional people if you are lucky. Or you realise those people aren't for you. At the same time your internal monologue sounds like a crazy person as you psychoanalyse the beings kn your environment and intrusive thoughts are at a frequency up the wazoo. 
Don't even get me started on things that are happening outside and around a conversation like, "look at that squirrel / what is that guy doing, anyway- (continue talking like nothing interrupted you)."

When all that is done, you wonder why people can call you lazy when you are absolutely wiped from those interactions and need a day of sleep at weird hours for no reason other than night is peaceful because it's not as noisy. 

And at the same time some people who care for you find you difficult because you're talking too much or not enough or you want something a certain way and they are out of patience to accommodate that. This is followed with an anxious internal monologue or picture reel in your head when alone of should have could have, why did I say that, did I embellish the story or am I misremembering it, can I trust them, I thought I had life and what I say more under control.


People with autism tend to work well with children if they have had some time with their diagnosis as we are good at finding different angles to explain things because things said to us sink in a little different. They also tend to have an incredible talent for something, music, memory, mathematics, science, drama, mimicry, languages, accents, art. 

Our productivity is an insane rate as well where we don't know when the next spike hits and when to hibernate and under a time crunch, although stressed, some of our best work is done with that because of an ability to hyper focus.

People with autism are some of the most interesting, stubborn and kind, selfish, passionate individuals you may ever have the pleasure of meeting, who will do anything for you once you've spent time over many years building an unbroken trust with them. They also tend to be very interesting individuals, self-conscious and sometimes self-centred whilst having no concept of self-awareness whilst being present in the moment. Cringing at what they've done just that day, let alone over the past. Give them patience and they'll give you light and life, just like Sean has breathed into his channel. 

We think you're awesome Sean, you have done amazing work and have continued to do so! So happy with your diagnosis. 👍

If anyone has any questions please feel free to ask, I'd love to help out and have some experience doing music therapy.

Content:
I'm in the process of being tested myself rn and it's such a strange thing, just overall. And ur so right about it going slow. It's taking FOREVER. I swear every appointment I've had has been months after what we agreed on the last time we met. My parents are convinced I have it, I have friends who think so, even my teacher believes it, but it's been kind of tricky tbh. I also worry about the fact that I'm both an adult now and a woman and how that impacts a possible diagnosis.  

Before the summer I was told that I scored high enough on the test itself, but that I essentially was "too normal" as a kid based ont he converation they'd had w my dad (even though I'd told them to talk to my mom and even gave them her number bc my dad's memory is kinda shit lol) as I understood it. I did kind of burst into tears in that appointment - partly bc of that - which was super embarrassing, but might have saved everything bc what kind of reaction even is that, so we agreed to meet again this fall, but I genuinely have no idea when that will be bc it's winter now.

A few years ago also I had a teacher who thought I should get tested for adhd. I did kind of feel like it was dismissed very quickly, but I also didn't push it so it kinda just died there. 

Anyway, I'm very glad you actually got an answer, I guess u can call it. I can imagine how sort of freeing it feels to have everything kind of "fall into place", so to speak.

Content:
When i was 18 i found out that I was diagnosed with autism at 12. I then spent 12 years hating myself and denying it which led to severe depression, ptsd from abuse trauma, and suicidal tendencies. I hate bright lights, i hate children screaming, i LOVE metal music but also LOVE ambient music!

Now that im in my 30s, i accepted it and it opened a whole new perspective! I saw autism in so many people! I developed a support system with so many people, i found my husband, i self published a book about vampires in a punk rock band who live a restricted life because they’re vampires and they want to achieve their dreams! It was an allegory for my experience living a restricted life growing up and unable to do what i wanted. I live independently since 21, dealt with shit jobs to make ends meet, and dealt with shitty people. I am now free from toxicity and living my best life.

Author: @elodiepollock7326
Content:
I am still only selfdiagnosed, but you are so right, having a label can open you up for so much compassion and understanding for yourself. I've started accomodating my needs (ear plugs with me always, don't leave the house without headphones either bc public transport without them is hell and so exhausting, as two examples) - something I wouldn't have done before because "I don't need this, I can do without." But how well? (Not well at all.) 
And it helps tremendously. Trying out different things to see if ot helps with my struggles - that is something I would not have done before just considering the possibility that I am autistic. I have learned that I don't have to do things the hard way. If I can make things easier for myself (with little effort and if it doesn't affect anyone), why wouldnt I?
Thank you for sharing this, I am sure that just like with your ADHD diagnosis, this time too many will see themselves in you and research or even seek a diagnosis!

0:29
This is why it's called ASD [short for "Autism Spectrum Disorder" (Keyword, "Spectrum")]. for some autistic people, there's no talking at all (basically real life versions of dopey, although i don't know if some people with this lack of communication also lack the ability to communicate by acting like Dopey does with the other dwarfs as well as Snow White), others struggle with being social [leading many of such people (like me) to be midtroverted at best], and others experience neither of these struggles, but have others, such as stimming by (literally) bashing their head on the wall (if you ever see a kid wearing a hard hat, that very well could be why). This is why people who actually know a thing or two about ASD always say "If you've met one person with Autism, you've met one person with Autism".

Author: @mellyuchiha641
Content:
I recently got diagnosed with ADHD at 26 even tho he didn't do a proper test, he just asked me which "symptoms" I have and when I told him, he just said "yeah I don't even have to listen to more, you definitely have ADHD, it's pretty obvious" and I'm on medication since 7 months but tbh, it's not really doing anything for me. I've actually also considered that I might be on the spectrum but I'm just not sure. As you said, ADHD and autism symptoms often overlap so.. yeah I don't know. I do know that I am hypersensitive to many things and struggle with certain social aspects but it's so hard to pinpoint where it's coming from. 
But I'm glad that you got your diagnosis and can learn to understand yourself better. It's hard and frustrating when people judge you because you just function differently. And I'm definitely not a fan of taking ADHD as an excuse for something but with the diagnosis, I feel much more comfortable with myself. I do work on certain behavior that bothers me or could really be a nuisance for other people but sometimes in my head I just go "You know what. You have ADHD. There are things that you just can't do and you often struggle much more than others but you're doing your best and sometimes it's just not enough and that's okay. You're not doing things because you're an asshole or lazy or whatever, you just sometimes can't control it and that's not your fault."

The diagnosis helps me to stop being so harsh on myself and hating myself because I can't do some things that seem so natural for others. But on the other hand, I can do many things that others can't and I've grown to find my brain fascinating. 
You're working extremely hard and I highly respect you for that. I hope people will treat you good, because you're a great, loving and hardworking person and you're doing absolutely great! Thank you for being so open with this, you're a big inspiration for many of us! Love you!♥

Author: @nightrogue5315
Content:
I'm happy for you because I can only imagine the relief you felt of having an answer. When I finally got diagnosed with ADHD about 3 years ago when I was 28, I felt such relief. Because I had an *actual* answer. It wasn't "oh you're just slap happy", or "oh you're just sensitive to caffeine" (whether that was from coffee or tea), or "you sure you're just not extroverted?"" 

My first doctor when I talked to her about getting diagnosed asked me these questions: "Were you diagnosed with ADHD when you were a kid?" Me: "No, I was never tested." Doctor: "How did you do in school? And did you graduate?" Me: "I did decent in school, and I did graduate." Doctor: "Ok, did you go to college?" Me: "I did go to college  but had to withdraw due to a family emergency that came up." Doctor: "Do you have a job, and if so what do you do?" Me: "Yeah, I've been at the same place since 2015 and I'm currently a supervisor." Her response... I KNEW when she responded she was full of shit and just didn't want to fully do her job.

She said, "Well, it's rare that kids go untested if they have ADHD. Not to mention you doing well in school and graduating, continuing to not only go to college but also have a job as a manager or supervisor. Generally people with ADHD don't have those things in common with people who don't have ADHD." I said ok and left. I got a new doctor. She set me up a referral to get tested and was so supportive. And I was  relieved because not only did I get that answer, but I was happy that my feelings and thoughts of my first doctor just being a lazy P.O.S. was true. Stereotypes regarding things is just hurtful. Not only to those who are stereotyped, but also to those who are ignored BECAUSE they don't "fit" those stereotypes.

Content: I’m just really happy that neurodivergancy(also other stuff) and mental health stuff is being talked about and accepted more on the internet. So I’m happy that hopefully now with how much it’s being talked about on here, some kid or some parent watching YouTube who doesn’t know they are or their kid is neurodivergent but are showing the signs, will be able to learn and identify the possibility that they have adhd or autism, get officially diagnosed sooner, and they won’t end up a mess like me. Author: @dyladventurer6045
Content: I was diagnosed with autism when I was a toddler or a baby, because specifically, I used to have low functioning autism. I would not talk, but point at random stuff that I wanted, like if I was playing charades, or being a mime. I would keep stuff “in order”, like by keeping all doors closed. Obviously, I would do that, because I had big OCD (Obsessive Compulsive Disorder). I still do have it, but it’s now small, it’s not that bad anymore. My ears wouldn’t handle everyday loud noises. My ears still don’t handle loud noises, but they can handle some of them, though. I would make loud noises by screaming and yelling, without saying any word, because I had low functioning autism back then. I would do that to get what I wanted. I would do that and point at stuff that I wanted. Mostly, my body wouldn’t deal with everyday clothing. So, as a result, I would wander around my family’s house, wearing nothing, but underwear. I also would be totally naked in my house’s pool, because underwear doesn’t go in water, swim trunks do. Now, I wear clothing, including swim trunks, that I find comfortable in my opinion. I would have so much anxiety. I still do, but not a lot, though. I do take a pill once every morning. My taste buds on my tongue in my mouth wouldn’t try new food, or drinks. I would shake and/or flap my hands as a way of “stimming”. I would also rock back and forth as another way of “stimming”. I don’t do those things anymore. At the age of four or five, at first, my doctor told my parents that he thought that I would never talk in my whole life, but he was wrong, because somehow, my mom was able to let me seek therapy to have someone make me talk for the rest of my life, permanently curing my low functioning autism, turning it into high functioning autism. I was taught by a nice woman, because she obviously cared about people with all kinds of levels of autism. And I know she still does care about them with their kinds of levels of autism. Many days of teachings later, I entirely learned how to speak on my own to say something about something and talk about an idea that I came up with. As a result, I began talking a lot, and even doing stuff, and more stuff that regular people would do. Later on in my younger life, I began to become creative. And I’m still creative to this day. Like for example, I’m good at coming up with stories. For another example, I’m good at building stuff in Minecraft. And for one more example, I’m good at designing pictures of mostly characters. Later on in my older life, I began to understand easy, and hard stuff. I also began to understand jokes. Speaking of jokes, I’m good at being, again, creative, also, speaking of which, at making jokes, because I have a great sense of humor. I’m full of funny jokes that I say. And now, here I am, still having high functioning autism, able to do regular stuff that regular people do, like talking.

Author: @AcerJones21
Content:
I was diagnosed with Asperger's (as it was then) at 24. A lot of people say that they feel relief when they get "answers" but I was devastated. I knew I was awkward and had issues and anxiety but before I was diagnosed I had hopes of fixing myself. Then I got a label that told me I was permanently broken. I am now Schizoid as well so it never got better. 

You are right that people have an idea of what autism is- either someone who is low-functioning or someone who is Sheldon Cooper. Female autism presents differently to male autism as well. My own mother doesn't know about my diagnosis. I don't have a good relationship with her anyway but I know she would either say "no you don't/aren't" or she'd throw herself a "what did I do wrong as a parent" pity party. She worked in a nursery for many years so I think she too has an "idea" of what autism is but those children who had a diagnosis at that age either had very involved, observant parents or, crucially, presented with symptoms severe enough to be diagnosed at a very early age. My parents know very well I'm mentally ill, but what they think is wrong is anyone's guess. They buried their heads in the sand over it. 

I've also had the "oh, you don't look like you have Aspergers" etc. How am I supposed to respond to that? People say it in a reassuring way but Aspergers isn't a physical disability, so people don't understand the issues and not looking/sounding like you have autism isn't a good thing if it makes people minimise someone's issues. I've been written up twice at work for "it's not what you said, it's how you said it". Good stuff.

Content:
LETS GOOO, WELCOME TO THE AUTISTIC FAMILY!!! :D 

Also, if you need resources: 
- NOT AUTISM SPEAKS. 
- AWANN (Autistic Women And Nonbinary Network) 
- ASAN (Autistic Self-Advocacy Network) 

Edit: Everyone else is sharing they're stories, so I might as well, too! I got diagnosed as autistic at the age of 14 (almost 15), just over a year ago. It was the best thing to ever happen to me. 
It made a lot of things make sense about me. I'd never really gotten along with other kids my age; I'd always tried to be kind, but most of the time, people took me as being rude or hurtful. People teased me for meowing like a cat- which, looking back, was my special interest at the time. I'd always had an aversion to meat, because of the texture. The hand dryers and automatic toilets scared me because the loud, sudden noise that hurt. 
I'm in highschool now, and when I was in freshman year, I was struggling so much. I was masking without even realizing it, that's how accustomed I've gotten to masking in public. Executive dysfunction and autistic burnout was hitting HARD. So I went to my mom, and said, "Mom, there is no freaking way that I'm not either ADHD or autistic". I will always be grateful to my mom for listening to me, and getting me diagnosed. 
As of now, I had an IEP plan that I use, I've met other autistic people who know what it's like, and I'm trying to learn how to unmask. I love being autistic; I love being me <3

Author: @TacoQueen33
Content: As a female with autism, autism is different for all of us. We have some differences, and some are silent or really loud. It all relies on how we view things, act toward things etc.. My mother says that it’s like a line. One end is the average person (no autism), the middle is middle/low autism, and the other end is high autism. On this line I’m somewhat near the middle. High autism is the kids or adults that cannot speak and act what people assume is “crazy”. The lower sides are like Jack and others like me. We can socialise, but we view or think things differently. The closer you are to the average person’s side, the lower your autism is. But that doesn’t mean you don’t have it. We supports your autism, Jack! Content:
I'm so happy for you!

I was also diagnoses this year, (in May, at age 21), but I've know I'm Autistic for 100% certain for about 2 years, and suspected it for many more before; I just didn't fit the stereotype so I had to take my own initiative to actually get diagnosed.

I've always felt outside, different, not good enough, and that it was all my fault.
My whole childhood, all I could focus on was fixing myself, fitting in, being "normal;" just masking so hard I didn't know who I was.
Breaking myself and burning myself out just to fail, be disliked, and called lazy.

Realising I am Autistic and getting diagnosed was just a HUGE weight of my shoulders.
I'm not just "sensitive, awkward, anxious, or depressed;" I have a concrete reason that cannot be "fixed," AND THAT'S OKAY!

Trying to love myself and my flaws, learning I don't have to fulfill the stupid expectations society has demanded of me since birth, and accepting that I have support needs that need to be filled; it genuinely saved my life.

What you do means so much to a lot of people, even though we're all just a bunch of strangers on the internet.

TL;DR:
 • Autism diagnosis is such a relief!
 • Society isn't accommodating enough yet...
 • We all have each other, as a community of neurodivergent strangers.

Author: @danbrittain9530
Content: As a kid I was always the odd one out who didn't really know how to take part in groups of friends, off to the side observing rather than joining in when playing, and preferring to get lost in computer games instead. Carried on into adulthood remaining socially awkward, able to communicate fine, but only if it's talking about something I'm really interested in. Hardly ever able to read people to know what they're thinking, so end up overthinking absolutely every possibility instead. Always struggled with depression, wondering why I never fitted in, really struggle with handling change, only like things I've always really liked such as computers, gaming and cars, I can't maintain friendships particularly well, etc, and don't really see anyone out of work nowadays other than my wife, kids and close family, so regularly feel unpopular and lonely outside of work. I don't appear to have ADHD or anything, was relatively good when in classes at school but had absolutely no interest outside of it and couldn't find any patience to revise or whatever, I was always better at learning something by being hands on rather than reading books, etc. My parents reckon I was a handful as a kid, and now I've got kids of my own, my youngest kept acting up and we suspected something was different. My parents would sometimes joke that I was the same when I was a kid, which got the cogs turning. We asked the doctors for support and was told there was a chance he was autistic, which then led me to think maybe I was the same and never knew. Got assessed two or three years ago, now in my 40's with the recent confirmation that I'm high functioning autistic or whatever else they'd prefer to call it at the moment. Most tend not to believe it since so many are still of the mindset that being autistic means you can't talk, rocking away in the corner for comfort, not being able to deal with loud noises, etc. You're right, it doesn't change anything, other than change how you see and understand yourself. You're still you, but just knowing your quirks a bit better lets you go easier on yourself, being able to understand rather than critique yourself all day long. I've certainly not been struggling to live with being me as much since I found out anyway, and hopefully it'll make things easier for you too. 👍

AUDHD GANG!!!!!
I got dx with autism at 23 (well literally the day before my 24th birthday lmao) and a few months ago at 27 I got dx with adhd, i truly feel like a boulder has been lifted off my chest, both diagnoses explain everything i struggled with my entire life.

Content: I have three diagnoses myself two of them is adhd and autism and I don't know how to say my third diagnos on English but I do have three diagnoses. I am sensitive to smells that I don't like, seriousl, I can't eat in the same room with something that I don't think smels good, I am also sensitive to how food tastes and feel in my mouth. My mom and dad realized that something was different about me when I was a toddler/very young child because I took longer to start talking then what "normal" children does. So they took me to some lady who could diagnose or something I don't remember, sorry, I have bad memory. Anyways this lady said that I had autism, I was too young to understand at the time so my parents waited until I started to realize myself that I am different. I don't remember how old I was when I noticed that I am different compared to the other kids in the school that I went to at the time but maybe I was 7, 8, 9, or 10 years old but, I do remember wondering if I was sick and I felt like an alien from another planet. My parents realized that I had realized that I am different so they told me that I had autism and I gated and I wanted to get rid of it because I just wanted to be a "normal" girl but you can't get rid of it. A while went by and my parents realized that I don't just have autism since I had outbursts in school and stuff so I had go get myself diagnosed and well it turned out that I had adhd too. So I began to take medicine for it and that made it better, I used to take the medicine everyday and I took another medication at the time but nowadays I don't take it everyday and I take another medication. I was 10, 11, or 12 years old when I found out that I have adhd and I didn't like that either. I gated my diagnoses for years but one day I just decided to accept and embrace my wonderful diagnoses because I wouldn't be the same person without them, sure, they can be a pain in the butt but they make me who I am and I really like them because of that so, even if it was a way for me to remove my diagnoses, I wouldn't do it because they are a part of me. I had accepted and embraced my diagnoses for a long while when I got diagnosed with the third diagnos, I was talking to someone since I had and still have issues anyways they realized that I had a third diagnose and I found about it if course but, I was just happoto know why things didn't go super well for me in school. I am 22 years old today, I am still speaking to a therapist but my mental state is so much better today then what it was years ago. I am trying to get myself a job and I hope that everything goes well for me and many other people. Having diagnoses, heck, being different is nothing to be ashamed of, being different, as long as it doesn't hurt you or anyone else, and having diagnoses and other stuff is a beautiful thing and that's something to be proud of. Sorry if I said something stupid and sorry for the long comment. Thank you Sean for speaking about this. ❤❤️❤️❤️❤️💚💚💚💚💚

Author: @NullandVoidArt
Content:
I love this new attitude going forward! It’s something that feels so needed. I’m also Autistic (sometimes suspecting ADHD as well, but I haven’t jumped much on it since my symptoms seem rather inconsistent) and have been on a *long* journey of self acceptance. I’m currently in my first year out of school, which has given me time to really focus on finding out how I work. It’s not always easy. It’s taken years for me to defeat the “why can’t I just be like everyone else” self-accusation “If they can do it with such ease, why can’t I?!”. I’ve come to accept it, but learning to be kind to myself about productivity, as you mentioned in the video, is also hard. Really hard. 

My next big life choice is what education specialty I’m gonna go into. At the same time I’m balancing a job with arts. I’d love to turn the latter into a career (if I could just tell stories for a living, I would be living the dream) but it’s also known for being a tough industry. And I fear, at my current self confidence and ability to function, I won’t enjoy much. I constantly doubt whether I could do it due to the massive pressure I put on myself to succeed and improve each day. And when I’m with likeminded people, a former teacher of mine, she tells me I have so much time, opportunity, and skill. *I HAVE the ability to and ENJOY putting myself out there.* And I *love* artistic spaces. It brings me such confidence when I manage to believe in myself even for just a moment. 
So I mean it when I say that I will be listening with bated breath as you steer into this conversation. Because *man* does it make me feel seen, and *man* does it need to be talked about. Welcome to the club, Sean. I can’t wait to hear more!

Content: I have a feeling that I have undiagnosed autism myself. My son was diagnosed at 5 after starting kindergarten 13 years ago. I saw a lot of myself in the things he did. Author: @MrBebopChamploo
Content: This was a great video! I can relate to a lot of what Jack is talking about. One thing I'd like to add for people who may be curious whether they have autism is that it's ok and valid to self-diagnose if you get to that point in learning about and identifying with autistic experiences. Official diagnosis might be reassuring, but it's hard to access and the process isn't always accurate, especially for women and femmes. For example, when I went through that process, the psychologist had to rely mostly on my parent for specific context of my childhood experience because I don't really remember it that well (on account of it being traumatic). But my parent said I didn't have trouble socially or with making friends. I may not remember my childhood that well, but that was absolutely not true - I peaked socially in like 1st grade lol and after that I always felt like an outsider or alien. I was constantly fixated on and stressed about trying to figure out how to fit in, negatively comparing myself to others, etc. Anyway I don't want to go into too much detail, the point is just that you are the authority of your own experience. If getting an official diagnosis is helpful and reassuring for you, and you have access to that process, then that's great! But if not, don't let that hold you back from the path to better understanding yourself, your experiences, and learning how to live more holistically and to hold yourself with greater compassion and love.

I'm 26 and I still have never held down a job for more than 2 weeks, can't drive, and can't function well outside of my home for more than a couple of hours. I can go non verbal a lot when I'm stressed but I'm not completely nonverbal. I stim a lot, have comorbities and have been in psych hospitals twice now. Content:
I'm glad Jack got diagnosed, I know exactly how it feels to grow up feeling like an alien because it feels like there's no other explanation as to why you have trouble in social situations or that you have problems with eye contact. It was an emotional experience for me learning about myself and reading the webpage they put up for me like I was reading about myself specifically! I know many other people have the same experience, If I can shout out Max Derrat, who made a similar video expressing his struggles as someone on the spectrum and the comments section was full of people saying they felt understood for the first time ever! My girlfriend says all the time she's an alien and it took me bringing it up for her to realize she just might be on the spectrum too. I find that a lot of the behaviors associated with autism are more learned behaviors (like masking) because of how we tend to over correct and be very hard on ourselves.

I'm so glad to have a voice as loud as Jack's speaking about this from a real place. There are far too many harmful stigmas out there and organizations like Autism Speaks are only making things worse.

Author: @JennDVidz
Content:
Thanks for sharing this with us! A lot of people have a misconception about Autism and how it works. They associate Autism usually with nonverbal Autistic persons, or there being some MASSIVE social divide between Autistic persons and neurotypicals... this is not the case at all. Autism is a spectrum, and every Autism patient has different sets of their own unique symptoms! There are LOADS of undiagnosed Autistic persons walking around in the world RIGHT NOW, going around masking, and even they don't know it! Autism isn't some obvious mental affliction that comes with clear signs and tells, it's a very complicated condition that can easily get missed in some individuals.

I wish I could get diagnosed, but American healthcare doesn't really like to cover mental health care in most cases. Fucked up, right? And then other countries why we're all so nutter butters over here. I'm obviously not going to claim anything or self-diagnose, but my behavior, thought process, reactions, etc. all seem to tick boxes for ADHD and Autism. I'm so proud of you Jack, thank you again for being so open, it's very inspiring!

Author: @Rain-fu9er
Content:
I think that the representation/misrepresentation of ASD on the media often distorts the reality of neurodivergence. A character who is on the spectrum is biblically both limited and revolved around this. This gives a single idea and presentation about ASD and ADHD. That if your life isn't brought to a stop because of ASD, you aren't on the spectrum, if you're not what is "typically" considered Autistic, then your not. This is not the case at all. Also, the person writing/making the piece of media might also just have little to do with neurodivergence.

Unfortunately, this cultivates the negative stigma around ASD, which could be the reason why many people who are on the spectrum do reject that idea. In short, neurodivergence needs more real and accurate representation on the media to push forward conversations about ASD as a potential for many more undiagnosed people, and normalising it so the negative stigmas are left behind.

Content:
I got my diagnosis (Asperger’s syndrome) in 2019, in the middle of my studies to become a sales assistant. Looking back there have always been signs, but they were never addressed.

When I was a taking a course on ‘being diagnosed with autism as an adult’ the first thing we learned was that it is often being in a stressful situation/point in life that reveals and amplifies the symptoms. 

For example; I was suddenly thrown into the service industry with no prior experience and having to work 8 hours Monday- Friday and 5 hours on Saturday. Due to this I developed new more severe symptoms, like having meltdowns where I either; can’t formulate words and stammer if I try to, or just keep repeating what I’m suppose to be doing and go on, on ‘autopilot’.

For me it was also very comforting to know and understanding why I feel like I do and really freeing.

Author: @moopotatokimchi
Content:
I have been sitting here peeling potatoes for the last 16 minutes and 38 seconds screaming "YES SEÁN!! YES!!!" 

I feel so validated. 

It's actually insane how validated I feel. 

I've been trying to get evaluated myself for a bit now (fuck American Health Care) just like you, I always thought autism was just the nonverbal, antisocial cases. But about a year ago I started learning more and more how NOT THE CASE that is. So I started researching, and I just keep finding myself in the symptoms - why do loud noises make me lose my shit? Why do I have to overanalyze every conversation, looking at every sign, analyzing every tone- only to realize I still didn't recognize sarcasm, rhetorical questions and the like - ultimately leaving me EXHAUSTED from social interaction? Why is the only reason I talk to other people because discord is audio only with no in-person commitments? Why do I stay obsessed with the same thing for YEARS while everyone else moves on???? 

I went and saw my doctor and she was like "yeeeeeeah. There's more going on" for reference, I'm ALSO bipolar. It's a very 'fun' combination. So I got referred, but insurance means it's either 800 dollars if I switch insurance, or 3500 dollars NOW if I pay.. only problem is... I haven't been able to maintain a 9-5 job in years because it overwhelms and exhausts me. Being a teacher was so unbelievably hard for me. And it took 7 years just to get that degree. I've been trying so hard to write a book, but when I am stuck with writers block, I struggle soooo much to buckle down and write. I don't know how to just 'pull it together" or 'fake it til I make it' because either I do what I'm supposed to and it's half-assed because a voice is screaming in my head "you'd rather be doing THIS" or I take a break and do what I want, only to have a voice screaming in my head saying "you piece of shit. Why can't you do what you're supposed to? You're a failure. You're disappointing everyone and you should be able to do it stop making excuses." So then I can't even enjoy my break, and I get no actual rest and just exhaust myself. 


So yeah. Getting evaluated doesn't change me. But maybe there are attention symptoms I could get treated. Maybe not. But just like you said, maybe I can finally fucking be kind to myself - have the validity of a recontextualized life. Maybe having that context will only ever look like excuses to others, but just because I do things differently doesn't mean I'm doing things wrong. Why in the WORLD are neurotypicals so convinced that divergent methods are 'wrong' or something to be 'ashamed' of? Why is it an 'excuse' rather than an explanation? 


All of this ranting to say, thank you for being open about this. Thank you for starting the conversation. Thank you for helping me be seen. Yeah, maybe I haven't been diagnosed yet, but everything is pointing to a type like yours - a type that is 'social' but really is just 24/7 masking. I feel seen, and I feel motivated that, hey, maybe just maybe, it IS worth still pushing for evaluation and figuring things out. I appreciate you so much!!

"im autistic" "but you're so social!?" "but you're just like everyone else..." people dont understand that that means we're masking pretty well, and its reinforcing that our mask is solid... which, isnt always a good thing. i hope this DX helps you learn more about you. figuring out i was an AuDHDer, instead of just ADHD, my life flipped upside-down, but in a good way. i finally looked back on many things and it made sense. i wasnt broken, i wasnt stupid, or lazy, or just over-emotional, the picky eating ( STUPID RAISINS >:(  ), and every other bad thing we've been told, and tell ourselves. "knowing is half the battle" but, sometimes, it feels like its more than half. knowing literally saved my life, because i couldnt understand why holding a job was so hard, why it felt like no one liked me, even when i had many people who genuinely loved being around me, just one perceived negative reaction to me was enough to send me into a bad spiral. but, now i know, i'm not alone out here, im not the odd one out, and im not broken, just different. i know how to regulate thanks to talking to other autistic adults who knew for longer, i learned to unmask and let myself be. 

thank you for being you all these years, being open, and making all of us feel so welcome to just exist for a while, and know that its okay to be us here.

Author: @NixyRose72
Content:
In the process of getting diagnosed as well. At nearly 52 years old. I had the same reactions from my closest friends when i told them that my shrin k suspected there was more than just my adhd. "Oh,well....yeah? Your shrink is just now noticing?" 
I reacted the exact same as you, "Why didn't you tell me?!?!" She said that she thought i knew lol

Same as you, this diagnosis is mainly to open up therapy avenues (I'm no longer functioning properly. Apparently, undiagnosed "high masking" women hit a point where the exhaustion of trying to fit cracks the mask. Mental health issues worsen, physical health issues worsen etc. Apparently for me,that point was about 10 to 11 years ago.) But the diagnosis is also to help me to understand myself.  The label helps me to stop labeling myself with derogatory labels. 

I've always had sensory and food issues. But we always chalked it and my son's stuff up to adhd, quirky genetics, and in my case, severe post trauma issues. 

Hearing you say so many familiar things is giving me the kick in the pants to finish my paperwork and actually go. 
But I'm scared. 
Mostly, I'm scared that I'm not, and I'm just broken instead of wired uniquely. But I am afraid. 
❤

Author: @ComicNelli
Content:
I also got diagnosed with ADHD first and the way you describe it is exactly how I felt. Both my ADHD and Autism diagnoses have come as an adult, so I have spent a lot of my life trying to figure out what was “wrong”. Getting one diagnosis is like having half of the puzzle, it explains some things, but you still feel like there are things left unexplained. 

When I got my autism diagnosis there was a lot of things that finally clicked. It doesn’t change who you are, because it has always been you, but at the same time it also opens a door for self acceptance. To understand why we are how we are, the struggles we experience and realising that we are not alone ❤ 
I still have a lot to understand about myself and autism, and it is a process to unlearn bad coping mechanisms I have created through my life, to learn to be myself and not drain all my energy hiding who I am. I wish you and everyone else good luck on your own journey of self acceptance and understanding as well ❤ Let us be us ❤

15:00 The thing is, there's a difference between being A Better You, and being a "better" you.

One is being true to yourself, being kind to yourself and others, while not sacrificing yourself for the approval of others.

The other is being "better" for the sake of everyone else's VIEW of you. Trying to portray the best version of yourself despite anything going on behind the scenes, or to "prove" some arbitrary point to yourself under the guise of being "better".

The desire for the second isn't *_bad_* but allowing it to control your life isn't healthy. Being Better shpuld be the first priority, and being "better" will usually follow suit once you do.

AYEEEEE LETS GO! Me too!! (also officially, by several doctors, at the hospital, also quite late as an adult) :)

It's notable that ID (intellectual disability) and ASD (autism) are different as the terms used to be synonymous.

I have yet to do one as I want to find meds that work before then so I can actually focus on the test.

Author: @IrisSonata
Content:
The way you see the world, hate how people today react or act, and the way you listed some of your feelings: Literally all *exactly* how i feel. It's insane actually, to hear and see someone actually feel the same way about ALOT of things, especially about the world and how depressing it is and wanting it to be better.

I think my downside is I have truly given up. I feel like *nothing* is going to fix the world or people's ways. And it probably never can or will be. Yet, even knowing that, it still depresses me sooo much that it can't be fix. And in turn, I dont feel like I could ever be myself. Even when I try to be and have tried to enjoy things, *every*, *single*, *time*, I loose that something/someone, get put down, or back-stabbed. For soo many years this happened.

And for those of you who do read this: no i aint 'suicidal'. But at the same time, you could say I'm already 'dead'. I really feel like I've lost alot of care or feeling. It's hard to impossible for me to care or understand 'love' or even 'empathy' now because of the world I see and what I went through. My empathy is already being put into the world of people who are suffering. Even the world itself.

Although Jack('s) video was inspiring, and did give me some hope to want to be that better person like him/you: i just can't do it. I just feel like I've fully accepted into waiting for my life to end whenever it does. Because time, places, money: i can't fathom how to balance and work that stuff to even feel like I have time to do what I want or try to fix things. Time feels so little to me.

But.. because of that, I also feel like for once I *have* accepted something of myself. Accepted that low point of myself. And it also feels like a little step forward. I'm still living and going and trying to do what I do enjoy and like. And enjoy the time with people that I feel I finally *have* as a true friend and someone that actually cares.
Yet, I doubt I'll ever try to get help. My trust in people, especially even in medical fields now, just feel like is fake and I will not find someone that would or could help. Many times I've tried different docs, and they are all the same: basic, not trying to actually help, and not even trying themselves to figure it out to help that someone.

But, I do hope you other people out there can find your peace, place, and help that you need that I can't find. Even if it means accepting your lowest point where you are first, to finally take a grab at the ladder up and take your time to get better.

Content:
And here I was wondering if you just misspoke on the recent charity steam with Gab (I don't Twitter). Welcome to the Late Diagnosed AuDHD club, Sean! 🧡 This is a fantastic video and I'm glad you're continuing to talk about and try to normalise (male) mental health like this. Author: @sora_tonin
Content:
I got diagnosed with asperger's syndrome/autism at around 14 years old (20 now) and it has always been an uphill battle. As a child I always felt different and on the outside and I never clicked with any of my classmates and never really made any friends. After masking 24/7 and being a people pleaser in hopes of people wanting to be my friend for over 10 years I pretty much stopped functioning and spiralled into a major depression. I didnt go to school or anything, and even after getting my diagnosis things just got worse. It was hard foe me to accept that I was autistic because I was used to people in school and other settings using the term 'autistic' as an insult. I have come to terms with it now, however it is still a struggle every single day. I still have depression and probably some type of anxiety, it's difficult to know when I am masking or people pleasing and not, and I struggle with self doubt and hatred all the time.
Seeing my favorite youtuber through my childhood talk so openly and being so accepting of this topic brings me so much comfort. Thank you Jack.
If anyone reading this is going through a hard time due to mental illness or a diagnosis, just know that there is always someone out there who will accept, love and help you. Keep up the fight, I believe in you <3

We offer more focused schooling for kids with these issues, and it, for example, gives the students a 6 to 1 student to teacher ratio to ensure they get their learning needs met. We also have many programs and ways to help students with these issues so they are not alienated as they often are in public schools. Our program is a day program as well as a boarding program where we take care of these students. It's truly and honorable place that I love so much. I have met so many wonderful students who wouldn't have had a good shot had they not been able to get the services a school like ours offers!

Author: @Haiyami
Content: I was also diagnosed with Autism and originally diagnosed with ADHD a long time ago. But in my opinion i think Austism is over diagnosed and it's too broad of  range because even if slight quirks now can be considered autism. Which I think is bad because within the last 10 years I've seen people use their diagnosis of autism as crutch and excuse their bad behavior. Autism diagnosis follows a very strict guide lines of signs. I admit the spetrium is large, but it's not as large as a lot of mental health places try claim it is.  LIke sean said there is one end with the nonverbal/low functioning autism and then there is the verbal/high functioning autism. But regardless of which side of the spectrum you are on, each side shares certain traits of. Which I'll list at times get stuttering of speech because their mouth can't keep up with their thoughts that move at a million miles an hour, or there is an impulsiveness over things or an idea and gets you laser locked into an idea or a behavior pattern that seems absolutely necessary (example: Like the OCD of having to always wake up eat breakfast shower and then brush teeth in that specific order because it doesn't feel right.), or even on the social side, sometime there is a disconnect that sometimes happens when having conversations. These are just random traits and not everyone with autism has all of these habits or traits as it varies. But again there is a strict medical diagnosis. As a fellow person with autism I"m very curious to hear more about Sean's story of autism.

Author: @AllisterMacDonald115
Content:
This may seem superficial but I prefer to say that I am Autistic, rather than I have Autism. It's important to me to frame it that way because to clarifies that I don't consider myself 'sick' or 'disabled' just due to being on the spectrum. Let me explain.

To "have" something generally implies that it's an ailment, in a linguistic sense. Something you caught along the way; something that may be perceived as going wrong or even just simply negative. Not always, of course, but the connotations of that wording are definitely there. But Autism is not an illness. It's not something that we ended up with and have to cope in spite of. We've always been Autistic. We were always going to be Autistic. It's not us plus or minus Autism. This is who we are. Who we were meant to be. There is no version of us that isn't on the spectrum. I think it's important to recognise that. We didn't get Autism, nothing made us Autistic. It doesn't make us lesser in any capacity, or does it inherent ail us in any capacity. Take care of yourself. I hope knowing this about yourself brings you comfort and helps you understand yourself, Seán, but remember that it changes nothing. This is who we are, and this is who we're supposed to be. We are enough

Author: @tessbauer3050
Content:
For who it might help, I'm a woman who got diagnosed with autism when I was 20. My diagnosis was autism and ADHD, I've been struggling with anxiety and depression all my life and after the official diagnosis I finally had sort of an answer as to why. 

No one believed I was autistic, not even my parents, because I didn't "act it". I'm social and know the proper social cues (sometimes better than other times), but I have a big problem with sounds and textures. For the longest time I wasn't allowed to mention my AUDHD in the house, because I was "playing victim". 
Safe to say, I had my answers, but I wasn't allowed to be comfortable in my diagnosis, which was a really tough time.

Nowadays it's a lot better, with my parents and friends taking my jokes and not giving me that look whenever I do. Just wanted to share this to let anyone struggling with anything close or even very much not close to what I went through that you're not alone :) There are people out there who will love and accept you as you are, and sometimes that takes some time and work on both sides, but you'll get there :)

Author: @bluemoose4826
Content:
4:32 i feel like working at a different pace is a small amount of disservice to both communities 

While both have very particular things that cause some inconveniences in "neurotypical" society, Im of the opinion that both have the clear and distinct advantages over the so-called "typical"

Both have the capability to excel faaar past the average when taught in the proper "way", not necessary "pace", and if taught in the proper manner taylored to the individual they will soak up the information and retain it deeper then any so called typical individual.

I also have peeves with the "neurotypical" classification. Having an inference to them being normal over another group being separate than normal, while if anything, those in the "typical" classification are at a stark disadvantage in comparison to most in the "divergent" community, if those in the divergent classification are being taught in an advantageous and conducive manners for how there mind works. The same care given to a "typical" individual doesn't net the same levels of success and excelling as that of those in the divergent group.

My entire household is "divergent", but i grew up not knowing i was and had to teach myself how to adjust accordingly  (society hadn't caught up yet -this was the 90s) and now, knowing how to handle things, my wife and children are excelling far past societal norms. Contrasted against when my children are in the care of other family or their biological mother, and they heavily regress.

Showing that if things are presented in the proper "manner" not necessarily a particular "pace" will net more positive progression.

I'm 36 years old, and am only just now being made aware of the struggles I had as a kid. As much as I knew at the time I struggled, I never attached potential diagnosis' to those struggles. Definitely considering a diagnosis now that you said intestinal issues also play a role, I NEVER would have thought to link that to Autism. But guess who has that as well... this guy!

Content:
The real "FUN" thing about having ADHD and autism is the amount of fuckin' contradictions there are.

I do certain things impulsively, but routine is what helps me feel mentally *okay*. I love to sit here and organize shit, but it also gets REALLY BORING if my ADHD is kicking my ass a little more than usual that day.
Spontaneous plans? Yeah! I'm down! But those plans get interrupted? ANGY. SAD. UPSETTI IN MY SPAGHETTI.
Impulsively making purchases for a new hyperfixation, like my recent interest in crystals or Pokemon cards? HELL YEAH! Hyperfocusing on researching the products to make sure what I'm buying is legit, and learning how to tell what's real and what's fake? YOU KNOW IT! And that snowballs into hyperfixating on a wide variety of topics while ALSO having long term special interests.

Struggling to be on time? Oh GOD yeah. Getting upset when OTHERS are a few minutes late? YEEEEP. Forgetting steps in plans? Yep. Needing plans to execute perfectly regardless or I get upsetti? YEP.

I didn't know I had ADHD until I was in my late 20s, and I finally got diagnosed in my early 30s. But that also led to me, while talking to my therapist, discovering that autism was part of the secret formula that makes my brain juice, and all the things that didn't click into place before suddenly did. Shit's wild, and it's so difficult to come to terms with it sometimes, especially after 2 decades and some change being considered lazy or weird or whatever. On the flipside... it's such a relief to know why the fuck I am the way I am. And I know sooo many people, especially people our age (millennials lol) have a similar experience. ESPECIALLY women, with the late diagnosis. We struggle so hard with that, ugh.

Author: @Steph-zo5zk
Content:
Hey Sean thanks for making this video! I'm unemployed, turning 30 soon and I finally got diagnosed with both earlier this year. You're right, it was hell on that waiting list for 3 years (still waiting for the NHS ADHD appointment.) I would research obsessively to try and validate myself because a few people in my life expressed scepticism and there was so much online hatred directed at young people self-diagnosing on TikTok (especially women). You and a few of my other long term beloved youtubers coming out with your ADHD/ASD diagnoses was so comforting to me because during my research I read about the double empathy problem and how neurodivergent people tend to gravitate towards each other due to the way we communicate. I can't explain how much it bolstered my confidence and kept me sane during that time hearing you and others talk about your experiences.  
I finally gave up on the NHS waiting list and fortunately was able to go private after 3 years waiting for both ASD and ADHD assessments and as soon as I got my ASD diagnosis through him the NHS ASD assessment finally came through, so I got double diagnosed within a couple of months which boosted my confidence. 😂The private ADHD assessment was harder as my mum was prejudiced against the medication for it and downplayed a lot of the disorganisation, lack of ability to motivate myself and forgetfulness and fidgeting that my she and my dad told me off for constantly growing up, saying she didn't remember. I didn't perfectly tick the ADHD boxes because I was a great student (up until I bailed on my degree in final year because I'd been depressed/suicidal since I was a young child without understanding why and I lost my creative abilities due to the university environment burning me out). Mostly all my teachers wrote in my reports was 'she rarely speaks in class' and it was because I was off in dreamland most of the time. Sometimes literally, partly because I had insomnia and partly because I would stay up til 3 or 4 am procrastinating homework by playing the sims or writing/reading fanfiction about my favourite shows (and youtubers lol). I regularly slept through religious studies but I aced every test so the teacher didn't care and I got an A* for my GCSE. There were only a couple of teachers who remarked on me losing and forgetting things a lot, they only really cared about grades and obedience at my high school. They didn't even have a counsellor/pastoral care system at the time.
One of my ASD symptoms was hyperlexia (unusually advanced reading ability) so I can easily teach myself online or memorise the textbook. I couldn't understand for the life of me why I needed to revise because I could see the page of the textbook in my head. (Though I didn't realise it at the time I was reading books about other girls my age so I could mask better, make friends and be told off less. Ended up so lonely, forgetting who the real me even was because I was masking my true self even around my family. Rejection sensitive dysphoria is the worst.)
Fortunately even though my reports were kind of borderline my psychiatrist still thought medication was worth a try. The first one cost 280 for a months supply and it didn't work for me, gave me weird side effects, and I felt so bad and doubted myself but now I'm on a different one that only costs 60 a month and it truly is like night and day! (I guess my ADHD is a cheap date lol) 
My psychiatrist said (unprompted) that it's the one that they usually prescribe for children, and I was like yeah that checks out lol. I've never felt so good and more like myself, and more at peace with who I am, even though educating my family has been hard work at times. My sister in law said to my face in front of my brother and parents that she could never respect an adult who stims the way I do in public. It was jarring to hear, and hurtful that no one stood up for me, but thanks to the knowledge I have, (and the medication making me less impulsive/sensitive) I was able to regulate myself and respond democratically where before I would have had a meltdown and run off crying and probably want to hurt myself. 
Now I understand that this attitude is a problem with her, and with society, not something I should feel ashamed of. Not my problem to fix. If I want to stim around her in public I bloody well will. I'm glad to see you're in the same place of no longer beating yourself up. I can also relate to how post-diagnosis, the more I talk about the symptoms and how they've affected me to friends and partners, the more they're realising that they have it too and are considering getting assessed. 
I love that we got diagnosed in the opposite order but figured ourselves out at similar times. I love you and everyone else in the community for opening up about their experiences and paving the way for us to accept ourselves and collaborate to improve the way society treats us. Thank you so much <3

Author: @misswetton
Content:
(Autistic small creator perspective): I think a way higher proportion of large creators are actually (high-masking) autistic compared to the general population, and I think that’s because some autistic traits are really advantageous in the initial stages of starting a channel. When you first start YouTube, in order to reach the point of monetisation you have to be:
1) knowledge enough in your specific area to make useful videos on it, and care enough about it to keep coming back to it again and again in great depth (hello restricted interests)
2) willing to put in many hours of work with no monetary reward, for the sheer love of the game - and not quitting for at least a year (hello hyperfocus)
3) able to perform socially to an audience (hello masking, we do that all day anyway!)
4) chronically online (hello struggles with daily life that lead to burnout and drive us onto the internet because it’s more accessible and there are lots of other neurodivergent people you can click with)

The qualities needed in the grind to become monetised as a creator simply suit a lot of autistic people, particularly those who are high-masking. Autism makes us obsessed enough, hyperfocused enough, and performative enough to make it happen!
While I don’t consider my autism a superpower, and to me it is disabling in many aspects of life, I’m also really grateful for some of the traits and how they’ve helped me, especially in setting up my channel.

They told me that because i am biologically a female, its hard for people of my sex to be diagnosed as they blame it on hormones and periods, pregnancy, or the "average young adult girl." So they told me that before i should assume, i should do research and i have. 

Ive done the most research i can from articles, websites, and friends who were diagnosed in general and told my parents about it. I was quickly shut down since i didnt have the same exact Symptoms as my cousins and therefore didnt make me Autistic.  Basically because i succeeded well in society, could hold eye contact, and wasnt nonverbal basically meant i wasnt ND. And thats not true. (I was also called the 'R' slur and yeah)


I can get myself around in society, hold eye contact for a few seconds, im very book smart, and i talk a lot. But i also cant pick up social cues, cant understand mood or tone, need food accommodations, stim a lot, need headphones on 24/7/365 (i have them on now), shut down, dont like rough fabrics, etc etc etc etc. 


Most of the time, those who are autistic dont show any signs. Its called masking where they try to fit in woth others, actung like them and not like themselves.

Author: @Adraeth
Content:
We're about the same age you and I, and back during our childhood, autism was considered literally something that can be seen physically.
It took that long, over two decades, for science to understand that autism is a very vast spectrum, and that "high-functioning autistic people" (as it used to be called, so basically people who don't show the stereotypical signs of it) are way more common than doctors would have said back then. The brain is something very complicated and we're barely scratching the surface, still. Autism isn't solely a bad deficiency that can be seen in a matter of seconds, and yet people still stigmatize it because the negative image from ten to twenty years ago is still strong.

It'll take time to break through that stigma, but as more and more "normal" people discover they have some type of autism and never suspected so, that mentality will erode away, bit by bit.

I'm considering getting tested as well, in my mid-thirties, partly thanks to seeing you normalizing it and talking about it openly like it's something normal (which it is, but it's not how our society make it out to be yet). Thankfully, I have the same outlook as you do. It's not gonna change who I am, it's just going to be answers to explain why I am how I am.
Wouldn't be the first discovery about myself from the last few years, and the others showed me that it's not a bad thing to understand yourself better.

Author: @spuburq
Content: Fellow irish autist, 0:30 is something you'll hear forever. Im not well versed with how it is to be diagnosed as a full adult, but i was diagnosed quite late in terms of males with autism, just before i was a teen. Hope you settle and accept this newly named part of yourself. As a young kid/teen, I was always of the impression I was fundamentally "wrong." I remember breaking into tears when i was told because i didn't want tobe viewed as "a retard" or "freak" while putting a ne on it gave me closure and helped me in the long run, it knocked an already bullied, self-hating, depressive kid right down to new lows because of misconceptions about ASD and preexisting mental hang ups. It puts past experiences all the way back to your birth in a new light for you and your family, and it can be deeply comforting to know that your personal struggles arent because youre some sort of pathetic failure who simply isnt good enough and failing despite having an identical struggle. You learn to forgive yourself and acknowledge the reasons for certain problems or behaviours. You realise the deeper reason for why you are who you are. Im glad you're getting diagnosed when you're at a stage in your life where you dont have to go through the deep, emotionally crushing initial steps that kids like me had to go through first. Good luck on your journey to understanding yourself, and thank you for aiding the destigmatisation of autism. If I had seen successful and likeable "celebrities" like you opening up about your diagnosis, Im sure I wouldn't have had the same level of negative reaction to my diagnosis that i did. Please dont downplay or understate the importance of this video because of modesty. People on the Autism spectrum who've just been diagnosed (particularly young kids, teens, and young adults) will likely appreciate having a role model like yourself being open and confident about their diagnosis. Thank you.

Author: @Ilikecatsismychannelname
Content:
I have a lot of the things you list off too! Well, the autism spectrum disorder, anxiety, depression, digestive issues, hypermobility, and joint issues. Amazingly no ADHD. I was diagnosed with what was then called Aspergers' Syndrome at 16. At the time it was a relief because now my doctors would stop prescribing pills that didn't do anything. I am now approaching my 40s. two or three years back I took a gene test to see if I had a genetic tolerance to my anxiety meds and if that was why they were barely doing anything. Turns out I have tolerances and resistances to all but 5 relatively new and expensive meds because my body metabolizes and flushes out everything else before it can do more than the barest of minimums. Also discovered I have a genetic mutation to the DNA sequence that produces the enzyme responsible for turning folic acid into something the body can use that causes my body to not produce nearly enough of that enzyme to get the B12 I need. Very useful test.

My autistic superpower is mimicry by the way. Well, that and all of the sensory hypersensitivities. Few things feel better when I'm having a bad day than wrapping myself in a blanket burrito of fluffy blankets and rolling underneath my bed. Makes me feel all safe, cozy, and warm. The joke in my family is that I am a hobbit. They aren't wrong. I am a burrowing creature at heart. I'd love to live in a hobbit hole. Also I'm on the short side, so even more hobbit energy there.

Author: @HayzTeeArt
Content:
one of us! glad you managed to also get a late diagnosis and noticed alas. The criteria of ASD has changed over the last many years. Its a fairly new diagnosis anyway, as the first person diagnosed as autistic died at 100ish years old only the other year. So theyve still a long way to go in understanding autistics, and now are listening to us more thankfully and thus the major overhaul of the criteria they look for.
WWhich is why so many are now being late diagnosed alas. Myself included.

The thing with being autistic is, its literally just a different neurotype. Our brain is just developed differently, and thus to be an "autistic" brain. Its why many of us now are asking for "autistic person" over "person with autism" terminology to be used. Because we dont just have a side dose of the tism, our whole brain is autistic. And thats also not a bad thing. Our brains are wonderful, but the problems arise mostly due to lack of accommodations and living in a world that has become sensory hell. And where we have to sing and dance to everyone elses social beat rather than our own.

Welcome to the community! Theres a lot of info out there now, and a lot of advocates who are trying to increase others knowledge on how autism actually impacts people and the current criteria and lived experiences. since most people think "meltdowns, trains, must be a boy, must never speak, must be unable to make friends, must stim all the time visably, echolalia". But, the autistic spectrum is a spectrum of traits, not a spectrum of slightly to very autistic like they previously thought. But theyre dragging ass in terms of re-educating the public about it. But are doing better educating the medical system as well as those who are freshly diagnosed on the new criteria and correcting past myths

Author: @wattsonthetube
Content:
Welcome to the club! Your description of the mental fortitude it takes to communicate is something that I experience too. I was diagnosed around 21 years old. I didn't fit in with children my own age growing up, mostly spoke as though I was an adult in a child's body. Didn't see much reason in interacting with kids my own age, because I often felt they were immature. It's only because my communication skills are quite adept, that I was told that I wasn't on the spectrum. It's only years later that the discussion has opened up, that I was able to receive a diagnosis. I still get some people saying that they don't believe me, when I tell them I'm on the spectrum.

You did list some of the other conditions people on the spectrum have, like intestinal issues, asthma, hyper flexibility, depression and anxiety, and they're all things that I've experienced at one time or another. In case you hadn't realised, my autism means that I'm way too honest and that tends to get me into trouble, but that's how I communicate.

My way of communicating is in part based on scripted conversations, where I analyse the words in intense detail. If I'm ever rundown or tired, then it really affects my ability to interact with people because I'm unable to figure out the nuances of a conversation. I'm always consciously listening for tone, posture, eye movement, context etc. not much of it is instinctual. It's super difficult to read certain people, because I can never tell if they're being light hearted or serious. On the plus side, my language skills are innate and particularly verbose, so I'm able to grasp complex concepts much quicker than most.

Content:
Hi Jack/Sean
I just want to tell you that, as someone who was diagnosed as autistic only last year when I was 27, and as an autistic woman, it is completely "normal" for people to be like "Oh, but you're so normal and social!" And I'll tell you this - it's fucking annoying!

I have so much pride in myself now that I'm "officially" autistic, and I love what my autism has done for me - some people take it badly, but I was one of the lucky ones. I have a good paying job, I'm in a relationship with someone who loves me, and my life is just so much better than it was prior to my diagnosis.

Also, cute thing: I have a boyfriend who openly says that he loves that I'm autistic and that I have so many special interests, and he even says "Is the tism kicking in?" if we see something that's linked with my interests, so it just shows that it just takes the right person to make your diagnosis something more positive.

Content:
I think the worst thing that happend for all sorts of Autistic people was the the DSM-5 summarizing all forms of Autism into simply AS. It makes distinctions between the cases for normal people basically impossible and on the other hand, Doctors are very quick to throw it out left and right to everyone. 

The Qustion you have to ask yourself is, what does it matter? Knowing you have Autism does not fix anything, you are already aware of your shortcomings and in the best case you learnd to cope with it. People tend to use the knowledge as an excuse "Be patient with me I have Autism", which is the WORST mindset you can have. A Mindset that stops you from trying to be better, to overcome your shortcomings, to fit in society and instead demand society to adapt to your needs in stead. 

For Parents with a kid with autism, they tend to get over protective and prevent their kid to develop independence. Sure a severe case of Autism like "early infantile autism" demands specal treadment, but ther are plenty of mild form of autism like aspergers- and to some degree high functional-autism that can run undiagnosed and life successful lives aslong they had propper parenting. 

Autism along with plenty of other Mental Illnesses are severely overdiagnosed and at the same time undertreated and Social-Media made everything just worse over the years.

Author: @xandamonium
Content:
I found out I was autistic through a video game. To The Moon handles the concept very subtly, with two characters on the spectrum, one unable to mask at all, the other permanently masked. When the latter described feeling like she had spent her life as an actress, unsure who she really was, I found myself crying. I didn't know why I was upset. Turns out that was me. I got so good at pretending that, at times, I felt like that was all there was to me. I get "you seem so normal" a lot, even from friends. Folks have no idea how much energy it takes to try and gauge reactions and motives, and formulate a natural-seeming response in every. Single. Interaction. It's exhausting. But it was good to finally know why I was always the weird kid. Why my brain does the things it does. And I'm glad you have that now, too.

This is incredibly relatable, and it's great that you're standing for visibility. Congrats on your diagnosis, and thank you for being open about it. You never know, you may be someone else's moment of clarity.
