Author: @lollibyte5727
Content:
It's lovely to have you in the tribe. 

As someone who got a diagnosis on "ADHD that displays some features of the autism" in 28 and having lived with that knowledge now almost 10 years soon... I was first lil scared to meantion it, being afraid people would treat me badly or think that I do that to get attention or to get away with not doing  my best or what not.... I learned through trial and error that admitting it actually like halved most issues I have with dealing with people, specially new people. 

Nowdays, if I know I need to be interractiong with a person a lot or in stressfull situation, I meantion it with "just in case you got trouble following what I'm saying or I seem distracted or might get confused and stuff so you know it's okay to ask what's up and don't feel like you are doing anything wrong or I'm trying to be a d**k." Most People are actually pretty cool about that. THey might be cautious,  curious or confused, but they'll be like "okay", maybe ask few things if they feel like it and then we go from there and go to the next thing. Sometimes people are lil'awkward, some might feel lil suspicious because their own package, but that's fine, they get over it. Some people don't have to information or have bad experiences and are sceptical what ever so they poke you around abit. As long as they are respectful it's cool. It's okay to feel uncomfortable and suspicious about things that are new, strange to you or feel fishy. I ain't fishy, they figure iot out if I give them a shot and show by example, that I ain't a monster but just a bit of a scatterbrained waffler, and they'll be cool with that. And it makes it so much easier to get through misunderstandings and figuring out how things are and all the hassle, because these people now know that hey, this person said their head is lil' funny, lemme try another thing or ask about this and that before making a hasty judgement.

But sometimes, the rare case of person being an absolute brick, I'm irritated, sure, but also grateful; now I know, and I will know exactly how much of my energy and attention I will waste to that person. I'll be respectful, sure, or try to be, because I think people deserve some base respect, but I ain't giving any weight and wasting any more breath to that person than I need to. I don't want to be surrounded by jerks that do not respect others, so if they don't wanna be around me, that's a win for me.

Content:
I was identified as autistic early at the age of five because i presented in the typical way for the time. Even then, my parents had to fight to get a diagnosis for me because i lived in the country for the longest time. And, even to this day, i find relief in learning new things about autism and that's why i made my mom cry by insisting i couldn’t do things i knew well how to do (PDA), i valued the company of my teachers more than that of other children and took the things they would say to me much harder than other kids and was inappropriately well-behaved because of that to make sure they respected me (RSD+PDA in a sense), and why it’s always been so hard to slim down for moves (i pack bond with inanimate objects).
But i'm also considering getting tested for ADHD as i learn about the overlap between it and autism. I was able to understand that ADHD didn’t present as the Ooh Shiny Disorder but was in denial for the longest time that it could apply to me because i have trauma involving a loved one's unwitting neuroableism regarding ADHD and also...I'm Autistic And Despise Change, Even If It Benefits Me. This video is cathartic to me because of that. I'm coming to terms with my emotional flooding and my executive functioning issues (both dopamine seeking and my fear of change) and my lack of hyperactivity being from masking for so many years.
I'm so so happy that you've been learning more about yourself in service of your emotional well being. Your videos got me through what i now suspect to be an OCD spiral (which is common in ADHDers and especially autistics) back in the days leading up to PMA and the infancy of PMA. Value your community that you trust with unmasking, and remember that everything you feel, be it relief or grief, is valid. Also, happy upcoming Thankmas! Ill try to be there!! Much love from Alabama.

Content:
I was fortunate to have been diagnosed with autism and adhd (or as it was called back then "add") as a child during elementary school. It definitely made it easier for how i view myself going down the road, but, as jack said in the vid, there's a lot of negative stigma attached to autism and mental health in general. 
Throughout middle and high school, i wasn't necessarily treated worse, but i was treated differently, both by other students and teachers, and lemme tell ya, it didn't feel good. Whenever I tell someone i'm autistic, the think one of two things: either they think im some sort of prodigy super genius, or they think i'm really stupid, and i mean THAT kind of stupid. Either way, it really did not help with forming any meaningful relationships. It's one of the reasons why now, whenever i meet a new person, i don't tell them I'm autistic. Not because I'm ashamed, but because neurotypicals (in my experience) have such little empathy or understanding of autism that it almost feels like they can't see me as just another human being.

Author: @tacthescribbler772
Content:
When I was a kid, I remember my doctor mentioning ADHD a couple times, but I was never actually diagnosed. I can hyperfocus on things if I find them engaging enough, but it's often video games and creative projects (like crochet or writing). I procrastinate a lot, but I used to be really good at forcing myself to do tasks I didn't want to do. Now, my usual methods don't work and I've often wondered if I deal with ADHD. I've always been introverted, and certain sounds just make me grind my teeth. I have very particular ways I like things to be in my apartment and I get really frustrated when my roommate doesn't leave things just so.

I spoke with my counselor about it a couple years ago and he gave me an ADHD questionnaire, but since I could overcome the symptoms really well, I think I downplayed my own struggles. Not because I didn't think I was struggling, but more because I've always lived with the internal baggage of, "I can make it work as I am, so it must not be as bad as I think." (Also, a childhood of really religious/strict parents meant I just kept my mouth shut to avoid criticism or being told no. I learned to just endure/tolerate what bothered me.) But the methods I've used to overcome my symptoms in the past (buckle down and complete 6 hours of work in 2 hours) is harder because the struggle to focus (especially when I'm not engaged with the work) is getting harder.

For a while, I told myself that I'm just being lazy, that I need to do more mental exercises to improve my focus, and "just do it, it's not that hard." But as I encounter more folks like you talking about your own situations, it's made me think that I should at least examine myself more closely and not be so dismissive of my own experiences.

So thank you. I'll be having another discussion with my counselor, it seems.

Author: @vicekillx
Content:
Thank you so much for this video - on American Thanksgiving, no less lol. I got diagnosed with auDHD earlier this year and was self-diagnosing before that and man, the weight it lifted off my shoulders. Suddenly it wasn't my fault I always forgot my homework or misplaced my cell phone or couldn't do anything but my special interest or cycled through hyperfixations every other week or couldn't let things go when I knew something was wrong, factually or morally. Like you said, it put my entire life in a completely new context and I was immediately, like instantaneously, so much kinder and more patient with myself. Now I've embraced it so much that if I had the option to not be autistic, I wouldn't take it. I just want the rest of the world to be more accommodating for people like us

I never understood the stigma against autism, but it is unfortunately very much still a thing. People definitely still think autism looks a certain way, but it doesn't - especially since we know now that autism and ADHD both often manifest differently in AMAB people (which all the old studies were based on) than in AFAB people, and thus a lot of people still think women can't be either. Now a lot of my friends are also starting to explore the possibility and I've been lucky enough to be able to help educate and support them. The only downside is now it's extremely obvious how oblivious neurotypical (or "neurotypical", since we're pretty sure neurodivergence is far more common than numbers suggest, most people just don't realize they are) people often are and how many assumptions they make about other people's intent every day

Anyway, I rambled a little bit, but yeah. This was a wonderful video to wake up to today. Thank you for telling people and for talking about it so openly - with 30 million people watching, I'm sure it will open a lot of people's eyes, and hopefully change their minds as well

At the risk of making a youtube faux pas and recommending another channel in your comments, I really like So I'm Autistic, Now What. She was a great resource for me and my friends and hopefully can be for you too, or for anyone else reading ♥

Author: @CrabMan2539
Content: I have autism as well, though I was diagnosed early in life. What I've learned is that autism, being a spectrum, has a wide scale of different traits. There are people who are very social, very anti-social (not to be confused with antisocial personality disorder), very chaotic, very calm, very smart, struggling to get past school, or may not be able to work a day in their life (this one doesn't mean they aren't smart). These are very dumbed down traits and there's a lot more but each person is different in their own way and it's good to get rid of stigmas and stereotypes (honestly just get rid of those in general). Least restrictive environment is important in schools and allows neurodivergent people to get exposure to what everyone else is learning thus better preparing them for the real world (this is worked out for each person individually. What classes and how many they should take mainstream). Presuming competence is important. It allows the person to do the most on their own and feel like they are capable of doing it instead of them thinking they are dumb. Positivity is massively important. I grew up learning to be kind and to respect others no matter what they look like or what their behaviors appear to be. Lastly (because this is getting pretty long), when talking about autism, never use definitive language when discussing it as a whole. Don't say "autistic people will" or "do", say they "might" or "can". It's also recommended to start with "some" so you're saying "some autistic people might". It prevents people from generalizing or assuming everyone does whatever you are saying. (Hope this didn't come across accusatory lol. I wanted to say this just to get it out there. Not a critique of this video.)

Content: It's alright having autism, and autism comes in a wide variety of ways and symptoms. I have autism myself and I'm on the higher functioning end, I presume somewhere near Jack's threshold. It doesn't make you any different than before, it just tells you what the exact description is and how it makes you _you_ . Sure, it might be a bit of a train hit - and trust me, I felt the same way - but like Jack said, you'll realize that it doesn't change anything. You just have more answers now, and gives you more avenues to find and navigate. I'm not saying that having Autism is a walk in the park by any means, and if anything, you might have different challenges or additional challenges compared to neurotypical people, but there is support for that, and there are upsides to it to some extent. And autism doesn't fully define you, it's just a label that gives you more answers. I recommend getting diagnosed if you do have it, at least to have more answers.

Content:
Hey jack! Im happy for you. Im sorry it wasnt found out sooner. 
Most of us late diagnosed have some really hard things to go through the first few years after diagnosis. 
(I also have autism and adhd)

Myself i had a year where i was realising that many of my past friendships, werent friendships, i was the clingy kid they couldnt get rid of because he wouldnt take a hint... i believed them every time they said they were bussy, and asumed that also was why they never were the ones to reach out, too bussy. :(
im 23 and im still processing friendships that werent friendships from elementary school and up. 

Feels pretty pathetic when going through it but you get past it. You have to.

Basically you will discover that things in your past wasnt the way you thought they were, and thats ok. We couldnt help it. 

Btw, unmasking, good luck with that. Its hard. Got no advice. 

Also none of us HAVE TO stimm, it isnt turettes, its not involentary, its a repetative movement we do to selfsoothe our nervoussystems, it can however be an instinctive reaction to stimm.
its usually bad for us if we supress those urges, and if u supress the need to stimm for too long, it can turn into chronic pain. So even tho it feels a little fake in the beginning when u start alowing yourself to meet your needs and stimm or pull back from a social interaction for a moment, it will help.
Dont be ashamed to stimm. 

You wouldnt love someone who hides you or is ashamed of you, so  dont do those things to yourself, because you deserve to love yourself, and be proud to be you. 

I think you are spectacular and ive always thought so. ♡ 
You deserve to think so too.

Good luck on all your jurneys, u have my suport. 

Really hope u get to read this because I wish i had a warning before i suddenly looked back and had all those realisations.

Author: @ChazMcClure
Content: I often times think to myself that ADHD and some forms of autsim arent a defect or illness as they are often labeled. I see it this way, some people have certain characteristics, these characteristics may be abnormal compared to more common characteristics but they are not mental illness. They are most often perceived as illness or disorder due to the fact that the world has been constructed to cater to the people with more average or common characteristics. I think its more healthy to not think of certain types of Autsim or ADHD as a disorder or disease/illness, but to think of it as "Im simply a different type of individual than most people". Just because you have uncommon characteristics doesn't IMO warrant the way it gets covered by media. Some of the most talented people ever born have these "disorders". This is the way I see autism and ADHD personally, and I have always hated the way it gets covered, the only reason it needs to be medicated is due to the fact that the education system and majority of the workplace has been designed to only fit typical human characteristics. School systems instead of catering to the child's way of learning decided it would be easier to simply put the child on amphetamines to force them to focus on something their brain doesn't perceive as interesting or important. I apologize if that's insensitive or closed-minded, I just figured I'd share my POV to see what others think of it and learn if this way of viewing it is wrong or mislead.

Author: @codyponce4118
Content:
0:15 "If you knew, why didn't you tell me?!"

Had a laugh about that because my own parents didn't tell me about my autism diagnosis for YEARS. I was diagnosed in the third grade, and found out about it on my own in eighth grade. When I asked my mom why they didn't tell me, she said it was because she didn't want me to associate myself too much with my older brother who has a more (for lack of better term) "severe" form of autism. I'm pretty good at communicating, and most of my traits come from regulating my emotions, a heightened sense of empathy and not being able to understand vague concepts. My brother has the whole nine yards of being nonverbal since he was a toddler, more violent stimming and even worse emotional regulation. 

However, I wish my parents still had told me before then, even if it wasn't directly after the diagnosis, because then I likely could've found better ways to cope with the issues I did have and recognize the more positive sides of it. For years I thought I acted the way I did and that people treated me the way they did because I was meant to be unlovable. I was bullied, teachers refused to understand me, and because of my poor grasp on emotions, it often led to me being in trouble instead of them. Had I been given a better way to reign those feelings by knowing my diagnosis, I probably would have had an a lot easier time. 

Either way, it be how it be. Welcome to the club Sean, even if you don't see this. We love you. 👍

I excelled in school with straight A's, but it would take me longer to do things than most classmates (especially when taking tests). Taking that test when I was young helped me understand myself better and know how to improve myself as I grew up and continued in life. When I was young I was given extra time for exams but now that I'm in college I don't need the extra time because I have worked on ways to help myself in that area.

Author: @rinb4599
Content:
One of us! One of us!
No but seriously, I was diagnosed with autism when I was around 3 and when my mother told me about what that meant when I was in elementary school I was elated. Like, that's why I found it hard to fit in with my classmates! But as I got older I've kinda started doubting my diagnosis because I don't present myself as the stereotypical autistic person -- I don't have special interests, I'm fully verbal, I'm good on most sensory things, and I don't physically stim. Hell, some days I feel like I have more in common with people that have adhd.
But I do stim, just with repeating songs instead of repeating motions. And I can't bring myself to go up to a cashier if there isn't a line already. I often have trouble falling asleep and getting up, I've been told to have hypermobility, and I have hyper fixations (thankfully not crippling ones).
All of this to say, thanks for "opening up a conversation." I think part of the reason autism is so stereotyped is because there are an endless number of autism symptoms, so its easier for us as a society to only focus on a few, highly noticeable ones. And I'm glad you're as excited about your diagnosis as I was when I was a kid! I hope things'll be a lot easier for you now. One of us!

Author: @damienmonik
Content:
I was diagnosed with autism at age 37, and I did go through the NHS. It took 1 year and 8 months and was one of the worst experiences of my life.

To begin with, my GP recommended me to a mental health clinic for an initial assessment. There, I was interviewed by the second worst doctor I've ever met. She didn't understand several words I used when describing sounds I hate, such as "slurping", and asked me to demonstrate. She would ask me a question and then interrupt my answer the moment she heard something she wanted to ask a new question about. In the end, she even told me she doesn't think there is anything wrong with me as I was able to answer her questions instead of shying away and saying nothing like most people do (ignoring the 25+ years of masking experience, apparently). She claimed there was nothing wrong with me and that I was just stressed due to the death of my Mum 2 years prior. By the time I got home that day, I was in a very dark place. I broke down and spent the next 6 months in a deep depression, having some very dark thoughts.

Eventually I contacted my GP, telling her that they had promised to get in touch with me within 3 months but it had already been 6. I got a call from the mental health clinic the next day profusely apologising, apparently they had forgotten about me (which was fantastic for my mental health). They immediately recommended me to my local autism assessment service, which then took another few months to get me an appointment. First my Dad and I had to fill out a form talking about my childhood behaviour and experiences, which wasn't easy because my Dad was usually away at work so I was primarily raised by my Mum. After that was a set of 2 interviews with 2 different experts a few months apart, the first was just a little chat talking about my life and childhood and the second was a series of embarrassing tests literally designed for children. The experts are then supposed to meet, discuss, and come to a decision. That's what's supposed to happen but when I finally got my results they said "Usually we need a lengthy discusion to decide but in your case it was immediately obvious, you are autistic." Wasn't quite sure how to feel about that but I let it slide.

Even after all that, though, it still provided much needed context to my life. I'm glad I did it, the relief of finally knowing was greater than I could have imagined. Now instead of telling people I have misophonia, misokinesia, OCD, social anxiety, regular anxiety, and paranoia, I can just tell them I'm autistic. Sure, some treat me like a child afterwards but it's better than the disdain or even anger that I got before, and there's significantly less mockery. More importantly, I know now that it's not my fault, there are lots of things I can't control and so I should focus on what I can.

Author: @kurasusoratobu
Content:
"It turns out that ADHD and autism are like a Venn Diagram."
When I was diagnosed in 1996 (yes, I'm one of your OOOOOOOLD fans), ADHD and autism could literally *not* be diagnosed together, because the 'ADHD' symptoms were so common among autistic/Aspergers (when it was a different diagnosis) people, it was assumed if you were autistic, you would have the same symptoms as ADHD. 

Basically, it would be like diagnosing someone with the flu as 'Feverish'. If they've got the flu, they're 99% chance to have a fever, so the moment you recognize they have flu, a fever is assumed. Having a fever doesn't mean flu, but having the flu means you have a fever. It was the same thing: not everyone with ADHD was autistic, but everyone autistic was *expected* to have ADHD symptoms. 

Things are different now in the diagnostics department, but the fact the two are *that* entertwined is still very much present.

EDIT: Because I wanted to add, while I am autistic (and very socially anxious), I am also an extrovert. I *like* being around people. I *like* the high energy of people around me that understand me, and it gives me strength. So it is completely possible to be an extrovert and still be autistic. Being socially anxious, or being bad at socializing, doesn't change that you may be someone who would *like* to 'People'.

Author: @Bluehousesys
Content:
I'm still trying to get diagnosed myself. I ALMOST had a psych diagnose that I was definitely autistic with mild need for accommodations, (verbal not written down), before I was sent to another person for a secondary testing, and then I had to move states before it was finished with either of them and ended up losing them. 

(Though even the second person I was sent to didn't think I had autism because I had /at least three friends/ and passed high school despite barely passing every year and going through special classes. Despite all my sensory issues and social issues and having a hard time holding jobs, etc. The first psych ended up apologizing for sending me to them, surprised at them because they were supposed to be a professional.)

It's not only expensive to get tested, but there's still a LOT of stereotyping out there even from professionals, and I've even recently learned that a lot of places have gender bias too, apparently mostly underdiagnosing AFAB people. I've had to be ping-ponged between different places before completion and I still am, but I'm still researching into everything extensively myself because I find it SO important to know how our brain interacts with the world, and by extension makes /us/ react, interact or perceive in unique ways.

Author: @vehicar
Content:
welcome to the club! it may not be a life threathening diagnosis but it can definitely be life changing :) 
as a high masking autistic person, before i got diagnosed i was told multiple times by medical professionals that "there's nothing wrong with me intellectually" or "i don't seem depressed". that was the most unhelpful thing to hear in that setting because for years i had deeply felt that there was something wrong with me, and i was at the point where i couldn't function and needed help. but no one understood or believed me when i tried to explain. 
eventually getting the diagnosis later in life made so many things make sense. i found that there was finally an explanation for almost every struggle that i had! i could start to understand myself more and be kinder to myself. it released me from a lot of the shame and guilt that i had carried inside me ever since i was a kid, and it felt so freeing. i look back at pictures of myself from before and i do not recognise myself. partly because of memory loss (seems to be common in autistics) and partly because i'm a different person now. i'm more comfortable being the way that i am, expressing myself in the ways that i want and sharing parts of myself that i was too ashamed to before. i'm still working on unmasking more in my workplace, testing the waters to see if it's safe. every autistic person deserves to be free to be who they are without fear of being shunned or mistreated. i hope we can all get there someday.
i admire you for making this video and i hope we can all talk about autism more. it's not a bad word or a bad thing to be, in fact i think autistics are cool as hell! rock on 🤘

Author: @laciereinheart9490
Content:
Maybe I should consider YouTube-ing...

Autism is not a bad thing. It presents differently in everyone, and we react to different things differently.

Most of us would hide in the corner at a party while everyone else girates, dances, and all the things... I did it just the other night.
I just... I dunno.
Sensory issues are a big thing with me. 
I also have an audio-processing disability. Someone can say a joke and while everyone else is laughing, I'm buffering. So by the time the laughter and responses are done, I burst out in laughter, and everyone's like, "Oh gosh; you're WEIRD."

I don't care that people are like, "Autism is what losers and weirdos have."
I like my autism. I don't like some of the stuff that comes with it, but I like being autistic. I am starting to like me more as well, now that I know...
Blessings and best wishes, Sean.
I hope you have a better time unmasking and learning about yourself than I have.

Content: The reason it’s very difficult to separate ADHD from Autism is that they have a very high comorbidity rate. If you have one, there’s a good chance you have the other, but it’s not a guarantee. That can make attempts to deal with one complicated, because we don’t have a way to tell where one ends and the other begins since there are a ton of similarities between Autism and ADHD. I hope this helps you understand your own mental health better. I was diagnosed with Autism pretty early in my life, and through a bunch of work I’m able to function pretty well in my community, but I recently sought help because I was beginning to understand that some of my behaviors weren’t just personal failings, they were symptoms of ADHD. Figuring out that I had ADHD changed my life, because I now have a way to work around my executive function issues because I know they exist.

Author: @LacrimosaTheNerd
Content:
This is an unsurprising surprise. I never thought it, but it makes sense. 
I have All Of The Things except asthma. My senses are also the worst. I literally gag around certain gross things, and my ears are so sensitive I'm almost always wearing headphones to block sounds out because certain sounds physically hurt. I have a weirdly extreme aversion to hazelnut too. 
I'm not officially diagnosed with autism, but I have like all of the other symptoms, and my family always knew. I never got diagnosed because my father's a nonbelieving dumbass and my mom was scared I'd be bullied. If it hadn't been stigmatized, I might have gotten help instead of adults and teachers bemoaning my wasted potential, that I'm too smart to be doing this or that. I was an overwhelmed child, holy heck.
Labels are powerful. As a queer person, finding words helped me better understand myself, that it wasn't just that I'm weird but it also kind of is, that I'm abnormal but in an understood way and there are others like me. Like, learning about asexuality explained a LOT. Everyone around me getting celebrity crushes and horny posting and going on dates and talking about how hot people are and I was just ??? I guess they're aesthetically appealing??? what's the big deal???? Having a name to what separated me from all those people was kind of comforting. I had a concrete reason. I'm not just wrong or bad, this is a Thing that happens with people.
And also knowing there's a REASON for your "shortcomings" and abnormalities and quirks  makes it a lot easier to not feel guilt, and to better find workarounds to problems. People just need to put effort into understanding.

Author: @zymstarz

"if you knew why didnt you tell me!" FELT. but truly so much of it is based on doubt and second guessing of both the self and of those around you [ie: your judgement on what is actually a similarity with you and other people and what is coincidence caused by the inherent variation of people existing]. that, and both misinformation and misunderstanding of autism as a concept alone - with those latter two exponentially building upon themselves and worsening the issue they both present and suffer from. the fact that people who know nothing about autism - and WHY they know nothing in the first place - assume it is exclusively a very "far end" of the spectrum [and dont understand it is, in its simplest terms, just a different radio frequency our brains are running on,] means that it is so infuriatingly easy to assume we are still incorrect in our judgements of if people are like us [if someone is even aware of what that means] or if we're still reading a ""normal"" [allistic] radio signal as our own. 
im happy for you to have the opportunity to get tested and a clear answer, and i hope said answer makes life more freeing for you. learning i was autistic was easily the greatest weight off my shoulders, knowing i wasn't actually "broken" and just didnt have my radio labeled right.

Content:
I was diagnosed with ADHD and ADD back when they were two separate things, specifically, I was five years old, I was put on a few different types of medication and none of them worked, At least that’s what the doctor/psychiatrist said and she was correct, none of them worked. 

Then one of the medication’s and this was the second to the last and it actually made a difference, it helped me to focus, it made me slow down to where I was able to be understood but after being on it for a few months, the doctor said nope that’s not working, even with me telling her several times that yes it was working, she took me off of it.

The last medication that I was prescribed, I did not know what it was and luckily my mom listened when I told her how it made me feel 

The last medication that I only took a single pill of before I never took any more of it again I learned later it was Adderall 

It made me feel like a zombie, I was super slow, I was extremely suppressed on how I normally was, I didn’t talk, how we normally talked, it felt like something was trying to suck me in and then spit out a version That was not me but when I told my mom, luckily, she listened, and she took me off of it, and I never went on medication again. 

Now at 27 years old, my ADHD and ADD are practically nonexistent, I have such a good control over them that they again practically notexist, they once in a while, and I literally mean once in a very, very great while kinda start showing again when I’m around my second oldest nephew, and without even him being diagnosed, I know for 100% fact that he has ADHD and ADD and probably a few learning disabilities as well but yeah.

I never want this to happen to anybody, but for me to be able to control my ADHD, and ADD to the point that I have now, I had to listen to my father every single day, for at least nearly a decade from when I was five years old till nine maybe 10 years old , tell me that I was faking it, and I was just doing it for attention and that ( mental illness does not exist ) To have such a good control over it, at six years old, I created a mask/façade, and at 12 years old I mastered it/perfected it to the point where not even a trained psychologist with 15 years of experience Can tell me anything about what I told her straight to her face, even when I told her the exact truth.

Do you wanna know the sad part and I mean seriously messed up part 

I can no longer take the façade/mask off, I have had it on so long that it’s become me 

There has only been a total of two people who have seen right through it, and those were two teachers one in fifth and sixth grade, and then one in my senior year of high school, those teachers I hope they are doing good in life.


Having anxiety I extremely, and I mean extremely dislike it, because along with the façade in a way, I started creating scenarios that yes, while millions of them have not come true, because they were rewritten with other ones, this is how precise my scenarios are. Like I can go get in my friends car and go to leave my house to go to my mom‘s house but if I just stop enough at the stop sign, make sure it’s clear and then go turn right instead of waiting the few seconds that I normally do, there won’t be a guy and his dog walking from right to left going back to his house.

I can because of the anxiety/scenarios, I can mentally finish anybody’s sentence/story They are going to tell me, but I have learned very quickly that it is not a very nice thing to do.

Also, I absolutely despise being an empath, but I have learned from many years of training/experimenting, I can almost bring the effect down to zero, but you can’t shut it off completely, so while I’m watching this video, I am feeling what Sean was feeling when he was making this video and I can also feel the emotions of the viewers whenever I look at the comments..





Thanks for listening to my ramble.

Author: @yasmeenahmaiden
Content:
I'm late diagnosed AuDHD as well. Diagnosed with both last year, at 38 and 39 respectively. Had the same response of just being very relieved to finally know what it was, that made it so I was always the weirdo and the one struggling with things others weren't struggling with. I've had so much external (and after years of that, also internal) pressure and ableism about struggling with things but feeling (and being told) that "everyone is doing such and such, so why can't you? Just do it, like everyone else, and quit whining and being difficult!". Now I know that I wasn't just being lazy, or difficult, or stupid or slow or whatever, but that I was just doing my best but working with a different operating system and with different abilities than others (neurotypicals) and that that's okay. Feels good to be nicer to yourself, definitely. 

So yeah, can definitely relate to so much you're saying in the video. I agree that it's very important to talk about it and show that 1. It's not anything shameful and 2. It's definitely not always the classic things (whether the non-verbal stereotype, or even the classic train loving socially awkward white guy). More and more women and POC are diagnosed and it can present in way other ways than just the aforementioned scenarios/types. This needs to be known, so both neurotypicals realise this and stop with the "But you don't look autistic" and also so those who are in fact neurodivergent but don't realise it because of only knowing the stereotypes themselves can have an easier (and quicker) time realising they might in fact be on the spectrum themselves. So thank you for speaking out and welcome to the club!

Author: @giszmo5099
Content:
I have been diagnosed with Autism (at the time still technically Aspergers but since the recent implenetation of the ICD11 Aspergers is now fully part of the Autism Spectrum) at the age of 20, almost 21, three years ago. I am also AFAB, and anyone that knows anything about not only Neurodivergency but just mental health in general is fully aware, that alot of the time research and what we know about mental health and the way it shows itself is based off of male individuals. So putting that together with this sort of sterilized and stereotypilized image of Autism online (im speaking YouTube, and tumblr specifically since i dont use any other platform) I always felt a little left out still. Even though I have been diagnosed by a Threapist that speciliases in Autism Diagnoses in Adults I always had that little voice in my head that was asking "but are you really on the spectrum? Are you not just making excuses?" and all that sort of crap. 
So now here I am, seeing You Jack talking about being Diagnosed. A Person i have been following since I was 15 (Jesus Christ that is almost 10 Years now) and that i always felt comfortable around saying that you have Autism. A person that is Nothing like the Idea of Autism that gets portrayed in TV Shows or on online Forums etc. (At least from my judgement of what I can see in the videos. I dont know what you are like in private) it feel like a relieve having someone that is more like me, more subtle and not as typical or obvious or whatever. Someone that is familiar with masking and overanalyzing in order to not stand out. It just makes me really happy to see.
Also something I want to put out there: Here in Germany (idk how exactly it goes in the UK or anywhere else) when I got diagnosed I not only had a questionaire to fill out about how I was as a kid and talked with the therapist about my past. It was part of the assessment, even getting my Parents involved (since my memories of the times when i was 3 years old arent that great) but my therapist told me when i got the confirmation for the diagnoses that If She had looked only at the parts about my Past, I probably would not have been diagnosed. In the talk with my Parents a key point came up about why that was: I have a little sister (Who later got diagnosed with ADHD) who is really got at being social and so what I did from a young age on was just copy her and develop such good Masking Strategies that noone ever even thought about me having any sort of Neurodivergency.
But Lucky for Me! The assessment has some other key Tests (as in actual tests that I gave answers to that were either Right or Wrong in some way or another) were I scored so obviously "Autistic" that there really was no second guessing with the actual Diagnosis.
Im talking one of the tests the cut off value for Autism spectrum was around 12 and I got a whooping 30, so like, yeah. No doubt here. I still sometimes look at those test results if im feeling really unsusre about myself.
Anyway, im rabling. Love you Jack, and im really happy for you partly from the selfish reason that i can go and point at you being like "Hey, Im kinda like that Guy, and he has Autism Too :D"

And this is a conversation that NEEDS to happen. AUDHD may not be life threatening to you, but it still can be life threatening. There are a lot of stats that make it hard to have hope for a long life with mental illness/disability and the world is not kind to it. 

Thank you for talking about it.

Author: @Tim8Bit
Content:
Something really important that I don't think is talked about enough is, you DO NOT need to fit a stereotype, to actually be something. I know that I myself have struggled a lot in learning things about myself because I felt and still feel, a need to match stereotypes, to be a certain way. This is especially important in the world of mental health. Jack talked a little bit in this video about how autism for a long time has been stereotyped to be a very specific way. But truth be told, autism is a wide spectrum, and really, all of mental health is. 

My point in saying this is, if you have even a slight suspicion that you have something, or could be something, don't be afraid to look into it, and get checked out for it. ESPECIALLY, if that thing is having a negative effect on you. Nothing bad can come from learning about yourself, and in most cases, it will improve your mental health tremendously.

Author: @CountryMusicMann
Content:
"If you knew why didn't you tell me?" Probably because they didn't want to make assumptions about you. From what I've observed having only joined the wider autistic community recently, it's somewhat frowned upon to run around assigning autism to various people without knowing them personally. It's about being aware that other people have their own lives to live, that not everything is about us, and giving others some privacy until and unless they themselves feel like sharing more about it.

I was still moderately young when I got diagnosed with autism (in 7th grade, I think), and so didn't really understand it, but in my Psych class last semester, I went out and read some actual academic research on autism, and it made me feel so much better about various things. I came to realize that I now had a term I could use to make sense of my own mind and learn more about it. I haven't changed, but a diagnosis and subsequently learning more about autism has opened a way for me to not constantly berate and punish myself for not living up to a standard that was not designed for people like me in the first place, though that's a habit I still am working to try to break.

Also in my personal life I'm very open about being autistic, reasoning that it's better for people to have that term leading to further reading should they choose. It's also a result of trying to open conversations about mental health and such, because autism is isolating enough to have, but it gets so much worse when you feel like you can't actually talk to anyone about it and are punished for things you simply cannot help.

Long story short, I agree with a lot of what you said, and heartily welcome you to the AA club: Awkward Autistics.

Author: @Reicha
Content:
First of all: Thank you for going public with this, the way autism has become a slur is upsetting and many stereotypes are harmful. So are misconceptions about the social part. Masking is a huge thing. Most of all you show people the HIGHLY empathetic, caring and looking to improve type of autism that has completely fallen under the radar. 

For a time it (or at least Asperger’s) was synonymous with sociopathy because not reading cues right was taken as not giving a bleep. 

Instead, the most empathetic people I know have all had or ended up with autism diagnoses - because the fact that understanding didn’t come (entirely (it varies from person to person)) naturally and sometimes they hurt people meant they _made an effort_ Even after learning how to read people that doesn’t just go away. 

Secondly, I have Asperger’s (I continue to use that nomer because that is what I was diagnosed with) and you were the main person whose ADHD diagnosis made me go “oh this makes me more sure I have that”, so this, well, makes me even more sure. Because of course it’ll click more for me with someone that also has both.

Author: @MjAnimus
Content:
Ah man, all the things you're saying; not fitting in as a kid, struggling in college, always liking the same things even when others moved on, yeah. Yeah I feel this. All my life I felt this. 
 I first thought I was autistic at 14, because I struggled so much with fitting in with my peers, I was never a "girly girl" and often felt left out. I first thought I had ADHD at 23. I got diagnosed with both almost 2 years ago, and it was so validating. This realisation that, no, there isn't something wrong with me, I'm not broken, I'm just built different. Like I've tried to explain it as imagine the whole world runs on iOS. It's the only operator. All instructions are for iOS, but you run on android, and the process for a lot of things is different. Alternatively I've said ADHD is like having 50 tabs open in my head and never knowing which is playing music 😂! Or; Autism is like "I will literally die if anything in this room changes" and at the same time ADHD is like "I will literally die if I can't rearrange this entire room right now."
 I'm still not medicated. Hoping to be soon. Eventually. Thanks for these videos. It feels less alone. Safe. Seen.
 Thank you for talking so honestly and openly about it 💜

Author: @timvermette3599
Content: Thank you for being so candid about this. You mentioned how someone asked you why you would be open with your diagnosis like it's a bad thing. I think that a big reason for them saying so, at least here in the States, is due to the image of autism still being incredibly stigmatized. Yes, the image is changing on what autism is, hence the spectrum. But unfortunately, many people still hear that word and conflate it to the child who has vocal or motor stims, who doesn't communicate through typical speech, etc., and society has always been one to look upon difference with disgust and distrust as opposed to open arms. But it's absolutely great that people are having more conversations about this, that public awareness is slowly changing on how the term is viewed, and I'm glad that people like you can feel good about having an answer to your questions that have gone unanswered for so long. I'm someone who hasn't been formally diagnosed, but am likely to be so, if for nothing more than a lot of what you said describes me as well. I appreciate hearing you talk about this more than you could possibly know. Again, thank you for making this.

Author: @Gear_Storm
Content:
Since you want to change things in the world for the better, I recommend looking into the types of problems people with autism face and seeing what you might be able to do about it with your platform. 

Theres problems like nuerotypicals especially news outlets or people in power talking about autistic people like theyre bugs in a jar or animals without emotions. 
Issues like autism speaks, a group that claims to support autism but is actually extremely awful. Its like the PETA of the autistic community, but important or influential people support it. 
Theres issues like how its extremely difficult for most adults to get a diagnosis because it costs thousands of dollars, and most doctors only work with autism in children where they havent learned to mask their symptoms yet and it results in lots of incorrect false diagnosis. 
Theres things like how the place in my area you have to go to in order to get diagnosed, that covers the entire lower half of british columbia in canada but is the only place you can actually get this diagnosis, has a limit of 100 kids per year because if your diagnosed as a child theres a monetary support the government now has to give your parents so they just start reporting any kids after that 100 mark as not autistic no matter what and you have to go through a terrible process to get signed up to be rediagnosed if you believe you were misdiagnosed. I didnt even get that far, I got put on the waiting list and they just never got back to my family after over ten years of waiting and now Im an adult.

Theres a lot of good someone like you could do to help raise awareness and maybe even change things. It would mean so much to so many people with autism have that support from someone who isnt going to just make it worse from their lack of true care or understanding.

Author: @daanmollema6366
Content: I know this view will probably not be highly appreciated in this commu itym however, you want to open up the discussion, let's have the discussion. IMO neurodivergence has been so extremely 'spectrum-ized' that it is hardly possible to make the distinction between a 'normal' person and a neurodivergent person. We all have quirks, and we all have difficulties in life. By making the definitions of neurodivergence so vague, we have fostered a generation that prefers upholding categorical labels as excuses for their shortcomings over taking positive steps to increase BOTH their functionality and their mental health. And we foster a generation with an attention need that is muchh vaster than society can provide (we'd need like 10% of our society to be psychologists). Does my friend who 'failed' his ADHD test by 2 questions while he has enormous study difficulty not deserve medication? For God's sake, let's stop dividing up our identities in vaguely defined labels and work with the concrete traits we have. That way, we see eachother as persons rather than amalgamations of mental illnesses.

Author: @potatolord8677
Content:
Man, I always felt like i need to justify merely wanting to get evaluated and undermine the chance I have it. I really needed this video. I fit so many traits, and so many things click into place when i view myself as autistic. The difficulty understanding certain cues, sarcasm; the way an interest can COMPLETELY consume me for HOURS and YEARS to the point EVERYTHING links back to it in my mind somehow; the physical pain I get feeling certain textures or smelling certain scents; that lingering feeling I get that I don't belong anywhere and kind of never will because there's no procedure or script to follow, just subtle and ever-changing etiquette I'll never quite catch up on.

But because I'm chatty and succeed in academic settings, because I'm "well-spoken," because I'm a woman, so on and so on, people brush me off. But I'm tired of feeling like a damn alien all the time! Like an alien wearing human skin and just REALLY successfully integrating but STILL unable to be fully "human"! I feel like this and at least getting evaluated may help figure out WHY this constantly hangs over me. So many friends of mine are diagnosed neurodivergent and were SHOCKED to find out I have no evaluations or diagnosis! Hell, some of them said they feel like they're the most "normal" person in the room when I'm around cause of how prevalent some traits get when I feel comfortable and accepted.

And maybe I'm not autistic! Maybe there's something else going on! But I felt so discouraged from even looking into an evaluation, even if I feel like it'd help me tackle the source of so many anxieties, because to many I don't "look" how they think autism should. Or any other diagnoses that may better match my life.

All this ranting and rambling to say: thank you for the video. It helped me feel less alone in my experiences, y'know? I function well enough in my day-to-day that no one takes me seriously when I say I'd benefit from getting checked, because they have no idea how tired I am of feeling like there's something between myself and "normal" people that I can't put a name to. Like there's a one-way mirror that I can't see through but everyone on the other side constantly tells me is transparent, and that it isn't hard at all to join their conversations despite the fact I can't see anything they're talking about. It genuinely really helps to hear you speak on this and your experiences.

Thank you, Jack.

Author: @HarrisonLovesSouthPark
Content:
Hi Jack!! Long time fan, probably like most on this video. I was diagnosed with autism earlier this year. It really feels validating to actually have it written down on paper, and it makes it a lot easier to understand and feel less, I don’t know, guilty for my struggles earlier in life. People use the term “high functioning” when they refer to me which isn’t offensive, at least to me, I’m aware it’s an outdated term, but it’s kind of weird to see how people react once they learn that about me. Sometimes they act condescending. Or speak on me like I’m not all there. It can be very frustrating and makes me feel even more out of place but at the same time I like that about myself. I know where my strengths are and what my struggles are. Having a diagnosis cleared so much up for me. A lot of people have interests like trains, sharks, horses whatever the common ones are, and for me it is South Park. Im proud of that. I take it at a deeper level than the satire. Being diagnosed with autism is never a bad thing, it’s a gateway to understanding yourself so much better, the only issue? How hard it is to get a diagnosis. Considering Jack is an adult and did not have that validation when he was younger could’ve changed a lot of things for him and that’s how it was for me. I wonder if I would be at a different place today had I known sooner. I wouldn’t have gotten my diagnosis had I not went through a private assessor. That’s so unfortunate because it took a lot of time and money for that. Healthcare won’t even acknowledge it half of the time if it isn’t what people stereotypically view as autistic. I’m glad society is learning that autism isn’t that at all though, it’s a spectrum. We aren’t less than for it. We are purely humans who think differently, like anything mental related. Jack, thank you, for your content and your recent content revolving mental health and sharing your personal experiences like this. For me, it makes me feel validated and your content means even MORE to me.

Much love, Harrison

Author: @SignoftheMagi
Content:
Even the concept of a "spectrum" of autism is now inaccurate. It's not a line. It is a sphere, a living, breathing globe that spans a wide variety of people, behaviours and senses. Being Autistic isn't a limited, set area of factors, but something to define when your brain communicates in a particular way. That's it. I have spent over 20 years working in the field of autism and I can tell you at least half the people I know with it, you could not tell without some hard observation. I have known doctors, lawyers, teachers, business leaders, police officers, and actors with it, and their co-workers never knew.

Let me say this. You are not damamged. You are NOT disabled. You simply see the world in a different way. And by God and Thunder we need people like that.

Author: @DiscoChixify
Content: My son has ADHD and Autism. I had read an article that said a small percentage of people who have ADHD are not helped by or satisfied with their experience of the medication for ADHD, and that a lot of the people who have that experience are also later diagnosed with Autism. And it makes them poor candidates for medication. So when my son was first diagnosed with ADHD I wanted to get him tested for Autism as well, just to rule it out. Because the doctor who diagnosed him said he might be a good candidate for medication. I wanted to make sure I was actually helping my son and not just causing him more distress. The article said that these individuals with both thought they were supposed to experience a total shift, and didn’t, and some of the symptoms they find most troublesome were symptoms that the medication didn’t manage. But those symptoms were the Autism. So I decided against medication for my son in particular, and instead he’s in ABA and doing other kinds of behavioral therapy disguised as play. He loves having friends who are going through similar or the same things he is. There’s a lot of support out there for children who have both now.

Author: @rubygaminghd
Content: I’M SO HAPPY THAT I GOT THIS NOTIFICATION!! I don’t even normally comment on here because of my anxiety but after years of waiting for a diagnosis I got mine this year in February and I am so happy to see that someone I’ve looked up to for years has gone through the same thing! It is so important that more people acknowledge that the spectrum is truly so diverse and it isn’t as simple as just “one way or another.” I am lucky that I was able to get mine relatively early in my life, but I can’t imagine what it must be like to have gone so long without knowing why you are the way that you are. Even before it was flagged up for me, I always had this feeling that something was off and I hope that anyone who sees this that can relate to what you and other autistic people have said about your experiences are able to get some clarity from seeking a diagnosis if they wish. There is seriously so much stigma around autism and at times I find myself being overly cautious about what I do or say around people who don’t know because of it. I really hope that other people who may be watching this that suspect they may have it feel more encouraged to seek further information, no matter how old they are or what their autism “looks” like. I also hope that next year and every year after, that you are able to embrace the differences that make you who you are and be your authentic self. Funnily enough, I’m in a similar vein in the sense that I knew I had one condition (for me it was the autism) but it doesn’t feel complete. I have suspected that I may have ADHD for a while now but I’ve never been able to seek a diagnosis especially because I don’t fit into the stereotypical depiction of someone who has it. I relate to a lot of the symptoms more specifically the inattentiveness aspect and maybe one day I’ll be able to look into that further. There is a lot of overlap between not just Autism and ADHD but as you said other conditions such as OCD and I appreciate you bringing attention to that. Thankyou so much for making this video and for the little jokes in between!! :)

Author: @WorldwideCookie-j7w
Content:
Watching this video really made my day. Thank you so much for speaking out and also giving support. Too many people don't know about autism, or think that it is bad, lame, don't take you seriously etc. I was starting to lose my motivation because I have been trying to get my autism and ADHD diagnosis for a year now. I am 23 years old, and in the country I live in they are not very good at diagnosing anyone that is not a child. The entire process so far has been very chaotic, since I have been sent from one place to another multiple times. 

I went from my doctor to a psychologist. The psychologist stated that I have some form of autism (as for the ADHD they didn't want to bother with that then and there), but they couldn't give me an official diagnosis for some reason, even though many other psychologists have given out diagnosis before. Then I went from a psychologist to a specialist. They denied the assessment request because in my previous psychologists notes some years ago, it was stated that I had good eye contact...and that was the time I was assessed for depression and not autism... After that, I went back to my doctor to be sent for second opinion, and now I'm working with another specialist (who is supposed to be specialized in working with neurodivergent people), who forgot to contact me for 5 weeks to give me a new appointment, and when they finally did, they mentioned that they will send me an SMS as a reminder. The SMS never came, and it has been 2 weeks since. :'') I have some people close to me that suspect I have both autism and ADHD, and I believe that too. I just want answers and to finally understand myself better.

So this entire situation has been dragging my mental health for a year now, and I got so happy after seeing the video. It made me feel not entirely alone. Reading the comments really warms my heart, especially seeing how many people have autism, some have been diagnosed later, others are considering getting a diagnosis etc. Now I know I'm not alone in this.

Love your videos Jack, have been watching your videos for many many years. You are a ray of sunshine, and give us a lot of motivation. Congratulations on your diagnosis 🥳❤

Content:
I got diagnosed autistic two years ago next month! Was a huge turning point for my mental health as like you said, I also suddenly went easier on myself and understood more. Processing it is kinda like the five stages of grief but randomised at any given time, so please do take your time with it as you figure out what it means for you. Maybe unmasking, maybe stimming more, maybe you will seem “more autistic” because suddenly your brain has been allowed to be itself. I like to call these discoveries expansion packs in my case lol. 
Also, I kinda knew you were autistic, but it’s not something you tell a person. It’s their own journey, and chances are if you’re autistic you’ll know there’s something missing and go looking for the answer. That’s not to say you shouldn’t suggest getting tested to others or kids, but some people need to figure it out on their own. 
Let yourself change as this processes. That’s my best advice. Hard as autistic people are usually not happy with change! But it is a huge part of identity. Just be a jellyfish. Morph around n shit. Idk. That’s what I’m doing and it helps.

Author: @kitsunehime3911
Content: Hi Jack, I love your videos and have been watching you for a long time. I just wanted to give my input on some of the differences between autism and ADD. I have ADD (I was diagnosed as a young child) but not autism. They are not the same thing. When a person has Attention Deficit Disorder (ADD) it means they have too few dopamine receptors in their brain which makes them struggle to focus on mundane tasks. For instance, they may daydream during a maths lesson and struggle to focus on it if they don't find it interesting enough. Dopamine is known as the "happy hormone" so without enough of it, people get bored easily and their brains literally can't focus on something monotonous even if they want to, so then they end up focusing on more interesting things like daydreams or a more interesting thing happening in front of them. That's also why people with ADD constantly misplace their keys or phones, etc. My body often goes on autopilot while I do mundane things like cleaning or putting down my keys and I then focus on my inner thoughts instead without meaning to, then I have to try to retrace my steps to find my missing keys or go look for them in places I would commonly leave them. On the other hand, autism is characterised by having an underdeveloped prefrontal cortex, and interestingly a lot of people with autism also have a highly developed hippocampus. The prefrontal cortex is a region of the brain controlling impulse control, emotional regulation, people's abilities to empathise with others and to pick up on social cues. That's why people with autism often struggle to notice sarcasm and read facial expressions. Autism varies in severity so some people with autism struggle to empathise with people more than others with autism do. The hippocampus is another region of the brain responsible for memory storage. So since people with autism often have a more developed hippocampus than others, there are very gifted autistic people that excel in a field that interests them since their brains can store a lot of information. A stereotypical example of a character with severe autism is Sheldon Cooper from The Big Bang Theory. ADD does not influence either the hippocampus or the prefrontal cortex like autism does. It is very surprising to hear you have autism since you seem very empathetic towards others, but maybe it is just mild autism.

Author: @megdawson7189
Content:
Dear Jack / Anyone Else Who Reads This and Vibes or Needed to Be Told:

I have ADD and a hint of autism too. I was never diagnosed (at least not with my autism) until high school because my mother was one of those parents who didn't to think something could have been wrong with her child (yes she has gotten so much better at understanding and accepting it's just a part of who I am), but also I came to find out when I was diagnosed as a teenager that because I hadn't been raised in a home where I was "coddled", I had much better motor and somewhat better communication skills than others the doctor who diagnosed me said she'd seen. Now, obviously this doesn't apply to everyone because I know the spectrum varies with severity and that not everyone reacts the same to the same environments, but I know for ME PERSONALLY, I learned how to be "semi-normal" and I really do think it had to do with my upbringing. Now I will be the first to say I still have my quirks; I was and still am the outsider most the time. I'm more of an introvert who spends way too much time on YouTube, I don't like crowded rooms or loud noises/sounds (earbuds with nothing playing just to mute down the noise level have been the best!!), nor do I do too well with strangers trying to get in my personal bubble. But all and all, I say there is no such thing as "normal"; were all a bit weird in our own ways, and we are perfect as we are, so owning it as a part of who you are is the best thing to! ❤❤❤

Author: @misshelenjunemain
Content:
Welcome to the late diagnosis club! ❤️🎉

For what it's worth I think what you say about not concentrating on being your best self next year - it's more that it's about separating your best self from what society says is The Best self. Like you my diagnosis was a relief because it made so much stuff make sense in retrospect, and it explained why I was an educated working professional but I couldn't cope with grocery shopping 😅 (sensory overload). Adjusting my understanding of what I need to be my personal best has reduced a lot of my self-loathing. I'm not pathetic because I struggle in loud and crowded places, I just need to remember to take breaks somewhere quieter and I can cope so much better. I don't have to stop myself from doing things I want to do but find daunting, because now I have so many tools and strategies that come from embracing how I function and finding ways to accommodate that instead of trying to brute force my way through life and getting overwhelmed and demoralised. 

Knowing and understanding yourself and how your mind works is an incredible asset. Having an official diagnosis doesn't "give" me anything - I'm long past needing extra support for school exams! - but it gives you an invaluable piece of knowledge that can change your whole perspective. I absolutely encourage anyone who thinks they might have any kind of neurodiversity to put themselves forward for assessment ❤️

Author: @L337Dratini
Content:
I've had the same experience of feeling relief and happier knowing I'm high-masking AuDHD. 
I was diagnosed when I was three, alongside chronic depression. I was told I have depression, but never told I was Autistic. I was given my ADHD dx when I was around seven, but still not told I am Autistic. I had a large/destructive meltdown sometime in college, and started looking up everything that could be "wrong" with me; when I found something that kinda fit (because I figured I would have been told I'm Autistic), I called my mother and asked her, "Do I have Down's Syndrome? I have something, do I have it and just don't have the physical characteristics?!" to which she laughed at and said, "No, you're Autistic. I never told you because I didn't want you to be treated differently."
Unfortunately I was treated VERY differently because of my AuDHD; adults and kids can be mean as hell when you're a little different. I am so happy I know now and I'm currently working on making life more comfortable for myself, but a close support system of knowledgeable fellow Autistics/AuDHDers is really important. If you're into it, reading books can help too (working through Unmasking Autism by Dr. Devon Price).

Author: @kronksstronkstonks6360
Content:
PSA: The golden rule of autism is that there is no golden rule. There's no defining trait like there is for depression (low mood levels) or a fever (high temperatures). There is no universal trait shared between autistic people despite the public assumptions around social awkwardness and aptitude for maths - that diversity of experience is why its called a spectrum. Even those with identical autistic traits experience those traits differently. This is why assessment and diagnosis has been ramping up in recent years because awareness is increasing, and why self-assessment is so widely accepted within the ASD community (despite social media's fetishism of the condition in recent years).

Another aspect not taken into account is the period of mourning after late diagnosis. If autism has affected your life dramatically there can be a lot of upset around the fact you likely went down the teenage hormones > anxiety/depression > trauma assumptions route before finally being diagnosed. that means you've spent all your formative years and beyond under the assumption you can get better, creating goals that you can only truly strive for afterwards, only to find out your struggles have been traits of an incurable neurodevelopmental condition. That you can't get "better" and therefore you could have been striving to be someone you actually can't be - even if still manageable its likely with immense burnout. This causes a kind of mourning because the person you wanted to be and thought you could be might very well be impossible to achieve and so you need to redefine your goals - professional, social and personal to fit who you are as opposed to who you thought you could be.

I was late diagnosed, I have a lot of thoughts about and experiences with the topic ahaha.

Content: Also AuDHD here! I was diagnosed at age seven in the 2000’s, and definitely was a bit more “stereotypically” autistic (stimming, no eye contact, social issues, taking things literally, sensory problems, really liked trains, etc), which is probably the only reason why I was able to get a diagnosis as an AFAB person in the 2000’s. I’ve finally started deconstructing that this year and learning to work with how my brain works instead of trying to work against it. I could say a lot more about it, I’m also pretty introspective, but I’ll leave all that here. I just want to say thanks for all you do. Author: @SteaknEla_The_Humble_Peon
Content:
I am also diagnosed autistic. I do have non verbal communication and difficulties with communication. 

If I'm forced to talk verbally and especially in a noisy environment I can lose the ability to speak. Masking is very temporary and painful. Neurotypicals brains don't understand, so I explain, in a cafe If I talk you hear me and you understand. When I'm in a cafe I hear the person's conversation on every table, the coffee machine, the chairs moving, the door opening, the traffic outside and your voice all as if they are of equal volume, and now everywhere plays music (wasn't the case 20 years ago) I can't process anything with music playing, I either listen to the music or a person and i can't listen to both or the other noises, because my brain doesn't know how to prioritize input. Everything is equally important. 

This is also why ASD people also get stuck doing the same thing or stuck on a sound. Echolalia is a big part of my autism, it's a form of stimming. 

I also have special interests and find it hard to do new things. I feel good doing familiar things over and over.

What a lot of people don't understand about autism is that with many things we can do things you can do, some of the time, then the rest of the time it either takes us a really long time or we don't accomplish what it was we wanted to do. This is when it can look like being lazy. No it all circles back round to being over stimulated. 

For me it helps, when I can't do a thing, I write down what I want to do, what are all the factors involved and the outcomes, and what I would do in each scenario. This can be as simple as you want to make lunch but you know it's not so simple because there's so many things to consider, and to do it safety, and then if you live with someone what if they want to use the space or interact with you? This thought process can spiral and it's hard to do checks of your thoughts when you're in them. 

I have over 40 years experience to share and I don't know how to convey this in a single message and in a clear way.

Content:
I don't think im going to get mine professionally diagnosed, but i do say I'm peer reviewed autistic.
This is a few reasons to keep in mind if you're looking into getting a diagnosis:
There are several legal and other disadvantages to an autism diagnosis, including:

Discrimination

People with autism may face discrimination in the workplace, including being fired or not hired if it's unsafe for them or their coworkers. However, the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) protects people with disabilities from being discriminated against at work, similar to protections based on race, color, sex, national origin, age, and religion. 

￼

￼

￼

Legal proceedings

An autism diagnosis can be relevant in legal proceedings, similar to a diagnosis of mental illness or mental retardation. 

￼

Guardianship

A court may determine that a child with autism is "incapacitated" and appoint a guardian to manage their affairs. However, many state guardianship statutes are restrictive and may not be able to meet the needs of a child with autism. 

￼

Cost

A diagnosis without insurance can cost thousands of dollars. Many psychologists who perform diagnostic testing do not accept insurance. 

￼

Disclosure

Deciding when and how to share an autism diagnosis with others can be difficult. While sharing can help others understand and offer support, it can also lead to misunderstandings and judgment. 


There are many advantages to getting diagnosed, but I dont want people to be diagnosed and have it be used against them.

Content:
To be honest, I didn't think you were autistic, but I'm not exactly shocked. Almost all of the creators I watch either have ADHD, autism or both, so you finding out you're autistic isn't that surprising haha.

I was diagnosed as autistic when I was 15, and I totally understand what you mean by not feeling like ADHD was completely right for you. After my diagnosis I've tried to mostly seek out other autistic people, because they can understand why I act the way I do and won't get mad at me for being "too quiet" or for openly stimming. 

I think that you being open about you being autistic can, as it did when you found out you had ADHD, help many others to get diagnosed and realize that they're not broken or that there´s something wrong with them, but that they're just autistic. If anyone reads this, it's never too late to get a diagnosis! Author: @tigervalley62
Content:
As someone who is also autistic. It bugs me to no end when normal people treat it as if it is some disorder or disease. It's neither of those things but rather an alternative mindset and personality that functions differently outside of the flock of sheep and hence why it is easily misunderstood. Everybody has their own set of weaknesses, austists just tend to have weaknesses socially. But just like everybody else for all the weaknesses we have strengths as well. A common characteristic of an autist is to latch on to one topic/field, then obsess over it and then excel in that given field. Because of this "obsession" we are perceived as geniuses and have competive advantage to climb ladders of success over our peers even though we cannot socially interact with them very well.

Bottom line, autism is not a weakness and in many instances can be classified as a natural human superpower and although the very minority on the extreme ends of the spectrum will have mental disadvantages, vast majority of us will be perfectly normal and functioning members of society. So please, stop treating it like a disorder and understand that we are just different from you. It's perfectly ok to be different...

Content: As someone who has autism (I have ASD, Autism Spectrum Disorder), I feel like we do as people never truly understand what Autism is. Heck, I've had it for 21 years (my entire life at this point), but even now, I have a slight clue, but I don't understand 100% what it is concretely. Autism is like...think of it as a tree. It has branches, leaves, and such, but there's different things to Autism, like types. I'm not an expert on the subject itself, despite having it for a long time, but I do know there's some parts of us that do inhabit some of those parts from the Spectrum. It could be high functioning, low functioning, mild Autism, it really depends on what you have if you are Autistic. If you are having some doubts about having it or if you believe that having it is a bad thing, trust me when I say that it's not a bad thing. It just means you're skilled at some things but may struggle with others. So, if you do have it, just know you're not cursed or anything, you're unique.

Did I miss a joke I should've laughed at or should I be making a joke now? What kind of joke? I never realized how blue their shirt was before this exact moment. Your announcement makes me feel a little less alone. Hopefully you feel less alone too.
Love your content Sean

Author: @mattkowal90
Content: Sean, as someone who was also born in 1990 (I was diagnosed in 1995 just before my 5th birthday), I too had to defy the stereotypes/stigma and my Mom advocated for me because there were no resources available to us. Intellectually to other people, they are amazed saying to my Mom that your son is a genius. I have unbelievable talents, but behind the scenes it was the exact opposite. I'm not afraid to comment any of these facts because it needs to be known. I was still wearing Pull-Ups in 1st grade because it took me a little over 6 years to learn how to use the bathroom (5 years how to go #1), it took me 12 years to learn how to wipe my own butt (I was afraid to get poop on my hands), fourteen years on how to tie my shoes (I was a Velcro/zipper kid). You should be glad you were diagnosed at 34, because if you find out at a young age (My Mom didn't tell me until I was 11), it will suck all the motivation out of you. I'm able to converse and be social to a certain degree but there is a limit because I don't understand social cues. I can make a model of an elevated train station, be a math major, self-teach himself the drums by just looking at Rock Band drum charts, pass his driver's test the first time, but doesn't understand sarcasm, misconstrues words, or do some simple tasks. Also, having PDD-NOS, Tourette's, and Alexithymia doesn't help. Sean, hang in there my man, no two cases are alike, hence the puzzle piece.
