Author: @KAW96
Content:
Just in case you, or anyone in a similar boat, gets to my comment - im diagnosed Autistic since 2017 and have learnt SO MUCH and have a hot take.

There are far more people that are actually both Autistic and ADHD - more commonly referred as AuDHD. People with both identify more with other who have both and most commonly the most late-diagnosed part of the community. Why? Both have a chance to balance eachothers pros/cons, difficulties, and abilities.

I personally theorise that AuDHD deserves its own recognition, that doesnt take away (because without meaning to, it does) from those with ADHD or Autism - basically thoae that dont have both. Yes theres cross overs, but they aren't the same.

I forget the term writing this - but your journey from diagnosis is your own. If you prefer diagnosis first language to person first - you are valid.

Just be careful about calling it superpowers, it gives the wrong impression, and the disabling parts get ignored by non-diagnosed people a lot. The discussion needs to have the pros/cons as us as individuals - the community thats built will be of people that relate to parts and less the whole as each person truly is different.

Im a believer in self diagnosis, as true self diagnosis involves all the questioning jacksepticeye did - you have to suspect you have it to seek a diagnosis as an adult. With or without a diagnosis, your born Autistic. Get the answer if you need, but find community with others that share some of your traits - tips and tricks to help improve your life, it is not taking anything away from diagnosed people.

Author: @MapleSamuraii
Content:
#1 Trait of Autism, telling other people you have Autism. Even when nobody asks. I had a coworker tell me she has autism right before leaving. Then months later my supervisor asked if I knew her. I said "Oh was she the girl with Autism." At first his response was "You can't identify people like that" then he pauses and realizes that's just what she told everyone. I wasn't speaking ill of her or judging she had autism, just identified her by the way she identified herself. It was a funny moment.

With that said, Autism is a evolutionary trait. It's not an accident or a disability. People with Autism were chosen by their partners because of who they are, and those traits were passed down. There are so many things in autism that could be justified in the past, being smart with lack of social behaviour would have been the normal before modern cities. The only reason why we notice it so much now is because everything revolves around being social. 

ADHD is the exact same. You could see why it might have been important for a warrior or a hunter to be constantly focused or energetic. In a time where your education is training to become a soldier do you think it really mattered that people couldn't sit still? We only notice it today because we force children to sit in a lifeless classroom for 6 hours a day. If it wasn't for school and kids were allowed to just be kids, we wouldn't be labeling anyone as ADHD or Autism. If 50% of jobs weren't just sitting in an office talking to people it would also be less evident. If you feel like you have ADHD or Autism and feel different. Just know you're not alone, you are normal, and it's mostly societies lack of understanding of the subject that gets ADHD and Autism labeled as disabilities when in reality they are evolutionary traits.

Content:
Thank you for this video. ❤️ I am currently going through the  journey of getting my ADD diagnosis reevaluated after 12 years of fighting to get the referral because the medication never truly helped me either. And this year it finally happened. The psychiatrist told me that the symptoms I was having gave her clear indications of schizotypal personality disorder and hearing somebody finally listening to me, somebody that finally took the constant feeling of being followed/under surveillance seriously, it made me so happy and I just started crying. Author: @ShaneBlackheart
Content: I suspected I was autistic for a long time, but was always in doubt because I didn't want to take up space where I didn't belong and all I knew was the highly stereotyped version of autism. After yet another falling out with friends that was severe enough to trigger my PTSD, and after realizing it was all over yet another bad miscommunication (my communication style makes people suspicious of me because I like to explain myself so I am sure I'm understood and not misinterpreted, which leads to people thinking I'm hiding something or am guilty which baffles me), an autistic friend started sending me autistic memes and relatable videos, plus I took a few assessments online that are close to the real thing and... yeah. It's not something I can deny anymore. I didn't see it because I'd been taught to be ashamed of anything 'weird' I did, and because I have an anxiety disorder, I grew up learning to hide anything that wasn't considered 'normal' in public. If I slipped up, I was chastized and told I was embarrassing myself. Now, as an adult who is struggling to find a proper assessment, I've accepted that I have to start to learn how to undo an entire life so far of masking (I'm 36). I started seeing everything I didn't notice before, such as stimming, echolalia, the executive dysfunction issues and meltdowns that literally feel like I'm dying when I'm overloaded, the sensory issues and sensitivity issues. It's all autism. Even things I didn't think were related my psychiatrist thinks actually are. It explains too why eye contact is so painfully uncomfortable for me. Thank you for being so open about your experience, I was going to give up on getting a proper assessment, but this inspired me to not give up and keep searching (I'm in the US and many places are for children, not many know how to assess an adult).

Author: @shorthelena
Content:
Oh my gosh, this describes my recent experience exactly. 

I'm 21, and the process of getting diagnosed with Autism has been just full of jumping through hoops because no one wants to be the one that writes that down. Figuring that out, the process of telling my close friends and family was all like "yeah, we knew." SO Y'ALL JUST DIDN'T TELL ME??? I had a hard time learning things. I was behind in learning how to tie my shoes, I had such difficulty learning cursive even though my mother put in extra effort to teach me. No matter how many times My grandma showed me how to crochet and sew it never stuck, I had to teach myself to sew and I still can't crochet. Learning how to do laundry took four years, and even now having to deal with foreign machines is daunting. When I eat a pack of gummies, I arrange them symmetrically by type and color and quickly eat the ones out of place while proceeding to symmetrically eat them. I stim ALL the time, and sensory overload happens to me multiple times a day. I never realized how dependent I am on my headphones. 

My childhood interests never evolved, I never lost interest in Minecraft, Sims, Roblox, Adventure Time, Miraculous Ladybug, and dolls. Dolls was a big problem for people, cause you're supposed to drop it as soon as you're a teenager. But I didn't start having the attitude of a teenager until I was twenty years old. I never sought independence until then. I tried to learn to drive, which has been a VERY difficult process with extra steps. So it makes sense in hindsight how I was the only one that didn't know. People would ghost me because I was too weird and always spoke my mind, especially once they found out I like dolls. People don't like to accept that your diagnosis can effect the people around you, that they should have to put up with it. You're supposed to somehow be able to grin and bear it for the sake of the people around you. I myself have a hard time accepting how dependent I am on other people. 

My diagnosis didn't change much for the people close to me, but it did for me. I felt like it validated everything about me. I have gastrointestinal issues, asthma, joint problems, high blood pressure, high cholesterol. When I found out I had autism, I started taking more supplements, cutting out artificial sweeteners, caffeine, lowering my sugar intake, doing more stretches to help my joints. It was like the worries of something deeper being wrong with me all went away. And that's important for mental health. I always had this deep rooted fear that I would die young. But I'm better now.

Content: As an 18 year old who felt sort of behind everyone else, i was brought to tears when my therapist even got close to mentioning the fact I could have autism. Not out of shame, but out of joy. It felt nice to actually have an explanation for why I felt so different. Getting a diagnosis could change the way you view your life and your expectations for yourself. It can genuinely change the expectations you set for yourself. For me personally, receiving a diagnosis for autism changed the way I view myself and the way I view the expectations of me from the people around me. Now granted this is also coming from someone who has a lot of problems with people pleasing, but honestly once I received my actual diagnosis for autism, I stopped caring about the expectations of the people around me. Because I felt like I no longer had to abide by them. The way I viewed myself was now on a completely different angle, and now I'm focusing on what I want and what I think is cool, not what some bum thinks. Getting a diagnosis would be massively beneficial. I urge anyone who doubts to do real research and look into the experiences of others who've been diagnosed with any mental illnesses. It's also just good to keep in touch with your mental health too. Just like your physical health

Author: @dingbat91
Content:
Hey Jack. I'm feeling a familiar pain in reverse, I was diagnosed with Autism when I was super young and now going through the ADHD assessment (which takes forever thanks to the underfunded NHS Services, ADHD is currently -five- years, over the two for autism)

Sometimes just knowing IS half the battle. Being able to be aware that yes, you aren't going mad, and being able to find the help you need can change your life. It certainly did with my Autism when I was young. It's good to be open about it and find the help you need, which can be hard even WITH the diagnosis ( I've been looking for work and so many people treat 'High Functioning' Autism as if it's perfectly healthy, just a 'mood', or even pure laziness. I -want- to work, I just want to also NOT have panic attacks because the situation overwhelms me while I'm trying to manage my autism, or put myself into a position where I'll do harm to myself or other people due to my own issues or misunderstandings.)

Autism is a lot of invisible work, as you said, having to put that manual effort into masking, non-verbal communication, and dealing with sensory overload. Even for 'High functioning' Autistic people (which I feel is just reductive to the issues people are facing, and right to be avoided). So getting that help can be crucial, yet society likes to ignore it at best, or be hostile to it at worst. But people deserve to get their diagnosis and get the help they need like any other. 

We need not just more positive voices in the space, but aware and understanding ones, so thank you for being one!

Author: @lawfulchaos9329
Content:
Hey Jack! Autism and ADHD here!
I didn't get diagnosed for a long time because my mom didn't want doctors to put me on medications. But a bunch of daycare workers knew I was autistic because I preferred to play on my own instead of with other kids.
And I'm sure some people dont think I can be autistic because I'm super good with social cues and I'm really smart with words, and I'm highly emotionally intelligent. (And extremely sensitive-)
But I also struggle with sensory issues a lot, and I feel you on that interests thing! My interests last. I got into creepypasta for example at like. Ten. And I was a dumb little kid who wasn't interpreting it right. But six years later, with changed views and opinions, I still love creepypasta! I bounce between interests sure but they never really go away like they do for other people. 
And I can't handle people being... mean. Like, jokingly. It's something a lot of people don't understand that comes with Autism and ADHD is RSD, rejection sensitive dysphoria. Even jokingly, I cannot handle people being mean or rude. I'll just cry. Forever.
But uh yeah I just wanted to throw in my experience too!

Author: @robbieh535
Content:
Hey, I am an autistic person, who is also doing their PhD about autism! (nearly finished!). You hit the nail on the head with this :) 

One thing that opened my eyes a lot is the 'double empathy' problem, coined by Damien Milton, which helped me reflect on some aspects I've experienced in the past. Much of what we know about these conditions comes from a third-person, deficit-based approach. "We can't do X" "We struggle with X" "We have deficits in X". It saddens me that this perspective still exists and is often the perspective of those who aren't familiar with autism above steryotyped and outdated perspectives.

There is now a shift towards a second-person approach in autism research, looking at the difficulties we experience (particularly social) as an inter-personal misfortune, rather than an individual deficit. The DSM is terrible for this, which trickles down the medicalised perspective. It states we struggle socially, but.. put us in a room with other autistic/ADHD people, and we reach a synchrony and communicate much easier! This tells us it is not an 'individual deficit' but a mismatch of two different ways of being. This is just a small small factor in my thesis, but one that hits home. I'm happy to answer any questions/have a dialogue about this.

Author: @sauseysandwich9215
Content:
you should be proud of being vulnerable in front of the world to advocate for positive change. you are amazing.

I have been dealing with mild sensory processing disorder my whole life. because it was mild, I always was right on the clinical threshold of being diagnosed and not. this really hurt me in the long run because insurance really likes clinically significant results to green light any treatment, AND people do not understand how I work until they *really* get to know me. 

being public spaces, noises, smells, touch, vestibular senses, driving, my art and more are all things that my hypersensitivity affects, whether in a positive or negative way. 

my IQ is above average for pattern recognition. and yet throughout my life I have struggled with reading comprehension and writing. In elementary school, I was the only one who excelled at math and struggled with language arts. 

I am currently applying to grad school so I can get my counseling degree, set my own hours, and help others with their problems, especially with sensory differences. 

you are one of the reasons why I got tested for autism. I did not meet the clinical thresholds for it, BUT it did help guide my treatment in a good direction and identify exactly how to proceed. since then, I have been going through new treatments and it has been doing wonders.

Thank you Sean. The community we have built is incredible.

Author: @rustic_cl0ver
Content:
I got diagnosed with autism earlier this year and it was probably one of the best things that has ever happened to me.
For such a long time, I would beat myself up about not being able to fit in and be "normal", just so people would like me and want to be my friend. But no matter how hard I tried, it would never work. I'd just be like "what's wrong with me?" "Why can't I just be normal?" Plus I didn't know that anxiety was a symptom of autism which is something else I struggled with.

But after my diagnosis, it's like all the pieces fell into place. I could finally be easier on myself and realised there's nothing wrong with me. This is just the way I am. The way I function. If other people can't understand that, then that's their problem.
And I got medicated for my anxiety and it's only after being able to feel good again that I realised how bad I had felt before.
Even reflecting on my past and the way I acted makes so much more sense now with my diagnosis.

I'm happy to have gotten this cause it's helped make a lot of things in my life so much easier and helped me build a better self image of myself. I'm not all the way there yet, but I'm much better than I used to be.

Author: @Lil-Dragon
Content:
Welcome to the family, Jack. I wasn't diagnosed (paid privately) until my mid-20s, but that's not because my signs weren't there. The system wasn't set up for people like me to be spotted as easily. I found out after figuring it out on my own after burning out in my third year of uni, God knows how I passed it. Obviously I masked until I couldn't function much anymore. 

I had support in school, luckily, because I happened to have a physical disability so that covered me during my academic years, and my sensory issues were attributed to my health issues like migraines. I know that without that, I definitely would've struggled even more had I got no support at all.

But there are some things I wish I had understood about myself as a child that I only do now, I know I'm autistic. But I'm now just focusing on processing that all before I'm moving forward in life because it's a lot to unpack, realising you spent 20+ years living life a completely different way to everyone else and didn't know.

Author: @dragonmumm
Content:
Working with children for a few years, I learned a lot about the “spectrum”. I learned that we are ALL on the spectrum to some degree, some more severely than others. What concerns me more than that is why there has been such a huge increase in the amount of people who are significantly affected by autism or other similar disorders now than there were before just 15 to 20 years ago. I used to wonder if there was something to the idea that immunizations were partially responsible, but now I am learning more about the toxic ingredients that are put in our foods and have been used more in the last couple of decades and if you do any kind of research, you will find that our country allows the input of horrible chemicals to be added
to our foods (just look into the origin of yellow 5 as one example and it will shock you) yet are illegal in other countries. Hopefully that will change as our FHA is changing and RFK has a calling to return our foods to being healthy. 

There’s obviously more to it than just one or two root causes, but we DEFINITELY need to find out why there’s so many people being affected by these disorders. Perhaps we can help the ones presently affected by reducing their symptoms and potentially reducing the number of people affected by these reduced to what it once was, when it was very rare. 

However it goes, I think you’re a GREAT source of information for people who seek knowledge and understanding about what they may be experiencing. You’re not judgmental, you are living with the symptoms you comment on, and you’re genuinely yourself. That’s the kind of thing we need in the conversations about these topics.

Author: @natedosmil
Content:
Hey! Me too! I'm 38 and I had thought for ages something was up.  I originally self diagnosed myself of Social Anxiety Disorder.  Then I realized I shouldn't self diagnose and just kinda discounted my thoughts for awhile.

Then in 2022 I got a job that I really liked, but I have social problems and have a hard time keeping jobs because of it.  I remembered that an ex of mine had said I was a lot like her dad, who had Asperger's (a diagnosis that has since been retired for Autism Spectrum Disorder levels 1-3).  So, eventually I pulled the trigger and asked my primary Doc for a referral.

My Neuropsych was booked way out, so even though I got my appointment in December of last year, I couldn't get my first visit til August of this year.  Then 2 separate visits here in November for testing for ASD, OCD, social anxiety, and several other things.  I got my diagnosis of ASD during the second visit (she was confident I was level 1), but I'm waiting til January to know about the rest, as well as to talk about what's next.

This has been an anxious time for me, but talking to someone really helps.  If you're on the fence, talk to your primary and ask for a referral.  I swear the first step is the hardest, but it gets better.

Sean, I'm glad you got your testing, your help.  I'm glad you're talking about this!

Content:
I was diagnosed a few years ago at the age of 37. Both me and my mom always strongly suspected I was on the spectrum, but it took that long to get a diagnosis. But getting that diagnosis, and learning from other autistic adults, has made my life so much better! It is a win for me to know, too. Content: Also quick correction they are NOT the same thing. Very similar in many aspects but adhd is a dopamine/serotonin disorder. Tends to thrive off chaos and just do it hence hyperfocus, quick learning, lots of struggle with schedule and timing, adhd paralysis when doing unrewarding tasks because you already lack in uptaking dopamine doing things that drain you make it far worse. Autisim often (not always) benefits from scheduling, patterns, great at organizational tasks, with the biggest thing being its social side effects adhd has some to but Autisim is a bit more. Holding conversation, reading between the lines, sarcasm, body language, and conversation cues tend to be alot harder for autistic people to understand. But they do have a large overlap not just in symptoms but I can't remember the exact number but I think it's like 30-40% of people with ADHD also are on the Autisim Spectrum as it affects similar areas of the brain.

Content: I honestly think one of the most common things that autistic people experience is feeling “weird” in their childhood. I ALWAYS felt weird, especially after I hit 12-13, everybody else seemed to Change from kid mode to preteen mode but I stayed the same. After I got diagnosed with autism I was in denial about it for a while, because as you said the picture painted of autism is different from how it presents. Eventually being diagnosed helped me a lot, it made me realise I wasn’t just Weird, my brain works differently. That my teachers and classmates weren’t picking on me because -I- was bad or wrong, they singled me out because I was autistic. This happens a lot, neurotypical people in social settings will often single out autistic people, most of the time not even intentionally. They pick up that something is “wrong” and act accordingly. All of my friends are neurodivergent, most of them autistic, and I surround myself with people who understand that I need breaks, that my social meter runs low on default, and that I prefer one-on-one time to group activities. It’s a wonderful thing to finally fully understand yourself instead of feeling like an alien who got stuck on earth.

Content: I was diagnosed with adhd and autism too, while I have really good pattern recognition it's really tough to confidently tell someone "I'm pretty sure you're autistic". It's seems a good chunk of people who get an ADHD diagnosis also gets an autistic diagnosis. As you learn to unmask things might get harder, it might take a lot more energy to do things than before. And that's ok! As you learn to accommodate yourself and find ways to regulate your nervous system it'll get a bit easier. For me I never realized how much I needed to stim, and have bought a bajillion fidgets to find what works for me. Otherwise I'll pick at my lips or skin unaware that that's the stim I unconsciously do. I wish you the absolute best on your journey! Never be afraid to ask for accommodations either! I suggest noise cancelling stuff for shopping trips because sometimes you won't even realize you're overstimulated until you feel the relief that rushes over when you do accommodate yourself and cancel noise or turn off lights.

Author: @SpoodleKiboodle
Content:
As an autistic person myself, when you know you have it, it's sometimes easy to forget you even have it, especially if you have the same habits others have.
And remember, Autism is a spectrum disorder. Everyone who has it is different and has different symptoms, myself included. I'm nonverbal myself, but I do love yapping abominably when it comes to stuff I like talking about at times. And stimming is also part of it, but not every autistic person stims.
Now that there's been more research on it and more people have come out with their symptoms, more and more people can get tested easier with a better diagnosis. I got diagnosed when I was ten and since then have been trying to live with this information for the past eight years and things have been going well. Just because you have doesn't mean you can't do half the things other people do. Like work and/or school. Remember, autism is not a good thing, but it's not a bad thing either. It's a daily struggle a lot of us go through, but try to remember that you were always the way you are before the diagnosis and will strive and continue to be. It's not a battle you have to win and it doesn't go away, but it doesn't make you any less of a human being. Welcome to our little community in the corner of the world. We have snacks and drinks here. :3
